A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Prime Minister Narendra Modi walking onto the stage and greeting other leaders. At the same time, the national anthem is being played, alleging that he disrespected it. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows PM Modi disrespecting the national anthem by walking on stage and greeting other leaders while it was being played.
Fact: The audio in the viral video has been edited, and the national anthem was added externally. The national anthem was not played in the original video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We did a reverse image search of the key frames from the viral video, which led us to the original video (archived) uploaded on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s official YouTube channel on 21 June 2025. The video shows visuals from a public meeting attended by PM Modi in Siwan, Bihar, on the same day. Upon reviewing the original video, we found that the national anthem is neither being played nor sung at any point. The video shows the organisers welcoming PM Modi as he arrives on stage, while he greets the leaders and people present at the event.
We also reviewed live footage (here, here) from the event and found no instance of the national anthem being played while PM Modi was on stage or addressing the gathering. This further confirms that the anthem audio was externally added to the viral video.
To sum up, this viral video, allegedly showing PM Modi walking and greeting leaders while the national anthem was being played, is edited.

Trump wants to be friends with Kim - but South Korea could pay the price
- Published
South Korea's annual military exercises with the US come to an abrupt end on Friday.
Ulchi Freedom Shield, which involves 18,000 South Korean troops and 11 other American ally nations, is being halted with only half of the scheduled programme complete - days after US President Donald Trump announced he had ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" the drill.
This revelation by Trump, who called the exercise "inappropriate and hostile" towards North Korea and costly to the US, caught his allies by surprise.
Seoul's Foreign Minister Cho Hyun tried to paint the decision as one of mutual agreement, but admitted officials did not know of Trump's intent to scale down the exercise in advance.
The move will also have rattled the likes of Taiwan and Japan, which have long relied on US security guarantees in the region.
Trump, who has also criticised Seoul for refusing to take part in action against Iran, has said he expects to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un later this year.
And while South Korea has long been keen on Trump reaching out to Kim as a means of maintaining diplomacy, it would not have wanted it to come with demands for cash and military assistance in Iran.
The US-South Korea alliance
Seoul considers the annual exercises with the US core to the alliance and a demonstration of US commitment to defend it against Pyongyang.
Although it has traditionally been happy to scale down or suspend the exercises in order to lure North Korea to peace talks, Trump's unilateral and sudden decision to pull his troops early has shaken South Korean confidence in the US as an ally, according to Jo Bee-yun, a Senior Research Fellow at the Atlantic Council.
There is a fear that Trump may go further and draw down the 27,000 US troops stationed in South Korea or even abandon the longstanding policy of denuclearising the North - all without consulting its ally.
The two Koreas are technically still at war since they did not sign a peace treaty after the Korean War. Reuniting with the South had always been a key, if increasingly unrealistic, part of the North's ideology until Kim abandoned it in 2024.
Despite this, the threats against the South haven't stopped. Days before the military exercise, North Korea launched ballistic missiles towards Japan and repeated a warning that it had the right to exercise its nuclear weapons should the country be threatened. More missiles were launched on Thursday.
A larger concern for South Korea this time is that the Trump administration no longer separates security and trade issues. Trump said he was unhappy with South Korea's refusal to join him in his war in Iran but he also has been unhappy with it as a trading partner.
His administration has complained that the country's $1bn (£734m) annual spending to host the US troops is not enough, that it is dragging its feet in investing the $350bn it has pledged, and that it is discriminating against US companies operating in the country.
Now that trade disputes are evolving into national security concerns, some have called for South Korea to reduce its reliance on the US.
Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute think-tank and a proponent of South Korea developing its own nuclear weapons, says Seoul must maintain its alliance with the US but also "take steps to acquire its own nuclear deterrence".
While the majority of its public supports a nuclear South Korea, the government has argued that acquiring the bomb is unnecessary and even harmful to the country's network of alliances. Such thinking could shift if the US withdraws further from Asia.
Meanwhile, South Korea has been trying to make the best of Trump's decision to end the drills early.
President Lee Jae Myung, who has sought to repair relations with the North, praised Trump in a post on X. "I believe [your social media post] was a bold decision that is the result of your deep consideration to achieve peace," he wrote.
Lee pledged to increase his country's defence spending and said he "fully agrees" with Trump's view the country should be responsible for its security.
Since Trump's first term, Seoul has seen his seemingly capricious approach to diplomacy as both a risk and an opportunity. With a mix of flattery and blind optimism, Seoul succeeded in setting up a first-ever meeting between a sitting US president and Kim Jong Un in 2018.
However, immediately after the meeting, Trump suddenly announced a suspension of joint military drills with South Korea.
He walked away from a second meeting in 2019 without an agreement when Kim refused to give up his entire nuclear facilities. Beyond the brief made-for-TV meeting at Panmunjom later the same year, the two leaders haven't engaged in any substantial negotiation.
Kim Jong Un in a strong position
It was Seoul that bore the brunt of Pyongyang's ire following these summits. North Korea demolished the South's liaison office in its territory and later swore off all communication with them. It introduced a new law making sharing of South Korean films and TV shows punishable by death, and codified the right to use nuclear weapons in its constitution.
Meanwhile Trump has maintained that he enjoys a "great relationship" with Kim, telling reporters on Wednesday: "He likes me".
But Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said in a statement that she knew nothing about Trump's claim her brother had contacted him recently, adding it "must be the only thing I am unaware of in our foreign policy".
She also repeated the North's position that it would never give up its nuclear weapons as they enhance the balance and stability of the region.
Kim Yo Jong also said the scaling down of the drills with South Korea "doesn't merit (her country's) interest nor comment", nor change their "hostile and offensive nature," she was quoted as saying in state media.
Although Trump said he would meet Kim Jong Un later in the year, few experts believe there will be another summit, especially while Kim is profiting from an alliance with Moscow and strengthening his relationship with China. Unless Trump is ready to publicly accept North Korea as a nuclear state, its key demand, there is no incentive.
The scaling down of the drills is already a major concession, not only for Pyongyang but also for Beijing, which shares the view that the exercises are a threat to its security.
It potentially also leaves the door open to further demands by North Korea at a time when the country appears stronger militarily.
Despite Trump's repeated claim that it poses no threat, the country has never stopped sharpening its fighting capability. It has tested nuclear bombs six times and has the capability to deliver them via long range missiles that can reach continental US.
More recently, the country has joined Russia's war in Ukraine, where it has supplied what is believed to be billions of dollars' worth of artillery shells and missiles, as well as at least 13,000 troops. While it has suffered thousands of casualties, its troops are now drone-savvy, having absorbed the lessons of the Ukraine war.
As Jo Bee-yun sees it, there isn't much South Korea can do to defend itself against the North, making its US alliance "a matter of life-and-death".

The calamitous collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the United States is a warning to nations worldwide that pursuing any kind of dialogue with the current US administration is doomed at the outset, according to observers who say this recent episode indicates seeking a fair deal is futile.
Andrea Lawlor, an associate professor of political science at McMaster University in Ontario, said: “No matter the closeness of the historical relationship, the American administration has signalled that it now prioritises its interests above those of some sort of global economic coordination or harmony.
“It feels like these talks ‘failed’. However, I’m not sure there was really a success to be had.”
The two countries are now in a deepening trade war after weeks of urgent talks fell apart shortly before the 12am EST (5am BST) deadline on Saturday, when the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods.
A defiant Mark Carney said on Saturday that he had rejected the deal because of last-minute US demands that would have undermined Canada’s sovereignty. The Canadian prime minister said: “They asked too much and they offered too little … you’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked.” He promised to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar”.
Donald Trump had initially announced the tariffs on 20 July,saying Canada had unfairly discriminated against American businesses.
The core example provided by the White House is Canada’s bans on the sale of US alcohol in eight of its 10 provinces and all three territories. The removal of US spirits, wine and beer from shelves came into effect after Trump’s first round of tariffs, slapped on Canada in early 2025.
The breakdown of talks came as a shock. Trump had claimed on Tuesday that a three-day extension would be applied to the tariff deadline, as an agreement was all but signed. On Wednesday, he told reporters that a “very fair deal for both” sides had been ironed out.
But as details of the agreement began to leak to Canadian media, there was growing alarm that Carney and his negotiators were conceding too much in exchange for lower tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars.
The premier of Manitoba, Wab Kinew, and his Nova Scotia counterpart, Tim Houston, confirmed this week that Carney had asked the provinces to return US alcohol to shelves in order to seal the trade deal.
Kinew told reporters he believed Canada “should fight” Trump instead, and that “you can’t get a good deal with a bad person”. He encouraged Canadians to avoid buying US alcohol, even if the premiers agreed to put it back on shelves.
Fears of capitulating to Trump also emerged in a high-level briefing call held by Canada’s ambassador to the US, Mark Wiseman, with the Canada-US trade council.
Sources told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that Canada’s former chief trade negotiator Steve Verheul had warned in the call that concessions now would only lead to further demands from the Americans down the road.
JD Vance the US vice-president, was also recorded at a private event, seemingly mocking Carney for standing down on “a lot of issues” as the trade negotiations were occurring.
Instead, Carney took the dramatic decision to bring his negotiators home to Ottawa, with no further meetings planned – and to launch a barrage of criticism against Trump, who in turn accused Canada of wanting “the benefits of being a state, without being one”.
Goods covered by the swingeing US import taxes include everything from anoraks to Christmas ornaments.
Lawlor suggested Canada would soon be back at the negotiating table, given the likely economic impact of the tariffs. But she said any negotiation with the Trump administration should be understood as prone to disintegrate at a moment’s notice.
She said: “We are very much in a state of constant flux, where even where negotiations do produce agreements, these should not be viewed as eternally binding.”

This week, two New York City renters filed a class action complaint alleging that a brokerage business called Compass—which has been boycotting posting listings on free digital platforms like Zillow—has now delisted so many rental units that it has created a fake supply shock that is artificially raising rents.
According to plaintiffs, Peter Castaneda and Haley Gelfand, Compass has bought so many brokerage firms over the past decade-plus that it maintains a monopoly, controlling “over 80 percent of the rental unit listings available for renters in Manhattan based on 2025 data.”
With that monopoly, Compass can “literally dictate pricing for as much as 80 percent of Manhattan’s rental units,” renters argued. And now, Compass is allegedly trying to manipulate prices on other platforms, as well.
Supposedly scheming to raise rents in order to raise broker fees often pegged to rent prices, Compass went to war with Zillow, the most popular free real estate platform that never charges broker fees.
In New York City, a Zillow-owned platform called “StreetEasy” makes it easier for New Yorkers to find a unit without paying a broker fee. However, seemingly hoping to force more people to turn to brokers to find homes that couldn’t be found on free platforms, Compass started delisting thousands of homes from Zillow earlier this year. Renters’ complaint cited a Compass “playbook” that allegedly “involves hiding listings from the public” in an attempt to “enable its own agents to double-dip to increase revenue per transaction, boost its stock price, and effectively ignore the consumer.”
In response to the mass-delistings, Zillow announced new standards excluding those private listings from ever appearing on its sites. That move was designed to curb the practice of hiding listings, since sellers likely wouldn’t want to lose the option of listing on Zillow if brokers can’t find a buyer. But the retaliation prompted Compass to file an antitrust suit, claiming that Zillow was the one trying to monopolize listings. However, Compass voluntarily dismissed that suit in March after a judge ruled that Compass was unlikely to succeed on the merits, writing that it seems clear that Zillow can’t have a monopoly if home buyers like to research across different platforms.

Before sunrise, Shameema slips on her worn rubber sandals and checks the insulated box – the ice packs inside must maintain the crucial cold chain at between 2C and 8C (35.6-46.4F). She hoists the container on one shoulder and steps out into the dark.
Tanzeela follows with her own pack, after quickly retying the laces of her canvas shoes. Both women live in Pulwama, a district where summer temperatures climb to 37C. Their destination lies higher, out of the valley where asphalt turns to dirt track and then to a barely distinguishable footpath along the floor of the mountain pine forests.
Shameema, 45, has worked as a vaccinator for more than a decade, while Tanzeela, 28, joined the programme three years ago. They form part of India’s army of 2.5 million frontline health workers – the human machinery behind the world’s largest immunisation campaign.
Shameema estimates she has administered polio drops to more than 3,000 children during her years as a vaccinator. She remembers a boy in her village who limped with a deformed leg, the legacy of a polio infection before India had fully eradicated it. It is this memory that keeps her going.
“I saw that child struggle to walk to school,” Shameema says during a pause near a stream. “His mother held him on her back until he grew too heavy. [People in] these mountains need protection too – the children here deserve the same health as those in the cities.”
This morning, they are walking towards Namblan, a meadow ringed by pine trees where nearly 50 dhokas, the seasonal mud-and-stone homes of Gujjar and Bakarwal nomadic families, are scattered over the hillsides.
Even before the paved roads end, the electricity lines stop far below these settlements. Horses are the primary transport for the families who spend the summer months with their livestock in these highlands.
The women climb more than 12 miles (20km) with the heavy insulated cool boxes, which hold vials of the oral vaccines, ice packs and the thick paper registers that document the day.
Tanzeela has given polio drops to about 800 children since she joined the programme. She wears the same shoes she uses for farm work. The soles have worn thin, but they grip the rocky paths better than the sandals of some colleagues, she says. One fellow worker walks barefoot for parts of the trail.
“The payment is small and the paths are steep,” Tanzeela says. “I think about my own nephews when I climb. The drops take seconds, but they change a life for ever.”
Their compensation is 125 rupees a day – about £1 – from the state government for the two-day vaccination campaigns, which happen four to six times a year during the national immunisation drives that target all children under five.
India’s polio programme represents a triumph of planning, vigilance and human endurance. The country has been certified polio-free since 2014 – with the final confirmed case in January 2011 in West Bengal – largely thanks to a surveillance network of 60,000 health workers, who monitor 40,000 reporting sites for acute flaccid paralysis, the signature symptom of wild poliovirus.
The oral polio vaccine uses a live but weakened form of the virus developed by a Polish scientist, Albert Sabin, in the late 1950s. The two drops placed on a child’s tongue stimulate antibodies in the intestinal lining that destroy the virus before it can enter the bloodstream and attack the nervous system.
The same gut immunity reduces viral shedding in infected children, ending the chain of transmission in communities where clean water comes from streams and springs. The oral formula creates communal immunity, protecting whole clusters of children who share courtyards and water sources.
This biological shield proves especially vital in the disputed region of Indian-administered Kashmir, where 73% of the 14 million population live in rural areas, with hundreds of thousands of children under six living in far-flung villages and mountain settlements.
Seasonal migration routes take the Gujjar and Bakarwal pastoral communities of about 1.2 million people far from clinics and hospitals during the summer. Reaching them requires coordination between state health departments, local panchayats (village councils) and the frontline workers who know the mountain trails.
The national immunisation effort targets 27 million children under five, and up to 1.7 million vaccinators can be deployed during a single day of a national immunisation drive. Those workers staff 750,000 booths, then fan out with mobile teams into forests, deserts and urban slums.
The scale of this operation dwarfs most military logistics exercises. Insulated boxes travel by foot, bicycle, boat and bus, but in regions such as Kashmir, the final leg of this journey is always down to women travelling on foot.
The dhokas sit miles apart, sometimes separated by ravines and streams that swell with melted snow. A mother might walk two hours to meet the vaccinators halfway, her baby strapped to her back. The workers record these encounters in their paper registers, marking the child’s name, age and the date of the dose.
Shameema and Tanzeela know the terrain and the communities, and time their ascent to reach the first dhokas as the families finish their morning prayers.
“The families welcome us with tea and bread,” Shameema says. “They know the value of these drops. Some remember the days prior to full eradication, when children in neighbouring villages fell ill.”
India’s greatest public health victory still depends on these health workers willing to make such critical journeys for little reward, dedicated to maintaining the country’s protection against the devastating disease.
By late afternoon, the final dhoka receives the vaccinators. A child opens their mouth, gets two drops on their tongue, another name goes on the register and the insulated box is a bit lighter as the women begin their descent down the same tracks they climbed hours earlier. It will be dark by the time they reach home.

'Super' El Niño didn't cause this year's fires and heat waves, but it's about to take us on a 'wild ride'
Ocean-warming phenomenon could be historic, as it combines with human-caused climate change, scientists say
Whether you call it a "super" El Niño or a "Godzilla" El Niño, the Pacific Ocean warming event that disrupts global weather patterns is back and packing a punch, at a time when many parts of the planet are already overheated.
This July was the hottest on record for North America and Europe, where successive heat waves have led to thousands of heat-related deaths, dried up rivers and fire-scorched landscapes. That includes Canada, which has already seen more than 4.1 million hectares of woodland go up in flames and produce thick smoke that blanketed much of the eastern half of the country and parts of the northern U.S.
Although this scorching summer aligned with the arrival of an El Niño and climate scientists say it's not to blame for those devastating extreme weather events. However, they note we may only be starting to see how this naturally occurring phenomenon could amplify extreme weather already super-charged by fossil-fuel driven climate change.
- El Niño is here, and it’s already looking like it could be 'mind-blowing'
- Sunken Nazi warships are resurfacing as Europe's drought deepens
"El Niño's impacts are going to be large and broad across a huge area," said Josh Willis, a climate scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
"Get ready, because it's going to be a wild ride."
Flipping the weather upside down
El Niños occur naturally every three to seven years, usually beginning in spring and enduring well into the following year, as the water surface temperature in the area of the Pacific where they form along the equator, rises at least 0.5 C above the average.
Willis says that warming heats up the air above the water and "rearranges the atmosphere."
"It flips the weather upside down," he said, causing drier places to get heavier rainfall and wetter regions to dry up.
Although this El Niño may have begun forming in May and June just as successive heat waves and fires began to scorch the northern hemisphere, Willis says they usually don't start to impact northern places like Canada until they peak in the late fall and winter.
But Muhammad Azhar Ehsan, a scientist at the Center for Climate Systems Research (CCSR) at New York's Columbia University, says this El Niño is so unprecedented that while he can't directly link it to current heat and wildfire conditions, he does wonder if the "exceptional" temperatures associated with it could be contributing to these disasters.
At the very least, he thinks it's grounds for more research
Ehsen says this El Niño is on track to rival those experienced in 2015-16 and 1997-98, the strongest El Niños since official records began in 1950.
What to expect when you're expecting El Niño
Models suggest much of Canada and the northern U.S. can expect a warmer winter than usual due to this El Niño, with British Columbia's normally wet south coast potentially seeing far less precipitation and a much lower snowpack.
The southern U.S., meanwhile, is likely to experience a much wetter winter.
There are also noticeable effects happening right now in the tropics that Willis says are likely associated with El Niño. He says the phenomenon "sort of juices up" conditions that may already be occuring.
Peru and Ecuador sit at the eastern edge of the El Niño region, where Willis says a lot of warm water has "smashed up" against the coast, posing a threat to fisheries.
- El Niño is officially here, and scientists say it will be particularly strong with widespread impacts
- 'Just stop burning fossil fuels.' Scientists stress that our smoky skies have only one true fix
Peru is also bracing for heavy rains and flooding in some areas and drought in many inland regions.
"But we're also beginning to see a lot of drought away from the equator," Willis said, highlighting a prolonged lack of rainfall in Panama, which is already affecting water levels in the lake that supplies the Panama Canal.
At the opposite end of the El Niño region are countries like Indonesia, which is already experiencing a much longer and more active wildfire season.
One thing people in North America can see happening now, Willis says, is the change to the hurricane season. In an El Niño year, there are fewer tropical storms and hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean.
"The jet stream, which is migrating a little bit farther south, tends to shear off the top of the hurricanes in the Atlantic," he said.
"And because we have all this warm water in the Eastern Pacific, it fuels storm generation there and tropical storms and depressions, which might not have been hurricanes otherwise."
The Eastern Pacific season has already recorded nine named storms ahead of peak season — including Category 5 Hurricane Genevieve in late July and Lala, which caused significant damage as a tropical storm on Hawaii's Big Island last week.
An El Niño born into a much warmer world
The record heat and wildfires this summer were the result of human-caused climate change, which has already been attributed for the past four years being the hottest on record, says Zachary Labe, climate scientist at U.S.-based nonprofit organization Climate Central.
"El Niño is just sort of a temporary boost on top of this long-term trend," Labe said.
But such a significant warming event happening in a world that's even hotter due to climate change could, he says, defy expectations climate scientists have based on previous data.
Labe says what's more certain is that we'll be dealing with the effects of this El Niño well into 2027.
"Because it takes time for that El Niño to have all that heat that's building up in the ocean to transfer into the atmosphere," he said.
"So, this will be around with us for at least the next six to 12 months."

As former cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan's health deteriorates in prison, several renowned cricketers from across the world have written a letter to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, renewing their appeal for Khan's medical treatment. According to reports, 22 former international cricket captains, including India's Sunil Gavaskar and Kapil Dev and Australia's Greg Chappell and Ian Chappell, have signed a second letter to Sharif in the past six months. The latest appeal from the former captains comes days after former Pakistan PM and cricket star Imran Khan was taken to a government hospital in Islamabad for a medical examination, with one of his sisters present for the examination. He was later returned to Adiala prison in Rawalpindi, with doctors declaring him 100 per cent medically fit. However, the cricket luminaries questioned the procedure followed during Khan's check-up and wrote, "Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered that Imran Khan be transferred to hospital for examination by a medical board that was to include his own personal physicians and his sister, Dr. Uzma Khan." The letter further read, "Concerningly, Mr. Khan’s hospital stay lasted only a few hours. He was examined by a state-appointed team rather than the board the court had directed, declared ‘medically fit,’ and returned to Adiala jail before that board could complete its work.” The former captains noted that, by writing the letter, they did not seek to interfere in the country's domestic legal process and had only written to Shehbaz Sharif “not as politicians, but as former colleagues and rivals (of Khan) who share a bond forged on the cricket field.” The letter comes roughly six months after a group of 14 former international cricketers expressed concerns over Khan's health. The letter, sent in February, came after Khan's family claimed that the former PM had lost roughly 85 per cent of the vision in his right eye, a claim disputed by the government. Later, authorities said Khan's condition was improving following medical treatment. The former cricketer's family had also accused the Sharif-led government of violating a court directive requiring him to undergo a medical examination at Islamabad’s private Shifa International Hospital. The government denied the claim over the weekend, saying doctors from the hospital had examined Khan and that security concerns prevented him from being taken there. The government, however, claimed that Khan’s supporters had begun assembling outside the private hospital despite a court directive barring them from gathering there to prevent inconvenience to other patients. Pakistan government rejects allegations It also rejected allegations levelled by Khan's family that he was being subjected to "cruelty, mental torture, punitive solitary confinement and medical neglect.” Pakistan's Ministry of Information told AP earlier this month that the former cricketer was not being held under a government order but as a “convicted prisoner” serving sentences handed down by courts following judicial proceedings. The government also rejected claims that the former prime minister was being kept in solitary confinement or prevented from communicating with his family. The ministry said Khan had received more than 900 visits from relatives, lawyers, doctors, political representatives and other authorised visitors since his imprisonment in 2023. It added that he had been permitted weekly meetings with his wife, along with phone and WhatsApp communication with relatives in Pakistan and overseas. Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay on Monday (August 24, 2026) announced reimbursement for three domestic LPG cylinders a year for eligible homemakers under the ‘Annapoorani Super Six Scheme’, which will be launched on Pongal Day in 2027. A total of 1,30,16,104 families will benefit from the scheme, which is expected to cost the government approximately ₹4,000 crore.
The provision of six free cooking gas cylinders was one of the major electoral promises of the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) in the run-up to the 2026 Assembly polls.
Making a suo motu statement, the Chief Minister said the money for the cylinders would be credited to the bank accounts of the beneficiaries. “The government would collect the list from the oil companies after the beneficiaries receive the cylinders post registration, and credit the money to their bank accounts,” he said.
Families with an annual income not exceeding ₹2.5 lakh, middle and marginal farmers, and families of persons with disabilities are eligible for the free cylinders.
Mr. Vijay said there had been a shortage of cylinders in the last four months following the war in the West Asian region, forcing families to opt for alternative fuels. The increase in fuel prices had also eaten into family incomes. “Though the government is facing a financial crisis, it has decided to reimburse the money for gas cylinders, taking into consideration the burden on the people, their welfare and to fulfil the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam’s poll promise,” he said.

A majority of India’s new-age tech stocks ended the week in the green, with Wakefit emerging as the biggest gainer after rallying 16.69% during the five trading sessions to close at ₹141.55. Shares of four companies – Klassroom, Zelio E-Mobility, Turtlemint, and Lenskart – touched fresh 52-week highs during the week. Overall, 34 of the 61 new-age tech stocks gained between 0.11% and 16.69% during the week. While Wakefit led the pack, logistics tech company LEAP India followed with an 11.75% rise to ₹162.15. The stock had made a muted market debut on August 14 (Friday). On the other hand, 27 stocks declined between 0.01% and more than 11%. SME-listed Yudiz and TAC Infosec were among the biggest laggards, while AI cloud infrastructure provider E2E Networks fell 9.68% to ₹622 after rallying for more than a month. Meanwhile, ecommerce enablement platform Shiprocket made a bumper stock market debut this week, taking the number of new-age tech stocks tracked by Inc42 to 62. The stock, which made a strong debut on August 19 (Wednesday), gained 8.58% from its listing price over its first three trading sessions. Shiprocket’s ₹1,617.5 Cr IPO comprised a fresh issue worth ₹885.5 Cr and an OFS of about ₹732 Cr. Early investor 500 Global clocked a gross return of up to 77.6X on the shares it sold through the OFS. Together, the 62 new-age tech companies commanded a market capitalisation of $166.84 Bn. With that, let’s look at some of the key developments that shaped the new-age tech ecosystem this week. The complaint was filed by the minor’s mother, Gurugram resident Anuradha Mehra. IPO Filings Galore: Consumer appliances startup Atomberg filed its DRHP with SEBI for an IPO comprising a fresh issue of up to ₹450 Cr and an OFS of up to 7.65 Cr shares. Manufacturing services unicorn Zetwerk also filed its UDRHP for a ₹2,600 Cr public issue. Meanwhile, online stockbroking platform Upstox reportedly began preliminary discussions with investment banks for a potential $400 Mn IPO. Kedia Backs Zaggle: Veteran investor Vijay Kedia-led Kedia Securities acquired 20 Lakh shares, or a 1.48% stake, in Zaggle for about ₹32.94 Cr through a bulk deal. Major Block Deal In Paytm: Vijay Shekhar Sharma-owned Resilient Asset Management offloaded 1.92 Cr shares in Paytm parent One97 Communications through a block deal worth about ₹2,948.9 Cr. Antfin, which retained the economic value of the shares under an optionally convertible debenture agreement with Resilient, will receive the proceeds from the sale. Y Combinator’s Groww Windfall: Y Combinator sold Groww shares worth ₹1,435.2 Cr through a bulk deal, marking another partial exit from one of its most successful India bets. The accelerator clocked a return of about 55.7X on the shares sold in the transaction. With that, let's take a look at the broader market trends this week. Smallcaps Buck Broader Market Weakness Indian benchmark indices ended in the red for the second consecutive week amid volatility driven by geopolitical tensions, elevated crude oil prices, and rising global bond yields. The Nifty 50 declined about 0.47% during the week to close at 24,252, while the Sensex fell nearly 0.60% to settle at 77,540.83. Ajit Mishra, senior vice president of research at Religare Broking, said geopolitical developments and elevated crude oil prices remained the dominant drivers of market sentiment. “Ongoing tensions in West Asia continued to raise concerns over potential disruptions to global energy supplies, keeping crude prices elevated. Looking ahead, Nair said the upcoming US inflation and GDP data would be key indicators for the global interest-rate trajectory. Wakefit Leads Weekly Gains Wakefit ended the week in the green, gaining 16.69% to close at ₹141.55. The rally coincided with the release of the D2C home and furnishings company’s FY26 annual report earlier in the week. Rare thunderstorm with lightning strikes wows southern B.C., causing havoc at Vancouver airport
'This was quite the system,' says CBC meteorologist
Lightning strikes lit up the skies across B.C.'s South Coast overnight in a rare display as a severe thunderstorm passed over the region, snarling traffic at Vancouver International Airport and causing flight issues in the process.
"This was quite the system, hundreds of cloud to ground strikes ... mainly in Vancouver/Richmond," CBC meteorologist Johanna Wagstaffe said.
Wagstaffe said the centre of a low-pressure system pushed onshore near Richmond after travelling from the equator, loaded with moisture.
The storm created havoc at Vancouver International Airport (YVR), causing multiple overnight delays and cancellations.
From 9 p.m. Saturday to 3 a.m. PT on Sunday, "flights could not depart YVR and many arriving flights were unable to taxi to the gate once landed, as it is unsafe to operate when there is lightning in the area," the airport said in a statement.
It said some flights are also being impacted Sunday as the airport works with airlines to get back to normal operations.
Travel advisory warns of possible road closures
Videos posted to social media also appeared to show significant flooding in parts of the airport.
YVR's website showed multiple delays and cancellations Sunday. People are urged to check their flights before going to the terminal.
The storm system also triggered a high streamflow advisory for the Central Interior, including the Pemberton area and its upstream watersheds, the Chilcotin River, the Bridge River and the Cariboo River.
The B.C. River Forecast Centre said it expected 20 to 25 millimetres of precipitation from the storm, with 30 to 60 millimetres falling in areas of the Cariboo to the Yellowhead region.
A travel advisory issued for most of the stretch of Highway 99 between Pemberton and Lillooet due to heavy rains near Pemberton also warned that the road could close on short notice.
B.C. Hydro reported numerous outages overnight. As of Sunday morning, over 3,800 customers were without power in the Lower Mainland and Sunshine Coast regions.

India’s technology ecosystem is entering another major transition. Over the past decade, technology leaders have navigated the shift to mobile, cloud, APIs, SaaS and digital-first distribution. Each wave changed how companies built products, managed infrastructure and scaled their engineering organisations. AI is now triggering another reset — but its impact is playing out alongside a second challenge. India’s largest technology businesses are themselves reaching a level of scale where decisions around architecture, infrastructure costs, reliability, security and engineering productivity have direct consequences for the business. According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, H1 2026, Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn in the first half of 2026, more than four times the $162 Mn raised during the same period last year. This came even as overall Indian tech startup funding declined 9% year-on-year. Meanwhile, the Google x Inc42 Bharat AI Startups Report estimates India’s AI opportunity could reach $126 Bn by 2030. For technology leaders, however, the harder questions begin after adoption. An AI workload that works in a pilot has to behave very differently once it becomes part of a product used by millions. Faster software generation also creates a greater need for verification. More compute can unlock new capabilities while materially changing infrastructure economics. And productivity gains inside engineering teams can eventually alter how those teams themselves are structured. Beyond AI, many of the toughest technology challenges also remain distinctly Indian. Companies are building for enormous transaction volumes, sudden traffic spikes, a wide range of devices and network conditions, cost-conscious customers and businesses where even small changes in technology economics can have an outsized impact at scale. At the same time, the engineering organisation is being reconsidered. AI-assisted development is increasing the output expected of individual engineers, the bar for junior talent is rising, while companies are reassessing layers of engineering and management that were built during an earlier period of aggressive technology hiring. Together, these shifts are bringing three questions to the centre of the CTO’s agenda: How do you build at Indian scale? What does an AI-native engineering organisation actually look like? And what happens to the critical layer of experienced engineering talent in the middle? Running across all three are decisions around security, infrastructure, reliability, governance and technology economics — the issues increasingly shaping the CTO mandate. These conversations have been building at Inc42 for years. Across 50+ closed-door technology roundtables, CTO dinners and leadership conversations, alongside platforms such as the Inc42 GenAI Summit and Inc42 AI Summit, we have brought together CTOs, engineering leaders, CISOs, founders and enterprise technology decision-makers to discuss the challenges emerging as technology moves from experimentation to scale. The Inc42 CTO Summit 2026 brings these conversations together into one dedicated room for India’s senior technology leaders. The Inc42 CTO Summit 2026 Is Here Taking place on September 30, 2026, at JW Marriott, Bengaluru, the inaugural Inc42 CTO Summit will bring together 175+ senior technology leaders responsible for building and scaling some of India’s most consequential technology businesses. The invite-only summit is being curated for CTOs, VPs of Engineering, Heads of Technology, CISOs, AI and ML leaders, architects, platform leaders and founders from growth-stage startups, unicorns and other scaled technology businesses. Across 10+ sessions, the conversations will be organised around the operating problems technology leaders face today rather than conventional technology categories. At this stage of the ecosystem, the more interesting conversation is no longer simply whether companies will adopt AI or move more workloads to the cloud. It is about what follows. Which architectural choices hold up as the business grows 10X? When does an existing system need to be rebuilt rather than continuously patched? How do the economics of AI change once deployments reach production? Which engineering capabilities become more valuable as software creation gets increasingly automated? And how do technology leaders balance speed, reliability, security and cost at the same time? The Four Conversations At The Centre Of The CTO Summit Building At Indian Scale For India’s scaled technology companies, architecture decisions increasingly carry direct business consequences. Infrastructure has to absorb large, unpredictable volumes without letting cloud costs outpace revenue. Platforms need to remain reliable as products, teams and markets expand. And systems built for an earlier stage of the company eventually have to be reworked or replaced — making the decision of when to rebuild almost as important as how. At the CTO Summit, we will delve into the architecture, platform, reliability and infrastructure decisions companies are making as their technology footprint expands. The emphasis will be on the choices behind scale: what held up, what became too expensive, what broke and what eventually had to change. The AI-Native Engineering Organisation Much of the first wave of enterprise AI discussion was centred on adoption. The harder phase begins when AI becomes part of how software is actually produced and operated. Coding assistants are accelerating development. AI agents are beginning to execute more complex workflows. Models are entering customer-facing products. But faster generation of software is also making verification, quality and human judgement more important. For CTOs, the question therefore goes far beyond how many developers are using an AI coding tool. It extends to engineering productivity, quality controls, team structures, platform and data architecture, software economics and ultimately the composition of the engineering organisation itself. The CTO Summit will examine what companies are learning as AI moves deeper into engineering and production — where productivity gains are showing up, where new bottlenecks are emerging, and which parts of the engineering organisation need to change around them. The Missing Middle AI is not the only force reshaping technology organisations. After years of aggressive technology hiring, companies are also reassessing how engineering teams themselves should be structured. Junior engineers face a higher entry bar as more basic development tasks become automated. At the other end, experienced architects and technology leaders capable of making complex decisions continue to remain critical. The more interesting shift could be happening in between. The experienced engineers and managers in this layer translate architecture into execution, mentor younger talent, coordinate increasingly complex teams and carry institutional context accumulated over years. The sessions at the summit will examine how this layer is evolving, what the changing mandate means for VPs and engineering managers, and what organisations risk losing if efficiency drives flatten teams faster than they can replace the judgement and context these roles provide. The conversation will also look beyond AI, factoring in the impact of cost resets, shorter project cycles and the broader restructuring that has followed the technology hiring boom of previous years. The Decisions That Cut Across Everything Architecture, AI and organisational design cannot be separated neatly inside a scaled technology business. An AI architecture decision eventually becomes an infrastructure-cost question. Faster development creates new reliability and security challenges. A flatter engineering organisation changes how technical decisions are reviewed, challenged and passed through the company. This is why infrastructure economics, cybersecurity, observability, governance, reliability and the technology P&L will cut across conversations throughout the summit rather than sitting inside isolated tracks. As technology becomes an increasingly significant component of both the cost base and competitive advantage of digital businesses, the CTO’s remit is expanding beyond engineering output into economics, risk, organisational design and business strategy. What To Expect At The Inc42 CTO Summit 2026 The CTO Summit is being designed as a focused room for leaders dealing with comparable levels of scale and technological complexity. The agenda will bring together technology leaders to exchange what they are seeing inside their own organisations — the architectures they are changing, the infrastructure economics they are trying to improve, the engineering structures they are reconsidering and the technology bets they are making next. That could mean understanding how another CTO brought infrastructure costs under control without slowing growth, how an engineering organisation is introducing AI into software development, how security architecture is evolving around new AI systems, or how another company is reconsidering the layers inside its engineering organisation. The objective is not to predict which technology wins next. It is to understand how India’s technology leaders are actually building, scaling and reorganising around the changes already underway. Attendance is curated, with seats capped to maintain the seniority and relevance of the room. If you are responsible for the technology decisions shaping how your organisation builds and scales, the Inc42 CTO Summit 2026 is where those conversations come together.

- Fable's new teaser ahead of Gamescom reveals a redesigned female character from their first showcase.
- The new female character design has softer facial features with a more traditionally attractive face.
- The change likely came to address the negative marketing the game had after the reveal of its first teaser.
Xbox has teased a small clip of Fable ahead of Gamescom on their socials, and it shows a vastly redesigned female character. Fable’s female character redesign likely came to address their biggest criticism yet.
From the very start, players have been complaining about how weird the female character looked in the game’s first teaser. Later, Fable showcased that players would be able to create their own characters, which removed some of the concerns from players. However, that initial image continued to haunt Fable, as many would bring it up to badmouth the game’s release.
Fable Revamps Its Female Character Design, Opting for a Softer and More Attractive Look
Xbox seems to have finally decided to change it and has completely redesigned the female character for the upcoming Xbox Gamescom lineup. In their little clip shared, players easily spotted the new female character, and her new features didn’t take time to spread in the community.
The new female character has much softer facial features, fewer freckles, and overall looks much more appealing. The change might be part of Xbox’s new drive to make sure their games succeed. Negative marketing has been one of the big problems many games have been facing nowadays before launch, and Xbox clearly wanted to avoid it for Fable.
The reaction of gamers towards the new face has been more than positive. One user replied to Xbox’s thread saying they would be pre-ordering the game today just because of this change. The reception seemed to be reciprocated by others as well. If Xbox was planning for more positive coverage, then they definitely made the correct call before Gamescom.
There has been a debate for some time now on how some developers are deliberately trying to have worse-looking characters for their games. Sometimes, the blame does look fitting, while at other times it feels hollow. For Fable, the blame was pretty spot on, but when the same was said about God of War Laufey, I couldn’t have denied it more.
But one thing is clear: game developers must have these conversations now before they plan to showcase their game, whatever their decision may be. So, what’s your opinion on Fable’s new female character redesign? Tell us in the comments below.

I tested the Premium plan extensively in the UK and briefly in Europe. It was quick and easy to set up in the Saily app and kept me connected as I roamed, offering decent speeds up to around 300 Mbps on 5G networks in city center locations, inevitably dropping off to 4G and around 15 Mbps in more rural spots. The specific speeds you’ll get depend entirely on the local network. Saily piggybacks on local providers, mainly connecting to EE and Vodafone during my month of testing.
The Ultra plan includes 30 GB of high-speed data. In this case, high-speed simply means unfettered; the actual speed you get depends on coverage where you are. After that 30 GB is gone, you get unlimited throttled data at up to 1 Mbps. In practice, I found this lower speed was enough for messaging, web scrolling, and navigation, but anything data-hungry, like video, is out.
It’s worth noting that the 30 GB limit is for the month. Most folks use around 20 GB of data in a month, so 30 GB sounds like a lot. But consider that you are probably connected to Wi-Fi most of the time at home or work, and you may not be when traveling. That 30 GB can disappear surprisingly quickly, and you should take advantage of Wi-Fi whenever you can on your travels. One of my top travel tips is to download videos and maps before you go, or when you’re connected to Wi-Fi.
If you’re only visiting one or two countries, it’s probably better to get a pay-as-you-go plan for that specific region or country. For example, Saily offers unlimited data in the UK for 15 days for $49, but there’s a fair usage policy that will throttle you after 5 GB in a single 24-hour period (until the next day). Unlimited data across Europe (35 countries) for a month will cost you $72, with the same 5 GB daily limit. You could also just buy 20 GB of data to use over 30 days for $23 in France or $31 in the UK.
Having used a few different international eSIM and regular SIM services for travel over the years, Saily compares favorably on performance and ease of use but is relatively expensive. That said, most other eSIM services don’t come with a bundle of extras.
Plenty of Perks
Saily Ultra will be a hard sell for most folks simply looking at the data, but frequent travelers will appreciate the plentiful perks. Here’s what you get:
- 1x Airport Lounge Pass per month: Airports can be noisy and uncomfortable, but airport lounges offer quieter spaces where you can work or relax, with fast Wi-Fi, comfier seating, and complimentary food and drink. If you’re stuck in an airport for a few hours, a lounge pass can make your wait as painless as possible. With Saily Ultra, you get one free pass per month for one person. It generates a QR code in the app that’s valid for 30 minutes. Here’s the complete list of supported lounge destinations. You also get a free lounge pass for that trip if your flight is delayed for more than two hours (contact support in the app).
- 1x Fast-Track Pass per month: You can skip the long security queue with fast-track and get straight through into the terminal. With Saily Ultra, you get one free fast-track pass for one person, generated as a QR code in the app. Here’s the complete list of supported fast-track destinations. Availability is far more limited than with the lounge pass, so I was unable to test this.
- Online Security Tools: You get access to NordVPN, NordPass, NordLocker, and Incogni with an activation code in the Saily app. Saily’s parent company is Nord Security, so it makes sense that its popular VPN service, password manager, and secure cloud storage are included. Incogni is a privacy tool that can help you remove personal data from the internet.
Saily lists several other perks on its website, including priority support, an ad blocker, and 8 percent back in Saily credits. The ad blocker is handy and also reduces your data usage, and you can use any credits you accrue to buy data plans or extra perks, like additional lounge passes. It's also worth noting that lounge and fast-track benefits rollover for up to three months if unused, though you can't share them. Saily also lists a ClassPass subscription on the site right now, but that wasn’t available when I tested. The perks are subject to change, so it’s important to check what’s included at the time of purchase.

78% of low-income elderly Hongkongers report heat-related distress, survey finds
Most respondents reported heat-related discomfort, while many lacked awareness of heatstroke risks and available government support
Nearly 80 per cent of low-income elderly people surveyed in Hong Kong reported physical or mental distress during periods of extreme heat, prompting calls for stronger government support and heat-prevention measures.
Data from the Department of Health cited by Greenpeace identified elderly people as the city’s demographic most at risk from extreme temperatures. The number of hospital discharges and deaths related to heatstroke among people aged 65 or above rose 16-fold between 2015 and 2024, from four to 68 – the sharpest increase among all age groups.
The city has been hit by sweltering weather this summer, with temperatures forecast to reach 33 degrees Celsius (91 Fahrenheit) on Friday. Earlier this month, Hong Kong recorded a maximum temperature of 36.9 degrees, the highest since records began in 1884.
For its study, Greenpeace interviewed 127 residents aged 65 or above across seven districts with rapidly ageing populations, including Kwai Tsing, Wong Tai Sin and Kowloon City. More than half lived in public housing, while 35 per cent lived in inadequate housing.
About 78 per cent of respondents said they had experienced at least one form of physical discomfort because of high temperatures, including dizziness, headaches, vomiting, difficulty breathing and a racing heartbeat. Some also reported mood disturbances and poorer sleep quality.
A total of 5.5 per cent said they had been hospitalised for a heat-related illness in the previous year.

Quick Answer
QuickLook brings macOS-style instant file previews to Windows 11. Install the free, open-source app, select a file in File Explorer, and press Space to preview images, PDFs, videos, archives, code, and more without opening another app.
If you are switching from a Mac to a Windows laptop or have already jumped ship, then among a bunch of cool things, there is a good chance that you might be missing that one tiny feature — tapping the Space bar to peek inside a file. On macOS, the file peeking feature has been around since 2007, and once you get used to it, selecting a photo, PDF, or video and instantly seeing what’s inside without opening a single app, going back feels like a step down. Windows, even with all the polish it has picked up over the years, never really bothered to catch up.
The Windows File Explorer still makes you double-click and wait for the right app to load, just to confirm whether you want that file or not. This is the gap that QuickLook fixes, as it brings the macOS-style press Space and preview feature to Windows 10 and 11 PCs. But it has more to it. Let us check it out.
Why does Windows File Explorer still lag?
No offense to Microsoft, but even after so many visual upgrades, Windows has never really implemented features that actually make a difference. For instance, it is not that Microsoft has never tried the preview feature. It has experimented with preview panes in File Explorer for years, and to be fair, the built-in Preview Pane (which you can enable through the sidebar from the View menu) does show images, PDFs, and a handful of document types. But it is quite slow and doesn’t support all file formats people actually deal with. On top of this, the preview pane needs a permanently open panel eating into your window memory. To put it in simple words, it was never designed to be instant but designed to be available if you go looking for it.
That’s a very different philosophy from what Apple built. Quick Look on macOS is designed so that you should never have to fully open an application just to look at whether the file is right or wrong. QuickLook for Windows brings that same philosophy and applies it system-wide, whether you are browsing on your desktop, a network drive, or even inside an Open/Save dialog box.
QuickLook is free and open-source
I love trying out new tools and software that bring more features and enhance the usage experience. QuickLook stood out because it is a free and open-source utility, and it has been actively maintained since 2017. One of the best parts about QuickLook is that it runs quietly in the background after installation, sitting in your system tray, waiting for you to select a file and press the Space bar. The moment you press the Space bar, a preview window pops open almost instantly; no loading spinner, no application splash screen, nothing.
What makes it genuinely useful rather than a gimmick is the long list of supported file formats it can preview. Out of the box, QuickLook handles more than fifty file types natively, including:
- Images (JPG, PNG, GIF, WebP, HEIC, RAW formats, and more)
- Videos and audio files, with actual playback controls inside the preview
- PDFs, rendered natively without needing Adobe Reader
- Source code files, with proper syntax highlighting for dozens of programming languages
- Markdown files, rendered as formatted text rather than raw syntax
- Archives like ZIP and RAR, letting you browse contents without extracting
- Fonts, showing a live specimen of how the typeface actually looks
- 3D model files, with the ability to rotate and inspect the model
Using QuickLook is straightforward
Once you are done with the installation, you can use QuickLook straightaway. All you need to do is click on any file, be it inside the File Explorer, your Desktop, or even inside a file picker, press the Space bar, and a preview window will open up, rendering the file’s contents without launching the actual application associated with it. Want to check the next file in the folder? Use the arrow keys to move your selection, and QuickLook updates the preview live, without you needing to close and reopen anything. When you are done, hitting Space again, pressing Escape, or clicking the close button dismisses the window immediately.
There is also a small but genuinely thoughtful touch. You can drag a file directly out of the preview window into another folder or application. This means that QuickLook does not just show you contents, but it can double as a lightweight way to move files around while you are inspecting them. For those who deal with folders full of similarly named files like screenshots, exported design assets, and scanned documents, this single feature removes an entire category of friction and saves a lot of time. Instead of opening five PDFs one at a time in a PDF Reader to find the right invoice, you tap through them in under two seconds each.
The plugin ecosystem is where it gets genuinely powerful
QuickLook’s native format support already covers most everyday use cases. But if you want to expand the list of supported file formats, the plugin system is what turns QuickLook from “a nice preview tool” into something closer to a universal file viewer. Community developers have built plugins that extend QuickLook to handle formats it doesn’t support by default. The best part is that installing one is refreshingly simple. You just need to download the plugin file, select it in File Explorer, press Space, and QuickLook prompts you to install it directly from the preview window itself.
Some of the more useful plugins in the ecosystem include:
- Office document viewers that render Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files without needing Microsoft Office or WPS Office installed at all
- ePub and comic book viewers, useful for anyone who reads digital books or manga and wants a quick way to confirm file contents
- PDF renderers built on WebView2, offering an alternative rendering engine for people who run into issues with the default PDF viewer
- SQLite database viewers, letting developers peek inside .db files without opening a separate database tool
- 3D model and CAD file plugins, handling specialized formats used in design and engineering work
It’s a similar philosophy to how tools like Winaero Tweaker approach Windows customization, where a small, focused core with optional extras layered on top, rather than a bloated all-in-one package.
QuickLook: Is this for you?
For anyone who regularly digs through folders full of screenshots, downloads, project files, or scanned documents, QuickLook solves a problem that Windows has quietly ignored for over a decade. It’s free, open-source, doesn’t collect telemetry, has no ads or premium tier hiding better features behind a paywall, and the entire project has stayed community-maintained since it first launched. Not only heavy file users, but casual users can also install it and use it in their daily lives, as it solves a core problem of having to double-click a file, use supported software, wait for it to load, and then preview the file. The setup takes less time than reading this article, and the payoff shows up the very first time you tap Space over a file and actually get what you expected, instantly.

'I didn't think I could do it': A 13-year-old N.S. girl fought a 711-pound tuna and won
Délynn Jacquard broke the previous record set in 2014, also in Nova Scotia
Five hours off the west coast of Nova Scotia, a 13-year-old girl broke a world tuna-fishing record during the 22nd annual Wedgeport Tuna Tournament and Festival.
Délynn Jacquard was aboard the Pelagic Predator when she reeled in the 711-pound (323-kilogram) catch Wednesday. If ratified, it will mark a new International Game Fish Association female junior world record.
The former record of 618 pounds was set 12 years ago by Nova Scotian Jenna Gavin in Ballantynes Cove, meaning Jacquard beat the record by nearly 100 pounds.
"I was thinking to myself, 'I don't think ... I might not be able to do this,'" Jacquard said in an interview Saturday. "But then I did it and I was just proud of myself."
Jacquard says it took just over an hour to reel the tuna in.
"It's a lot of work," she said. "You're hooked on to the rod and to the chair. Once you see the tip of the rod start coming closer to you, that's when you start twisting the line and pulling it in."
Jacquard’s father, Camille Jacquard, captains the Pelagic Predator. He has participated in the tournament for roughly 20 years. But this year was Délynn's first outing as a relative newcomer to the world of big-game fishing.
Délynn said she's not sure if she'll be back for next year's tournament.
2026 is going to be known as the year of records- Brandon Doucette
Brandon Doucette, a board member for the tournament, said it could take up to six months for the record to be official, though he is confident it will be confirmed.
Doucette said that IGFA records are based on the weight of a fish before it is gutted, whereas the Wedgeport tournament counts the weight after partial gutting. Jacquard’s tuna weighed 711 pounds fresh out of the water and 635 pounds after being partially gutted.
Doucette said that "2026 is going to be known as the year of records," as another vessel reeled in the heaviest tuna in tournament history. Capt. Brent Pothier caught an 801-pound bluefin aboard the Lucas & Noah, a vessel named for his two sons, who were also on board for the catch.
It is the first fish to clear the 800-pound mark in the tournament’s 22-year history, breaking the previous record of 796 pounds set in 2014 — the same year Gavin made her record-setting catch.
"When they started yelling the weight out, the excitement was unbelievable," Doucette said. "We were just so excited to have not just one world record, but also a Wedgeport Tuna Tournament record."
Doucette said the annual tournament is as much about community history as it is about records. Between the 1930s and 1960s, Wedgeport hosted anglers from around the world for its International Tuna Cup Match, earning a reputation as the sport tuna fishing capital of the world.
"We’re able to come out, celebrate our culture, and it's really such an incredible event for our community," Doucette said.
As for the thousands of pounds of tuna landed during the event, Doucette said that all catches fall within the region’s commercial quota.
"It's going to end up either in a restaurant or on somebody's plate in their house," he said.

Ramban, Aug 24: Three families comprising 10 members were evacuated as a precautionary measure after land subsidence and cracks in residential houses were reported in a village in Ramban district of Jammu and Kashmir, officials said on Monday.
The land subsidence at Kulthi Chakka Kundi in Tehsil Rajgarh, along the banks of the Chenab River, triggered panic among the local villagers, particularly in the wake of recent heavy rains that have affected several areas of the district, they said.
Administrative, revenue and rescue teams rushed to the affected area and shifted the affected families to safer locations.
Tehsildar Rajgarh Major Singh said one non-residential structure belonging to Bhagat Ram was washed away, while cracks had developed in the residential houses of Chaat Ram, Chaman Lal and Bhushan Lal due to land subsidence over the past couple of days.
Singh said he visited the affected area along with an State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) team and shifted the affected families. They were provided tents for temporary accommodation.
The Naib Tehsildar and other officials are stationed in the village and are closely monitoring the situation, he said.
Locals, however, reported cracks and damage to several other houses, including those belonging to Dev Raj, Hari Ram, Santosh Singh, Fallal Singh and Shashram.
BJP Ramban district president Neelam Kumar Lange also visited the affected area and demanded compensation and rehabilitation for the affected families.
He also expressed concern over the absence of any minister or MLA from the National Conference-led government at the site, alleging that no minister or MLA had visited the affected area to assess the situation.
Local residents apprehended that recent water releases from the Baglihar Hydroelectric Power Project following heavy rains may have contributed to ground instability.
However, officials said the exact cause of the land subsidence and cracks is yet to be established.
One person, along with a sand-extraction boat, who was swept away by strong currents in the Chenab River near Pul Doda in Doda district Monday morning was also rescued by the SDRF.
The rescued person, a non-local worker employed as an operator of the sand-extraction machine, was engaged by a private company that had been awarded the contract for sand extraction in the area, officials said.
They said efforts are currently underway to retrieve the machinery from the river.

The Indonesian volcano known as Anak Krakatau, or Child of Krakatau, emerged in the 1920s from the underwater ruins of the larger Krakatau volcano that erupted devastatingly in 1883. Here, the volcano erupts in 2018.

The Indonesian volcano known as Anak Krakatau, or Child of Krakatau, emerged in the 1920s from the underwater ruins of the larger Krakatau volcano that erupted devastatingly in 1883. Here, the volcano erupts in 2018.
Credit:
FERDI AWED/AFP via Getty Images
The first telegram arrived in Singapore on a Monday, sent from the city of Batavia in the Dutch East Indies (now Jakarta, Indonesia). “Terrific detonations from Krakatau (volcanic island),” it reported. Soon afterward: “Stones falling. Village near Anjer washed away.” The wires continued clattering out news of bridges destroyed, boats smashed, lighthouses “disappeared.” By noon on Tuesday, the scope of the natural disaster was clear: “Where once Mount Krakatau stood the sea now plays.”
Within days, the source of the destruction was known worldwide. On the morning of August 27, 1883, a volcanic eruption had obliterated two islands in the strait between Java and Sumatra, and most of a third. More than 36,000 people perished, the majority in devastating tsunamis that raced outward from the colossal explosion.
Thanks to Victorian-era telecommunications, it was the first time in history that people around the globe could begin to document, in near real time, the immediate and long-term effects of a catastrophic volcanic eruption. What they learned over the next few years laid the foundations for the modern science of volcanology. And it was an especially eye-opening lesson in how the biggest eruptions can influence climate, agriculture, and even the course of human history.
Global effects
In the months after Krakatau, drifting volcanic particles high in the atmosphere circled the globe, causing violently colored sunsets that contemporary artists captured in paintings, likely including the psychedelic background of Edvard Munch’s The Scream.
But the key climate-driving component of the volcano’s emissions was sulfur from the molten rock that fed Krakatau. Once sulfur erupts into the atmosphere, it can form particles called aerosols that reflect sunlight and cool Earth. In the months and years after the eruption, average summer temperatures fell 0.6° Celsius (1.1° Fahrenheit) in the non-tropical regions of the Northern Hemisphere.
Fast-forward more than a century, and researchers now understand that climate changes, especially rapid ones, have transformed societies by affecting agriculture, public health, and living conditions. With what they’ve learned from Krakatau and other eruptions, volcanologists today are identifying past catastrophic blasts that may have contributed to historic events like droughts, famines, epidemics and societal unrest.
“In so many different ways societies were affected … a failure in harvest or flooding or a cold summer or a really cold winter,” says Katrin Kleemann, an environmental historian at the German Maritime Museum in Bremerhaven.
While they can’t prove an eruption caused the demise of a regime, volcanologists have uncovered some intriguing links, including some that could inform our understanding of how today’s society might react to a rapidly changing climate.
536 and all that
The first challenge in making volcano-society connections is to find physical fingerprints of past eruptions. In the year 536, scribes in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia wrote about bizarre weather, including a haze that shrouded the sun for 18 months. Temperatures plummeted, harvests failed, and within a few years, the first documented global plague began.
These early medieval chronicles strongly suggest a major volcanic eruption—but the hard evidence lies deep in polar ice. Scientists can infer that big eruptions happened at certain times in the past by looking for sulfur and ash deposits in ice cores from Greenland and Antarctica. These cores, drilled into ice sheets, preserve an annual record of whatever was circulating in Earth’s atmosphere as it settled onto the surface each year. Researchers can read these frozen layers back in time like turning the pages of a book.
It turns out that polar ice cores do contain large amounts of sulfur dating to 536, a distinct signal of a major eruption. But which volcano went off at the time remains a mystery. There is no known written record from anyone living close to the eruption—Iceland, where it may have occurred, was not yet populated.
Large volcanic eruptions cool Earth’s climate by injecting tiny particles of sulfur high into the atmosphere, where they reflect a portion of incoming sunlight back into space for periods of months or years. The 1257 eruption of the Samalas volcano in Indonesia dwarfed others in recent history as measured by sulfur output, and has been shown to have chilled the climate across the Northern Hemisphere for several years afterward. Other significant eruptions shown have also influenced Earth’s climate enough to affect human societies.

Empire falls
There is better evidence pinpointing the volcano that may have helped topple the Mongol Empire seven centuries later. Until 2013, researchers knew only that some eruption—the biggest in the last few millennia as measured by sulfur output—occurred in 1257. In 2013, an interdisciplinary team radiocarbon-dated the ash, pumice, and other deposits around Samalas, a volcano in Indonesia, tying it to the 1257 eruption.
Tree-ring studies, which analyze annual growth layers on trees to determine which years had good and bad growing weather, show extensive cooling across North America and Eurasia from 1257 to 1259. Among other impacts, bad harvests led to starvation in England, and wet, cool summer weather in Japan damaged rice production.
Some researchers have speculated that it was the Samalas eruption that helped seal the fate of the Mongol Empire, which ended after its last ruler perished in a 1259 epidemic in China that could have been linked with the eruption-caused climate changes.
The Black Death
A century after Samalas, volcanologists have found, there was yet another intriguing eruption-disease connection. Between 1346 and 1352, perhaps half of Europe’s population died in the Black Death plague, from infection by the flea-borne bacterium Yersinia pestis.
Historical records from Europe and Asia suggest that skies were darker than usual around that time, perhaps because of a volcanic haze. Ice-core records support that interpretation, documenting a big eruption, or perhaps several, around the year 1345—though the location remains unknown.
To see how this volcanic activity might have affected climate, an interdisciplinary team led by Ulf Büntgen, a tree-ring specialist at the University of Cambridge, used tree-ring data to confirm that the summers of 1345, 1346, and 1347 were unusually cold and wet in southern Europe.
Büntgen and his colleagues note that as crops failed in the bad weather, Europeans imported grain from farther east. The grain ships arrived with rats harboring Y. pestis, leading the researchers to argue that the mystery volcano erupting in 1345 may have set off a chain of events that ultimately killed tens of millions of people.
Iceland’s toxic fogs
Connecting volcanoes to human events may be a challenge even today, but in 1784 an American ambassador to France named Benjamin Franklin was astute enough to link a strange haze that rolled across the countryside in the previous year to a distant eruption.
The source turns out to be Laki, an Icelandic fissure that spewed lava for eight months starting in June 1783. The eruption killed at least one-fifth of Iceland’s people, and much of its livestock, through toxic fog and climate changes that ruined harvests. Though the event was well-documented in Iceland, observers in England, France and elsewhere across Europe who saw the volcano’s haze and sometimes smelled its foul odor could only guess what was going on in a disconnected, pre-electronic world.
“They wouldn’t get news alerts on their phone, they wouldn’t see livestreams of this eruption — they would have no idea,” says Kleemann, who has studied the eruption.
Connections grow clearer
Though it happened just a few decades after Laki, one of the largest eruptions in recorded human history offers a much more detailed picture of how a volcanic climate shock can change history. In 1815, a mountain in Indonesia named Tambora exploded, sending sulfur into the upper atmosphere and triggering broad climatic changes.
Tambora’s eruption caused cooling across much of Europe and North America, where crops failed and 1816 was dubbed the “year without a summer.” The volcanic weather that year kept the writer Mary Shelley cooped up while traveling in Switzerland, where she wrote the novel Frankenstein.
The bad weather brought famine to Switzerland, Ireland, and elsewhere; grain prices and malnutrition soared in parts of Europe, prompting tens of thousands of people to emigrate to North America. Eastern Europe and western Russia, in contrast, had relatively better growing conditions under the post-volcanic climate and enough grain to export it to other nations. Port cities like London and Hamburg enjoyed greater access to imported grains, while prices rose sharply in the hinterlands. Those bright spots show how access to transportation and trade networks can make societies more resilient in the face of disaster.
“Human society has a lot of susceptibilities and vulnerabilities,” says Clive Oppenheimer, a volcanologist at the University of Cambridge who coauthored a 2026 Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences paper on volcanoes, climate and society with Büntgen. “Some climate shocks will come and go…. At other times, the climate shock will come … when there are greater societal vulnerabilities.”
These lessons may hold particular relevance today, because researchers see the historical fallout of past eruptions as a clue to how humanity might respond to present-day climate change. Big volcanic eruptions cool the planet rather than warm it, but they represent the same sort of rapid planetwide shocks that societies are coping with now as Earth heats up.
And as historical volcanology teaches, it is only a matter of time before the next big blast. In the era of satellites and social media saturation, the whole world will know the moment it happens—but it is only by studying past events like Krakatau and Tambora that we can have an idea of what will happen next.
