If there’s one thing young moviegoers seem to fear these days, it’s the idea of the in-between. The term liminal horror has gone from niche internet speak to Hollywood trend, thanks to the acclaimed TV show Severance and the recent smash-hit movie Backrooms. Stories like these mine the unsettling feeling of nondescript office corridors and basement halls that seem to self-replicate into infinity; this spring also saw the U.S. release of the excellent Japanese film Exit 8, a video-game adaptation about someone getting trapped in a subway station with seemingly no way out. Now there’s It Ends, a low-budget bit of creepy cleverness with a punchy pitch: What if you got lost driving down a road that never ends?
That this type of premise has grown more commonplace makes sense. Such a film typically needs only one set (for example, a long, lonely road, flanked by trees), a small cast of characters, and a spare, intentionally circular script. It Ends uses that scrappy charm to its advantage, the lack of frills dialing up a sense of realism. The film, written and directed by the newcomer Alexander Ullom, follows James (played by Phinehas Yoon), Day (Akira Jackson), Fisher (Noah Toth), and Tyler (Mitchell Cole), four friends who are headed on a celebratory graduation road trip. Their drive is occupied by the sort of nonsensical, wandering conversations young people love to have; there’s no real sign of anything being wrong until Tyler notices that he’s missed his turn.
The horror builds gradually, spikes, then slows to an existentially brutal crawl. The group realizes that there’s no way off the road, but when they get out of the car to look around, swarms of people emerge from the woods and fight to enter their vehicle. As the friends continue on in search of safety, they notice that the gas tank never goes empty, they never feel hungry, and nobody needs to sleep. They’re in a sort of limbo, condemned to keep moving despite having no destination. It’s essentially a Gen Z take on Sartre’s No Exit, a gentle riff on hell being other people, with a few jump scares tossed in for fun.
But while prior small-scale horror movies such as The Blair Witch Project and Paranormal Activity had an unseen villain guiding the scares, It Ends thrives on an utter lack of information about what is happening and why. The terror of liminality is how effortlessly it evokes the creepiness of a bad dream, the kind that begins in the middle of the story and seems just off. There’s no monster around the corner, no demonic puzzle to be solved. The characters of It Ends initially debate what’s going on, keeping track of patterns occurring around them in search of some explanation. While James keeps doing so as a way of staying sane, the others start to accept their frozen existence; the strangers in the woods, it seems, are also confined to the road’s environs.
That Ullom manages to squeeze a feature-length movie out of such a mundane premise is impressive; it helps that his cast is charming enough to carry it off. As the film plods on, it starts to skip further and further ahead in time, warping the viewer’s sense of chronology. It Ends is more aggressively aimless than other recent entries in the genre: Exit 8 sees its heroes try to figure a way out of their infinite subway station (it was based on a video game, so some resolution is built into the plot); the protagonists of Backrooms discovered a world of non-Euclidean corridors and lobbies in a basement, then found out that opportunistic corporate villains were plundering it; such a revelation hints at sequels that could expand its lore.
The simplicity of It Ends, by comparison, is wonderful and jarring, as is the total inability for future properties to spill out of it. Part of the dread that liminal horror mines is the drudgery of the never-ending scroll, a familiar feeling for anyone who’s been on social media; no matter how much you look, you’ll never hit bottom, only summon more of whatever the algorithm wants to serve you. It Ends is set entirely outdoors but captures that same fear of being stuck without any touchstones to distinguish simulation from reality.

A post is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) claiming that US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and that the US was in talks to adopt India’s EVM system for the 2028 election. It further claims that Trump praised India’s EVMs as secure and called for an end to mail-in voting. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
Fact: The viral post is fabricated. In his original post, Trump mentioned CEC Gyanesh Kumar’s interaction with the US administration and praised India’s voter ID system while urging Congress to pass the SAVE America Act. However, he did not say that the US was in talks to bring India’s EVM system to America for the 2028 election. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports or official information confirming that US President Donald Trump said the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
We then reviewed the social media accounts (here, here, and here) of US President Donald Trump to check whether he had made the statement mentioned in the viral post. However, we found no post from Trump stating that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
During this process, we found a Truth Social post (archived) by Trump dated 18 August 2026. In the post, Trump stated that earlier that month, India’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar had asked his administration how the US could conduct elections without valid photo ID. Trump also referred to India’s last election, which had 646 million voters, noting that less than 1% voted by mail and that every voter had to provide a valid photo identity document. He concluded by calling for the passage of the SAVE America Act.
The post was also reposted (archived) by US Ambassador to India and Special Envoy to South and Central Asia Sergio Gor on the same day, stating, “President Donald J. Trump is absolutely correct! 646 MILLION voters, every single one, required an ID in India’s last election. Congress should pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT.” This further confirms that the viral post claiming Trump discussed bringing India’s EVMs to the US is fabricated.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) about Trump’s post, in which the US President praised India’s election system and called for the passage of the SAVE America Act, referring to the conversation with CEC Gyanesh Kumar. However, none of these reports mentioned that the US is in talks with India to bring its EVM system to America for the 2028 election.
The SAVE America Act (H.R. 7296), or the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act, is a proposed US federal law that would require people registering to vote in federal elections to provide documentary proof of US citizenship and require voters to present an eligible photo ID when voting. The bill was introduced in the US House of Representatives on 30 January 2026 and referred to the House Committee on House Administration. As of 20 August 2026, it has not (here, here) become law. The legislation concerns voter eligibility and identification and has no provisions related to adopting or importing India’s EVM system.
To sum up, this viral post alleging that President Donald Trump said the US plans to bring India’s EVMs for the 2028 election is fabricated.

It was meant to be an outing for Black children in Berlin and their families, offering them an exclusive afternoon at an outdoor pool set up by a local theatre.
But the plans, slated for earlier this month, had to be scrapped after they were seized on by rightwing and conservative voices to whip up outrage, leaving organisers fending off racist emails and threats.
Berlin’s Volksbühne theatre said it had extended the invitation in hopes of dismantling some of the barriers that would normally keep these children away from the pool. While other groups had similarly been invited to use pool exclusively without incident, the idea of Black children enjoying a private afternoon at a public pool proved to be controversial among some.
“Berlin is a livable, diverse, colourful and free city. So why do we need safe spaces?” a local Christian Democrat politician, Aileen Weibeler, said on social media, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland co-leader Alice Weidel described it as “an apartheid” in which “white people are temporarily denied access”.
It was the latest in a long list of incidents linking swimming pools to racism. Across North America and Europe swimming pools have often acted as a flashpoint for wider racial tensions and exclusions.
Earlier this summer, an open-air swimming lake in the eastern German city of Halle made headlines after it refused entry to bathers who did not speak German. In the Netherlands, the Institute for Human Rights recently ruled against a pool after it was found to have singled out a Black child for an identity check.
The list of incidents spans decades. In 2013, the Swiss town of Bremgarten moved to restrict asylum seekers’ access to swimming pools. In Bulgaria, Roma have sounded the alarm about being discriminated against at public pools, while in 2022, a swimming pool in Romania was fined just over €2,000 (£1,716) for barring entry to Romani children.
Some of the association between racism and pools most likely comes down to the intimacy of these spaces, said Jeff Wiltse, the author of Contested Waters: A Social History of Swimming Pools in America. “They’re visually, physically, and socially intimate spaces, and I think that continues to pique people’s social anxieties,” he said.
Wiltse has long studied pools in the US, recasting them as sites that reflect the wider tensions in society at any given time, from James Brock in 1964 pouring hydrochloric acid into a whites-only pool where Black men were swimming, to the Texas police officer who in 2015 pinned an unarmed Black teenager to the ground and drew his gun as he sought to break up a pool party.
In the US, “throughout much of the 20th century, swimming pools were homogenous spaces”, he said. “There was explicit racial segregation of public pools.”
In the late 1940s, as public swimming pools in the US began to be racially desegregated, private pools began to spring up, particularly in suburbs that were almost exclusively white. Many people came to see swimming pools as “a certain type of social space in which the people there are all socially similar”, said Wiltse, who advocates tackling the issue by increasing public investment in community pools that could bring together people from different ethnic and racial backgrounds.
The racialised history of pools – and its continued legacy today – has helped to give rise to a stark racial divide when it comes to swimming ability, one that has had deadly consequences. In the US, the fatal-drowning rate of Black and African American children is three times higher than that of white children.
The statistics are even worse in England, where recent data found that children from Black, Asian and minority ethnic communities are 3.5 times more likely to drown than their white counterparts. Recent figures from Sport England suggest that 95% of Black adults and 80% of Black children do not swim at all.
In 2022, Katrice Rodrigues set out to change this with the launch of Unity Swimming, a community organisation that runs weekly classes aimed at Black and Asian communities.
“People get angry at that, saying: ‘How can it be inclusive if it’s just for Black and Asian communities?’” said Rodrigues, who is also a keynote speaker on diversity in aquatics. “My thing is that we’re making the whole of swimming more inclusive by creating these safe little spaces, which lead to more people swimming, and that makes swimming, as a whole, more inclusive.”
The success of the programme has relied on Rodrigues and her team confronting the wide range of cultural barriers that keep minorities out of the pool, from having parents who are terrified of water to concerns over feeling out of place, dressing modestly or protecting Black hair.
Other barriers have proven more enduring. “There’s a myth and a stereotype that Black people can’t float and can’t swim,” she said. “It’s not true, but I’ve had to correct two experienced swim teachers who thought that was a thing.”
As summers become hotter across the globe, sending more people into rivers, lakes and pools in search of respite, the imperative has grown to ensure that as many people as possible know how to swim, said Rodrigues.
“It’s the only sport that’s going to save lives,” she said. “If you’ve got water safety knowledge, you could help save someone else’s life as well as your own and your whole family. So this has a knock-off effect on families, on communities and for generations.”

Seven people, including five Americans, were killed when a safari helicopter crashed on Wednesday morning in a remote part of northern Kenya, according to local police and the state department.
Among the dead were an executive with Telemundo, the US-based Spanish-language network owned by NBC Universal, and the director of Ecuador’s national intelligence service.
The helicopter crashed at 9.13am while flying from the Loisaba Conservancy to the Ewaso Nyiro area in Samburu county, according to the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, which said in a statement that an investigation was under way. It said there were seven people onboard – six passengers and the pilot.
Late on Wednesday, David Nkoroi, the police commander for Samburu, told reporters that all seven people onboard had died.
In Washington, the state department said five of those killed were US citizens. “The US embassy is in touch with local authorities and is providing consular assistance,” it said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones on their loss.”
The identities of the victims were not revealed but a local television station in Miami, Florida, said that José Suárez, 55, president and GM of several Telemundo stations in Florida, was among those killed.
“We are heartbroken to learn the tragic news that José was killed in a helicopter accident in Kenya,” the NBC affiliate in Miami quoted from a joint statement from NBC Universal and Telemundo leadership.
The helicopter crashed in a rugged area in the foothills of Mount Ololokwe, a popular tourist destination in the country, local media reported. The helicopter, owned by local company Lady Lori Helicopters, was carrying guests with the travel company +Beyond.
Lady Lori Helicopters said in a statement that the aircraft was operating a charter flight when it crashed.
Tropic Air Kenya, a local safari operator, said in a statement that it dispatched two of its helicopters to aid search and rescue operations.
The aviation authority said the aircraft was a Eurocopter EC130 B4.
Ecuador confirmed later on Wednesday that Michele Sensi-Contugi, director of the country’s national intelligence center, died in the helicopter crash in Kenya.
In a statement posted on X, the presidency said: “In this moment of deep sorrow, the government extends its heartfelt condolences to his family, loved ones and close associates.”
Sensi-Contugi was visiting Kenya as a tourist with his wife, Stephany Hollihan Vasconez, who also died in the crash. She was a US and Ecuadorian citizen. They are survived by their two children.
Helicopter crashes have happened with increasing regularity in Kenya, which has a thriving tourism industry that depends on domestic carriers to ferry visitors to distant places like Mount Ololokwe.
In February, a legislator was among six people who died after a helicopter crash in a hilly area of western Kenya.

Shigellosis has surfaced again in Keralam, with a three-year-old child from Kottukal in Thiruvananthapuram district admitted to SAT Hospital with the infection.
Following this, health officials have renewed public health warnings, urging people to be cautious about the food and beverages they consume outside their homes, especially during the festival season.
According to reports, the child had travelled with her family to Nagercoil on August 12. On the way, they reportedly consumed cold drinks from a wayside vendor. The child developed diarrhoea and vomiting the following day and was later admitted to SAT hospital, where she is now recuperating in one of the paediatric wards. The case was confirmed on Tuesday (August 18, 2026).
One more case of shigellosis was also reported from Vizhinjam in Thiruvananthapuram on Tuesday; and three scattered cases from Pazhayannur in Thrissur; Kattipara in Kozhikode and Noolpuzha in Wayanad.
Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) is a highly contagious bacterial diarrhoeal infection caused by shigella, which is contracted through contaminated food or water. The disease can present with mild symptoms or as severe cases of diarrhoea.
Health officials point out that cases of shigellosis are reported sporadically throughout the year from all districts in Keralam, with some cases triggering small local outbreaks.
The infection spreads through contaminated water, food and contact from infected surfaces.
While shigellosis is self-limiting in healthy adults, it can be fatal for children under five years, in whom the highest mortality is reported. The elderly and immunocompromised individuals are also highly vulnerable.
Symptoms usually appear within one to two days of infection and include fever, diarrhoea, vomiting, nausea, blood in stools, and painful, frequent urges to use the washroom.
The Health department has advised that affected persons use solutions of oral rehydration salts so that dehydration is avoided and that they seek treatment if there is no respite in diarrhoea.
It was in June this year (2026) that Keralam reported major Shigellosis outbreaks, with over 225 cases and six deaths reported from Kozhikode, Malappuram, and Wayanad districts. Outbreaks were officially declared in Kozhikode (77 cases), Wayanad (27), Malappuram (37), Thrissur (15), and Alappuzha (5). Cases were also reported from Thiruvananthapuram (20), Kollam (15), Kannur (14), Palakkad (6), Ernakulam (4), Idukki (3), and Pathanamthitta (1) during June and July.
As of August 18 this year, as many as 441 confirmed cases, 106 probable cases and eight deaths due to Shigellosis have been reported in the State. Last year, a total of 133 cases were reported, with zero deaths.

'Up front next week?' Guehi proves Maresca's midfield masterstroke

Enzo Maresca might have been expected to keep his head down and not make any curious team selections in his first Premier League game in-charge of Manchester City. Instead, he made the surprising decision to field Marc Guehi in a holding role and, eventually, it turned into a midfield masterstroke.
All the heat prior to kick-off had been on rivals Manchester United and free-spending Tottenham following their demoralising opening game defeats but for 84 minutes on Sunday, that unwanted focus looked set to shift to Etihad Stadium.
City had suffered a chastening 3-0 defeat by champions Arsenal in the Community Shield last Sunday and were heading towards back-to-back defeats to start the season.
But a late rescue act courtesy of a towering header from Guehi - who all the attention was on - and Josko Gvardiol's cool finish salvaged an unlikely comeback victory against Bournemouth.
Eyebrows were raised before kick-off when Maresca decided to fielded a team consisting of six players that can play as defenders, but the serious questions cropped up during the warm-up.
With the back four going through their routines with a City coach, it appeared England centre-back Guehi would be deployed as holding midfielder. When referee Jarred Gillett blew his whistle to start proceedings, it became clear that this was the reality.
But instead of the story being about Guehi being played out of position, the former Crystal Palace skipper scored to help switch the narrative to it being an Ingenious move from the new manager.
Pundits and supporters were taken aback by the switch in position and so too was the player himself.
Guehi told Sky Sports: "It was just an idea the manager had, we worked on it in the week. We're trying different things, trying different solutions for the team.
"I'm glad today it paid off in the end."
He also told BBC Sport he had not played in midfield too often, adding: "I enjoyed it simply because I got so much help from so many people. When you have that you feel comfortable to just go out and play and do what you can for the team."
Boss Maresca told BBC Match of the Day: "Marc Guehi has never played as a midfielder, today he was very good, so I am happy with the effort from the players.
"Sometimes you visualise things. I know Marc from Palace and I always thought he could play as a midfielder because he is very good. So we tried it for a few days and I think he was quite good."
City 'completely changed' but still 'expected to win'
The Guehi experiment may end up being a long-term fix with Maresca saying afterwards he provides "a solution" in the middle of the park.
Maresca had started Mateo Kovacic on the bench, so was the Italian boss sending some sort of message to those in the corridors of power at City?
The former Chelsea manager replaced the legendary Pep Guardiola in the summer and has not hidden his desire for the club to bring in new signings before the end of the transfer window on 1 September.
But just 50 minutes before kick-off BBC Sport reported that City had agreed an £86m fee to sign midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille - Maresca said he had no idea about the deal as he has not yet spoken to the decision-makers
At the tender age of just 18, the Moroccan sensation has a massive price tag on his head and has huge boots to fill at City following the departure of 2024 Ballon d'Or winner Rodri to Barcelona, as well as Tijjani Reijnders heading off to Saudi Arabia.
Bouaddi will play in the pivot alongside club-record signing Elliot Anderson, who played an hour on his Premier League debut for City, and showed glimpses of what he will bring to the side, covering plenty of ground and often snuffing out the danger.
But Sunday's surprise midfield partner Guehi showcased his versatility by scoring the 10th Premier League goal of his career with an 84th minute header.
Overall, Guehi won all three of his tackles - more than any other player on the pitch - while also managing a 94.9% pass completion from 59 attempts and winning eight of his 11 duels.
Asked where he will play next week, Guehi jested: "Who knows? Maybe up front. We'll see."
Former City goalkeeper Joe Hart added: "I think City look OK. It's obviously interesting when they have had such settled world class players that they have almost mixed and matched.
"Anderson and Guehi is an interesting one in midfield but that won't be a long-term thing, especially with Bouaddi coming in. I think with people coming back late from the World Cup, Maresca is just trying out things in-season, in-game.
"That's just where Manchester City are at the moment, they've completely changed everything about themselves but they're still expected to win."

Break-up of Villa's Europa heroes leaves cracks for Emery to fill
- Published
Aston Villa's European heroes are already part of history.
They ended a 30-year wait for a trophy by lifting the Europa League in May against Freiburg but the club could have sold six of the starting XI by the end of the transfer window.
Ezri Konsa's imminent £51m departure to Arsenal is the latest high-profile exit at Villa Park this summer as Unai Emery's squad undergoes drastic change.
Istanbul goalscorers Youri Tielemans and Morgan Rogers left last month, Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea a record for an English player.
Lucas Digne was sold to Paris St-Germain and Villa must also find a solution for goalkeeper Emi Martinez after his failed move to Juventus and the signing of his replacement - Zion Suzuki.
Al-Hilal may also test Villa's resolve again before the 1 September transfer deadline for Ollie Watkins, with the Premier League club reportedly tabling a new contract to try to keep the striker.
That would leave Matty Cash, Pau Torres, Victor Lindelof, John McGinn and Emi Buendia as those who remain from the 11 that started in Istanbul.
- Villa £18m bid for Harwood-Bellis rejected by Southampton 
  - Published10 hours ago
- When is the Champions League draw and who is in each pot? 
  - Published22 hours ago
Why are Villa a selling club?
Like many, Villa are a selling club, mainly due to necessity, and have been for a number of years.
They must comply with Uefa's squad cost ratio (SCR) which restricts them to spending 70% of their football related revenue on player and staff wages, transfer fees and agent fees.
They have already been fined twice by Uefa for breaches, being hit with a £9.5m sanction last year and a £19.4m fine in June, although £12.9m was suspended after Villa came to a settlement agreement with Europe's governing body. But it has meant the club's hands are tied in the transfer window.
The Premier League's Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) also limited financial losses to a maximum of £105 million over a rolling three-year period.
In their latest accounts, ending 30 June 2025, Villa had a post-tax profit of £17m but their two previous years showed losses of £119.6m (2023) and £85.4m (2024).
The regulations have now been replaced by SCR, which sees the Premier League fall in line with Uefa's model
"It's necessity because of the rules," one former Villa executive told BBC Sport, when asked about the sales. "The PSR, the SCR, issues are well documented.
"It does seem slightly unfair they're having their ambition capped at this level. But it has forced this very big churn of players, which is unfortunate.
"Some will be forced due to PSR, some will be player demand. Combined it makes a big problem for Emery and certainly it is a lot to swallow in one go and to try and replace. "
This summer has crystalised their situation further because of the high profile nature of the departures.
Villa had raised just over £200m with the sales of Jhon Duran (£71m), Douglas Luiz (£42.5m), Jacob Ramsey (£40m) and Moussa Diaby (£50m) over the past two years.
This window will see them bank, once the Konsa deal goes through, around £212m, including £9m for Lewis Dobbin who never played a senior game for Villa before leaving for Southampton.
The academy has also paid its way comfortably with Jaden Philogene and Cameron Archer being bought back to be sold again, while Burnley spent £12m on Aaron Ramsey in 2023.
Internally, when Villa first returned to the Champions League in 2024, it was recognised it would be harder for academy prospects to break into the squad which left Villa more open to selling them.
Last summer their gross transfer spend was £71m which was dwarfed by Manchester, City, Chelsea and Arsenal who were all over £200m while Wolves, who finished bottom last season, were £109m.
It justifies Emery's argument Villa are not part of the elite, especially when they spent months working on a deal for Conor Gallagher only for Tottenham to be the ones to step in and buy him in January.
Rogers' £117m move to Chelsea this summer was the easiest way for Villa to comply with Uefa's financial rules.
The plan came after their first fine last year and under it they must break even in 2026-27.
Their run to the Champions League quarter-finals in 2024-25 banked them close to £70m and the main reason they managed to turn a profit in the latest accounts.
Winning the Europa League means Villa guaranteed themselves around £45.6m, which includes the minimum earned for qualifying for next season's Champions League.
Despite the departures optimism remains. Last week's battling Super Cup defeat in Salzbug to Paris St-Germain still showed Villa's competitiveness and Emery's powers of adaptability.
Emery has constantly needed to roll with the punches during his three-and-a-half years in charge but he has consistently improved Villa, having taken over when they were 14th following Steven Gerrard's reign.
In Austria, skipper John McGinn pointed to the fact they still have Emery while others - Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea - have new managers and that Villa's structure remains intact.
"We have a structure in place, standards and rules which have made us a success. I am really excited about the new Aston Villa," said McGinn.
That includes Brian Madjo after Villa won their battle with Fifa to register the 17-year-old earlier this month.
The striker scored on his debut against PSG, eight months after initially signing from Metz for £10m, and could prove one of the surprises of the season.
The drive towards younger players comes after Roberto Olabe replaced Monchi last September as president of football operations with a long-to-mid term directive on transfers.
Midfielder Joao Gomes, 25, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki, 23 and defender Matteo Ruggeri, 24, have joined this summer after 20-year-old Johan Manzambi became the club's record buy in July.
They have also had an £18m bid rejected for 24-year-old Southampton defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis.
The loan signing, with an obligation to buy, of Alejandro Garnacho from Chelsea allows Villa to spread the cost while Aaron Wan-Bissaka is due to move from West Ham on a similar deal.
"The problem is they may now be at the end of a chain of transfer deals, with the players involved and their transfer targets dependent on other moves happening first," said the former Villa decision-maker.
Above all, though, Emery remains Villa's biggest asset and he has overhauled them before. This time it would be one of his biggest achievements.
"There's a lot of hope and ambition resting with the manager," said the ex-Villa Park executive.
"He's the ace card they've got left and everybody's hoping with his experience and knowledge they can pull through.
"It's a lot of pressure on him and you've got to wonder if he's trying to think 'maybe I need to go somewhere else with more resources?'
"I don't think it'll be this season but, at some stage as a manager, you get fed up juggling all those demands."

'Ghana was the crime scene': The country leading the demand for slavery reparations
- Published
This year has seen a dramatic change in tone in the global conversation about the transatlantic slave trade.
The demand for formal apologies, debt relief and financial compensation from nations and institutions that benefited from slavery has become increasingly forceful.
In March, a resolution was passed at the United Nations recognising slavery as "the greatest crime against humanity" - though the United States voted against the resolution and every European nation abstained from the vote.
The UK, which alongside Portugal dominated the transatlantic slave trade, has consistently rejected the idea of paying reparations, which is perhaps unsurprising given estimates of what Britain "owes" in damages to nations affected run into many trillions of pounds.
This resistance has not deterred the country that has become the leading voice on reparations: Ghana.
Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable"
It was Ghana that tabled the UN resolution, and in June, a summit on reparations was held in its capital, Accra, with delegates from around 80 countries, who concluded that recompense was long overdue.
"Ghana has always been a pan-African leader. We're the first country to attain independence in sub-Saharan Africa and to prove that it is possible to fight imperial might, and win," Foreign Minister Samuel Okuzeto Ablakwa tells me.
Ghana has been given special responsibility by the African Union to be "champion for reparatory justice" and it is clearly a role the country's political leadership is taking seriously.
In part that is because about 10-15% of the estimated 12 million Africans who were forcibly removed from their homes, torn from their villages, and dehumanised on a scale never before seen, were from what is now Ghana. Even more were shipped from its shores.
"Ghana was the crime scene where these atrocities took place, so Ghana cannot afford to be silent on ensuring that we hold perpetrators accountable," Ablakwa says.
The minister has called for a system of reparatory justice that funds educational grants, venture capital for young African entrepreneurs and research into enduring health issues that some argue may trace their roots back to the severe malnutrition and inhumane conditions of enslavement.
And though he insists that this is not about direct financial gain for African leaders, one of the demands laid out at the recent summit on reparations clearly talked of debt relief and debt cancellation.
He also wants individual institutions that benefited from the slave trade to be held accountable and pay compensation. Among these is the Church of England.
In the 18th Century, the Church's missionary wing ran plantations and owned hundreds of slaves, which helped fund its work across the Americas and beyond.
Many Church of England clergy independently owned slaves, and a recent report by the Church's endowment fund reported the institution made large investments in the slave trade from which it made huge sums of money.
In July, the leader of the Church, the Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally, visited Ghana in one of her first international visits in the role.
She travelled to Cape Coast Castle, one of the many coastal fortresses that had been run by the British, and where enslaved people were held before enduring the brutal "Middle Passage" to the Americas.
As she toured the dungeons where slaves were held and walked through "the door of no return" through which they were forced before being loaded on to ships, Dame Sarah looked emotional and stopped to pray.
"I felt the weight of the depth of evil that the transatlantic slave trade was. You can't help but be deeply moved by the horrific conditions that people were kept in," the Archbishop said.
She also prayed in a 17th Century chapel that was positioned directly above the dungeons.
"For me that is such a stark illustration of the way the Church was involved in the slave trade," she says. "How can the church have sat above the horrors that were going on below?".
"The Church of England has apologised for the part that we played in the transatlantic slave trade but we've also said there needs to be action that relates to that," Archbishop Sarah said.
The Church has set up a £100m ($135m) social impact fund designed to benefit communities thought to continue to feel the enduring legacy of the slave trade today.
But within the Church, the establishment of the fund has encountered resistance, just as the global push for nations to pay reparations has done.
One of the key counter-arguments centres on the fact that some Africans were themselves complicit in the capture and sale of their fellow people.
But Foreign Minister Ablakwa emphatically rejects this narrative. "I think that there's a strategy to divide and conquer and to create a very contrived confusion," he argues.
He stresses that the entire architecture of chattel enslavement was curated by Western slave-owning powers, who simply utilised local actors to help carry out their plans.
The foreign minister points out that when the laws, insurance policies, and financial architectures of the trade were being drafted, "there was no African at the table".
"We denounce and totally reject those claims that Africans are as guilty and complicit as those who masterminded this whole atrocity," he says.
Yet, within Ghana itself, the conversation around African complicity is far more nuanced, and for some traditional leaders, acknowledging the past is a vital prerequisite part of healing.
King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, the Ga Mantse, leader of Ghana's Ga people, recently took the step of publicly apologising for his ancestors' involvement in the slave trade.
"I think that the transatlantic slave trade was the greatest crime against humanity, and ancestors also took part as players in that trade," says the king.
The Ga people became middlemen who traded with Europeans. They sold gold, ivory and ultimately enslaved Africans, often those captured in local conflicts, in exchange for the manufactured goods brought mainly by the British and Dutch, including textiles, alcohol and guns.
But the king felt he needed to say sorry not just for his own people's complicity, but the complicity of other Africans too.
"I stand on the same point of apologising on behalf of all traditional authorities and my ancestors and forebears for the part they also played in the slavery of our brothers and sisters.
"It has affected lives and societies up to now, and to be able to go forward, you have to look at your past. It dawns on us to admit our fault and correct it," he says.
The king believes strongly in the need for those who benefited from the slave trade to pay reparations and acknowledges that he, too, needs to commit to making financial amends.
"I believe that it underpins a state of moral courage and credibility."
For the Ga Mantse, admitting fault does not dilute the guilt of European empires; rather, it solidifies Africa's moral standing and sets an example as to how to move forward.
But Ghana is leading the way in another aspect of trying to heal the damage done by the slave trade. The country has run a high-profile campaign inviting the African diaspora - particularly African-Americans - to visit the continent.
It has been promoted as a means of bringing people together in the shared story of their traumatic past, with "reparations" quite literally focussing on "repair" at a very human level.
Yaw Asare, now a Ghanaian PhD student at Howard University, previously worked within the President of Ghana's Diaspora Office, which ran the campaign.
Initially, the gathering of black people from across the globe was, he felt, "a beautiful, profound experience devoid of capitalist motives". But he says in some respects the initiative soon morphed.
"The Ghana Tourism Authority also latched on to it and then used it to enhance their tourism project," Asare explains, saying the initiative started to become less about "repair" and more about hitting tourism quotas.
Asare says the campaign has often viewed the returning diaspora simply as a means of foreign cash flow, raising prices and negatively altering local economies.
"Now (local) people are finding that they cannot afford basic things," Asare says, describing how local Ghanaians were economically sidelined.
More devastatingly, he feels the commercialisation of the initiative overshadowed the deep, psychological work that is desperately needed for locals as well as "returning" members of the diaspora.
"We are dealing with humans, we are dealing with people. We cannot reduce them to, 'come see this site, pay this entrance fee'," Asare says.
He also questions - in an initiative that was partly supposed to be about addressing the trauma of Africans in the diaspora - why they were required to pay entrance fees at the same rates as European tourists at, for example, the coastal castles where slaves were trafficked.
He says all of this means a missed opportunity to address deep-rooted trauma some of which he feels is etched into the very geography and psychology of modern Ghana.
"Go to Jamestown (in Accra), people are huddled together because there is the fear of 'if I live far away, I could be taken'," Asare says, pointing to how centuries-old concerns dictated why people built their houses so closely together.
Jamestown is one of the oldest districts in the city, a community originally built around a British coastal fort where slaves were brought, traded and then sent on ships to the Americas.
For Asare, true reparatory justice must prioritise human connection and healing over financial transactions.
"We have to remove the band-aid and then look at the sore, the gaping wound that's present," Asare says about what he sees as real "reparations". "And see how we can dress it and nurse it and heal".

Nanda Malini, one of Sri Lanka's best known voices of protest, dies at 82
- Published
Nanda Malini, a famed Sri Lankan singer whose voice was seen as a soundtrack to some of the country's political and social upheavals, has died at 82.
Songs from her album Pawana, which touched on social issues and urged people to stand up to injustice, were banned from national airwaves in the 1980s, during a particularly turbulent period of Sri Lankan history.
Her political advocacy continued well after those years, and today Malini is remembered as one of the most prominent figures of the Sinhala music industry.
She died at her home in Nawala, just a few days shy of her 83rd birthday.
Born on 23 August, 1943, in a village in Kalutara, Malini was the fourth in a family of nine children.
She went to school in the capital Colombo, where she won a poetry singing competition in 1956, which was seen as the start of her music career.
In the 70s and 80s Malini became known for her songs about social justice, from satirical lyrics about corruption to rallying calls for Sri Lankans to look past racial and religious divides and stand up against tyranny.
Sri Lanka at the time was undergoing a period of upheaval, as Leftist activists spearheaded an anti-establishment movement, airing frustrations against youth unemployment, social inequality and the elite class.
It was also a time of ethnic tensions, which culminated in the eruption of civil war in the 1983.
Authorities at the time banned Malini's songs from being played by national broadcasters - though that did not stop fans from listening to the tracks and attending her concerts.
Her 1987 album, Pawana, which contained songs about human rights and state oppression, is remembered today as the defining music of those turbulent years.
Her advocacy continued even as the country's political landscape transformed over the decades.
In 2022, as the country saw large-scale anti-government protests amid a spiralling economic crisis, Malini was a vocal supporter of the movement and performed to a gathering of demonstrators.
The months of protests led to the toppling of President Gotabaya Rajapaksa.
The Sri Lanka government has declared a three-day mourning period for Malini, as tributes poured in for the veteran singer.
In a statement on social media, Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake said he was "deeply saddened" by Malini's death and called her a "true musical legend of our time"
"Her timeless music inspired generations of Sri Lankans, young and old alike," he wrote.

Is a liquid-cooled PC worth it?
Liquid-cooled systems look amazing, but come at a cost premium compared to air coolers.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
A liquid cooling system can be one of the star components of a custom-built gaming PC, but are they really worth the money? After all, they're usually a lot more expensive than traditional air coolers. AIO (all-in-one) liquid cooling systems often look flashy and can sometimes be tricky to install, but there's a reason they're all the rage with high-end PC builders.
Let's get into how liquid coolers work, the main differences between them and traditional heatsink models, and when it makes sense to opt for an AIO system over a tried-and-true air cooler.
Liquid CPU coolers vs. air coolers: The key differences
At their core, both liquid and air coolers perform the same function: they move heat away from a PC's CPU. Where they differ is in the methods used to transfer the heat. Air coolers use a heatsink and pipes to regulate a processor's temperature, whereas liquid systems use coolant. Air coolers are generally simpler in their makeup than AIO models, consisting of only a cold plate, pipes, a fan and a heatsink. Liquid coolers are a little more complicated, being composed of a plate, pump, tubing, coolant, a separate radiator and accompanying fans.
Liquid coolers are typically aimed at a different market than their air alternatives. AIO systems are good for high-end gaming PCs where 4K output at console-beating frame rates is the priority. Aiming for 120FPS gameplay in Ultra HD puts a lot of load on the CPU. To prevent overheating and thermal throttling, a liquid cooler with a large radiator dissipates heat more effectively than an air cooler. On the flipside, while air coolers aren't as well-suited for top-of-the-line gaming processors, they're ideal for budget or mid-range PCs where the CPU is less likely to be under constant heavy load.
How do liquid CPU coolers work?
A liquid cooler regulates the heat of a CPU by directing heat away from the processor via a water block, cooling pump and a radiator. When you install a CPU for the first time, you apply thermal paste to the top of the chip to help the cooler transfer heat more effectively. Once the paste has absorbed heat, it's passed onto the water block's copper plate, whereby the heat is transferred into liquid.
After this step, the cooler's pump directs this liquid towards the radiator, which is most commonly installed above a PC's motherboard. Once the liquid reaches the radiator, the heat from the coolant is dissipated by its fans, and the newly cooled liquid is then sent back to the water block in a cycle that constantly repeats whenever your PC is running.
Custom loop cooling systems work a little differently. Unlike an AIO unit where all the components come in the box, custom loops let you choose every part of the cooler (including the water block, radiator, tubing, fans and reservoir. The reservoir is what stores the system's coolant while also feeding the pump. If you like, you can also set up custom loops to cool more than just the CPU. With the right tweaks, you can integrate a GPU water block into a custom loop system to help regulate the temperature of your graphics card.
Should I go with a liquid cooler or an air cooler?
If you own one of the top gaming CPUs, like the AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, you should definitely go with a liquid cooler. I've had the aforementioned processor for a couple of years, and I'm glad I decided to pair it with the NZXT Kraken 360. This high-end 360mm AIO cooler offers comprehensive customization via the NZXT CAM app, allowing me to set precise performance targets while also providing an abundance of RGB lighting options.
The added thermal headroom a liquid cooler grants my custom-built PC allows me to run the best and most demanding PC titles at 4K/120FPS without ever having to worry about overheating. Top-tier liquid coolers like the Kraken 360 can also run at whisper-quiet levels, and they look so much sharper than the fan alternative. It's worth noting that cheaper liquid coolers can get a little noisy. In general, models with larger 280 and 360mm radiators can dissipate substantially more heat compared to air coolers, making them the go-to choice for cutting-edge PC builds.
Of course, there are downsides to going with a liquid cooler, though none of them should be considered deal-breakers. High-end models can cost upwards of $200, which is way more expensive than even the best air coolers. AIO models are also trickier to install, as you're not just dealing with the pump; you also need to secure the radiator inside your case. Maintenance is another issue. Whereas air coolers need very little tinkering after being installed, the pump of a liquid cooler will wear over time. There's also the (fairly low) possibility of leakage, which could damage other components inside your PC if it does occur.
Moving onto air coolers, they're the best bet for all but the most hardcore of PC players. Unless you're rocking a rig with an Intel Core i9-14900K and a Nvidia GeForce RTX 5090 (our review), you probably don't need a liquid cooler. If you're a casual Steam user with a mid-range system that houses a relatively modest CPU, an air cooler will work just fine. As they're cheaper, easier to install and have generally longer lifespans than AIO models, they're the ideal processor-cooling solution for folks who aren't obsessed with aesthetics. As long as you don't mind staring at a big heatsink if you have a case with a transparent window, air coolers are the most sensible option for the majority of PC gamers.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
Good morning. After the news about Moderna and Merck’s mRNA cancer vaccine came out yesterday, someone resurfaced a great Sharon Begley story on personalized cancer vaccines from early 2016. I recommend reading it if you’re interested in a primer on “turning your cancer against itself.”
Major cancer group cancels alcohol fundraiser
The American Cancer Society has canceled its upcoming Wine and Spirits Industry’s Gala, a spokesperson confirmed to STAT’s Isabella Cueto. The news came less than two months after Isa and our colleague Lev Facher reported that the group had for years raked in at least $22 million from wine and liquor executives, creating at times an unsettling conflict of interest given alcohol’s known links to cancer.
“Can you imagine the American Cancer Society hosting a tobacco industry gala? This is basically the same thing,” said public health professor Michael Siegel, who called the decision to cancel the gala a wise one. Read more from Isa.
Who is Heidi Overton?
While health secretary Robert F. Kenendy Jr. has been the public face of the MAHA movement and the Trump administration’s health care efforts, Heidi Overton has been the top policymaker behind the scenes, STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo and Daniel Payne report. Now, President Trump has nominated Overton to run the nation’s food and drug agency.
Overton has spent years as a Trump loyalist, having served in the first administration. Some industry leaders are worried about her close association with former director Marty Makary and the White House. On the other side, many MAHA activists are convinced Overton is to blame for stalled and slow-moving policy initiatives. So how might Overton fare at the FDA? Read more.
When hospital chatbots actually come in handy
Modern electronic health records are bloated. As health systems started experimenting with generative AI tools, the idea was that the technology could be used to find a needle in a haystack — the key piece of information, hidden in pages of records, that could explain a clinical mystery and potentially save a patient’s life. Today, a number of health systems are moving toward broad implementation of chatbots for EHRs. But as STAT’s Katie Palmer reports, it turns out that solving diagnostic mysteries is the least of their selling points.
The dominant application of AI chart summarization tools is decidedly less cinematic: Doctors are using them to save time as they prepare to see patients. Still, questions remain about how many errors are worth accepting in the name of efficiency, and ideally, the rare needle-in-a-haystack discovery. Read more from Katie on where things stand.
Inside a 5-year-old brain organoid
For years, scientists at Harvard rented space to the longest-living brain organoids on record. But they rarely actually studied them, as the longevity became an intimidation. “What if you make a mistake and the experiment doesn’t work and all of a sudden you cannot go back to a sample that is so unique?” Paola Arlotta, a developmental biologist in the lab, told STAT’s Megan Molteni.
Eventually, one junior scientist had the courage to analyze the specimens. A study published yesterday in Nature details what the team found. Over more than five years, the organoids had developed and matured in the same way that our own human brains do. Read more from Megan on the science and how it could be used.
Contrasting legal decisions on gender-affirming care
Last week, a federal appeals court ruled in favor of the Justice Department’s efforts to obtain gender-affirming care patient records from the telehealth company QueerDoc. While most judges have categorized such requests as overreaching or for an improper purpose, two out of three judges on the panel ruled that there was nothing out of line about the QueerDoc request. (Some legal experts believe that the case could be a candidate for en banc review, meaning the entire court would review the case again.)
The QueerDoc case was the first of many quashed requests to be appealed by federal law enforcement. But since oral arguments were made in March, the DOJ has taken a different approach to other subpoenas, concentrating its efforts in a Texas district court with a strong conservative reputation. At least one subsequent criminal subpoena, for records from NYU, has been temporarily blocked by a New York federal court.
Most recently, transgender patients and advocates logged a victory in court, as a district court struck down a Trump administration rule that attempted to exclude gender-affirming care from the “essential health benefits” that Affordable Care Act marketplace plans are required to cover. While only a handful of states explicitly include transgender health care in their list of essential benefits, the care is often covered as part of another protected category, like prescription drugs. The judges ruled that the administration did not use proper procedure to propose the change — an argument that probably won’t work against a similar rule barring Medicaid from covering the services.

Japanese power prices jumped to the highest in more than three years as hot weather boosted electricity demand and Middle East energy supply disruptions increased fuel costs.
The nationwide next-day power price rose 20% on Monday from the previous week to ￥25.18 ($0.16) a kilowatt-hour, the highest since January 2023, according to data from the Japan Electric Power Exchange.
The Japan Meteorological Agency issued a warning for unusually hot weather across the country from Wednesday. The regions around Tokyo and Kansai are predicted to see highs of 35 degrees Celsius Tuesday and Wednesday, according to the agency, while Nagasaki could see 37 C on Wednesday.
Spot prices for liquefied natural gas (LNG) in Asia are currently more than double levels from before the U.S. and Israel began attacks against Iran in late February. That’s boosted the cost of Japan’s biggest source of power.
Visible shipments of the super-chilled fuel through the Strait of Hormuz have been at a standstill since an Iranian attack on a Qatari-owned tanker in July. Washington’s vow to isolate Tehran economically has further dimmed prospects for a full reopening of the waterway, which carried about a fifth of the world’s LNG before the conflict.

Norwegian star actor Kristofer Hivju (“Game of Thrones,” “Red One”, “Beck”) will play opposite Friday Hallgren (from Oscar-nominated “As It Is in Heaven”) in the upcoming Swedish-Croatian rom-com “True Love” (working title).
Helmed by actor-turned writer, director and best-selling author Martina Haag, the SF Studios project, now in pre-production, will be pitched Aug. 26. at Haugesund’s Nordic Co-Production Market.
“True Love” marks Haag’s second collaboration with seasoned screenwriter Peter Arrhenius (“Clark,” “Welcome to Sweden,” “Beck”) after the seasoned actor’s directorial debut “Little Did I Know,” which landed a Best Film Award at the Monte-Carlo Television Festival in 2024 before turning into one of Sweden’s biggest box office draws of 2025.
Popular on Variety
As with ‘Little Did I know,” “True Love”’s starting point is deceit and divorce and how to bounce back when you’re over 50.
According to the logline, when Ellinor (played by Hallgren) is dumped by her husband after 20 years of marriage, she loses faith in life.
	When she wins €40 million ($46 million) immediately after, she finds it even harder to trust anyone. But then she meets Henrik (Hivju). The latter grew up at the elite Lundsberg boarding school, where his mother worked as a cleaner. To fit in, he learned to lie, and became an irresistibly charming master of deception. Their relationship should never work, but what if they’re exactly what the other needs?
“As both main characters are flawed and a bit extreme in the beginning of the film, it was important for us to find great actors that are warm and relatable: Real people in exaggerated situations, that we want to be with and see get better,” said Hivju and Hallgren Haag. 
	
They added: “Both Frida and Kristofer feel grounded and are capable of going from being extremely funny to super sensitive. And of course, the chemistry and dynamics between the actors is super important in a romantic comedy. If the spark isn’t there, it doesn’t matter how great the story is. We’re so happy to have Frida and Kristofer on board!”
Added SF Studios producer Helen Ahlsson: “Frida is a wonderfully warm and talented actress, and one audiences have taken to their hearts over the years. Kristofer has never really played a romantic lead before, which was perhaps a new challenge he was very keen to take on. In this film, you’ll discover a new Hivju like you’ve never seen before,” she enthusiastically shared with Variety.
Haag said catering for mature audiences came naturally. “I love stories about and for women – and men – over 50,” she said. “I really can’t understand why we don’t see more of them as a whole scope of relatable, life altering relationship questions appear after surviving Project Family and raising the kids. One being deceit and divorce – as in “Little Did I Know” – but also how to be able to trust and love again.”
“This story is about that,” she added. “Who we were, who we are, who we try to present ourself as, and who we really want to be. How can anyone dare to let their guard down and risk being hurt once again? We take that premise to the extreme in this film.”
Teaming up again with Arrhenius was a no-brainer.
“It is rare to find a writing partner that both has a skillset that completes your own and at the same time can respect and see your own strengths, like the yin and the yang,” she said, pointing out that “Peter is very interested in structure and serves up a lot of drastic jokes and situations, while I tend to focus on grounding these ideas in character and ”what would a real person do in this situation.”
“When that works, what you get is drastic, funny situations happening to characters that feels true. Real emotions without being kitchen-sink drama. We share that desire to both touch an audience, but in an entertaining way,” she observed.
Seasoned producer Ahlsson who’s worked mostly on dramas for film and TV – from Alicia Vikander’s Swedish debut “Pure” to Rojda Sekersöz’s upcoming “Will You Care if I Die” – said she couldn’t resist boarding her first rom-com after reading the script.
“It’s got the magic of British comedy hits such as “Bridget Jones’s Diary” or “Mamma Mia,” which balance believable, engaging characters with lightness, humor and emotions. It’s a tricky mix that you can’t take lightly,” she said.
Filming between Sweden-Stockholm, Dalecarlia-and Croatia is due to start Oct. 8, with delivery pencilled for fall 2027.
The feature is produced by Scandi giant SF Studios in co-production with Croatia’s Kinorama, SVT and NRK, with funding from the Swedish Film Institute, Film Stockholm, Film i Dalarna, and a Croatian tax rebate.
	Ahlsson said she will discuss global sales at the New Nordic Films market unspooling Aug. 25-28 at Haugesund, Norway.

(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Ramya Kannan writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
Did cataclysmic events happen over the week in healthcare - developments that made us sit up and take note, fume a little, wonder much and record everything? Bringing to you, five major themes that caught our attention this past week, and then, some more.
AI technology is forever invading our columns here, opening up the possibilities of what can happen in the future, and indeed, bringing the future to our door steps today. The last week, there was news about researchers using AI to design, hold your breath - viruses. A particular type of virus actually - a bacteriophage. Infectious Diseases specialist Dr. Abdul Ghafur explains what happens when AI begins to design pathogens. Referring to the Stanford experiment that produced the bacteriophages (bacteria- eating viruses), he explains: “It does not show that AI can casually manufacture dangerous human viruses; it shows that computers are beginning to move from analysing biological information towards proposing biological designs that scientists can physically build. This requires appropriate governance and safeguards.”
“The computer did not create a virus. It did not touch a test tube or handle a living cell. What it did may ultimately be more consequential: it helped decide what the virus’s genome should be,” he writes. Of the 285 AI-generated designs physically synthesised and tested in the laboratory, 16 produced functioning phages. Some were able to overcome bacterial resistance that defeated the original virus. What is new, is not the physical manufacture of a virus. AI has entered the design stage of biology. For medicine, that creates remarkable opportunities. For biosecurity, it raises equally important questions, he says.
Further, in the cardiac diseases sector, AI heart disease prediction tools show promise but are not ready for clinical use, Afshan Yasmeen writes, quoting a review. Published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, an open-access journal. The review assessed 30 studies published since 2017 on AI-based models developed to predict future cardiovascular disease among adults without established heart disease. Researchers say “Many models demonstrate good discrimination, but very few studies examine whether the predicted risks correspond to what actually happens in different populations.” For more on this, hit the link above.
From AI, to another cutting edge research segment - genetics. Dr. C. Aravinda and Dr. Veera Rajagopal step into that highly niche area and highly technical area: turning off genes. What we can learn from nature switching off human genes, they ask, based on a study from Pakistan.
Imagine the human genome as an enormous instruction book, they describe, containing the information needed to build, run and maintain the body. Its 23 pairs of chromosomes are like chapters, and the text is written in DNA, using an alphabet of just four chemical letters - A, T, G and C. Within this text, genes are individual instructions or recipes, each made from a particular sequence of these DNA letters. Proteins digest food, transport substances, build tissues, transmit signals and act as the antibodies that defend us against infection. Genetics studies how these instructions are inherited, altered and sometimes naturally switched off.
This is something you might want to read too, if genetics is what floats your boat. D.P. Kasbekar here, writes on how a Hyderabad scientist found out: Scientists find why a debilitating genetic disorder - FRDA - affects only Eurasians.
While at it, do check out this really interesting piece on What can genetics usefully do in your consultation room today? by Dr. Alok Kulkarni. “It can reduce blame. A mother did not cause schizophrenia by being ‘too strict’. A father did not ‘transmit’ bipolar disorder through a moral failing. Biology matters and families often find that acknowledgement to be a relief,” he writes.
Moving on to cancer, we had a comprehensive article on why vital chemotherapy drugs are in short supply in India, with inputs from all the bureaus across the country. India is facing a critical nationwide shortage of two key chemotherapy drugs, cisplatin and carboplatin, driven primarily by the soaring global platinum raw material costs, West Asia shipping route disruptions, and domestic price caps. While government hospitals in several States have managed to stabilise supplies, private hospitals in many parts are still facing a crunch. For patients, this has meant interruptions or delays in life-saving treatment. In response, the government last month raised temporarily ceiling rates for the two drugs by 50%, to help restart halted domestic manufacturing lines. Do read more at the link.
In significant news in the sector, the Supreme Court asks 19 States and UTs to declare cancer as a ‘notifiable disease’ for early detection. This was after it was informed that only 17 of the 36 States and UTs have so far notified cancer as a notifiable disease in light of the recommendations made in a parliamentary standing committee report.
In this podcast, Zubeda Hamid discusses with Dr. Rajeev Jeyadevan about the consequences after Three common medicines were declared carcinogenic. What does this actually mean for patients? The International Agency for Research on Cancer earlier said that three commonly prescribed medicines, hydrochlorothiazide, used to treat high blood pressure, voriconazole, an antifungal medicine and tacrolimus, an immunosuppressant were classified as carcinogenic, or cancer causing, to humans. For the details, click on the link.
This past week, we also featured a number of stories focusing on the gendered aspect of health care. Women with endometriosis are at a 46% higher risk of developing diabetes, a study suggests. Endometriosis causes severe pelvic pain, painful periods and fertility challenges. Researchers, led by those at the George Mason University in the US, followed nearly three million women in the Utah Population Database between 1996 and 2021, including nearly 100,000 diagnosed with endometriosis.
Staying on the subject, Can weather affect your periods? And when should you seek medical help? Athira Elssa Johnson explains that extreme heat, humidity, cold weather and changes in routine can make periods harder to manage. However, persistent changes in cycle length, bleeding or pain should not simply be blamed on the weather; it is important to seek medical attention then.
Continuing our neglected women in science series, I write on Jean Purdy: an unrecognised contributor in IVF, and whose work was critical in the birth of the first test tube baby Louise Joy Brown.
Bindu Shajan Perappadan quotes experts who advise that identifying and addressing health risks in both prospective parents could improve reproductive and pregnancy outcomes, in the article Rising obesity among Indian women underscores need for preconception interventions.
Switching gears to nutrition, recording other top news, Supreme Court slams FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products. The Bench went as far as to ask the country’s food regulator whether it does not want children to grow up healthy. “You should be concerned about the health of young children. They are addicted,” Justice Pardiwala added.
Also read this article A timely reset for the Food Security Act, by Dr. V. Mohan, Dr. Soumya Swaminathan, and Dr. Ninja M. Nazar. They write on the significance of the draft National Food Security (Amendment) Bill, 2026 that links Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) entitlements to household size. The policy challenge is to correct inequity without reducing existing foodgrain access, while creating a pathway towards nutrition security, the authors say.
