Questions remain over Vieira deal amid Senegal uncertainty
- Published
The arrival of Patrick Vieira as the new coach of Senegal comes at a particularly difficult time for the national team - so much so that there is the possibility the former France captain may not even take charge of the Teranga Lions.
The 50-year-old's appointment has been announced despite him not having signed a contract, and the date of his official presentation remains unknown.
Senegal's football federation (FSF), which is currently riven by off-field issues, said discussions regarding the "administrative and contractual arrangements" for Vieira are continuing between the two parties.
The ex-Arsenal and Inter Milan midfielder was unanimously approved as the man to succeed Pape Thiaw at an FSF meeting on Monday, with former Netherlands international Patrick Kluivert among the other names considered.
However, uncertainty surrounding the termination of Thiaw's deal remains.
Vieira's predecessor was sacked following the dramatic last-32 exit to Belgium at the Fifa World Cup without Senegal's government, which funds the national team, formally endorsing the decision.
He is demanding the payment of several months' worth of outstanding wages as well as various bonuses, with the total reportedly amounting to almost $815,000 (£600,000).
Meanwhile, a ruling on the election of the current FSF leadership - which has been contested for the past year - is expected from the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) by Friday.
With the FSF leadership increasingly isolated, without the backing of the government or the general public's support, and constrained by the impending Cas ruling, it nevertheless had little choice but to act quickly to fill the Teranga Lions hotseat.
The calendar will not wait, with Senegal back in action in the qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) on 23 September when they travel to Mozambique in their Group J opener. A meeting with Ethiopia follows days later.
The Cas ruling in Lausanne could call into question the legitimacy of the FSF hierarchy and potentially even the choice of Vieira as head coach.
Moreover, for all his achievements as one of the greatest footballers of the modern era Vieira's record in management has been less impressive.
A long-awaited homecoming
Beyond all of that, Vieira's connection with Senegal carries a deeply symbolic significance.
Born in Dakar in June 1976 to a Cape Verdean mother and a Gabonese father, Vieira began kicking a football around the sandy streets of the capital until the age of eight.
His family moved to France and his life went in a different direction, becoming a Premier League icon during his time with Arsenal, amassing over a century of France caps, and helping Les Blues to the World Cup in 1998 and the European Championship in 2000.
He faced Senegal only once as a player, in the opening game of the 2002 World Cup when France suffered a shock 1-0 defeat against a generation led by Aliou Cisse and including Thiaw - the two men whose coaching legacy he is now following.
But Vieira never truly severed ties with the country of his birth.
Indeed, one of his most significant contributions came towards the end of his playing career when he made a major investment in the creation of the Diambars Institute.
It would go on to become one of Africa's leading football academies and, less than two decades later, one of the foundations of Senegal's recent success.
Diambars has produced players including Idrissa Gana Gueye, Bamba Dieng and Abdoulaye Seck, all of whom have played a part in Senegal's story since 2018.
Crowned champions of Africa for the first time in February 2022 at the delayed 2021 Afcon, the Teranga Lions secured a second title with a 1-0 win after extra time in January's Afcon final. However, the ultimate destination of the trophy will be settled by Cas after Thiaw called his side off the pitch following a controversial penalty awarded to hosts Morocco in stoppage time.
The challenge facing Vieira is the rebuild of a team attempting to look towards the future after one of the most successful chapters in its history.
There is plenty of promising young talent coming through but those players will have to carry the weight of a formidable legacy left by the old guard of Sadio Mane, Edouard Mendy, Kalidou Koulibaly and Gana Gueye.
The shortlist for the new coach included Kluivert, Vieira's compatriot Patrice Carteron and two former Senegal internationals in Habib Beye and Oumar Daf.
The Frenchman dropped a series of hints that he was in the running to take charge, most notably during the unusually high-profile coverage of his recent holiday in Senegal.
Vieira's mixed coaching record
Vieira amassed a glittering list of honours as a player but has found similar success hard to come by as a manager.
He began his coaching career with New York City FC in 2016, leading them into the play-offs in both of his two seasons at the helm, only to see his team lose twice in MLS conference semi-finals, including a 7-0 aggregate hammering by Toronto FC.
He then guided Nice to creditable seventh- and fifth-placed finishes in Ligue 1 before being sacked in December 2020 and joining Crystal Palace in July 2021.
Vieira earned praise for an attacking style as he led the Eagles to a 12th-placed finish in the Premier League and the FA Cup semi-finals in 2021-22, but was dismissed in March 2023 when Palace were three points above the relegation zone following an 11-match winless run in the league.
Then-chairman Steve Parish said the decision was taken with "enormous regret" but in order to keep the Selhurst Park side in the top flight.
Then came a year at Strasbourg and another mid-table finish in Ligue 1. The Frenchman's most recent job was at Italian side Genoa, whom he departed by mutual consent last November with the team winless and bottom of Serie A.
International management presents its own challenges and, with defeated candidate Mady Toure contesting last August's election of FSF president Abdoulaye Fall, Vieira may find his long-awaited return to Senegal far more dramatic than he intended.

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.

Enes Kanter Freedom gets tossed from arena after courtside clash with WNBA star
Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night's WNBA game between the Indiana Fever and Chicago Sky after a confrontation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.
Freedom was seated along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female."
With 1:22 remaining in the third period, the Fever called a timeout after Cloud scored inside. Cloud shared a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking toward Freedom.
Cloud, 34, began yelling and pointing at Freedom, 34, as she approached him. Freedom stood up, extended his arms, and took a step onto the court before security personnel and several Sky players stepped between them.
"There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we're just going to focus on the game," Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky's 113-90 loss.
Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team.
"I told her she wasn’t," Marsh said. "I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash."
Freedom stopped near the basket to argue his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out to encourage a response from the crowd as he walked toward the front lobby.
He spoke with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.
"I didn’t see it, we were talking about the next play in our huddle," Indiana star Caitlin Clark said, "so I think that’s probably a question for Chicago."
Cloud met with team and league security after the game but did not speak with the media.
The WNBA has recently been the focus of debate over whether transgender women — individuals assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to compete in the league. No transgender athlete has ever played in the WNBA.
Although the league's collective bargaining agreement states it is restricted to women, it contains no specific language regarding gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
Fever guard Sophie Cunningham stated in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls' and women's sports. Freedom and another former NBA player, Royce White, have declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women.
Freedom joined a small rally supporting Cunningham outside Wintrust Arena before the game.
Asked if he had a message for Freedom, Marsh praised the league and its players.
"If you come to a game you should probably come to enjoy the basketball," he said, "and that seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that too."
There were no major issues between Sophie Cunningham and DiJonai Carrington in Indiana's 113-90 victory over Chicago on Sunday night. Cunningham scored three points for the Fever in 11 minutes, while Carrington recorded seven points for the Sky in 18 minutes.
It was the first matchup between the teams since Cunningham was brought down by Carrington on a fast break earlier this month. Carrington was listed as questionable with a left foot injury, but was cleared after warmups.
Cunningham downplayed any lingering animosity between the teams going into the game. Indiana had dropped two straight games.
"My mindset has never changed. I think it is what it is," Cunningham said. "I’m locked in on tonight. ... I think we’re just out here trying to get the win."
Cunningham and Carrington both checked in for the first time with 3::green-background[04] remaining in the first quarter, with no notable disputes between the players all night long.
Sky coach Tyler Marsh said he had no conversations with his players before the game about the tense atmosphere from their previous matchup.
"That kind of was what it was last game and anything that came out of it kind of lasted for that time," Marsh said. "But for us, again, it was on to the next one in front of us."
Cunningham was going up for a layup in the first quarter of Indiana's 90-86 win on Aug. 8 when Carrington came from behind and struck her in the head and neck, knocking her to the court as the shot went in. Cunningham got up, charged Carrington and pushed her as she was held back by a teammate.
The referees reviewed the play and upgraded it to a Flagrant 2 after citing windup, impact, and follow-through, resulting in Carrington's ejection.
Shortly after being thrown out, Carrington posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" on social media and tagged the Fever. Carrington is Black and Cunningham is white.
Days later, Carrington said she never claimed the Flagrant 2 assessment resulted from white privilege, though she did not elaborate further.
"I (couldn't) care less about what she does, what she tweets, any of that," Cunningham said before Sunday's game. "I’m here to play basketball.
"There's going to be people who are going to talk about it ... but to me, it’s just another basketball game."

In global commercial real estate investment markets, data centres are all the rage. While stock markets continue to suffer bouts of volatility as sentiment oscillates between concerns 
artificial intelligence
 (AI) will fall short of expectations and fears it will prove more disruptive than many think, the fundamentals of data centres are exceptionally strong.
According to JLL, global data centre occupancy was 97 per cent at the end of last year while 77 per cent of all capacity under construction is committed to tenants. Hyperscalers – leading technology companies and cloud service providers such as Amazon and Meta – occupy more than half of all data centre space, providing 
security to landlords
. This is why data centres account for a fast-growing share of global commercial property fundraising.
However, the market has reached an inflection point. The rapid growth of AI workloads has amplified constraints such as power availability, land access, sustainability requirements and community acceptance. In the United States, a fierce 
backlash against data centres
 has become “a structural constraint on AI infrastructure” that “has expanded to broader anti-AI sentiment”, Jefferies said in a report.
In the first quarter of this year, at least 75 data centre projects worth around US$130 billion were delayed or blocked by local opposition, close to the total value of schemes stymied by local resistance during the whole of 2025.
Last month, New York moved to become the first US state to impose a temporary ban on the construction of large new data centres because of fears that the scale and speed of development put too much strain on energy and water resources.
Lawmakers in more than a dozen other states are mulling temporary bans on the facilities. Research group Data Centre Watch said “moratoria [have] expanded from local exceptions to a multi-front political battle”.

U.S.-Canada trade talks collapsed last night. Punitive Trump tariffs will now go into effect. Canada will reciprocate with retaliatory tariffs of its own.
The story may not be over. Donald Trump is notorious for issuing threats, then reversing them. Wars are on, off, on again, off again, then on a third time—but only as a “little detour.” This is not an administration that thinks even one move ahead. But without a supersized Trump TACO, the U.S.-Canada impasse likely won’t resolve soon.
The Trump administration has one big idea about Canada: The U.S. is larger, stronger, and richer than Canada, so Canada must sooner or later surrender to Trump’s demands. That one big idea is wrong.
Yes, Trump can hurt Canada more than Canada can hurt Trump. That part of Trump’s thinking is true. But wars are not decided only by the question Who can inflict more pain? Wars are also decided by the question Who can endure more pain? Trump’s failure to accept this truth is why he lost the Iran war—and why he is losing his trade wars.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has much more political permission to accept pain from a U.S.-Canadian trade war than Trump does.
To read current Canadian polling is to see a country united under its political leadership—and energized by its dislike and distrust of Trump’s United States. A majority of Canadians view Trump’s America as a more immediate threat to their security than Russia or China. Two-thirds favor the government taking a hard line in trade talks; fewer than one-quarter regard the United States as trustworthy. Meanwhile, Carney is backed by the Canadian public, polling at about 60 percent approval, a remarkable figure in a multiparty political system.
The Canadian economy has definitely suffered because of Trump’s hostility. Exports were down last year, and growth slowed. But this year, Canada got an unexpected bailout: Trump’s Iran war and Trump’s inflation have boosted prices for Canadian oil, gas, minerals, and food products. Canadian incomes are rising again. Meanwhile, Canada’s low levels of public debt have kept inflation low. Whereas the U.S. government must pay 5.3 percent to borrow money for 30 years, Canada pays 4.2 percent.
By contrast, Trump is facing an omnishamble. “Trump’s Economic Challenge: $40tn Debt, 6.7% Mortgages and $5 Diesel.” That’s a headline in today’s Financial Times. The paper could have added one more: 33 percent job approval, and falling fast.
Trump’s tariffs are costing the typical American household $1,100 a year in both direct collections and indirectly in higher prices, according to the Yale Budget Lab. Although teasing out Canada-specific costs is tricky, one indicator is the price of aluminum. In 2024, about one-fourth of the aluminum consumed by Americans came from Canada, the U.S.’s single largest source of imported aluminum. Result: Whereas European and Japanese consumers now pay about $3,000 a ton for aluminum, Americans pay almost $5,000, driving up the cost of everything from a can of beer to the construction of a new hospital.
Although Canada’s economy is much smaller than the U.S.’s, Canada’s government has a more rational and intelligent leadership—and can therefore target its retaliation in ways that better serve national ends. U.S. alcohol exports to Canada have collapsed by 80 percent as Canadian provincial liquor stores ban U.S. wine and spirits. Canada’s booze boycott hurts more than one might expect given the comparatively small size of the Canadian market. Alcohol exporters to Canada prepare special labels for their products to meet Canadian legal requirements. More than 1 million bottles of wine intended for Canadian markets now slumber in U.S. warehouses, unsellable anywhere else without costly repackaging.
More than 30 percent of Ohio’s exports go to Canada, and almost 40 percent of Michigan’s. Both states will this year elect a U.S. senator and fill open governor’s seats. Not only is Trump putting at risk his party’s position in purple Michigan, but suddenly the races in beet-red Ohio look in jeopardy too. With these states, may turn control of the Senate—and Trump’s chances of facing meaningful accountability next year for his law-breaking and corruption.
Trump’s theory of his trade war, like his theory of his Iran war, is that the bigger bully always wins. Size counts for a lot, but not for everything.
As Trump has declared over and over again, his ultimate goal in this trade war is to add Canada as a 51st state. Why? To make the United States look bigger on the map. For that goal, which excites ultra-MAGA crackpots, Trump is hazarding not only America’s most important trading relationships, but very possibly every other political equity he holds, including avoiding investigations and accountability by a Democratic House and Senate after January 2027.
Against Canada, Trump is fighting a trade war that very few Americans support, under leadership that most Americans reject, to achieve results that virtually all Americans would dismiss as pointless if not crazy.
Against Trump, Canadians are fighting a trade war that the great majority support, under leadership that commands broad assent, to defend their independence and self-respect. That’s a war that even the weaker side can win, especially if it needs to hold on only a few months longer to survive.

U.S.-Canada trade talks collapse just before deadline for tariffs
Trade negotiations between the United States and Canada fell apart on Friday night, shortly before a midnight deadline for 50% tariffs to take effect on $20 billion worth of Canadian products.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement, shared on social media late Friday, that "Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses."
Carney said important progress had been made in recent weeks toward "improving Canada's position as having the best deal in the world with the U.S." That progress, however, did not meet Canada's objectives, he said, adding: "As a result, this evening, I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the U.S. and have directed negotiators to return to Ottawa."
The prime minister blamed the U.S. for the collapse in negotiations. "Last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said, concluding, "Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future."
Shortly after midnight, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer responded to Carney with a statement posted on social media saying Canada had "declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week."
"Despite the U.S. offer to Canada to receive the best treatment of any major exporter to our market, new demands and walk backs of other commitments by Canada have upended the careful balance reached in the past days," Greer said.
He added that earlier this week "the United States agreed to provide even better treatment to Canada, offering significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos, and lumber."
"The offer would have led to supply chain coordination on aerospace, complementary actions to address unfair trade practices, critical minerals cooperation, increased enforcement against imports produced with forced labor, and the announcement of formal U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) negotiations," Greer said in his statement.

There will be no settlement talks meeting Monday between Paramount and a coalition of state Attorneys General after all.
California AG Rob Bonta cancelled the scheduled sit-down late Sunday after reports of an August 21 meeting with the David Ellison-led company oozed out.
“Not only did Paramount leak the alleged substance of settlement discussions, but they misrepresented these discussions, demonstrating a lack of good faith,” the AG said in a statement provided to Deadline “As soon as Paramount stops playing games and engages sincerely, my office is happy to meet again.”
News of behind the scenes talks in the bitter battle over Paramount’s $111 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery were actually first confirmed publicly by none other than Gov. Gavin Newsom. “I know there are many meetings that are going on, and there’s a lot of conversation,” the presumed 2028 presidential candidate said on August 21.
Watch on Deadline
It should be noted that Deadline actually heard details of the August 21 preliminary gathering to set the agenda for the August 24 meeting from a variety of sources, if you know what I mean?
Paramount did not respond early Monday to request for comment on Bonta’s pulling of the meeting plug. The New York Times first reported the meeting cancellation.
Though expectations for the August 24 meeting were “intentionally low,” sources told Deadline Sunday, there seemed to be several hot ticket items on the table for the parties.
Specifically, representatives of the 12 state AGs who sued Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery in an antitrust action on July 13 wanted CEO Ellison to sell a swath of WBD’s still lucrative cable channel stable. As well, the elected officials sought to have Paramount and WB remain two separate studios, with Donald Trump pal Ellison ( and to some extent his father and backer Larry Ellison) practically cordoned off from running the place he just bought.
“David’s not going to go along with any of that, and Bonta knows it,” a studio exec told Deadline Sunday of the discussion points put on the table. Clear non-starters with Ellison and Para execs, the agenda points also reflect the figurative and literal distance between the AG, their lawsuit partners the WGA and the Melrose lot.

The USS Lincoln has been at sea for 270-plus days. Here’s why conditions on board fell apart
Iranian attacks that devastated a key US base in the Persian Gulf forced the Navy to resupply the aircraft carrier from a faraway island in the Indian Ocean. Now it’s steaming home
The food shortages and other problems that sparked outrage over substandard conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln stemmed from Iranian attacks that devastated a key Navy base on the island nation of Bahrain — leaving the ship to rely on supplies from an outpost about 2,200 miles away.
The Navy's Persian Gulf base, known as Naval Support Activity Bahrain, is the headquarters of the Fifth Fleet, which in 2004 unveiled a $25 million, state-of-the-art nerve center to support maritime military operations across the Middle East.
But the site was largely destroyed by missiles and drones that hit it February 28, the first day of President Donald Trump's war against Iran, according to The New York Times.
A short time later, the Navy began using its base on Diego Garcia — a faraway UK-administered island in the middle of the Indian Ocean, south of the Maldives — as a new logistics hub, an unidentified military official told the NYT.
The situation led to supply shortages on the Lincoln, whose crew of about 5,000 sailors and Marines has set a post-Vietnam War record of more than 270 continuous days at sea since the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier left its home port of San Diego on November 21, 2025.
It also denied the crew the use of a nearby “liberty port” that would have provided the opportunity for shore leave.
On Thursday evening it was reported that the ship was heading back to the U.S. and was expected to arrive back in San Diego in a few weeks.
The Pentagon referred an inquiry from The Independent to U.S. Central Command, which didn't immediately respond.
A White House spokesperson re-released an earlier statement that said President Donald Trump “cares about our troops more than anyone, and he is ensuring our brave servicemembers have all the resources they need to be successful as the United States Military continues to economically strangle the Iranian regime.”
In recent weeks, relatives of some crew members went public with tales of skimpy, inedible meals, moldy showers, broken toilets and sporadic laundry service on the Lincoln.
Military mother Danielle Rappa told NBC News that her son, who's serving on the ship, “describes the overall experience as a scene out of the [Fox TV show] American Horror Story, where he feels like everybody is dead but they don't know it yet.”
One sailor went overboard August 3 wearing a life vest and was rescued after nearly an hour in the water, and others were prevented from also jumping off the ship, according to reports.
Another mother said her son had told her that there were crew members who “weren’t doing well.” She said: “One person had just given up; they weren’t reporting for duty. They were wanting to get sent home.”
She said she’d been told that conditions had improved in April after parents started complaining.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth claimed August 13 that conditions on the Lincoln were being “completely misrepresented” in news reports, saying, “We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment.”
Trump also described the Lincoln's deployment as "not nearly long enough" while speaking to reporters August 14.
The president made the stunning remark a day after The Wall Street Journal reported the Navy was planning to replace the Lincoln with the USS George Washington, which the WSJ said had recently been operating in the South China Sea. On Thursday the Associated Press reported that the USS George Washington was now operating in the Middle East.
Trump’s comment also came the same day Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao in a prepared statement that the Lincoln's crew had "crushed their deployment and will return home soon as part of a planned rotation."
On August 15, Central Command — which is responsible for a region that stretches from northeast Africa into Central and South Asia — said its commander, Admiral Brad Cooper, had just completed a 10-day trip to the Middle East.
It included a visit to the Lincoln, where Cooper addressed the crew members and thanked them for their dedication and courage.
“The Lincoln Carrier Strike Group is a strong team of high-achieving Americans standing tall with immense, justified pride in everything they accomplished,” Cooper said in a prepared statement. “History will record this deployment as one of the most operationally intense and consequential of the modern era.”
In a social media post Thursday, Central Command, known as CENTCOM, posted a photo of sailors working on the Washington's flight deck “as the aircraft carrier transits the Arabian Sea.”
“The George Washington Carrier Strike Group is operating in Middle East during a scheduled deployment after arriving in the CENTCOM theater yesterday," the caption added.
Iran followed up its February 28 strikes against the Navy base in Bahrain with other attacks over the ensuing months, according to a late June report by the WSJ.
An analysis of satellite imagery and social media video, as well as interviews with current and former service members, revealed extensive damage to the base that the Pentagon hadn't publicly acknowledged, the WSJ said.
The base's command headquarters, at least a dozen other buildings and two satellite communications terminals were all hit hard, but the military told the WSJ that no one had been killed and U.S. operations weren't significantly impacted.
Only a small staff remained on the ground after most personnel were evacuated, the WSJ said.
Iran’s attacks against the base in Bahrain and others across the region have the Pentagon considering whether to reduce America’s military presence in the Middle East after the Iran war is over, The Washington Post reported Thursday.
Shifting logistics operations away from Bahrain may have prompted Iran to fire two medium-range missiles at Diego Garcia on March 20, according to the NYT.
A Navy warship shot down one missile, and the other fell short and splashed into the Indian Ocean, the NYT said.
The U.S. looks no closer to ending the war with Iran nearly six months after Trump started it, despite repeated claims of an imminent deal. This week Trump threatened an “economic D-Day” against Tehran and any countries aiding it.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Thalles de Souza. It has been edited for length and clarity.
In March 2016, on a Sunday morning, police entered my house, shouting and shooting. At only 13, I woke up screaming, not sure of what was happening. When I walked into the kitchen, I was nearly shot. Turns out, the police were looking for a family member of ours.
Shootings were common where I lived in Vila Kennedy, a community in Bangu, in Rio de Janeiro. I witnessed so many deaths — countless deaths.
I lived there with my mom, a single mom, and my three older siblings. My mom had always done what she could to protect us, given what she experienced as a child. After her parents died when she was 10, she became homeless. By 19, she had four children. She did what she could to keep us safe, but she couldn't hide what we saw in our community when we walked out the front door.
My mom decided to move us to the US
There were a lot of gangs and so much corruption. Every day, people were killed. It was a normal occurrence to be playing soccer with my friends, right next to dead bodies lying in the street. I learned to navigate life in these spaces surrounded by danger, but it was normal — it was my reality.
On that Sunday in March 2016, my mom decided she had to get out to keep her children safe.
She had quietly been saving small amounts of money, taking out loans, and applying for our visas so that we could travel to the US. She kept it quiet to make sure no one got in the way of her plan.
Three months after the shooting in our house, we moved to Cape Cod, Massachusetts, and we never left. It became our home, our new community.
I went to community college to save money
After graduating from high school, I attended our local community college to save money and decide what college I would transfer to later.
In community college, I worked hard. I had perfect grades, became a member of the Massachusetts Board of Higher Education, participated in clubs, served as student body president for two years, and served the community I lived in, wanting to give back to the people who had welcomed my family.
Last year, I started looking for which college I was going to transfer to. I knew Yale had produced some of the best lawyers and judges — what I hoped to become — so I went for a visit.
I applied to Yale, thinking I wouldn't get in
When I got out of my car, I said to myself that this place wasn't the kind of place that would accept someone like me. But I applied anyway. I knew there was only a 1.3% acceptance rate, but I had to try.
When I saw I had an email from the admissions office, I called my mom and older sister into the room with me to find out the result.
I got in. I got into Yale, one of the most prestigious universities in the world. Not just that — I had a 100% full-ride scholarship.
I still can't believe it, even though I'm starting in September.
Where I came from didn't determine where I could go. I might have started as just another unlikely statistic in society's eyes, but that isn't what I'll become.
On a visit to the campus a few weeks ago, my mom looked at me and said how amazing all of this was. She's so happy. She tells everyone. She sacrificed her entire life to get her children safe. And the result was far better than she could have imagined.
I'm so glad I've been able to give her the gift of knowing her sacrifice wasn't for nothing — it was all worth it.

It might be possible to outrun your next rent payment — if you live with roommates.
Nike is offering a unique — and highly relevant — prize to two winners of a street race in New York City on August 29: "1 month of free rent."
"Step to the starting line on Orchard Street for a chance to win one month of rent paid," the company says.
Participants, who will be chosen by a random drawing, will race in a series of 100-meter dashes, advancing through an undisclosed number of heats before racing in a final round.
At the end of it all, the two fastest participants will each earn up to $4,000, which Nike is marketing as enough for a month's rent.
For many New Yorkers, though, that might not cover it.
The median Manhattan rental price for a market-rate apartment, where the race is set to occur, soared to $5,000 last month, according to an August report from The Real Deal and appraisal firm Samuel Miller.
Should the winners of the races hail from Queens or Brooklyn, the $4,000 prize will likely be enough, but not by much. According to data from Apartments.com, the average rent for a one-bedroom in Queens is $3,605. In Brooklyn, it's $3,082.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made lowering the city's astronomical housing costs a centerpiece of his administration. His signature rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments takes effect this fall, while City Hall is pursuing a broader plan to build and preserve 200,000 affordable homes over the next decade.
Representatives for Mamdani did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
The race comes as Nike tries to recapture some of the cultural cachet it's lost in recent years. CEO Elliott Hill, a Nike veteran who returned to lead the company in 2024, has been working to refocus the brand on sports, rebuild relationships with retailers, and revive product innovation after years of losing ground to competitors like Hoka and On.
The turnaround has shown signs of progress in North America, but it's been slow going. Nike's shares remain well below their 2021 peak, while weakness in China and other challenges continue to weigh on the company.

Fast-moving wildfire in Nevada forces nearly 90,000 to evacuate was human caused, sheriff says
‘Please get out if you can right now,’ the sheriff urged
An uncontained, human-caused wildfire in northwest Reno, Nevada, has destroyed homes and prompted authorities to urge around 90,000 residents to evacuate on Sunday.
At least six people were injured, according to officials.
The Hawk Fire started Saturday and quickly expanded to 20 square miles (53 sq. km.) across the Peavine Peak area of the Humboldt–Toiyabe National Forest, where rugged foothills are surrounded by homes and businesses near the California state line.
The blaze moved at an extraordinary speed Saturday night, leaping over fire engines and obstructing emergency responders trying to reach hotspots while residents fled, Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said.
"It was extremely confusing," the sheriff said, describing how shifting winds sent flames in multiple directions.
Multiple structures were destroyed, and those injured included three civilians alongside three first responders, officials reported.
Authorities provided no further details on the origin of the fire, indicating it remains under investigation.
Approximately 42,000 residents are under mandatory evacuation orders after the "GO NOW" zone expanded to the edge of the University of Nevada at Reno.
An additional 45,000 people were placed in an adjacent warning zone. Officials urged everyone to leave and prepare to stay away for several days, as shifting and intensifying winds were expected to make the blaze even more unpredictable.
"Please get out if you can right now," the sheriff said.
Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the Nevada National Guard.
The deployment includes two helicopter crews for aerial firefighting and 60 troops helping police protect evacuated neighborhoods, joining 800 fire personnel on the scene.
Nearly 10,000 customers remained without power in Washoe County on Sunday, down from 60,000 on Saturday.
Portions of U.S. Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed. Reno, home to more than 280,000 residents, is Nevada’s largest city outside metro Las Vegas.
Emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center for evacuees, though pets were not allowed; owners were directed to leave small and large animals at two separate locations. Casinos in Reno offered room discounts to displaced residents.
The fire was so small Saturday morning that it was not a concern, said Tyler Duvall, who was camping over the weekend. By Sunday, his home was inside the evacuation zone and inaccessible.
"The wind really blew it up," Duvall said, adding that he knew of several homes that burned roughly a mile from his property.
Strong, gusty winds, low humidity, and dry vegetation are continuing to fuel the blaze, according to Truckee Meadows Fire & Rescue in Reno.

Amid growing concerns over a government-ordered Instagram censorship drive in India, political parties and leaders are now reporting restrictions on their posts, with Meta citing “legal requirements” but providing little information about the basis for the action. Content linked to the Cockroach Janta Party protests, political parties and creators has all been caught up in the restrictions.
Over the past few days, several social media posts and accounts have been geo-blocked in India. On Instagram, users’ posts are either removed citing legal requirements or restricted from being viewed in India. Several opposition organisations and leaders have also faced such restrictions, with their posts suddenly being taken down.

On August 6, the Aam Aadmi Party, and on August 7, the Congress party’s youth wing, the Indian Youth Congress, posted on social media to say that their Instagram posts were being repeatedly removed by Meta.
Modi ji, IYC se Dar Gaye Kya…
Meta se overtime kara rahe ho…
Aur Spineless @Meta walon, Tum Platform ho Ya BJP IT CELL ki Franchise? pic.twitter.com/Y7awNsZOcF
— Indian Youth Congress (@IYC) August 6, 2026
No explanation. No accountability. Just silence.
Democracy demands transparency, not secret restrictions and automated acknowledgements.@Meta, stop hiding behind silence. Tell India why accounts are being restricted on your platforms and whose orders you are acting on.… https://t.co/50a21ApBNo pic.twitter.com/p8tIi97ynw
— AAP (@AamAadmiParty) August 6, 2026
Clicking on a removed post shows a notice stating that it has been restricted by Meta’s automated systems in India, in accordance with legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.
Opposition Leaders’ Posts Restricted Earlier as well
This is not the first time that posts by political entities have been restricted under these rules. Earlier, posts by Congress and TVK leaders related to Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay had also been removed from Instagram and Facebook, citing the same provisions.
On May 11, Goa Congress president Girish Chodankar posted on X, asking whether Prime Minister Modi was so afraid of a Congress-TVK alliance that even a video of the chief minister’s swearing-in ceremony was being blocked. Similarly, TVK leader Aravind shared a screenshot on social media showing that his Facebook post related to Tamil Nadu chief minister Vijay had been removed.
Shame on you @narendramodi 🤦 pic.twitter.com/ujHKwW8VfI
— Aravind TVK (@Aravind8282) May 11, 2026
Around the same time, Meta blocked a reel featuring Rahul Gandhi and C Joseph Vijay, citing the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules. Following widespread criticism, Meta restored the reel.
The Union ministry of electronics and information technology said at the time that the action was the result of an internal error by Meta and had nothing to do with the ministry.
More recently, Meta itself restricted a video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressing students for a few hours. Meta later apologised, calling it a technical glitch. However, the incident too lacked transparency, as Meta did not publicly explain the nature of the technical glitch that had led to the restriction.
What is the Legal Provision?
The legal framework behind these restrictions is Section 79(3)(b) of India’s Information Technology Act. The provision was originally intended to determine when platforms could lose their “safe harbour” protection, or immunity from liability.
Put simply, if online platforms and social media intermediaries fail to expeditiously remove material flagged by the government after receiving notice, they may lose their legal immunity for third-party user content. This could make the social media intermediary directly liable for the material.
However, digital rights activists argue that the government is using this provision as the legal basis for a content-blocking mechanism while bypassing Section 69A, which involves greater procedural safeguards and requires written and reasoned orders.
Lack of Transparency
A serious flaw in this process is the lack of transparency. When the government sends a request flagging a post, users are not told who made the complaint or on what basis the order was issued. Instead, they see a generic notice stating that the content has been restricted in accordance with legal requirements.
Users are neither provided a copy of the order nor a case number. They are also not told which official or authority sent the takedown request.
ALSO READ: Content creators decry Instagram censorship, call restrictions a ‘digital emergency’
An even bigger problem is that ordinary users have no concrete and reliable mechanism to challenge such action. Digital rights organisations such as SFLC and IFF have been assisting some users, but the large-scale removal of posts has exposed the absence of an effective redressal mechanism.
At its core, the mechanism is unbalanced. Content is removed first, without users being given a clear reason or an opportunity to be heard. The entire burden of seeking an explanation or having the post restored is then placed on the user.
According to a recent report by The Indian Express, the government issued around 195,000 blocking orders between March and July 2026. Of these, nearly 100,000 were sent to Instagram and around 80,000 to Facebook. In addition, around 15,000 blocking orders were sent to YouTube.
A senior government official told The Indian Express that a significant share of the blocking orders — particularly those involving Instagram — were issued during a period when protests were gathering momentum.
The report also stated that Meta has integrated its API (Application Programming Interface) with the Sahyog portal. As a result, content marked on the system under government directions can be removed from Meta’s platforms automatically, without separate human review by the company. This automation leaves Meta with no meaningful opportunity to independently review or object to the directions before acting on them.
On August 20, the Press Information Bureau (PIB), the government’s nodal agency, shared details about the matter. It said that the Sahyog portal’s API was integrated in 2025 at the request of Meta, Facebook and Instagram’s parent company. This enables state governments and central ministries to notify IT intermediaries about allegedly unlawful content.
According to the PIB, around 298,000 URLs were sent for takedown between March and July 2026. Of these, 244,000 URLs, or 82%, were sent by state governments. This included 51,000 URLs sent by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) in connection with cyber, infrastructure and stock-investment scams.
How does Meta’s ‘Automated System’ Actually Work?
The most confusing and opaque aspect of this entire process is Meta’s “automated system”. Notices on restricted posts state that Meta acted under an automated system, but users are not told what criteria this system uses.
Does it automatically restrict content flagged through the Sahyog portal? Or does it operate on the basis of certain keywords, images, non-compliance with AI-labelling requirements, or other factors? There is little transparency around these questions.
During the recent students’ protests in Delhi against alleged irregularities in NEET-UG, reels posted by journalists, media outlets and student activists showing police action were also restricted. Posts by creators producing content related to the CJP protests were subsequently restricted as well. Alt News has published detailed reports on both instances.
More recently, an Alt News post that mentioned “Burhan Wani” was repeatedly removed by Instagram. In another instance, an Alt News fact-check was restricted for using the word “Khalistani”. we later discovered that searches on Instagram with ‘Burhan Wani’ or ‘Monu Manesar’ do not yield any result. We wrote to Meta asking whether there is a list of words that are not allowed on the platform or whether there is a government order to that effect, but we are yet to receive a response.

Ukraine-Russia war latest: UK Storm Shadow blueprints given to Zelensky by Burnham on Independence Day visit
Ukrainian drones spark fire at a logistics hub belonging to online retailer Ozon, after weeks of attacks targeting Wildberries
Andy Burnham has arrived in Kyiv to honour Ukraine’s Independence Day, just hours after at least three people were killed in a Russian attack on the outskirts of Kharkiv.
It is the first overseas visit for the British prime minister, more than a month after entering Downing Street, and it comes as Kyiv and Moscow continued to exchange devastating attacks overnight.
He is set to announce that Britain has agreed to allow European missile manufacturer MBDA to release classified information on UK-made components used in the SCALP long-range cruise missile, according to his office.
"Ukraine's security is our security," Burnham said in a statement, adding that Britain would stand by Ukraine "for as long as it takes".
In Kharkiv, emergency services have rescued and evacuated eight people, some of whom were injured, governor Oleh Syniehubov said, adding the search was ongoing to identify any other possible casualties.
Meanwhile, two people were killed and two more injured in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian border region of Belgorod, local authorities said.
Ukrainian also hit another online retailer, setting fire to Ozon's logistics hub in Makhachkala in the Russian republic of Dagestan.
Ukraine not ready 'to simply surrender' to Russia, Zalensky says
Ukraine is not ready “to simply surrender” to Russia at any price, Volodymyr Zelensky said in a defiant speech marking Independence Day celebrations.
Standing in a traditional Ukrainian embroidered shirt in front of the golden-domed St Michael's monastery in Kyiv where burned-out Russian tanks are on show, the president reiterated that his country will not surrender territory.
He said Russia's demand - repeatedly rejected by Ukraine - that Kyiv cede the remaining part of the eastern Donbas area that is not in Russian hands after 4-1/2 years of war would not be enough to stop the war.
"We will not let them (Russians) seize the initiative, deceive Europe and the entire world into thinking that we simply need to give up Donbas and everything will be over soon," Zelensky added.
Paying tribute to the people and soldiers defending Ukraine in the war, he again urged allies to bring Russia to the negotiating table and hit it with more sanctions.
Two people killed in Ukrainian drone attack on Russia, authorities say
Two people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian border region of Belgorod.
Local authorities said two others were also injured in the attack earlier today.
In the past week, Ukraine has been targeting Russian logistic depots in the region.
In pictures: Ukrainians mark Independence Day as Russia pummels second-largest city
EU unveils further £5.2 billion in aid for Ukrainian defence
The European Commission has unveiled a further £5.2 billion in aid for Ukraine - for new defence systems, such as air defence, missiles, ammunition and radars to repel the worsening Russian attacks.
This latest aid package comes on top of £13.6 billion of previously approved procurement plans, of which £7 billion had already been disbursed, the EU said.
"As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a statement.
Why is the SCALP missile so important for Ukraine?
The SCALP missile is the French-manufactured version of the prized British Storm Shadow.
It is a long-range, air-launched cruise missile, designed to hit high‑value fixed or fortified targets with precision and low observability.
It has a strike capability of over 155 miles , which means that it would potentially allow Ukraine to attack targets deeper into Russian territory.
This will be a massive boost to Ukraine in its efforts to target military sites in Russia.
Downing Street said the decision will allow France and Ukraine to go ahead with assembly of the missile on Ukrainian territory.
It follows efforts by the two countries to expand local production of long-range weapons, so it does not have to rely entirely on deliveries of complete missiles from abroad.
Britain was the first country to provide Ukraine with Western long-range strike missiles when it supplied Storm Shadow back in 2023.
Minister says Ukrainian elections are ‘internal matter for the people of Ukraine’
A UK government minister has insisted whether to call an election on Volodymyr Zelensky premiership is an “internal matter for the people of Ukraine”.
Zelensky has faced pressure to call an election in recent weeks after sacked defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for a contest.
Defence minister Luke Pollard told Sky News: “When to have an election is an internal matter for the people of Ukraine, the government of Ukraine.
“If I look at the parallel with the United Kingdom during the Second World War, while there was war waging in Europe, we didn't have elections, but that will be a matter for them. B
“But having spoken to both President Zelensky and the former defence minister you mentioned in the past, I know that both of them are committed to the defence of their nation and seeing through their nation to get to a peaceful conclusion to the conflict. It is up to them and their system about how they handle those internal affairs.”
Germany's Wadephul to urge Rubio to take more active role on Ukraine
German foreign minister Johann Wadephul plans to speak to his US counterpart, Marco Rubio, by phone today to urge him to become more personally involved in diplomatic efforts related to the war in Ukraine, he told radio broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.
Wadephul, who was recently in Ukraine, told the broadcaster that US diplomacy had so far been handled largely by presidential envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
Negotiations between Russia and the US to bring about an end to the conflict in Ukraine have largely stalled amid the war in Iran, and the Kremlin said last week that it had no information yet on a possible next visit by Kushner and Witkoff.
Russian deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov had said in an interview on Friday that Russia was ready to listen to Rubio's new ideas and continue dialogue with Washington.
"I may be able to encourage him (Rubio) myself to do more there," the German minister said, adding that Berlin was pursuing other channels to help restart negotiations.
Ukraine hit Russian fighter aircraft and two vessels in Black Sea
The Ukrainian military struck a Russian MIG-29 fighter aircraft and two Russian vessels in the Black Sea overnight, Ukraine's drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said on Monday.
Brovdi said on Telegram that one of the vessels attacked was a tanker, and the other was a bulk carrier.
Attack on another Russian logistics hub tanks company’s shares
Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12 per cent on the Moscow Exchange on news of the attack, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13 per cent.
Ozon has become Russia's second e-commerce giant, after rival Wildberries, to be targeted in Ukrainian drone attacks. Work at a logistics centre in the Samara region was halted after the first Ukrainian strike on the company's facilities on 22 August.

Doctor who reportedly wrote a paper on violent teens killed in alleged plot involving her daughter and friends
‘Those few girls who kill tend to kill family members,’ Tamela Dutcher reportedly wrote in an article over 20 years ago
An Ohio doctor who reportedly once published a paper on “violent and homicidal” adolescents and what leads teens to kill was allegedly shot dead by her 18-year-old daughter’s boyfriend and his friend.
Tamela Dutcher, 55, was allegedly shot in the face by her daughter’s boyfriend, Christian Evans, and his roommate, Dajameous Payne, during an invasion at her Delaware County home on August 14, NBC 4 reported.
Her teenage daughter, Bryanna Dutcher, is charged alongside Evans, 20, and Payne, 21, in the murder. Bryanna Dutcher has not entered a plea.
Deputies with the Delaware County Sheriff’s Office were called to the home just after midnight when Tamela Dutcher’s husband called 911 to report she had been shot.
While on the phone, he also heard a second shot and reported someone running out of the front door of the home. First responders were called to the home and rushed Tamela Dutcher to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.
Over two decades ago, Tamela Dutcher co-authored an article in the International Journal of Adolescent Medicine and Health titled “The violent and homicidal adolescent. Hearts darkened before time,” according to NBC4.
“The vast majority of youth arrested for homicide are males. Those few girls who kill tend to kill family members,” Dutcher reportedly wrote in the article, which was published six years before her daughter was born.
Authorities interviewed the daughter, who had been home at the time of the shooting. The teen said she heard gunshots but did not see anyone enter the home.
However, police noted in a probable cause affidavit: “It is believed that Bryanna repeatedly lied to law enforcement about her knowledge of the circumstances involving this incident, which delayed identifying leads and suspects,” according to the document, which was obtained by Oxygen.
During the investigation, the 18-year-old told authorities that she was quietly dating Evans because she didn’t want her “very racist” parents to know she was dating a black man.
She told police that if her parents found out about the relationship, they would have kicked her out of the house. However, she told police that Evans “was okay with her parents being racist.” She also denied that he was involved in the shooting.
Bryanna Dutcher told police that on the night of the shooting, she vented to Evans over the phone about a fight between her and her mother, and he allegedly replied, “If I were you, I would have killed her.”
Later that night, Evans and Payne stopped by the family’s home, but Bryanna Dutcher wasn’t allowed to leave because she didn’t complete her chores, according to Oxygen.
The teen said that she heard a gunshot about 15 minutes later.
Phone records later revealed deleted text messages between the teen and Evans, including one from him that allegedly read, “Once they both pass away” and “Also I believe you should also get a gun.”
The affidavit noted Bryanna Dutcher allegedly told Evans “Alr shes living room he’s basement where you’re here lmk.” He allegedly replied, “Were getting ready,” “Getting gloves” and “Take them both out at the same time.”
Evans and Payne were later identified as suspects after police spotted them dumping a bag into a dumpster outside of their apartment.
Bryanna Dutcher, Evans and Payne have all been charged with aggravated murder and are being held in Delaware County Jail.
Carlos Crawford, a defense attorney for Evans indicated he would file a written plea of not guilty by reason of insanity for his client and have the court evaluate his competency.
“[Evans] is suffering from mental decline there at the jail,” Crawford said, according to Richland Source. “He does have a significant history of mental health disorders.”

September 11, 2001, will be remembered as one of the darkest days in American history. As the 25th anniversary approaches, National Geographic, in collaboration with the 9/11 Memorial and Museum, is marking the occasion with a new documentary miniseries: 9/11: Reunited. The three-episode series revisits the personal stories of several survivors of the terrorist attacks, with a twist: It reunites people whose paths crossed at that time to celebrate the bonds they formed 25 years ago.
Director Julian Jones was a producer on NatGeo’s Emmy-winning 2021 documentary miniseries 9/11: One Day in America. The experience inspired him to return to direct 9/11: Reunited. “What emerged for me [while making the 2021 documentary] was a sense of people showing up for each other, a selflessness and everyday heroism,” Jones told Ars. As the 25th anniversary of the attacks approached, he and National Geographic decided to commemorate the milestone with a documentary series focused on that aspect.
“We wanted to bring people together to offer gratitude to each other, to answer unanswered questions, to talk about things that maybe they weren’t ready to talk about until now, and also to remember their fallen comrades or friends,” said Jones. “After 25 years, who do they want to meet? What questions have they got? I think we also wanted to tell the story of what many in the 9/11 community call 9/12, that’s the rest of your lives—the journey, and in many cases, the psychological and physical struggles.”
“The challenge was not to impose a story onto anything,” said Jones. “It was to let the story emerge organically in a way that would feel meaningful to our participants. Our job was to really listen to our participants and be guided by what they wanted.”
Jones and his team had vast amounts of archival footage at their disposal, and selecting which footage to use—and how much of the often gruesome details to include—proved to be a delicate balance. There is no footage of the desperate people jumping to their deaths from the burning North Tower, for instance.
“You can’t sanitize history,” said Jones. “You can’t sanitize what happened. But at the same time, you have to be sensitive. The horrible images we all remember of people falling or jumping—those people are someone’s husband, wife, child, or parent, and we have a duty to be sensitive to that. We tried to choose archival material that reflected the experiences our participants were having at that moment.”

Among those featured in 9/11: Reunited are John Paczkowski, George Phoenix, and Jan Demczur. Paczkowski worked on the 67th floor of the North Tower; Phoenix worked on the 74th floor. They had just entered the elevator to get to work that morning when Demczur, a janitor, jumped in at the last minute with his gear. The first plane hit the North Tower as the elevator approached the 65th floor; the car plummeted 15 floors before the emergency brake kicked in.
Trapped in the elevator with smoke pouring in, they managed to pry open the doors only to be faced with a wall. Undaunted, Demczur used his squeegee blade to carve a hole in the plaster so the men could kick through the wall to escape—a process Demczur re-enacts for the series. They ended up in the 50th-floor men’s room and managed to evacuate down the stairwell with other survivors before the North Tower collapsed.
Debbie St. John was taking the subway to work that morning, unaware that the North Tower had been hit. She disembarked to find police officers directing passengers to the street exits. She was walking down the street when the second plane hit the South Tower. So was Stefan Herlacher, a bond trader who worked nearby. He spotted a large piece of wreckage falling toward him and thought he would be hit; the wreckage hit St. John instead.
Herlacher braved the falling debris and panicked people running through the streets to help her and was horrified to find the fragment had cut through her back. He waved down a passing ambulance driver who transported St. John to a hospital. She was the first 9/11 patient admitted and the last to be discharged 18 months later after 50 surgeries. St. John spent years working on her rehabilitation, marrying her fiancé, and having children, but she never forgot the man who saved her life.
“I remember speaking to Debbie on the phone and she said, ‘I’d love to meet Stefan,’” Jones recalled. “I asked, ‘Well, what would you like to do?’ And she said, ‘I want to take him horseback riding.’ Because she had such terrible injuries and couldn’t walk. She just said, ‘I want to show him how far I’ve come thanks to him.’ So we did that.”
Cmdr. Craig Powell was working at the Pentagon when the third plane hit, as was Lt. Col. Marilyn Wills. Wills had been in a meeting and recalled a fireball flying past and singeing her bangs. Trapped in the burning wreckage, Wills led a group of survivors down the corridor, crawling, because she knew there was a window there. The window was bomb-proof and initially wouldn’t open, but Wills and her commanding officer kicked until it popped open. They were on the second floor, so Powell and others on the ground below formed a fireman’s catch as people jumped, one by one.
“You get a second chance, live life.”

It was Powell who caught Wills, one of the last to jump to safety. He initially thought Wills was dead when he passed her off to a teammate for CPR. “In that situation, giving a person CPR [on site], I didn’t hold out much hope,” Powell told Ars, although he later learned she had lived. As for her second-story jump, “That takes a lot of courage,” he added, since it was the equivalent of a fourth-story jump from a regular building. He remembers being in considerable pain the following day—“catching all those people is not easy on your body, and I was inside the room when the ceiling came down”—as well as needing a shower. “I stunk, and it wasn’t BO,” he said. “When the shit hits the fan, so to speak, your body dumps all these endorphins; it’s literally the smell of fear.”
Powell admitted to some apprehension about reuniting with Wills, mostly because of the cameras, but Wills took control of the situation and helped him through it. “I wanted to participate to close the loop,” said Powell. Despite his experiences with active combat, the events of 9/11 hit differently. “It was an attack on American soil,” he said. “It really hit close to home and made me very concerned about the safety of my family.” He was diagnosed with leukemia in 2015, related to his rescue work at the Pentagon that day, but the treatment worked, and he was able to walk his daughter down the aisle for her wedding. “My greatest appreciation is that my kids are alive and I got to watch them grow up,” he said.
Kevin Shea had just joined the FDNY’s Ladder 35 unit, and his shift was ending when the first tower was hit. He volunteered to stay on, and his supervisor agreed, but there was no room for him on the trucks. Shea planned to find his own way to the site and meet up with the team there. But when he reached the staging area, he couldn’t find Ladder 35. His crewmates were filmed walking into the South Tower several minutes before it collapsed—the last time any were seen alive. Shea was standing just outside when the tower collapsed. It’s the last thing he remembers.
Paramedic Al Kim was working triage in the South Tower Marriott lobby and survived the collapse. He recalled hearing beeping alarms sounding in the wreckage—motion sensors worn by all the firefighters that trigger alarms when the wearer stops moving for a prolonged time. Kim started combing through the wreckage looking for survivors when he came across an unconscious and badly injured Shea, and he salvaged medical supplies from one of the burning ambulances to stabilize the firefighter.
When the North Tower started to buckle, he moved Shea to the safety of an underground parking garage nearby, leaving him in the care of another physician who had taken shelter there. Kim never saw Shea after that—until they were reunited for the documentary—and found no other survivors. Shea spent several weeks in the hospital. He had broken his neck in three places and credits Kim’s on-site care not just with saving his life, but with preventing him from becoming quadriplegic.
A beacon of hope

Bill Spade of FDNY Rescue 5 on Staten Island was on site helping evacuate people from the North Tower when he met John D’Allara of NYPD’s Emergency Services Unit coming down the stairs. They ended up chatting for about 25 minutes about their respective wives and sons; Spade recalled that it was almost as if they were writing their own obituaries. Then everything went eerily quiet, and an evacuation order came through due to fears that the North Tower might collapse. D’Allara was hurrying others through the exit door when it fell. Spade curled up in a ball under falling debris, having lost sight of D’Allara, who was later confirmed dead.
Spade was only one of two Rescue 5 members to survive, but he never forgot D’Allara and contacted his widow, Carol D’Allara, a few years later. But D’Allara’s sons were still too young. Spade, who volunteers at the 9/11 museum in Manhattan, thought the 25th anniversary was the right time to reconnect with the family and let the sons know their father “was thinking of them right to the very end.” D’Allara saved 20 lives that day; his son Nicholas also joined the NYPD and even carries his father’s old badge.
Perhaps the most well-known story—depicted in Oliver Stone’s 2006 film, World Trade Center—is the rescue of Port Authority Police sergeant John McLoughlin. McLoughlin and colleagues William Jimeno and Dominick Pezzulo were on the main concourse between the two towers when the South Tower collapsed, trapping them in the rubble 30 feet underground. Pezzulo was attempting to lift debris off his comrades when the North Tower collapsed 30 minutes later and he was buried by falling debris. McLoughlin was buried up to his elbows, slowly being crushed under the weight, and recalled hearing Pezzulo take his last breath—but not before firing a single shot into the air to alert any rescuers to their location.
Meanwhile, above ground, Scott Fox had joined the rescue effort, despite having retired nine months earlier from Rescue 5, as the FDNY formed makeshift companies out of surviving firefighters. So did John Busching of the NYPD’s Emergency Services Unit. They risked their lives navigating increasingly unstable debris to help dig out first Jimeno (after 13 hours), then McLoughlin (after 22 hours)—a small victory in the midst of tragedy.
McLoughlin was gravely injured and spent six weeks in an induced coma, underwent 27 surgeries during his three weeks in the hospital, and then went through rehabilitation. He still walks with a slight limp. But thanks to Fox, Busching, and several others, “I got to see my kids grow up and meet my grandchildren. How do I thank you for that?”
These are harrowing stories, and it almost seems cruel to ask the survivors to relive that trauma yet again. Per Jones, it helped that there were pre-existing relationships with many of the survivors because of the earlier documentary, which helped establish trust.
“It’s a big deal to ask someone to share the story of the worst day of their lives,” said Jones. “It is emotional, and it is hard for them, but I was astonished by the bravery of the people who participated. They wanted so badly to meet the person who saved them, or the person they saved. In those fleeting moments, amidst all that chaos and horror, these incredible bonds were formed that can never be broken. Many survivors also have a real sense of gratitude and of a duty to keep telling their stories, to remember that day and all the people who didn’t survive.”
Fair warning: 9/11: Reunited is an undeniably powerful documentary series—how could it not be, given the subject matter?—and exquisitely well done. But it’s not an easy watch, and for many who lived through that day, even 25 years might feel a bit too soon to relive those painful memories. (As a former New Yorker who had just moved to DC four months before the attacks, I couldn’t bear to watch more than one episode at a time, and felt pretty wrecked by the end. But nonetheless, I’m glad I persevered.)
“It’s a tough watch, and it is emotional,” said Jones. “But I hope what comes out of the series is a sense that, out of all this tragedy, this was a day when people turned up for each other. There was a human instinct to help each other regardless of what you look like or believe in. People just wanted to help. Personally, I found that incredibly moving.”
9/11: Reunited premieres August 21 on National Geographic. It will be available for streaming on Disney+ and Hulu the following day.

Vieira named new Senegal head coach
- Published
Former Arsenal and France captain Patrick Vieira has been appointed as the new head coach of the Senegal men's national team.
The 50‑year‑old replaces Pape Thiaw, who was sacked in the wake of the country's last‑32 exit at the 2026 Fifa World Cup.
Born in Senegal's capital Dakar, Vieira will now manage the country of his birth, having moved to France aged eight before later winning over 100 caps for Les Bleus and lifting the World Cup in 1998 and the European Championship in 2000.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) said the appointment reflects its "desire to strengthen its high-level technical staff" and is "perfectly aligned" with the nation's sporting ambitions.
Details of Vieria's contract and his starting date in the role are still being discussed.
His first matches in charge of the Teranga Lions are expected to come next month in qualifiers for the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon).
Vieira joins the West Africans after he left his role as Genoa head coach by mutual consent last November, with the team bottom of Serie A.
He won eight and drew nine of his 26 games during the 2024-25 season to guide the Italian club to safety and a 13th-place finish.
However, he left the club after managing just two wins in 25-26, with both of those victories coming in the Coppa Italia.
During his playing career, midfielder Vieira won three Premier League titles and four FA Cups at Arsenal, as well as silverware with AC Milan, Inter Milan and Manchester City.
He retired in 2011 and became the manager of New York City in 2016 before returning to Europe with Nice and leading them to seventh in Ligue 1 in his first season.
Vieira was sacked in December 2020 and became Crystal Palace manager the following year, guiding the Eagles to 12th in the Premier League and the FA Cup semi-finals in 2021-22.
He was dismissed in March 2023 after a 12-game winless run, before joining RC Strasbourg as their first appointment following a takeover by BlueCo, the company which owns Chelsea. He left Strasbourg by mutual consent in July 2024.
His predecessor Thiaw was at the centre of controversy in January when he ushered his Senegal team off the field when Morocco were awarded a stoppage-time penalty in the 2025 Afcon final.
The players eventually returned after a delay of about 17 minutes before Brahim Diaz's penalty was saved and Pape Gueye scored an extra-time winner.
However, Morocco were declared the winners of the tournament in March when the a Confederation of African Football appeals board overturned the result of the final following Senegal's walk-off.
Senegal have lodged an appeal against that decision with the Court of Arbitration for Sport - with the case due to be heard on 8 October.
