While the photo is authentic and shows Trump in Moscow, it is from a visit he took to the Russian capital in 1996, when he was 50. Dubinin was not the nation's ambassador to the U.S. at that time.
Over the years, people have shared an image allegedly showing a 41-year-old Donald Trump during his first visit to Moscow in July 1987. Users' posts claimed Yuri Dubinin, the Soviet Union's ambassador to the U.S., invited Trump to the event. The posts promoted the long-standing claim that the future U.S. president has secret ties with Russia.
The black-and-white picture features Trump standing at a gathering of men in a large room, wearing a tie and overcoat, holding a drink glass and surveying a buffet table.
For example, on Aug. 18, 2026, a Reddit user posted (archived) the image with the caption, "Future reality tv show host, Don Trump, 41 years old, in Moscow at the invitation of Soviet Ambassador to the U.S., Yuri Dubinin. July 1987."
(SteveNtheseagulls accessed via Reddit)
Other users have shared the picture and rumor on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), LinkedIn (archived) and X (archived). Some posts featured additional claims about Trump's plans for a Moscow hotel and his 1988 purchase of the Plaza Hotel in New York, as well as the claim that officials for the KGB — the former Russian secret police and intelligence agency — recruited him as an asset.
Trump's 1987 book "The Art of the Deal" says a Dubinin invitation did take the 41-year-old future president to Moscow for the first time in July 1987, in part to survey sites for potential Trump hotel properties.
Beyond the claim's age and year inaccuracies, no available evidence has credibly and conclusively confirmed Russia secretly recruited Trump as an asset. We previously reported the facts about a former Soviet and Kazakh security official claiming the KGB recruited Trump in 1987, finding no solid proof for the claims.
The Associated Press credited photographer Igor Tabakov with taking the picture in question on Nov. 5, 1996. The AP's caption read, in part, "In this Nov. 5, 1996, file photo, American real estate mogul Donald Trump, left, visits a reception, as he checks out sites in Moscow, Russia, for luxury residential towers."
The rumors presented alongside the photo follow the trail of other Trump and Russia claims, in particular Russian involvement in the 2016 U.S. presidential election. A Republican-led Senate Intelligence Committee report published in 2020 detailed findings on that matter, telling of a "grave counterintelligence threat" and that Trump associates expected to benefit from the Kremlin's help.
This article documents some of the information known about the other claims that have appeared with the picture on social media.
Trump's first visit to Russia in July 1987
In Trump's "The Art of the Deal," the author describes Trump meeting Dubinin at a luncheon, apparently in 1986. The book describes Dubinin's daughter as being familiar with Trump Tower:
A prominent businessman who does a lot of business with the Soviet Union calls to keep me posted on a construction project I'm interested in undertaking in Moscow. The idea got off the ground after I sat next to the Soviet ambassador, Yuri Dubinin, at a luncheon held by Leonard Lauder, a great businessman who is the son of Estee Lauder. Dubinin's daughter, it turned out, had read about Trump Tower and knew all about it. One thing led to another, and now I'm talking about building a large luxury hotel, across the street from the Kremlin, in partnership with the Soviet government. They have asked me to go to Moscow in July.
Later in the book, the author continues, saying Trump flew with his first wife, Ivana Trump, to Moscow on July 4, 1987:
In January 1987, I got a letter from Yuri Dubinin, the Soviet ambassador to the United States, that began: "It is a pleasure for me to relay some good news from Moscow." It went on to say that the leading Soviet state agency for international tourism, Goscomintourist, had expressed interest in pursuing a joint venture to construct and manage a hotel in Moscow. On July 4, I flew with Ivana, her assistant Lisa Calandra, and Norma to Moscow. It was an extraordinary experience. We toured a half dozen potential sites for a hotel, including several near Red Square. We stayed in Lenin's suite at the National Hotel, and I was impressed with the ambition of the Soviet officials to make a deal.
Later that July, Trump reportedly (archived) told the Press of Atlantic City, a New Jersey-based newspaper, that the Moscow trip did not go well, saying he had given up hopes of building a hotel after Russian officials offered only a joint venture with Trump having a minority control of the property.
A Reddit user posted a photo allegedly showing Donald and Ivana Trump standing in Moscow during the July 1987 visit. That post got the city wrong; the photo was taken at St. Petersburg's Palace Square. A Washington Post article captioned the photo as, "Donald Trump and his then-wife, Ivana Trump, visit St. Petersburg in 1987."
(chennai94, accessed via Reddit)
The Plaza Hotel
Users who shared the black-and-white Trump photo captured in 1996 (not 1987, as they claimed) presented the timing of Trump's Plaza Hotel purchase as suspicious.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) alleged, in part, that during Trump's 1987 visit to Russia he received loans from 16 banks and purchased the Plaza Hotel for $407.5 million.
Research in newspaper archives via Newspapers.com located past reporting on that matter.
In 1988, The Business World, a New York Times Magazine publication, reported Trump received a $425 million loan "provided by a consortium of banks led by Citicorp," as well as that he allocated $407.5 million of the total to his purchase of the hotel and 22 Central Park South.
At the time, Trump spokesperson Howard Rubenstein reportedly credited (archived) Trump's interest in purchasing the Plaza Hotel with Trump admiring the property from his office window. "He keeps looking out and seeing things. That's how he got involved in the [Wollman] skating rink, and now this."
In 1995, The New York Times published news of Trump selling the Plaza Hotel to a Saudi Arabian prince and one of Singapore's leading entrepreneurs. According to the article, banks in the U.S. originally lent money to Trump for his 1988 purchase, with banks in Japan holding a mortgage on the property. The story did not mention Moscow or Russia.
Trump's November 1996 Moscow trip
On Nov. 7, 1996, USA Today reported (archived) Trump as telling The Moscow Times about his trip to Russia, "We're looking at building a super-luxury residential tower, which I think Moscow desperately wants and needs."
The newspaper printed the article two days after Tabakov captured the black-and-white photo of Trump and nearly a decade after his first visit to Moscow.
Voice of America and The Washington Post published further reporting providing more details of Trump's past pursuits to expand his real estate empire in Russia.

Ferrari delay in moving Leclerc costly - Hamilton
- Published
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari's delay in moving team-mate Charles Leclerc out of his way could have cost him second place at Sunday's Dutch Grand Prix.
Hamilton finished fourth in Zandvoort, with Mercedes taking second and third - championship leader Kimi Antonelli finishing as runner-up after his Mercedes team-mate George Russell was ordered to let him past.
Hamilton came up behind Leclerc mid-race when he was on fresher tyres and asked to be let through so he could optimise his race against the Mercedes drivers.
But after asking Leclerc to pit, the Monegasque resisted, was left out for a further lap, and then ordered to come in again.
Hamilton said over the radio at the time: "Great way of wasting time, guys. Great job."
Hamilton later caught Russell in the closing stages of the race but ran out of time to pass him, his attempts hindered by a late virtual safety car.
McLaren's Lando Norris won the race.
Hamilton, who is 59 points behind championship leader Antonelli, said the race was "definitely frustrating".

"I'm here to win and i think this team can win," Hamilton said.
"We couldn't win this race but to win championships you have to pick up every point and the last few races have been difficult with penalties and stuff.
"And then today I lost several seconds behind Charles, which I think ultimately could have made the difference in the end.
"My goal is to try and lead this team to the championship. We've got some work to do, for sure."
He contrasted Ferrari's actions with those of Mercedes.
With Russell in second, and caught by his team-mate Antonelli and the two Ferraris behind, Mercedes ordered the Briton out of the way of his team-mate late in the race. That was to ensure Antonelli lost no time and consolidated second place.
Hamilton said: "What's clear is I'm looking at them and seeing Mercedes. They executed. They got the car, they are fighting for the championship and did it straight away.

"We didn't want to tell [Hamilton] the strategy at this stage, because we didn't want to disclose it to the competitors, because we wanted to keep him on track until the end [of the race].
"He was able to keep Antonelli behind him, and I think it would have been the right call. Charles was supposed to pit. We extended one lap, and it was a kind of confusion, but I'm not worried about this - everybody will be back in the briefing, they will have a clear picture about the race."
Hamilton also urged Ferrari to upgrade their engine as soon as possible.
"The one thing I'm definitely really proud of the team for bringing an upgrade here this weekend.," he said.
"We are getting closer to them, but it's just half a season we've been down in power.
"We really need to pick up the power if we're going to be anywhere near trying to fight for them, closing the gap to them."
He said Ferrari were losing 0.4secs on the straights to Mercedes at Zandvoort.

India is home to more than 1.4 billion people, thousands of communities, hundreds of languages, and five major language families. Many communities have historically practised endogamy and in some regions, consanguineous marriage. This is both a social and a biological fact with medical consequences. India is not one genetic population. Indians carry a layered inheritance shaped by ancient migration, mixing, isolation, ecology, language, culture and marriage patterns.
Our political map shows States and districts. Our genetic map often shows boundaries shaped by communities that lived near each other but did not always marry into each other. This matters, because genes influence inherited diseases, drug response, disease risk prediction, and the success of screening programmes.
Ancient layers
There is no single Indian genome. The oldest layer of Indian ancestry goes back to early modern humans who reached South Asia tens of thousands of years ago. This ancient ancestry forms the deep foundation of the subcontinent’s population history. Later came other ancestry layers linked to populations associated with the Iranian plateau, the Indus Valley world, Steppe pastoralists, and Tibeto-Burman-speaking groups. These movements were not like a single flood covering the whole land evenly. They came through different doors, at different times, and settled into different social worlds. That is why a Punjabi agrarian group, a Tamil caste group, a tribal population in Central India, a North-Eastern community, and an indigenous island community from the Andaman and Nicobar Islands cannot be treated as genetically identical. Some remote island populations preserve deeply distinctive ancestral lineages because of long isolation. But even here, caution is needed. No living community is a fossil.
Genetics can complicate community pride. A community may have a strong language, faith, identity, regional history, or story of origin. These identities matter. They give people belonging. But genes do not always obey the neat boundaries of culture. A group may preserve a language or ritual for centuries while carrying ancestry from multiple ancient sources. Two neighbouring communities may share a landscape but remain genetically distinct because they did not intermarry. Another two groups may speak different languages but share some older ancestry. Cultural continuity does not require genetic purity. It is a story of movement, mixture, separation, adaptation, and memory.
Marriage and disease patterns
After ancient mixing, many Indian communities became socially closed. Endogamy–marriage within a social group, and consanguinity–marriage between biological relatives, became the norm. Both can increase the chance that two parents carry the same rare recessive disease variant. We inherit two copies of most genes, one from the mother and one from the father, and in recessive diseases, a person with one altered copy remains healthy (called a carrier), while persons with two altered copies get the disease. If two carriers of the same disease-causing variant have a child, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of producing an affected child. This is why a child can be born with a serious genetic disease even when both parents are healthy. The family may have no known disease history, but the risk gene may have travelled silently through generations.
When a small community remains genetically closed for centuries, a rare variant present in an ancestor can become more common among descendants. This is called the ‘founder effect’. This is central to India’s public health future. Sickle cell disease is more common among several tribal populations in Central, Western, and Southern India. This pattern reflects old malaria pressure, population structures, and local history. Thalassaemia and other haemoglobin disorders also show region-specific and community-specific patterns. Some metabolic disorders, neuromuscular conditions, inherited hearing disorders, and rare recessive conditions may cluster in particular groups.
The correct message is that specific populations may carry specific risks, and knowing those risks can prevent suffering. Genetics should not be used to label communities; it should be used to guide screening, counselling, diagnosis, and care.
Testing and counselling
Genetic testing without counselling can do harm. A carrier may wrongly think that they are diseased. A family may blame the mother. A marriage proposal may be rejected because a test result is misunderstood. A whole community may feel stigmatised. This is why genetic counselling is not an ornamental part of modern medicine. It is the ethical bridge between a laboratory report and a family decision. Good counselling explains risk without panic. It tells people that being a carrier is common and usually harmless. It helps couples understand reproductive choices. It protects autonomy. It avoids coercion. Carrier screening, when voluntary and confidential, can help couples know their risks before the birth of an affected child. Newborn screening can identify treatable disorders early. Better rare disease diagnosis can end the long and exhausting journey that many families face, moving from one hospital to another without an answer.
Data gap
India does not yet have a large, deeply characterised, health-linked biobank comparable to resources such as the U.K. Biobank. Such a resource would not merely store DNA. It would connect genetic data with health records, laboratory results, imaging, drug response, and long-term outcomes. It would include India’s internal diversity, not only convenient urban samples. It would also require trust, consent, privacy protection, community engagement, and strong ethical governance.
Large population datasets can help identify new disease mechanisms and molecular targets for new medicines. This gap matters. A genetic risk score for diabetes or heart disease developed mainly in European populations may not work accurately in Indian populations. A drug-response marker common in one ancestry group may be uncommon in another. A rare disease variant important in one Indian community may be missed if reference databases are dominated by non-Indian genomes. Precision medicine will remain imprecise if the populations behind it are mismatched.
Mapping medical futures
India’s genetic mosaic is not merely an ancestry story, but a medical map. It can help prevent inherited diseases, improve newborn screening, guide safer prescribing, diagnose rare disorders earlier, and support drug discovery. But the map must be read carefully. Genetics should not be used to make claims of purity, rank communities, or frighten families. Its value lies in the responsibility to turn knowledge into care.
The Indian genome is not a single national portrait. It is a mosaic made of many tiles some ancient, some recent, some widely shared, and some found in small communities and still barely studied. Medicine now has the tools to read this mosaic. Our task is to read it responsibly, without cultural arrogance, without stigma, and without delay.

New Tata boss to face formidable challenges
- Published
The shock resignation of Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran earlier this month has left corporate India's top job vacant. But finding his successor will be no easy task for the country's most revered conglomerate, whose sprawling $300bn empire spans Jaguar Land Rover and Air India as well as manufacturing iPhones for Apple.
Chandrasekaran resigned amid a deadlock over his reappointment and a widening rift with Tata Trusts - the charity arm which owns controlling shares of the unlisted commercial holding company.
The disagreements are said to have centred over a public listing of Tata Sons as well as capital allocation for the group's various new unlisted businesses, including semiconductors, e-commerce and aviation, all of which are bleeding money.
The group has been in the middle of the largest ever capital investment cycle, with tens of billions of dollars being deployed on everything from building India's first chip fabrication plant to manufacturing EV batteries and turning around Air India, which the Tatas bought from the government in 2022.
The new person at the helm will need to have an ability to assess and absorb the risks that have come with this breakneck expansion as well as rise up to numerous other challenges, Hetal Dalal from Institutional Investor Advisor Services (IiAS), a governance advisory firm, told the BBC.
"It is an incredibly difficult role not just for the individual who will get it but also for the selection committee to find someone. It requires a multitude of skillsets and experience from managing the Tata Trusts to the Tata Sons board, understanding various new businesses and being able to also have strong relationships with regulators and the government," Dalal said.
"There aren't many people running such large, diversified conglomerates. And will they leave their current roles to join the Tata Group?"
The complexity of the role has risen in recent years as the "collective losses of the new businesses are more than the cashflow generated by older companies like TCS, the group's software arm whose business model has been challenged by AI”, Nirmalya Kumar, who previously headed strategy at Tata Sons, told the BBC.
TCS has been the group's cash cow, contributing to some 85% of cash flows, but is no longer the pillar of support it once was.
According to Dalal, even though losses at privately held companies have mounted, the performance of publicly traded, CEO-run Tata companies has been strong.
The group has a good bench strength of internal candidates who could throw their hats in the ring. Yet, finding a candidate who's a straight "plug and play fit" will be difficult, she says.
"I think any person who comes in will have a set of skills and experience, but must be also groomed for the role."
Kumar, on the other hand, isn't convinced the internal names doing the rounds will fit the bill.
"The people internally are good executors of existing business models. Companies like Tata Steel and Tata Motors are almost running on auto-pilot with a CEO in charge. The new chairman will have to understand new business models of the four unlisted businesses that are losing money," he said.
For investors, the resignation is likely to usher in a period of prolonged uncertainty.
New leadership will bring a change in strategic direction at the group in terms of how a new chairman approaches the ambitious expansion Chandrasekharan undertook, say experts.
"Some of the bleeding businesses will need a strategic plan to be made profitable. [The new person] will need to decide whether to scale back or exit some investments," says Dalal.
Kumar says they will also need to communicate a clear plan to the market on how much further investment is needed and when a break-even is expected on these ambitious bets.
But most importantly, he adds, the focus will have to be on "driving alignment between the Trusts [the dominant shareholder] and Tata Sons".
The group's most successful run was under JRD Tata and Ratan Tata, when the relationship between the biggest shareholder and the operating company was frictionless as they were at the helm of both entities.
It broke down under Cyrus Mistry when there was a separation of the roles. Chandrasekharan's exit is the second instance where the chairman has resigned because of the rocky relationship with the Trusts.
The fact that the principal shareholder was not aligned on business strategy was perhaps a fundamental problem in the relationship breaking down, Mukund Rajan, former brand custodian at Tata Sons, told, external India Today news channel.
"You cannot have companies being run where the majority shareholder is either feeling ignored or not aligned with the way the company will be run going forward," Rajan said.
Repairing this relationship will have to be a key priority for whoever is next in the driving seat.
For now, the ongoing turmoil has dented the group's brand image, say experts.
Clear communication has been a major challenge with the Tatas, which does not bode well for the public markets, according to Dalal. While the holding company can argue that it is not publicly traded, what happens there has a direct impact on shareholders of the listed Tata universe, she adds.
"The priority should not be the volume of communication but about reducing uncertainty," Minari Shah, a communications advisor who previously worked with Tata Motors, told the BBC.
"That means demonstrating that governance mechanisms are working, reassuring stakeholders that business continuity is unaffected and providing clarity around the process for leadership transition. It is okay not to have all the answers immediately, as long as stakeholders have confidence that the disagreeing parties are in dialogue."
As of now, nearly two weeks after Chandrasekharan's resignation there have been no detailed public statements on either a succession roadmap, or the way ahead from either Tata Sons or Tata Trusts.
The former's annual general meeting also had to be adjourned because of a lack of quorum, leaving several governance and succession related decisions under a cloud at exactly the moment when shareholders of India's most iconic company will be looking for the greatest clarity.

India’s campaign at the FIH Men’s Hockey World Cup 2026 is on the brink, but a narrow route to the semifinals remains open ahead of its must-win Pool E clash against Argentina at Wagener Stadium, Amstelveen, on Monday, August 24.
How India Can Qualify
1. India must beat Argentina by at least two goals
This is non-negotiable.
A two-goal win takes India above Argentina on goals scored.
A win by three or more puts India ahead on goal difference.
Anything less than a two-goal win eliminates India.
For example, a 3-1 win for India keeps the qualification door open.
2. The Netherlands must beat England by at least three goals
This is the crucial second half of the equation.
If India wins 3-1, its final tally would read:
Goals scored: 6
Goals conceded: 8
Goal difference: -2
If the Netherlands beats England 3-0, England would finish with:
Goals scored: 5
Goals conceded: 8
Goal difference: -3
India would therefore finish above England on goal difference.
The simplest path: India beat Argentina by two goals + Netherlands beat England by three or more goals = India through.
The State of Play
India goes into the match bottom of Pool E without a point after a 1-3 loss to host the Netherlands, leaving it with a goal difference of -4 (3 scored, 7 conceded). Argentina’s 3-1 win over England on Saturday kept the group alive for India, and left England and Argentina level on three points apiece. The Netherlands leads the pool with six points and has already sealed its semifinal berth.
England faces the Netherlands at 10:30 p.m. IST, four hours after India takes on Argentina at 6:30 p.m. That gives England the advantage of knowing exactly what it needs to do to qualify.

Russia's second-biggest online retailer targeted in Ukrainian strikes
- Published
Warehouses belonging to Russia's second-largest online retailer have been hit by a wave of Ukrainian drone strikes.
Ozon said its logistics facilities in the southern regions of Krasnodar, Dagestan, Stavropol and Adygea were on fire and several people had been injured following overnight strikes.
Ukraine has for weeks struck sites belonging to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, describing the firm as a legitimate target because it supplied components to the military, which Moscow denies.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday that Ukraine had opened "Pandora's box" by striking economic targets and that Russia would hit back at Kyiv's "most sensitive economic sectors".
Russia has targeted Ukraine's civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, and recent Russian attacks have hit Ukrainian warehouses and cargo terminals.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Ozon said "a fire broke out" at a logistics centre in Makhachkala, in the southern region of Dagestan, following a drone attack at around 05:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on Monday.
The company said earlier that a "major fire" was burning at one of its logistics centres in the city of Krasnodar, 700km (435 miles) to the east of the Dagestan site.
Russia's defence ministry said three children had been killed in Krasnodar following a Ukrainian drone attack. Russia's children's rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova said they were aged 13, 15 and 16, while six more children had been taken to hospital.

Meanwhile, Ozon workers in Adygeysk, in the Adygea region, and Nevinnomyssk, in the Stavropol region, have been evacuated.
Videos posted on social media of the Ozon attacks have been verified by the BBC. One shows a drone hitting a warehouse in the Orenburg region, while another shows a large plume of smoke and flames rising from its warehouse in Dagestan.
Shares in Ozon fell by as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday morning, while shares in its major shareholder, private equity firm AFK Sistema, fell by almost 13%.
When asked on Monday whether the Russian government would provide state support to Ozon, the Kremlin said it was "working with business representatives to develop various options for providing support in this difficult situation".
The overnight strikes comes a day after Ozon's site in the Samara region was hit. The company said a number of its workers had been injured.
Following that strike, Ukraine's defence ministry said on Saturday: "Systematic strikes on dual-use goods storage centres complicate the enemy's logistics and negatively affect the Russian economy as a whole.
"After Ukrainian units hit 15 of the largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it was Ozon's turn."
Meanwhile, in Ukraine's Odesa region, overnight strikes targeted food storage facilities and energy infrastructure leading to five people being injured, the region's head Oleg Kiper said on Telegram.
Founded in 1998, Ozon is one of Russia's first online retailers. The company is second only to Wildberries in terms of scale and presence, with its pick-up posts and delivery boxes stationed across the country.
Both the Ozon and Wildberries logos are often seen together in Russia at shared pick-up points.
The targeting of these online retailers has had the effect of bringing the war closer to ordinary Russians.
Both companies have been described as "Russia's Amazon" and it is estimated that they are used by 85-90% of Russia's economically active population.
In many remote places lacking accessible shops, Russians depend on them for much of their clothes and household appliances.
But unlike Amazon, which sells goods directly alongside its marketplace business, Wildberries and Ozon act almost entirely as marketplaces, connecting independent sellers with buyers across Russia, storing and delivering their goods and handling payments.
This means many of the losses incurred in the attacks have been borne by those businesses.
The Kremlin has denied that online platforms are used for army supplies.

As USS Lincoln heads home, mental health experts tally the stressors of life at sea
The USS Abraham Lincoln — which has been participating in U.S. military operations in the war with Iran — is now on its way home. The roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard that ship have spent a grueling nine months at sea with little relief.
Reports have emerged of deteriorating conditions — and of deteriorating mental health, including apparent attempts by crewmembers to jump overboard. The Navy has not confirmed those reports and NPR has not independently verified them. "A small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life," Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said in a statement last week.
Experts say while the physical circumstances are difficult, a lack of careful and consistent messaging from leadership at the highest levels also contributed to the crews' mental distress.
The USS Lincoln is like a small city, according to Armen Kurdian, a retired U.S. Navy captain who served aboard the aircraft carrier in 2005. The labor aboard the carrier, he says, can be uniquely physical and difficult.
" It takes a toll on your body," says Kurdian. "The plane captains are out there on the flight deck — you know, these 18-, 19-, 20-year-olds lugging these 100-pound chains on their backs in 120-degree weather."
He describes dehydration and exhaustion as pilots have to take off and land on the carriers, sometimes at night and in bad weather, and "then just being mentally prepared to go fly because lives are at stake."
In the off-hours, Kurdian says there is little to no privacy, with people sleeping in crowded quarters.
While difficult, these conditions can be bearable, he adds. But experts say once uncertainty is thrown into this equation, it can push people to their mental brink.
Jack Stuster is a retired behavioral scientist who spent decades studying human performance.
"In conditions of isolation and confinement," says Stuster, "one of the worst things that you could do to the person is to tell them they're gonna come home at a certain time, and then you say, 'No. It's gonna be delayed.'"
Return is overdue
The Abraham Lincoln's deployment was originally scheduled to end in May.
In addition to the Navy, Stuster worked with NASA and scientists operating in small groups in places like Greenland, where return flights home were often canceled at the very last moment — even after their would-be passengers had dragged their duffle bags right up to the flight line.
" People have described to me going out there for the third time … only to be told that it wasn't gonna happen," says Stuster, which caused them "to break down in tears."
Then there's the issue of duration. A three-month deployment is ideal, says Stuster, or even six. At nine months, he says, things start to become untenable.
Dr. Phillip Hunt was for years a Navy physician who deployed on several submarine missions. His background is in emergency medicine, but Hunt says in the Navy much of what he treated was mental health. " I was kind of the father confessor, psychologist, what have you," says Hunt.
With a crew of 5,000 people on a ship, Hunt says it's inevitable that some people will struggle with mental health — even in the best of deployment conditions. "You'd have guys getting anxious. You'd have guys getting depressed."
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says reports of poor conditions aboard the Lincoln are overstated. President Trump recently called the deployment "not nearly long enough."
Hunt says a lack of certainty or reassurance from leadership at the highest levels can trickle down to impact everyone's mental well-being. "Denial of this unit's deteriorating operational conditions is highly detrimental to the crew's morale," says Hunt. "The result can include anger, anxiety, or eventually mental exhaustion and depression."
Hunt says he blames leadership at the highest levels for the lack of recognition of this hardship.
" I just, I feel so badly for that crew. It's just tragic," says Hunt. "Just thinking about them almost brings me to tears."
If you or someone you know is struggling with their mental health, please call or text the number 9-8-8 to connect with a counselor.

This affordable fix may be all you need to improve earbud sound quality
Improved noise canceling and punchier bass? Yes, please.
Apple's courageous decision to drop the 3.5mm headphone jack in 2016 seems to have worked in the company's favor. The AirPods are by far the most popular truly wireless earbuds globally. Competition has also caught up in terms of sound quality and features, and it's generally pretty difficult to end up with a bad pair of wireless earbuds these days. With most higher-end offerings touting active noise cancellation, lossless audio codecs and customizable EQ settings, the purchase decision often comes down to comfort and ecosystem benefits.
Most truly wireless earbuds ship with ear tips that are made of silicone. It's a material that's cheap to manufacture and flexible enough to accommodate a wide range of ear shapes. Manufacturers often throw in two more pairs of ear tips in different sizes to maximize the chances of users finding a fit that works. Unfortunately, human ears come in a vast range of shapes and sizes. In fact, a multi-ethnic study involving more than 1,400 people found that the human ear is a reliable biometric identifier, not unlike a fingerprint.
Besides not providing a secure and comfortable fit, the wrong set of ear tips can also negatively impact sound quality. Unlike over-ear headphones that create a wider seal around your ears, earbuds rely almost entirely on the ear tips to form a proper seal. If it's not a good fit, sound can leak out, and outside noise can get in. This results in weaker bass and noticeably poorer noise cancellation performance.
Foam ear tips are the solution
Silicone ear tips are easier to clean and can last virtually as long as the actual earbuds do, but they shouldn't be your first choice if you're looking for the best comfort. There are a handful of renowned third-party manufacturers that sell foam ear tips. If you use memory foam pillows or insoles, you know what I'm getting at. Unlike silicone ear tips that come in a few preset sizes at best, foam tips expand to match the shape of your ear canal and create a much better seal.
I'm one among the lucky souls who don't have a problem with how most earbuds fit. When I picked up a pair of AirPods Pro 2, though, I decided to go all out and replace the stock silicone ear tips with a set of memory foam alternatives. The first thing I noticed was how much of a better fit they provided. I was no longer adjusting my AirPods every few minutes to keep them in place. The bigger difference, however, was how much more punchy the bass felt.
Now, switching over to foam tips won't magically make your earbuds sound better, but by minimizing sound leakage, they can help music sound fuller and more impactful without you having to crank the volume all the way up. Since foam ear tips create a tighter seal, they dramatically improve passive noise isolation. Not only does this help improve the performance of active noise cancellation when you turn it on, but it also makes it so you don't have to rely on ANC as much in the first place.
How to pick the right earbud tips
Comply and Sonicfoam are two reputable brands you can shop from, but make sure you check compatibility with your earbuds first. For instance, AirPods feature a proprietary snap-fit mechanism that requires a specific type of ear tip. Though Engadget has not formally tested them, I can personally vouch for the quality of the memory foam ear tips that Sonicfoam sells — I've been using them for over two years now.
Foam ear tips have their fair share of downsides, though. For starters, they wear out rather quickly. If you use your wireless earbuds every day, you can expect your foam ear tips to last around two to three months, although they start losing their ability to fully expand well before that. They also tend to get dirty and attract dust more easily than silicone tips.
Pricing can range from $10 to $40, depending on the brand and the number of ear tips included in the package. Once you've found a pair of foam ear tips that work well for you, it's worth checking if the brand sells refill packs that contain only your preferred size. This way, you don't spend money on smaller or larger ear tips that you'll never use.
Foam ear tips also make it quite clear when it's time for a replacement. If you pinch them and they don't expand as well, they're not going to create the same tight seal in your ear canal. Ideally, you'd also replace them when you notice any visible deformation or damage. A final helpful tip: It's best if you clean them regularly. I've made it a habit to give mine a quick wipe before each use since any buildup of earwax or skin oils can leave them smelling less than pleasant over time.

We then reviewed Swami Ramdev’s official social media handles (here, here, and here), but found no record of him making the alleged statement.
We also reviewed the official website and social media handles (here, here, and here) of Navbharat Times, whose watermark appears on the viral graphic. However, we found no report or post carrying the alleged quote.
We found posts featuring statements by Swami Ramdev on NBT’s platforms (here, here, and here). The viral postcard appears to have been created by editing one of these original postcards. It appears that the text in this section has been edited and replaced. The comparison can be seen below.
On 21 August 2026, Navbharat Times (NBT) refuted the viral claim in a post on X (archived), stating that several fake posts using NBT’s name had been circulating on social media in recent days to spread misleading and false information. NBT urged users to rely only on its official social media handles and platforms for authentic news and information.
To sum up, this viral NBT graphic alleging that Swami Ramdev praised the Congress party and apologised for previously tarnishing its image is fake.

- The claim that U.S. President Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp is a cancer survivor cannot be independently verified by Snopes. Because Snopes looks for primary sourcing and evidence to rate our claims, we are leaving this claim unrated.
- The rumor stems from social media posts criticizing a senator for referencing Harp while mocking Trump in August 2026. These posts said Harp was a cancer survivor, while other posts argued there's no proof of that claim.
- The claim that Harp had cancer is based on her own accounts of her experience battling a rare bone cancer, which she wrote and spoke about in 2019 and 2020. In Harp's account, she was told she'd have to wait for certain treatment options to be approved before she could continue treatment after failing two chemotherapies and being rejected from a clinical trial for an investigational drug. Harp credits Trump's right-to-try law, signed during his first term, for enabling her to be treated with an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug that wasn't approved for use in treating her cancer.
- Based on the available evidence, much of Harp's experience, as told by her, is realistic and believable. Bone cancers in general are rare and often resistant to chemotherapies. Immunotherapy drugs, which are still relatively new and frequently researched, are a promising possible treatment for many bone cancers. Many such treatments are not yet approved for use for treating bone cancers because the cancers are rare and difficult to treat.
- However, there are a few details, largely in her descriptions of cause and effect, that could potentially be inaccurate, based on our research. For example, she credits Trump's right-to-try law for saving her life, when her description of the drug that finally made a difference for her better aligns with a drug that she would've been able to access through an FDA system that has existed for decades.
- Snopes reached out to the White House by email to ask if it could share details about Harp's history with cancer that could potentially be verifiable, such as the name of the drug used in her treatment. The White House did not answer our questions.
In August 2026, news reporting about one of U.S. President Donald Trump's aides, Natalie Harp, intensified, particularly after Sen. Jon Ossoff , D-Ga., referenced her in criticism of Trump, drawing increased attention to the once little-known aide.
Many conservative figures then criticized Ossoff for referencing Harp, who they said was a cancer survivor, in his attacks on Trump. For example, one X post (archived) said, "Harp is a 35-year-old cancer survivor who works in the White House. Ossoff chose to make her part of an anti-Trump attack because he thought it would score points with the Democrat base and generate attention."
The claim surfaced elsewhere on X (archived) and Facebook (archived). Other social media posts (archived) cast doubt on whether Harp ever really had cancer. Some Snopes readers searched the site or sent emails asking whether it was true that Harp was a cancer survivor.
Harp first rose to fame by sharing her account of suffering from Stage 2 bone cancer and how a Trump-signed "right-to-try" law apparently saved her life. Snopes cannot independently verify Harp's account and medical history, so we're unable to rate this claim true or false.
However, we can compare the details of Harp's account with the current medical research available to get a sense of which details, if any, may sound unrealistic in her story.
Harp's account
Harp's claims about her history with bone cancer came from a LinkedIn blog post she wrote and an interview with Fox News in June 2019, as well as a speech she gave at the Republican National Convention in August 2020.
The LinkedIn post, her earliest public description of her experience with cancer, didn't give any details about the specific cancer she was diagnosed with except that it was rare.
She shared slightly more detail two days later in her appearance on Fox News. Brian Kilmeade, co-host of "Fox & Friends," opened the interview (0:04) by saying Harp had Stage 2 cancer. Harp went on to say her illness was terminal (2:10), Kilmeade Said Harp had Stage 2 of a rare bone cancer (2:18) and Harp confirmed she was "the youngest person in this rare bone cancer" she had (2:52).
The cancer diagnosis is not where Harp has begun any of her accounts, however; instead, she has frequently highlighted a medical error she suffered before that.
"On November 9, 2015 — a year to the day Donald Trump would win the presidency — a nurse mixed up my IV with the deadly substance of sterile water leaving me housebound and searching for care," Harp wrote on LinkedIn. She said her physicians offered her medications for managing pain and even Death With Dignity instead of diagnosing her condition.
On Fox News, she said it took two years for doctors to figure out what was wrong with her. Harp also said in that interview that this medical error is one that "no one has survived" (0:52). At the Republican National Convention, Harp said (0:38) she was a victim of a "notoriously deadly medical error," but survived "only to be diagnosed with a rare and terminal bone cancer." Harp then presented the care she was offered afterwards, which is in contrast to her other accounts in which she described receiving these offerings prior to diagnosis of the cancer.
Notably, the web article Fox News published alongside the video of the interview said Harp "has battled stage 2 bone cancer for most of her life," even though the above descriptions make it sound like her struggles with the cancer developed in the several years prior to that interview.
In all of her accounts, Harp described the available chemotherapies failing to address her cancer and being denied participation in clinical trials. At the Republican National Convention, she claimed (1:22) that no one wanted her in their clinical trials because she'd "make them look bad" after failing the chemotherapies.
Harp said her doctor told her she'd have to suffer through symptoms for either several more months (LinkedIn) or more than a year (Fox News interview, 2:43) for the next round of FDA approvals for the clinical trial drugs she was denied.
She wrote that her doctor did not tell her she had other options, so she went to another doctor who was willing to try a different approach: prescribing an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug for an unapproved use. She credits that experimental treatment for her recovery, and Trump's Right to Try Act for that treatment even though she acknowledged that some may argue it was repetitive of existing law.
Snopes emailed the White House to ask if it could share more verifiable details about Harp's experience, such as which unapproved drug was used in her treatment, but 
Right-to-try law
The right-to-try law Harp credits for saving her life essentially allows patients to access drugs without FDA approval for treatment in specific circumstances. According to the law's text, an eligible patient can consent to the use of an "eligible investigational drug" that has completed a Phase 1 clinical trial and "has not been approved or licensed for any use." The drug manufacturer is allowed to decide it won't permit the patient to access the unapproved drug.
A contradiction between the law and Harp's story immediately jumps out. The right-to-try law applies specifically to drugs that have not been approved for any use, but Harp claimed her lifesaving treatment was an FDA-approved immunotherapy drug being used for an unapproved use.
Such a drug could still theoretically be used to treat Harp's condition under a different process that existed prior to the Right to Try Act: expanded access. Expanded access also allows patients who have exhausted all other treatment options for a serious or life-threatening condition to use an investigational drug instead. Investigational drugs eligible for use in expanded access have not been approved by the FDA "for their specific use."
FDA researchers wrote that the agency has been facilitating access to investigational drugs since the 1970s, and regulations describing the pathways to accessing these unapproved drugs have existed since 1987.
A chart by Triage Cancer, a nonprofit organization focused on practical and legal issues that may affect cancer patients, both expanded access and right-to-try require a physician and the drug manufacturer to approve a request to use an unapproved drug. Expanded access also requires approval from the Institutional Review Board and the FDA, which right to try does not.
FDA data says that between fiscal years 2019 and 2023, the FDA approved anywhere between 97.1% to 100% of expanded access requests, depending on the year and the type of request.
Harp's description of events suggests that her physician, and potentially drug manufacturers, would not approve her request for expanded access. Such obstacles would also to be an issue for Harp under the right-to-try law; based on her story, it sounds like Harp became able to use an unapproved drug treatment because she got a new doctor, not because of the new law.
Comparing Harp's story to actual research
While Harp's story may be vague on specifics such as names and dates, it does have enough details to compare it to reality.
In 2008, the Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority reported that bags of sterile water were being mistaken for IV solutions because of similar appearance, and that these mistakes were capable of causing serious harm to patients, sometimes even killing them.
It's unclear whether Harp suggested that such a medical error led to the development of her cancer, but in any case, Snopes could find no evidence that such a mistake could cause cancer. According to the Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority, the IV error is dangerous is because sterile water can cause red blood cells to break down too soon.
Based on the report's description of a patient who survived the sterile water injection, others have survived the medical error that Harp claimed no one else had survived. The less-extreme version of Harp's claim, in which she calls the error "notoriously deadly," is accurate.
Bone cancers are rare in general, and there are many different specific kinds of bone cancers. The American Cancer Society even suggests seeking out clinical trials because these cancers are rare and difficult to treat.
In fact, the University College London wrote that bone cancers are frequently resistant to chemotherapy. The American Cancer Society says that "in recent years" researchers have developed non-chemo drugs, including immunotherapy drugs, to help treat some bone cancers.
The Cancer Research Institute says that while surgery is often the main treatment method for early-stage bone cancers, immunotherapies may be used in treating more advanced or far-reaching forms of the cancer.
The FDA first approved an immune checkpoint inhibitor, the kind of immunotherapy drug often used for treating these cancers, in 2011, according to the Osteosarcoma Institute. (Osteosarcoma is a type of bone cancer.) The institute says no new treatment options for the cancer have been approved in 40 years.
The research above does suggest that much of Harp's story about her battle with cancer is plausible. Bone cancers are rare, so it's expected that whatever kind of bone cancer she'd have would be rare itself. Many bone cancers are resistant to chemotherapy, which would explain why Harp failed such treatments twice.
It also makes sense that the unapproved treatment she and her doctor tried would be an immunotherapy drug. Cancer research organizations point to immunotherapy drugs as a promising avenue for treating some forms of bone cancer. New immunotherapy treatments are still emerging today, and so it wouldn't be surprising if the drug wasn't yet approved 10 years ago.
On top of all of that, the rarity of bone cancers can make it difficult for emerging treatments to be tested with large enough sample sizes in trials to quickly move through the approval process.
For further reading, Snopes has recently fact-checked a number of claims about Harp, including whether an image of her and Trump in a helicopter is authentic.

Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is no longer just a problem of hospital-acquired or health care-associated infections. Clinicians in Keralam are worried that the resistance profile of primary antibiotics used to treat even acute diarrhoeal diseases like Shigellosis is going up, which has important implications for antibiotic use in the State.
Data from Keralam’s KARS-NET (Kerala Antimicrobial Resistance Surveillance Network), one of the strongest AMR surveillance systems in the country and which has been tracking the AMR profile of Shigellosis since 2023, says that the resistance profile of primary antibiotics used to treat the infection is growing.
Increased resistance
Ciprofloxacin, which continues to be included in national guidelines for treatment of Shigella dysentery and which used to be an important treatment option for bacterial dysentery, has a resistance profile of 96% and can no longer be relied upon for empirical treatment of Shigellosis.
What is worrying is that pathogenic resistance to the next available drug, Ceftriaxone, a third-generation Cephalosporin class antibiotic, has also gone up to 36% as per KARS-Net data.
“Till now, community-acquired AMR had not been a problem in the State. If you, as a citizen, have never been worried about AMR, you should be now, because it is showing up right at your doorstep. Our arsenal of effective and affordable antibiotics for common infections in the community is shrinking,” points out R. Aravind, head of infectious diseases, Government Medical College, Thiruvananthapuram, who is also the convener of KARS-Net.
Most acute diarrhoeal diseases are self-limiting and do not really require treatment with antibiotics. Shigellosis, too, is largely self-resolving with proper rehydration but in vulnerable populations (children below five years and the elderly), the infection can lead to severe dehydration, sepsis and neurological complications, requiring the use of antibiotics.
Shigella is primarily an enteric/community pathogen, which spreads from person to person through contaminated food and water and is thus a sentinel organism for detecting what is happening to AMR in the community.
“Clinicians have been using Ceftriaxone for treating Shigellosis in patients who get admitted to hospital. But the clinical implication of growing resistance of Shigella to this drug is immense. For Shigellosis patients with severe dysentery going into septic shock and multiorgan failure, it is absolutely important that the correct antibiotic is administered within an hour and that it is 100% sensitive. This means that for such serious patients, we can no longer depend on Ceftriaxone and have to go for high-end drugs like Meropenem which belongs to the Carbapenem class, widely considered the last-resort antibiotics,” explains Dr. Aravind.
Major outbreak
Shigellosis is reported sporadically from all districts in Keralam every year. But the State reported one of the major outbreaks ever in June this year, when 225 cases and six deaths were reported from Kozhikode, Malappuram and Wayanad districts.
The fact that loss of lives was unusually high this year should be read alongside the information about the rising AMR profile of Shigellosis, clinicians warn, even when there is no exact data to say that AMR led to the death of patients.
Emergence, a decade ago
Keralam documented multidrug-resistant Shigella and ESBL-producing strains more than a decade ago, signalling the emergence of Ceftriaxone resistance. ESBL-producing strains are bacteria that release Extended Spectrum Beta Lactamases enzymes, which can break down important third-generation antibiotics, rendering them ineffective.
The 2018 study published by clinicians in Government Medical College, Alappuzha, which studied the antibiotic susceptibility pattern of Shigella isolates (2011-2016) had reported that 91.6% of the isolates were multi-drug resistant and that eight of the isolates were resistant to Ceftriaxone/Cefotaxime. It had also reported that five isolates produced ESBL enzymes, making third-generation Cephalosporins less effective. This was one of the first studies from Keralam that had given a clear indication that AMR was no longer confined to just the older drugs.
What it means for patients
Rising drug resistance means more treatment failures, longer hospital stays, greater use of high-end antibiotics and increased health-care costs, apart from the threat that more drug-resistant pathogens might emerge in the community.
“Most cases of acute diarrhoea do not require antibiotics. But even when antibiotics are genuinely indicated, particularly for severe bacillary dysentery caused by Shigella, our treatment options are steadily narrowing. This is certainly a wake-up call for everyone that we need to be very careful about using antibiotics,” a senior health official points out.

Arbeloa v Alonso: Benitez on his former players turned managers
- Published
When former Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez is asked whether he had expected his then-players Xabi Alonso and Alvaro Arbeloa to become managers, his response is brutally honest.
"Alonso, yes. Arbeloa, not really," he says. "For me, Arbeloa was a surprise."
Almost 20 years after Benitez brought them together at Anfield, the pair will go head-to-head as Arbeloa's Fulham host Alonso's Chelsea on Monday.
The pair won the 2010 World Cup and two European Championships with Spain, along with domestic league and cup triumphs when they both joined Real Madrid after Liverpool.
They played together for seven years at club level and shared the pitch 262 times for club and country, and their careers have remained closely intertwined since.
Arbeloa was promoted from Real Madrid B to replace Alonso when he was sacked by the Spanish giants in January last season.
"He was in Castilla [Real Madrid's academy], which was similar to how I started, and then he went to Madrid in special circumstances," Benitez said of Arbeloa's rise to Real manager.
They both returned to England in July to take up their first Premier League managerial roles and now lead clubs whose stadiums are only two miles apart.
"With Alvaro, he knows the Premier League," Benitez told BBC Sport. "But his experience is shorter than Xabi's. We need to know how he can cope outside Real Madrid, which protects you in a way. Outside, you are on your own."
It's no surprise that, having played as team-mates – including under Jose Mourinho and Carlo Ancelotti at Real Madrid, and Vicente del Bosque with Spain – socialised off the pitch and even gone on holiday together, the pair are, in the words of Arbeloa, "very good friends", despite being "rivals when the game starts". He explained they spoke to each other in the lead up to Monday's match, but not about football.
Other similarities will see the duo live close to each other in Cobham, Surrey, with their children attending the same school.
In the words of Arbeloa, their friendship "will never change".
'He was someone who was always thinking'
Alonso was one of Benitez's first Liverpool signings in 2004 as he looked to overhaul Gerard Houllier's squad, Arbeloa then joining in 2007 from Deportivo after rising through the ranks at Real Madrid.
Benitez explained that Alonso has experience of "coaching at a different level in a different country", having had success in the Bundesliga at Bayer Leverkusen by winning a league and cup double in 2024.
Alonso, in particular, had "vision" on the pitch, says Benitez, while his experiences playing at Liverpool, Real Madrid and then under Pep Guardiola at Bayern Munich would have "opened his mind" to a range of coaching approaches.
Benitez recalls a moment of magic from Alonso in a 2009 game that displayed his football intelligence.
In a match against Sam Allardyce's Blackburn at Anfield, Alonso ignored an instruction to deliver a free-kick to the far post. Instead, his ball to the near post allowed Fernando Torres to head in his second goal of the match as Liverpool went on to win 4-0.
"He was someone who was always thinking," said Benitez.
'They always take something from you - I'm happy with that'
It is not just Alonso and Arbeloa who are among Benitez's former Liverpool players to have moved into management.
He reels off more than 20 names who have become coaches or managers, a list including Wales boss Craig Bellamy. He also points out that Djimi Traore is now an assistant coach at Seattle Sounders.
"I sent him to the shower at half-time in the Champions League final [in 2005]," he recalled of the defender, who was expecting to be substituted after a poor first-half before an injury to Steve Finnan saw him reinstated for Liverpool's historic second-half comeback and eventual victory on penalties against AC Milan in 2005.
He added: "They always take something from you. Maybe two or three things they can use [as a coach], and I'm happy with that."
It has been more than 40 years since Benitez began coaching at Real Madrid and, this summer, he finds himself in the unusual position of being without a job.
Now 66, Benitez says he is "waiting for another challenge", adding that his passion for the game is undiminished, as is his desire to "improve teams and players".
He felt he delivered in his most recent role at Panathinaikos, securing the top-four finish he had been tasked with achieving when he took the job in October, but was still sacked in May.
Explaining his continued motivation, Benitez said: "I was a PE teacher before and was trying to improve young people. It was the same as when I had Anthony Gordon at Everton."
The former Newcastle and Chelsea manager remains a Uefa technical observer and speaks about adapting to the modern game, using social media, artificial intelligence and increasingly sophisticated data as part of his approach.
"I had some offers," Benitez said, having recently been linked with the Scotland job.
"Maybe it is a national team, as a lot of teams will change after the World Cup, but there has to be something where you feel you can achieve something, whether that is promotion, like we had at Newcastle, with amazing fans.
"I know football now is more demanding. You have to be patient because, if not, if you change with the pressure of social media and change every seven months, then you don't have any project. That is the difficult thing."

15 flights diverted from Delhi airport as city hit by heavy rain, thunderstorm
12 of the flights were diverted to Jaipur, while two were redirected to Chandigarh and one to Lucknow.
As many as 15 flights to Delhi's Indira Gandhi International airport were diverted on Monday after heavy rains and thunderstorm hit the national capital.
12 of the 15 flights were diverted to Jaipur, while two were redirected to Chandigarh and one to Lucknow. Among the 12 flights diverted to Jaipur, three were international flights.

A red alert for very heavy rains was issued for parts of the national capital, while a yellow alert for moderate showers was sounded for other districts of Delhi.
South East Delhi, East Delhi, Shahdara, Central Delhi, North East Delhi, South Delhi, New Delhi, South West Delhi, West Delhi, North West Delhi and North Delhi witnessed heavy downpour earlier in the day.
The heavy rainfall led to waterlogging and traffic snarls across the city.
IMD's rain forecast for Delhi
The capital is likely to receive multiple spells of rain on Monday. However, the weather is expected to turn largely dry from Tuesday, with the IMD forecasting little or no rain for most of the rest of the week.
For Tuesday, the IMD has predicted only the “possibility of” very light rain during the afternoon. On Wednesday, a spell of very light to light rain is expected at a few places before noon. From afternoon to evening, another spell of very light to light rain is likely at many places, while moderate rain is expected at isolated places.
From Thursday to Sunday, the IMD has stated that no rain is expected, with partly cloudy skies likely to persist.
The IMD also issued a yellow alert for Ghaziabad, and an orange alert for Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad till at least 2 pm on Monday.

Only four in 10 healthcare facilities worldwide meet basic sanitation standards for accessible and usable toilets, the United Nations said on Tuesday (August 18, 2026), while 11% have no sanitation services at all.
In a report, the UN’s health and children’s agencies said only 40% of healthcare facilities last year had toilets that adequately met the needs of patients and staff, including people with limited mobility.
The report from the World Health Organization and UNICEF for the first time provided global estimates of basic sanitation services in healthcare settings.
Its 2025 estimate found significant gaps in access to basic sanitation standards, which it said required usable facilities including at least one toilet dedicated to staff, at least one sex-separated toilet with menstrual hygiene facilities and at least one toilet accessible for people with limited mobility.
Relying on data from 70 countries, the report showed that sanitation levels in healthcare facilities varied widely between regions, with only 23% of facilities in sub-Saharan Africa providing basic services, compared to 55% in central and southern Asia.
It found there was no sanitation service at more than one in 10 health facilities globally, serving 936 million people.
In addition to sanitation, the report estimated access in healthcare facilities to water, hygiene, environmental cleaning and waste management.
It found that an estimated 85% of facilities last year had basic water services, 72% had basic hygiene services and 71% basic healthcare waste management services.
Only 59% of facilities meanwhile met basic so-called environmental cleaning standards, which require both cleaning protocols and trained cleaning staff and is core to infection prevention and control.
A full 18% of facilities, serving around 1.5 billion people, met neither of the environmental cleaning requirements, said the report, which for this category relied on data from 54 countries.
The situation is particularly dire in poorer countries.
The environmental cleaning standard was met by just 24% of facilities in the world’s least-developed nations.

One Kashmiri Pandit employee said they would not be intimidated by the threats and would neither be scared nor leave the Valley
A fresh threat letter was allegedly circulated on social media targeting Kashmiri Pandit employees serving in the Kashmir Valley, prompting the All PM Package Employees Forum Kashmir to seek enhanced security from the Jammu and Kashmir administration.In a letter to chief secretary of Jammu and Kashmir on Monday, the forum said the purported threat poster, allegedly issued by an outfit calling itself the United Liberation Council (ULC) and dated August 23, contains the names, addresses and vehicle numbers of some employees.
The forum said the authenticity of the poster has not yet been verified by police or security agencies but warned that its repeated circulation was a matter of “grave concern”. In its letter, the forum said, "The authenticity of the poster is yet to be verified by the Police and security agencies. However, the repeated circulation of such threat letters and posters, particularly those containing sensitive personal information, is a matter of grave concern.
"One Kashmiri Pandit employee said the threats would not force them to leave the Valley. “We will neither be scared nor run away this time.
Kashmir is ours also. It is our birthplace,” the employee told ANI.The employee said a similar threat letter had surfaced earlier this month and urged authorities to investigate the source of the latest threats and how the alleged perpetrators obtained sensitive personal information.
The forum, citing previous targeted attacks on Kashmiri Pandit employees, sought immediate security cover, a review of arrangements at workplaces and residences, and protection for employees whose personal details may have appeared in the alleged poster.

World 100m champions Oblique Seville and Melissa Jefferson-Wooden roared to victories at the Silesia Diamond League on Sunday, as Armand ‘Mondo’ Duplantis wrapped up another dominant pole vault display.
The assembled field was outstanding in Poland. Of the 260 athletes appearing in Silesia, 55 were Olympic medallists, 101 have made the podium at world championships, and 68 were European championships medallists.
Quality shone throughout the meet, in front of 40,000 spectators at the Stadion Slaski, none less so than when Jamaica’s Seville blasted to a meet record of 9.83 seconds for victory.
Americans Kenny Bednarek (9.87) and Christian Coleman (9.93) completed the podium.
The women’s blue riband event was won by their teammate Jefferson-Wooden, in her first head-to-head over 100m with Olympic champion Julien Alfred, in a season’s best of 10.78 seconds.
Alfred, of St Lucia, came in second, at 0.05 seconds.
Duplantis had an uncharacteristic three failures in the pole vault, before girding himself for the business end of the showdown with Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis.
The US-born Swede eventually claimed victory with a best of 6.20m, 20cm higher than Karalis. One attempt at what would have been a 16th world record, at 6.32m, was enough before Duplantis called it a day.
One of the stand-out performances on the track was Brazil’s Alison Dos Santos, unbeaten this season, holding off Karsten Warholm in a thrilling 400m hurdles to win in 46.43 seconds, the sixth fastest time ever run.
The world-leading time smashed the meet record of 46.82 seconds set by Warholm last year.
“I expected a fast race, the line-up was amazing - everybody was here,” said Dos Santos.
“I knew that to win here I had to give my best.
“It was a great race today and a great time.”
The Brazilian made it four wins from four outings in Silesia and also four wins this season over Warholm, who claimed a fourth European title in Birmingham this month, as well as a second gold as part of Norway’s 4x400m mixed relay quartet.
“You cannot be mad if you set a season’s best,” acknowledged Warholm.
“Of course I always want to win. But 46.5 is really good coming out of the European championships, which really took its toll. The other guys have not been racing in a month and they were fresher.”
Ingebrigtsen fourth in 1,500m
Warholm’s teammate Jakob Ingebrigtsen, fresh from winning European 5,000m gold, made his first Diamond League appearance in a 1,500m in two years.
Ingebrigtsen clung on to finish fourth in a race won by American Ethan Strand, in 3:30.77, ahead of Kenya’s Phanuel Kipkosegi Koech and Olympic champion Cole Hocker of the US.

Ethan Katzberg and Camryn Rogers, who ensured hammer throw domination for Canada with two golds at last year’s Tokyo worlds, dominated the two events here for victories with bests of 82.92 and 77.09m respectively.
Italy’s Leonardo Fabbri, with a best of 22.08m, held off a quartet of Americans headed by Jordan Geist in the men’s shot put.
Olympic and 2023 world champion Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic won the women’s 400m in 48.87 seconds, but there was no such luck for Morocco’s two-time Olympic 3,000m steeplechase champ Soufiane El Bakkali, beaten into second by Ethiopia’s Gemechu Godana, who clocked a meet record of 8:02.74.
World record holder Ja’Kobe Tharp claimed the victory in the 110m hurdles in 13.05 seconds, while teammate Alaysha Johnson won the women’s short hurdles in 12.52.
“This victory means a lot to me, especially in this strong field,” said the 20-year-old Tharp.
“My coach would not be too happy about the race, some hurdles were not really good. But hey, I won this Diamond League race, so I cannot complain.”
Ukraine’s Yaroslava Mahuchikh equalled the meet record to win the women’s high jump in 2.00m.
And Botswana’s world 400m champion Busang Collen Kebinatshipi smashed the meet record set by world record holder Wayde van Niekerk in winning the one-lap race in an impressive 43.59 seconds.

What is a VESA mount and how to know what type your TV has
The VESA dimensions tell you where the mounting holes line up, but you still need to check the mount's weight limit and hardware.
Thankfully, VESA 400 × 400 isn't another TV resolution you need to learn. VESA stands for Video Electronics Standards Association, and in TV-mount shopping, a VESA size or VESA pattern describes the spacing between the mounting holes on the back of a TV or display. A VESA mount isn't one particular style of bracket; it simply supports one or more of those standardized patterns.
What does a VESA size such as 200 × 200 mean?
Look at the back of a typical mountable TV and you'll find threaded mounting holes, usually arranged in a square or rectangle. The VESA pattern describes the distance between those holes, measured in millimeters.
The first number is the horizontal distance and the second is the vertical distance. So a TV with a 400 × 200 pattern has mounting holes spaced 400mm apart from left to right and 200mm apart from top to bottom. A 200 × 200 pattern measures 200mm in both directions.
The VESA numbers don't describe the TV's resolution or screen dimensions. Larger TVs often use larger mounting patterns, but screen size alone doesn't tell you which pattern a particular model uses. Checking your exact TV model is more reliable than guessing from its screen size.
You also don't need a mount limited to that exact VESA size. Many mounts support multiple VESA patterns, so you don't need a bracket labeled only for your exact size. Your TV's pattern just needs to appear on the mount's list of supported patterns.
How to find your TV's VESA pattern
The easiest method doesn't require a ruler at all. Look up the exact TV model in its manual or on the manufacturer's support page and find the wall-mount or VESA specifications. Manufacturers commonly list the mounting-hole pattern in millimeters.
If you can't find the specification, you can measure the mounting holes yourself. Measure from the center of one mounting hole to the center of the corresponding hole horizontally, then do the same vertically. Write the result as horizontal × vertical, in millimeters.
For example, if the mounting holes are 400mm apart horizontally and 200mm apart vertically, the TV has a 400 × 200 VESA pattern. Measure in millimeters so you can compare the result directly with the mount's specifications.
A matching VESA pattern isn't enough
A matching VESA pattern tells you the bracket can line up with the TV's mounting holes. It doesn't tell you whether the mount can safely hold the TV, so the next specification to check is its weight limit.
Compare the mount's maximum load with the weight of your TV. A bracket can support the correct VESA pattern and still be unsuitable for a TV that's too heavy.
You should also check the hardware required by your TV. VESA compatibility also says nothing about how the bracket should attach to the wall. Once you've confirmed the pattern and weight rating, use the TV manufacturer's instructions to check the required mounting screws and follow the mount manufacturer's instructions for attaching the bracket to the wall.

An Indian children’s entertainment company has brought its debut original animated series to Netflix.
“Emomee: Big Skills for Little Ones, Minis,” from the Mumbai-based brand Emomee, features 20 episodes of some 11 minutes each, centered on characters E, Mo and Mee as they navigate everyday adventures designed to build confidence, curiosity, kindness, emotional intelligence and problem-solving in preschool-age viewers.
“This launch represents much more than a new distribution platform. It is another milestone in building Emomee into a global entertainment company. Every step we’ve taken – from growing a loyal audience to expanding onto streaming platforms – is helping us build a long-term franchise that will extend beyond content into consumer products, licensing and live experiences,” said Pooja Jauhari, founder and CEO of Emomee.
Popular on Variety
Founded by Jauhari, a former CEO of WPP-acquired creative agency The Glitch, and Varun Duggirala, co-founder of The Glitch, Emomee reached one billion views across more than 100 countries and built a subscriber base of 2.5 million within 15 months of launch. The company drew further attention on “Shark Tank India,” where all five sharks made offers at the founders’ asking valuation of INR50 crore ($5.2 million). Suraksha Subramaniam rounds out the founding team, overseeing legal and IP compliance.
Emomee has positioned itself around what it describes as a “life-skills-first” approach to children’s content, in contrast to the algorithm-driven, high-stimulation formats that have drawn scrutiny from parents and educators globally.
The Netflix debut is part of a broader expansion push that spans consumer products, licensing and live experiences. Emomee plans to attend Mipcom later this year to pursue new deals across distribution and licensing.
