Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.
Excel in Interviews With These AI Tools
AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Exponent Practice and Interviewing.io make more sense for technical candidates, Yoodli is particularly good for communication and behavioral practice, while MyInterviewAI works well for resume-based preparation. Big Interview helps with overall delivery, Huru AI makes quick job-specific practice easy, and Ophy AI covers the widest range of interview-preparation needs.
Whichever tool you choose, don’t stop after one mock interview. Upload your latest resume and the actual job description, complete a practice session, review where you struggled, and repeat it after fixing those areas. Two or three focused mock interviews will be far more useful than memorizing dozens of AI-generated answers.
Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.

The Swift space observatory has been in operation since 2004. It specializes in gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the most energetic electromagnetic explosions known in the universe. Its original mission was supposed to last just two years. More than two decades later, it continues to explore some of the most violent phenomena in the cosmos. Now it is nearing the end of its life.
Swift doesn’t have a propulsion system capable of significantly raising its orbit. Although it is hundreds of kilometers above the Earth’s surface, there are still atmospheric particles at that altitude that exert a small but constant drag on the satellite. With each orbit around Earth, it loses a tiny amount of energy and, little by little, altitude as well. If this process continues without intervention it will eventually reenter the atmosphere.
NASA knew that Swift had limited time left. Some models had indicated that the observatory could remain in orbit until the 2030s, but increased solar activity during 2024 changed those projections. Energy from the sun heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Estimates eventually placed its likely reentry before the end of 2026.
Faced with the rapid deterioration of Swift’s orbit, NASA decided to attempt a rescue maneuver straight out of a movie. The plan was simple in concept but astonishingly complex to execute. A robotic mission would catch up to Swift, capture it with mechanical arms, and use its own thrusters to raise the observatory to a safer orbit, where it could continue operating. To do this, NASA turned to the company Katalyst Space Technologies and its LINK spacecraft.
LINK was launched into space on July 3, 2026. However, problems arose soon after. The spacecraft suffered failures in its attitude control system, which is responsible for keeping it properly oriented and stable in space. For weeks, engineers worked to regain control.
On Wednesday, NASA canceled the rescue mission. In a statement, agency administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the decision was due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system. LINK will no longer capture Swift or raise its orbit. The spacecraft will continue to approach the observatory to conduct demonstrations of rendezvous, navigation, and close-proximity operations. The agency hopes to use this attempt to gather information that can be applied to future missions aimed at repairing, relocating, or extending the lifespan of satellites in orbit.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future. We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow,” Isaacman said in a press release.
The agency had warned from the outset that this was a high-risk mission. Swift was not built to be captured or repaired in orbit, while LINK was developed and launched against the clock in response to the observatory’s rapid descent.
“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” Isaacman noted.
Without an intervention to raise its orbit, Swift will continue to lose altitude until it reaches the denser layers of the atmosphere. During reentry, much of the observatory will be destroyed by intense heating and aerodynamic forces. It is still too early to determine exactly when and where this will occur.
For now, NASA estimates that Swift will likely reenter the atmosphere before the end of the year.

Two dead and others missing after Tunisian migrant boat travelling to Europe capsized
A boat carrying migrants has capsized off southern Tunisia, leaving at least two people dead
At least two people have died and 12 remain missing after a boat carrying migrants overturned off the southern coast of Tunisia, the national guard confirmed on Saturday. A single survivor was rescued.
Guard spokesperson Houssem Eddine Jebabli informed state news agency TAP that two retrieved bodies were taken to a hospital on the nearby island of Djerba. Speaking to national radio station Mosaique FM, he added that approximately 15 people were thought to be aboard when the boat launched between Zarzis and Ben Guerdane.
The boat set off early on Thursday morning. A commercial vessel discovered the lone survivor wearing a life jacket on Saturday, according to details reported by Mosaique based on the survivor’s account.
A helicopter and coast guard boats were deployed to the location to search for additional survivors, an Associated Press photo journalist at the scene said. The migrants were believed to be travelling towards Italy.
Zarzis has long served as a key departure point for Tunisians and individuals from across Africa and beyond seeking to make the Mediterranean crossing to Europe.
The city experienced a similar tragedy in 2022 when a vessel carrying 18 people disappeared. That event triggered weeks of demonstrations, with relatives accusing officials of failing to conduct adequate searches and burying several recovered bodies without establishing their identities or contacting their families.
Migrant departures from Tunisia have fallen sharply since the European Union and Tunisia signed a comprehensive pact in 2023. The agreement included EU financial assistance and technical support for border control and coast guard training to curb irregular migration and deter human traffickers in the Mediterranean basin. The EU allocated 105 million euros ($121 million) in migration support to Tunisia in 2023 alone.
The drop in numbers has not stopped dangerous crossings from Tunisia’s southern coastline, where families in Zarzis have spent years searching for relatives missing at sea.
Human rights organisations have raised concerns over the treatment of migrants and asylum seekers in Tunisia since the EU deal, pointing to reports of collective expulsions, racial violence, arbitrary detention and abuses against Black migrants.
In July, Amnesty International stated that EU support for border security in Tunisia was continuing to fuel grave rights violations, adding that refugees and asylum seekers were being "deliberately trapped in a system that offers neither protection nor a safe way out."

When I ask Jack Schwartz how much he’s charging for a table at his upcoming party in Manhattan, he offers to “show” me instead of answering with words. Then, the 21-year-old reaches into his black leather jacket, pulls out a white envelope containing $27,500 in cash—neatly separated into three stacks—and slides it across a countertop at WIRED’s office in New York, his right hand flashing a $10,000 diamond- and sapphire-encrusted gold ring.
Schwartz is the founder and CEO of MyPlots, a party promotion and ticketing company he started after throwing a series of legendary ragers in Los Angeles beginning at the precocious age of 14. He’s been building a cult of personality since high school, teasing his parties on Instagram and Snap to create FOMO and then packaging highlights in Reels and Stories afterward. “He was like The Great Gatsby,” says Zane Harwin, a 19-year-old former high school classmate of Schwartz’s who now does marketing for MyPlots. “That’s what we would all call him.” Harwin has traveled to New York with Schwartz for the party, and to try to raise money for their app. He’s wearing a $500 white Chrome Hearts T-shirt, a 424 jacket, and a claspless silver “permanent” bracelet he got at Coachella.
MyPlots launched its namesake app in January 2025, in part to promote “after-prom” events for high schoolers. Today, it’s the go-to app for under-21s in LA and boasts more than 1 million users. The app is also expanding its user base to older (of-age) attendees. Daniel Herring, a 30-year-old promoter who works with MyPlots, says that when he moved to LA three years ago, most events were promoted on Partiful, but “over the last year, it’s definitely been damn near all MyPlots.”
On MyPlots, a host will sign up, create an event, and invite people. The app allows promoters to target people who have attended their parties in the past and text guests updates, but it does not share phone numbers with promoters or third parties for off-platform use. Guests RSVP and purchase their tickets through the app, and the company takes a 20 percent cut of all sales. (When it launched last year, the ticketing feature distinguished MyPlots from competitors, but they’re catching up. In June, Partiful announced it would be offering in-app ticketing.) To use MyPlots, users technically need to be 18, but Schwartz concedes that “people find ways around that.” Stripe, which is integrated into the app, allows users as young as 13 if they have a parent enrolled on the account.
It’s not really the tech that sets MyPlots apart, which feels amateur compared to competitors like Partiful. Rather, it's the cool young crowd using it for exclusive, luxury parties—and how MyPlots markets to them. Scanning the app in mid July 2026 turned up an all-ages rap show at downtown LA nightclub The Mayan; a mansion party in Encino boasting “CELEBERTIES [sic]”—with a disclaimer that organizers aren’t liable for “anything negative that could happen” before, during, and after the event; and an 18-plus Daybreak Festival at the W Hollywood hotel featuring “VIP cabanas” and Schwartz’s bolded name as a headlining DJ. Ticket pricing is often tiered, sometimes varying based on gender, timing, or VIP access. A “Euphoria Mansion Party” from last spring, which did not specify an age restriction, boasted 500-plus expected guests and offered 30 minutes of “bedroom access” for $75.
No longer just a rite of passage or a chance to score clout at school, teen parties are now full-blown moneymaking enterprises for entrepreneurs savvy enough to take advantage. In addition to MyPlots, there are promoters like 310 Events, Off Campus Events, and LA Social, and ticketing apps like Plots and Turnt, all catering to young crowds.
“If you get real creative, there's always a way to make money—even without even leaving your house—if you know how to market and you can use the internet,” says Schwartz, whose role model is billionaire Mark Cuban. “So many young people are just on their phones all day.”
Standing at 5'8", Schwartz wears his dirty blond hair slicked back, and often has a pair of Oakleys perched on top of his head. He speaks with the bullish confidence of a tech founder, the occasional "like" reminding you of his age. As he tells it, he first became an entrepreneur at 14 years old. While a freshman at Palisades Charter High School—a well-known public school known as “Pali” by locals—he started a streetwear line called Loonar Clothing. His marketing strategy was to wait outside of celebrity haunts like Boa Steakhouse and the Saddle Ranch Chop House “for like 8 to 12 hours” and ask stars like Addison Rae to wear his T-shirts, sunglasses, and other swag on camera—prompting an Inside Edition story. Just before the Covid-19 pandemic hit, Schwartz threw three parties in succession, building a name for himself at school. “Everyone was like, who is this Jack Schwartz kid?” he recalls. “Every kid at Pali, even the seniors, are going.”
The first was in a rec room at his dad’s apartment complex, with his dad working security and collecting payments; the other two were on Hollywood Boulevard, where he paid $2,000 cash to rent the space. Schwartz says it wasn’t hard to find venues willing to rent to minors. “If you go to Hollywood, some of these venues … they'll do anything for business.”
His parties weren’t always hosted at official venues; they popped up at warehouses, offices, even friends’ houses. “A lot of the time, the parents … wouldn't care,” Schwartz says. “They would be upstairs, and it would be in their backyard.” But this wasn’t always drama-free: One of his New Year’s Eve parties, held at a warehouse, got shut down prematurely because the cops showed up and Schwartz claims the venue didn’t have the right permit.
Schwartz isn’t the only promoter who says it’s relatively easy for underage kids to find a party venue in LA—if they have money. Matt, a venue operator in his twenties who caters to brands and celebrities, started a party-promoting Instagram account as a teen and recalls renting corporate space and buying insurance for the night on sites like Eventhelper.com or Eventsured for a couple hundred bucks. (Neither website returned a request for comment.) Asked how he secured insurance as a minor, he says he “probably” put it under his dad’s name or figured out another way of getting around it. (WIRED has given Matt a pseudonym as he’d like to avoid professional repercussions.) “Some people are desperate for money,” he offers, by way of explaining why adults would work with children and take on the liability that comes with it.
And the liabilities are many. Matt recalls that a dance studio in Brentwood, which he rented for an event while in high school, hosted another party with teen guests months later. The floor broke under the weight of the crowd. Los Angeles Magazine reported that it sent “rowdy rich kids spilling into the streets.” As a venue operator, Matt says he’s worked with “really kind, sweet high schoolers” and teen promoters who cut corners. Some hire their friends as security guards or sneak alcohol in via staging equipment. The underage guests themselves present additional problems, sometimes showing up visibly drunk and getting aggressive when they’re not allowed in.
In 2024, Schwartz appeared in Social Studies, an FX documentary series about the highs and lows of teen social media use. According to the doc, in 2022, Schwartz hosted his own birthday party, in concert with another friend. In a social media post about the event, guests were explicitly advised against bringing “visible alcohol.” Nonetheless, the show depicted the party’s debaucherous turn: drinking out of containers, smoking, hooking up, a fight among two girls, and a teenage boy hanging off an indoor balcony railing. Guests interviewed say someone threw up before passing out on the ground. His friends called an ambulance, but not before dragging him a few blocks to avoid getting the party planners in trouble. “That’s scary,” Schwartz tells the camera in a follow-up interview. “That’s also why we purchased insurance.” When asked about the FX series, Schwartz tells me he was misrepresented by the filmmakers. He now claims the birthday party in question wasn’t his, that he didn’t organize or manage it, and as such, he didn’t get insurance. FX declined to comment.
In Schwartz’s junior year, when Covid-19 lockdowns lifted, teens were desperate for in-person connection; he decided to go hard, throwing parties under the brand MyPlots—“plot” is slang for something to do—and advertised them on Instagram. But it was “messy,” he says, with people sending him money via Venmo and Zelle or paying cover charges (typically $20) at the door. Sometimes security guards would pocket the money. “There had to be a better way to facilitate these events, make them safer, and provide people with more security,” he recalls. “So that's why I created MyPlots.”
To bolster his business, Schwartz grew his TikTok following to 1.6 million by doing man-on-the-street videos asking people how much their fits cost; he also inked a deal with Snap’s Spotlight monetization program for a “lot” of money, picking up a “ton of followers,” he says. (Snap did not respond to requests for comment.) In 2023, during his senior year, Schwartz used proceeds from his parties to buy a blue BMW M340i that he says cost $50,000.
Zane Harwin was a freshman at Pali when Schwartz was a junior. The former captain of the school’s surf team, Harwin is 6'4”, with a mischievous smile and has brown hair that flows in beachy waves. He towers over his boss, but has always looked up to Schwartz. Harwin fondly recalls rolling up to one of Schwartz’s giant house parties in Brentwood, seeing cars lined down the road and Schwartz dutifully running the door. “He’s the man of the party,” Harwin says, adding that his proximity to the enterprise means some girls have offered to do “anything” to get into the events. (He says he would never take them up on that.) As a duo, they’re a modern-day Spencer Pratt and Brody Jenner—Schwartz is the brains of the operation, and Harwin the charm.
They speak with nostalgia about the chaos of their high school raging—parties in iconic LA neighborhoods like Beverly Hills and Bel Air—some so crowded that people would fall into the hot tub. Another Pali classmate and now MyPlots’ head of marketing, Lucas Ward, remembers seeing a kid “literally get knocked out cold” during a fight. “Kids would make it a mess, but it was authentic high school parties,” Harwin says.
MyPlots likely could not have been born anywhere but the affluent neighborhoods of West LA, where many teens have easy access to cars, envy-inducing houses, wealth, and the jaw-dropping beauty of the Pacific Ocean’s coastline. Zillow pegs the average home price in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood at just over $3 million. Pali High is so iconic that there was once a popular TikTok account devoted to sharing the outfits of its students. As is typical for kids in this area, both Schwartz and Harwin grew up well-off. Schwartz's mother runs a marketing agency while his father has a corporate job; Harwin is the child of a tv personality/producer and a restaurateur/hospitality real estate developer.
“It's like the number one place if you want to be an influencer,” says Harwin. “Social media is the biggest here. Hollywood, everyone knows a person in LA, and like you post one video here, it'll go viral.”
Rachel, a Culver City–based mother of a 17-year-old son and 15-year-old daughter, says both of her kids and their friends attend ticketed parties thrown by other teens, which are promoted on social media; her son’s friend has a “business” throwing parties at other people’s homes. Teenagers in the LA area “can stay out really late and, you know, just take a Waymo and be very independent,” she says. The fact that “everyone has their parents’ credit card on their phone” is a game changer, she adds. “Kids are just kind of absent-mindedly spending a lot of money.”
Outside of lavish locations, these teen parties are markedly different from the ones you hosted in the backyard when your parents went out of town. Rachel’s daughter, Amber, says parties are typically advertised on Instagram and Snapchat, and the location is dropped the day of the event. Usually, girls’ tickets cost less than guys’, and kids can prepay, showing a barcode at the door. The hosts, some of them teens themselves, use an app to sell tickets. Most crucially, they’re making real money off parties that 20 years ago would have just gotten you grounded.
In May 2025—just a few months after the launch of MyPlots—Schwartz and Harwin threw an “after-prom tour,” hosting parties for seniors to attend once their school proms ended. Harwin advertised the party “tours” on Instagram, filming from exotic cars and penthouses with stunning mountain views, sometimes using stacks of cash as props. “Nobody else in the world has done a tour like this,” he said in one reel, sitting on stone steps behind a swimming pool. Their strategy for selling tickets was getting popular high school seniors to act as brand ambassadors—a role that Harwin filled when he was still a student at Pali.
As is common with after-prom ragers, things sometimes got out of hand. Several attendees of one party say security for the event got aggressive and shoved students. Schwartz brushes this aside, first claiming that the security came with the venue and later that too many students tried to get their friends in for free. “It was like a shit show,” he says. “The crowd was so disrespectful.”
Raine, a 16-year-old who lives in Venice, attended a backyard party in the Rancho Park neighborhood advertised on MyPlots and Instagram last March. (Rachel, Amber, and Raine are all pseudonyms, in order to protect their privacy.) As they were leaving, at around 10 pm, Raine saw a girl, clearly intoxicated, lying on the grass in the front yard. The fire department showed up. The account promoting the party later posted an Instagram story with the text: “two drunk ho** ruined the party for yall NEXT ONE GON BE CRAZY.”
Schwartz wants to distance himself from promoters who use his app. He says the technology is simply facilitating ticket sales and that he has no connection to the majority of the parties on MyPlots—nor does he bear any legal responsibility. “I have no idea who 95 percent of [the promoters] are,” he says, adding that he’s very selective about what events he personally throws. “It's not worth the liability to make a few thousand dollars.”
Marley Majcher, who plans events in LA through her business The Party Goddess!, is skeptical that young party promoters are free from liability, even when they have single-night insurance. Majcher organizes high-end events, including sweet sixteens and bar and bat mitzvahs in locations like Beverly Hills and Malibu. She says her own lawyer has stressed the importance of airtight contracts to account for things like accidents and drinking and driving. “There's just no way that these people have the coverage for what they need to have … especially here, where we're very sue-happy and affluent,” says Majcher, who is 56 but tells me that she looks younger “due to the amount of Botox and skin treatments I have on a regular basis.”
William Lemmon, the principal broker at Broadway Insurance Services, says that a party host would generally need a special event permit, an occupancy sign-off if the space isn't zoned for a crowd—like a warehouse or office—the fire marshal's approval, and a permit for alcohol sales, which a minor can't apply for. Instant online insurance is perfectly fine when everyone's an adult, but if “a teenager is charging a cover at a warehouse with booze, that's about as far from the intended use as it can get,” he says. He also points out that minors generally can't be held to contracts, so the carrier could argue the policy is invalid. Liability for these events is a “pile-on” that would involve the promoter, tenant, property owner, whoever bought alcohol, and possibly parents if the party thrower is underage. “Here’s what it really comes down to: Take that same party and make everyone 21, and it’s insurable. Add minors and alcohol, and no carrier will knowingly touch it.”
For now, the business is working. Following the successful 2025 after-prom tour, Schwartz and Harwin say they took a monthslong European vacation, flying first class and hitting Amsterdam and Ibiza, among other spots. Despite Ibiza’s reputation as one of the party capitals of the world—with clubs open all night and after-hours gatherings that last the entire next day—the guys decided to throw their own event at their villa.
“We go to this post office, we create a flyer, and we're printing out like hundreds of flyers,” Harwin recalls, detailing how they went to the massive outdoor club Ushuaïa and threw the posters into the crowd. “The next thing we know, we go back to the villa, and there's already a line.” They claim they charged $100 a head and walked away with around $10,000. When I ask why they felt the need to work during a vacation, Harwin says they missed the hustle: “This is what we do. We’re good at this.”
By early June 2026, Schwartz had transitioned to throwing parties for an 18-plus crowd—and taken his talents to the East Coast. A few hours after the meeting at WIRED’s office, I head to HK Hall, a two-story nightclub in Manhattan’s Hell’s Kitchen neighborhood. Schwartz and the MyPlots team are hosting an after-party for Houston rapper Don Toliver’s Madison Square Garden show—the one with a $27,500 table fee. It’s their second big New York City event, the first being a Playboi Carti after-party last November.
By 10:30 pm, a couple dozen young-looking people are in line at the door, which is being manned by Ward and Schwartz. A woman tries to haggle with Schwartz to get a discount on the $100 entry fee. He offers it to her for $75, but when she gets to Ward, he still charges her $100, telling her the extra is “tax.”
A white guy in a Bathing Ape shirt, with beaded box braids, is smoking a joint outside. It’s Daniel Herring, the aforementioned event promoter. Schwartz and his collaborators flew him out from LA. He’s a few feet away from a sign prohibiting drugs but says that, because he’s a VIP, security is holding on to his half-ounce of weed. “I chose MyPlots over a lot of these guys,” says Herring, who promotes his parties on MyPlots because he favors its customer service. “They’re very driven, they’re very humble, and they’re genuine. They’re not out here sharking or doing bad business by anybody.”
Inside the club are bottle girls with sparklers, people smoking hookah, and at least a couple of influencers livestreaming. Eight TVs repeatedly flash MyPlots’ purple logo. The place fills up quickly; By midnight, hundreds of people are lined up around the block. Schwartz says he paid “a substantial amount of money” for Toliver’s 2 am appearance.
MyPlots is in the middle of a search for angel investors, hoping to raise $10 million to set up a permanent office and hire a sales team to book talent for parties. It’s also planning a 10,000-person festival on Santa Monica beach for next summer. Schwartz is currently taking a hiatus from pursuing his economics degree at UCLA, explaining, “Every kid you know, from back in the day, they wanted to be a policeman, a firefighter. Now everyone wants to be a YouTuber, a streamer.” His ambitions go far beyond nightlife. He says he wants to eventually sell the company and start a new business: “Something in AI.”
Harwin puts the long-term goal more plainly: “Make as much money as I possibly can—as soon as I can.”
“It’s very possible,” Harwin says, “we're going to be doing something bigger than Coachella once we get older.” You know, once they’re 25.

Tamil Nadu will launch the ‘Chief Minister’s Elderly Health Insurance Scheme’, covering nearly 38 lakh senior citizens aged 70 and above. The scheme will provide free medical treatment, including cancer care packages, advanced cardiac surgeries, organ transplants, and high-end diagnostic services, at empanelled government and private hospitals, with no ceiling on income, Health Minister K.G. Arunraj announced in the Assembly on Monday (August 17, 2026).
The Minister made 115 announcements for the Health Department at a total estimated outlay of ₹2,997 crore. It covered areas including policy reforms, universal free health services, new posts creation, infrastructure projects, equipment and procurement, direct beneficiary programmes and digital health initiatives.
The 87-year-old Tamil Nadu Public Health Act, 1939, will be replaced with a modern, comprehensive Act to address contemporary and future health challenges. Dr. Arunraj said a new provision would make unsupervised home births outside hospitals a punishable offence. Noting that Tamil Nadu was known as the country’s health capital, he said that ‘TN Medicity’, a world class integrated medical hub comprising clinical services, research, medical tourism, and AYUSH, would be established. The government will allocate ₹10 crore for the preparation of a Detailed Project Report in the first phase.
‘Nalam 360-Annual Free Health Check-up for All’ scheme will be rolled out. Under this, everyone aged 30 and above will receive 14 basic tests annually, free of cost, across 1,257 government health facilities in the State.
This will include blood pressure, ECG, haemoglobin, complete haemogram, random blood sugar, urea, creatinine, total cholesterol, serum bilirubin, urine albumin, and VIA screening. For the first time in the State, the Health Department will introduce Home Based Diagnostic Services — sample collection and testing services — in metropolitan areas on a public-private partnership model, he said.
Policy reforms
The department will come up with a ‘Positive Health Policy’ to promote holistic health and wellbeing at the community, family, and individual levels, accompanied by the “Nalam 360” mobile application. A new legislation ‘TN Institutions of State Importance in Health Care Act’ will come up to create institutions of State importance to provide world-class medical services.
Addressing a long-standing demand, Dr. Arunraj said 2,500 permanent posts of staff nurses would be created. Existing contract nurses on consolidated pay will be absorbed into regular time-scale pay. A total of 1,695 nursing posts on consolidated pay will be created at a cost of ₹42.72 crore.
A total of 3,594 medical staff across 24 categories, including pharmacists, nursing assistants, village health nurses, and ophthalmic assistants, will be recruited through the Medical Services Recruitment Board. Additionally, the department will create 284 temporary super speciality posts across 25 specialities such as neurology, cardiology and nephrology on time-scale pay to take advanced medical care to the district-level.
These posts will be created to accommodate doctors who complete their post-graduation every year and are posted in government hospitals on bond conditions. A number of announcements for infrastructural development such as new hospital buildings and medical equipment were also made.

An Indian court has sentenced a high-profile former editor of an investigative news magazine to 10 years in prison after convicting him of raping a junior colleague, overturning his acquittal in a case that drew nationwide attention.
Tarun Tejpal, 63, the founder and former editor of Tehelka magazine, was accused of raping a journalist in the lift of a five-star hotel in the western coastal state of Goa during an event in November 2013. He was arrested and spent seven months in jail until the supreme court granted him bail.
A court in Goa acquitted Tejpal of charges including rape, sexual harassment and wrongful restraint in 2021.
The government of Goa challenged the acquittal before the Bombay high court, which set aside the trial court’s verdict and sentenced him to 10 years in jail on Thursday.
“He has been convicted to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment. He has been given two weeks’ time to surrender,” the police investigator Sunita Sawant, who led the case against Tejpal, told reporters.
The court also ordered him to pay a £3,900 fine, he said.
Tejpal, 63, said he would challenge the conviction in the supreme court.
He had initially blamed the assault on “a lapse of judgement” but later alleged the case against him was part of a vendetta by the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) government in Goa.
“For the past 13 years, they have been pursuing me as a part of a political vendetta,” he said after conviction.
Sawant told reporters: “This is a sentence where a girl has stood up for her rights … so this judgment is very important for women who are working in any sector.”
The case emerged at a time when India’s handling of sexual assault cases was under intense scrutiny after the gang-rape and murder of a 23-year-old student on a Delhi bus in December 2012.
That attack triggered nationwide protests and international outrage, and prompted the government to strengthen the country’s rape laws.
Tejpal’s case severely damaged the authority and credibility of Tehelka, which had historically championed women’s rights and social justice.
The magazine continues to operate under new leadership, but it has failed to regain the influence it had before the 2013 case.

Tropical Storm Moke to cause more flooding as Hawaii recovers from Lala
A tropical storm in the Pacific Ocean will bring additional flooding and gusty winds to Hawaii as the state recovers from damage from last week's Hurricane Lala, according to forecasters.
Tropical Storm Moke is impacting the Big Island of Hawaii and will bring rain to other islands through Monday, according to an advisory by the NOAA NWS National Hurricane Center issued late Saturday night, local time.
"This rainfall may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides for the windward and southeast Big Island, especially in deep terrain and over areas that were recently affected by Lala," the center said in the advisory.
The center of Tropical Storm Moke is not expected to make landfall and will pass to the south of the Hawaiian islands, but up to 15 inches of rain could fall across Big Island and 3 to 6 inches of rain are expected to fall on eastern Maui, the center also said.
Potential damage from Tropical Storm Moke is set to occur less than a week after Hurricane Lala battered the islands.
Hurricane Lala, now downgraded to a tropical storm and moving northwest across the Pacific Ocean away from Hawaii at a slower speed, did not make landfall either, but dropped more than 30 inches of rain on some parts of Hawaii in a short period of time.
That heavy rainfall triggered floods and mudslides that destroyed roads and bridges. Floodwaters swept through several towns, lifting homes from their foundations.
More than 8,000 people were still without power as of Saturday morning, and full restoration of the electricity supply is not expected until Sept. 8, according to the local grid company, Hawaiian Electric.
At least one person, a 90-year-old woman, died in a flood caused by the hurricane, according to Hawaii Public Radio. Hawaii Gov. Josh Green on Saturday signed a request asking the White House to declare an emergency in the wake of the earlier hurricane, Lala.
Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda on Sunday encouraged residents to prepare for another battering, with the strong winds and heavy rains expected from Tropical Storm Moke.
"Please anticipate interruptions in power and communication and hazardous road conditions," Alameda wrote on social media.

Fab Four and Fleming on the phone - England's first-Test takeaways
- Published
England's crushing victory over Pakistan was the ideal start to Joe Root's second reign as Test captain.
The home side could not have wished for a more straightforward beginning to a new era as they look to move on from the chaos of the past year.
England's innings win comes with the context of a desperate performance from Pakistan, so any judgements on progress should be reserved for now.
Still, Headingley taught us some things. Here are the takeaways.
Fab Four keep England in the fast lane
England are rebuilding their bowling attack for two reasons.
First, the retirement of Ben Stokes has robbed them not only of inspiration, but of balance.
Secondly, Stokes has followed Stuart Broad, James Anderson, Chris Woakes and, most likely, Mark Wood out of the door. That is 1,871 Test wickets lost in less than three years.
The first stab at a post-Stokes team included four frontline seamers – Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson – supported by the part-time off-breaks of Dan Lawrence.
In helpful conditions, it could not have gone better for England. Robinson and Tongue took eight wickets apiece, while Archer and Atkinson improved after a rusty first innings when they struggled to adapt following a month playing in The Hundred. Lawrence bowled only one over in the match.
Clearly, there will be times when England need a frontline spinner, but there is no consistently Test-class spinner in the country right now.
There is an argument to be made that England should continue to stack their attack with seamers because they are the best bowlers – Root said they "don't know how good they could be".
The likes of Sam Cook and Brydon Carse wait in the wings to step in or provide different skills if necessary, meaning England have a large squad of pacemen to choose from.
A trip to Bangladesh in February will mean England have to find some spin. For now, they should stay in the fast lane.
- 'Plug him in as attack leader' - England-Pakistan player ratings 
  - Published15 hours ago
- It would be 'nice to have choice' over Ashes venues - Root 
  - Published13 hours ago
Cox rocks
Jordan Cox has waited a long time for a proper opportunity in Test cricket. Now that it has finally arrived, the Essex batter looks at home at the highest level.
Deputising for the injured Jacob Bethell at number three, Cox impressed with an assured 73. He showed patience and sound judgement, though still had the range of strokes to push the scoring along at a healthy rate without taking risks.
Admittedly, the Pakistan attack Cox faced was far from the most fearsome in Test cricket. None of their seamers had the pace to test his ticker against the short ball.
But, occasionally, players come along and appear instantly suited to Test cricket. Cox seems to fit into that bracket.
His blemish was missing out on the really big score that would have made it impossible for the selectors to leave him out when Bethell returns. Cox potentially has four more innings in this series to make himself undroppable.
If the 25-year-old does demand a place in the XI for the December tour of South Africa and beyond, it leaves England with a dilemma.
Is opener Emilio Gay vulnerable? Bethell is now England's opener in one-day cricket, while Cox opened for Kent at the beginning of his first-class career.
Cox can also keep wicket. Might he put pressure on Jamie Smith? Speaking of whom…
Smith behind the sticks
Smith was one of the players who most noticeably wilted under the pressure and scrutiny of the Ashes tour.
He was not helped by a lack of attention to his wicketkeeping in training. Whether it was because a threadbare backroom team was overworked, or England's overall attitude was not good enough, Smith was rarely seen doing the hard yards with the gloves on.
There has been a change this summer. Since joining the coaching staff, former England women's wicketkeeper Sarah Taylor has worked closely with Smith, who has also been able to do more wicketkeeping training with his county Surrey since recovering from a finger injury.
Another circumstance was an injury to Surrey's regular keeper Ben Foakes, one of the best glovemen in the world. It gave Smith three consecutive games behind the stumps in the County Championship in the early part of the season.
The result has been a definite improvement in Smith's keeping for England. It's not as if the 26-year-old ever looked out of place behind the stumps in Test cricket, but he has shown off a greater range of skills this summer, particularly standing up to the fast-medium of Robinson.
At one point, in the third Test against New Zealand at Trent Bridge, Smith even stood up to the pacey Archer.
Not all progress is linear. Smith's Test batting average has dipped below 40 and he needs to avoid developing a habit for maddening modes of dismissal.
The man who somehow got out to a Marnus Labuschagne bouncer in Sydney tamely holed out for 25 on Friday morning when there was an opportunity for a much bigger contribution.
If Cox or Lawrence fill their batting boots this summer, then England's top-order will become congested. Smith must ensure he does not become vulnerable.
Flem on the phone
Stephen Fleming, England's new Test coach, is not here. Brendon McCullum's replacement is not due to arrive in the UK until September, by which time the Pakistan series could be over.
Fleming was appointed last month, yet will not take charge of England in a Test until South Africa at Christmas.
The delay has not fully been explained, apart from perhaps a desire to give Fleming a break after almost two decades with Chennai Super Kings.
You will have your own opinions on that one. Being in charge of an Indian Premier League team is intense, but CSK's last match was on 21 May, seven months before England's first Test against the Proteas. Could Fleming, now with one of the biggest jobs in coaching, not have been part of a month-long series against Pakistan?
Either way, Root revealed the New Zealander had been in daily contact during the Headingley Test. "It's been great to have him on the end of the phone," said the captain.
Fleming's influence is not immediately obvious, simply because England were not tested in Leeds.
Should things get more difficult in the remaining two Tests, or if a crucial selection decision needs to be made, perhaps vital input will come from the Flemphone.
- 'I fear for them' - pundits lament 'desperate times' for Pakistan 
  - Published13 hours ago
Pakistan problems
A win is a win for England, much needed after only two in their previous 10. However, they should have been better than two wins in 10, and the dismal nature of Pakistan's performance means Root's men can only take limited encouragement from their week in Leeds.
Nothing went right for Pakistan, from the moment captain Babar Azam was ruled out with a thumb injury. Their batting was brittle, their bowling scattergun and their fielding shoddy.
Babar's team beat West Indies in Trinidad earlier this month to earn a 1-1 series draw, yet that was Pakistan's first Test win away from home in more than three years.
They are heavily reliant on winning Tests on spinning pitches, which is why they switched to worn tracks on England's last visit to Pakistan in 2024. When pace bowling becomes the dominant weapon, Pakistan have neither the bowlers nor batters to thrive in the conditions.
Now they head to Lord's, where not one over of spin was bowled in England's shootout win over New Zealand in June.
The surface at the home of cricket could be much different this time around, or a sporty pitch could act as a leveller between the two teams.
Still, the smart money is on another England victory to complete their first series win against anyone in almost two years.

What to try when an Android app keeps crashing
Get back to doomscrolling or swiping right as quickly as possible.
The Google Play Store is home to millions of apps, and it's also where developers push updates that introduce new features and squash bugs. I've been an Android user all my life, and in my experience, app crashes have mostly been caused by buggy updates rather than something being wrong with the phone itself. So, if an app has been acting strangely, heading to the Play Store is one of the first troubleshooting steps worth trying.
To do so, tap on your profile picture in the top-right corner, select Manage apps and device, and under the Updates available section, check to see if there's a newer version of the troublesome app waiting to be installed.
If there are no pending updates for you to install, you can dig a bit deeper into the app's settings. There are two ways to go about this. You can either long-press the app's icon on your home screen or app drawer and tap the tiny "i" icon to access the App info page, or head to Settings > Apps and select it from the list of installed apps. Depending on your phone's version of Android, these options may be labeled a bit differently.
While you're in the App info settings, tap on Storage & cache and select the Clear cache option. Head back, tap on Force stop and try launching the app again. Clearing the cache removes temporary files the app has stored that could have become corrupted. Android has had this neat cache management system on a per-app basis for years, which can also help speed up apps that have become sluggish over time.
Clear the app's data
If clearing the app's cache and force stopping it didn't do the trick, you can attempt to fully uninstall it and download it from the Play Store again. The downside to this approach is that you'll wipe any data the app has stored locally. This includes credentials, media files and other preferences. If the app has the ability to sync data to the cloud, all you'll have to do is sign back in. However, if you haven't enabled cloud backup for the app, you should consider setting that up before uninstalling it so you can preserve your data.
Alternatively, you can also head to the App info page for the app and tap on Clear data. This saves you the hassle of having to download the app again. That said, if you're connected to a decently fast network, reinstalling the app from the Play Store is the more thorough option if you're trying to fix persistent crashes.
Though you don't need to do it regularly, restarting your phone can sometimes be a surprisingly quick fix for a lot of issues. You can force restart most Android phones by holding down the power button until the screen goes black and the logo appears. Some models may require you to hold down either the volume up or volume down buttons in addition to the power button.
It's also worth checking if your phone itself has any updates available. Apart from getting to enjoy new features, staying on up-to-date software ensures you have the latest bug fixes and security patches, some of which may address system-level issues that could be triggering app crashes. Navigate to Settings > System > Software update and install any pending updates you find.
Install an older version of the app
One of the beauties of Android as an operating system is how it lets you sideload applications relatively easily. Though Google is implementing a stricter security process for sideloading, you can still install apps outside the Play Store. On newer versions of Android, you will first have to enable developer mode by navigating to Settings > About Phone and tapping on Build Number seven times. You will be asked to restart your device as a preventative security measure. After a one-day wait, you can allow installation from unknown sources. This is a one-time security process that's designed to protect you against social engineering attacks.
You can now proceed to download an older, stable version of the app that's been giving you trouble. I recommend using APKMirror to find the installation file, since it's a source I trust. Remove the app from your phone and install its older version using its APK file by opening it from your file manager. Some apps that use split APKs may require you to use the APKMirror Installer app.
Keep in mind that this is a temporary fix until the app developer publishes an update that addresses whatever bug was causing the crashes. When this happens, you will have to remove the app and install it back via the Play Store to make sure you receive future updates normally.
Alternatively, if all of this is a hassle, you can simply resort to using the app's web version in your browser for the time being. Most popular apps that also have a web version are optimized reasonably well for mobile browsers. You can even enable notifications for supported websites and pin them to your home screen for quicker access.

What to know about Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump's pick to lead the FDA
President Trump posted on Truth Social that he is nominating Dr. Heidi Overton to be the next FDA commissioner.
Overton would fill a vacancy left by Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned in May after leading the agency for 13 months.
Overton trained as a surgeon. Her current role is deputy assistant to the president for domestic policy at the White House.
Dr. Joshua Sharfstein, who was the principal deputy commissioner at the FDA during the Obama administration, says that moving from the White House to the FDA could be eye-opening.
"In any administration, there are White House advisers who are walking around saying, 'Why can't FDA just do this? What FDA should really do is that,'" he says. "And then you get to the FDA and you realize there's actually another side of the story."
He says that side includes hearing from career scientists with deep expertise in analyzing the safety of medications, for example.
In Sharfstein's opinion, leading the FDA might be the hardest health job in government. It has a staff of around 18,000 people, and is responsible for regulating food, drugs, and medical devices — as well as tobacco, cosmetics, supplements and other products.
Successful FDA commissioners, in Sharfstein's experience, need a good brain — but also a strong spine. In other words, you have to be smart but also tough. "There's all kinds of pressures — there are political pressures, there are business pressures, there are advocacy pressures coming all the time," he says.
When Overton worked at the conservative America First Policy Institute, she wrote papers opposing gender-affirming care for minors. She also has questioned the safety of medication abortion and suggested the FDA was wrong to allow it to be prescribed via telehealth.
On Aug 10, President Trump issued a controversial executive order pushing to change the childhood vaccine schedule, and dredging up debunked theories linking vaccines to autism. Speaking at the press conference, Overton called Trump's order "a historic action."
She also backed his call for the production of individual vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella. Those vaccines are often given together in a single shot known as MMR, or sometimes MMRV, if the chickenpox vaccine is included.
"We do still recommend the measles vaccine for all children, but we want parents to be informed about the timing and to have the option to separate them out," she said.
Sharfstein and other public health experts have pointed out there's no science to support giving the measles vaccine in a separate shot from the mumps and rubella vaccines.
Unbundling those vaccines and manufacturing new ones could raise costs and increase the chance that children miss doses.
Overton still needs Senate confirmation to become FDA commissioner. Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash. has already said she will vote no. Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana and gastroenterologist, also voiced concerns on social media but didn't say how he would vote.
NPR reached out to the White House to set up an interview with Overton but had not received a response at the time of publication.

South Korea says US cancels joint marine drill over Iran war
The cancellation follows US President Donald Trump's order last week to scale down the separate annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises.
SEOUL: South Korea said on Monday (Aug 24) that the United States had cancelled a large joint amphibious landing exercise scheduled for next month due to constraints on force availability caused by the war with Iran.
The biennial Ssangyong drills involve marine forces from South Korea and the US and are designed to strengthen combined operations, typically involving warships, aircraft and ground forces rehearsing amphibious landings.
The cancellation follows US President Donald Trump's order last week to scale down the separate annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, cutting the joint drills from 11 days to five.
Trump at the time cited their high cost and said they sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea, while highlighting his relationship with its leader, Kim Jong Un.
"The US Marine Corps formally notified our forces in June that its ability to deploy forces during this year's Ssangyong exercise would be constrained due to the situation in the Middle East," Han Seung-jeon, a spokesman for the South Korean Marine Corps, told reporters at a news briefing.
Seoul and Washington were continuing consultations on resuming the amphibious exercise, he said, without giving details.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Seoul's announcement.
Trump's order last week to scale back the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise came as he seeks to revive the relationship he developed with Kim during his first term.
The US president said Wednesday that it was important to "get along" with Kim, adding that Pyongyang now had 57 "very powerful" nuclear weapons.
Seoul estimates that North Korea has around 80 to 120 such weapons.
Trump and Kim met three times during Trump's first term, but Pyongyang accelerated its nuclear programmes after their second 2019 summit in Hanoi collapsed without an agreement on North Korea's denuclearisation.

Malayalam actor S. Devan, who recently quit the BJP, on Monday (August 24, 2026) said he has decided to join Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay-led Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) party.

He merged his party with the BJP in 2021 following a meeting with Union Home Minister Amit Shah and was subsequently appointed the party’s State vice-president.
After recently quitting the BJP, Mr. Devan had said he was not getting enough “space” to function within the party.

Trump made more than 1,000 trades in June totaling millions, financial disclosures reveal
Trump’s trades in June come as Congress debates stock-trading ban
Donald Trump undertook a shuffling of his stock portfolio in June and sold nearly $30 million in shares that month as Congress debates whether those in power should be allowed to trade stocks at all, according to financial disclosures.
The president put his businesses and financial interests in a blind trust during his first term to separate himself from the appearance of corruption. In his second term, Trump appears to have abandoned this approach as his businesses and investments have run almost in sync with his presidency.
A CNBC review of his most recent financial disclosure revealed that the president’s portfolio went under a major reshuffle in June, with the president buying tens of millions of dollars of securities and selling others.
The form, which does not show exact figures, shows purchases of at least $49 million and sales of at least $28.5 million in total. The largest transaction was a sale valued between $5 million to $25 million of shares from the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation Index Fund ETF, while the largest purchases included shares of Home Depot stock and Fidelity National Information Services. The portfolio conducted more than 1,000 trades over the course of the month.
Trump’s appearance of profiting off of the presidency has been labeled a conflict of interest by his critics since he returned to the White House without the shackles of his first-term separation from his financial endeavors. A White House spokesperson denied to CNBC in May that a string of first quarter FY 2026 investments could be construed as such.
“There are no conflicts of interest,” spokesman Davis Ingle told the news outlet. “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public — which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses from the fake news media.”
Overall, over the course of 2025, the Trump family saw their wealth grow by a combined $2 billion a total that includes more that $1.4 billion solely from cryptocurrency enterprises his family began during his years out of office. It was also a total that was more than three times the amount his businesses had made just a year earlier — when he was still a private citizen.
Earlier this year, it was revealed that Trump had made hundreds of stock trades in April of last year just days before his administration launched what would become a global trade war by announcing reciprocal tariffs on dozens of countries.
During a gaggle with reporters on July 1, he responded to questions about his financial gains and credited the stock market for his successes, but the president’s explanation did not account for the hundreds of millions of dollars he’s attracted in foreign investments to his World Liberty Financial crypto business. His response also didn’t acknowledge the roughly $60 million he made licensing his brand overseas during his first year back in office.
"Well, you know why I'm profiting? Because the stock market's going up — everybody's profiting. Do you have a 401(k)? … So we're all profiting. I'm profiting because I have a lot of money and a lot of cash,” Trump told reporters in July.
Congress is currently debating a ban on stock trading by members while in office, but the legislation was trimmed down to remove such restrictions from the president or vice president in an effort to get more Republicans on board. The legislation passed the House, but is currently stuck in the Senate without much hope for passage. Polls have shown that Americans broadly oppose members of Congress being allowed to trade stocks given their access to nonpublic information.
Surveys have similarly shown that Americans largely agree that the president is using his office for personal gain.

Since getting laid off from a big bank in March, Lamar Rogers has used AI to help him apply to nearly 200 jobs.
He turns to Claude to tailor his résumé, uses an AI-powered dashboard for every interview, and recently vibe-coded a résumé-review app. Yet Rogers draws the line at letting AI apply for jobs on his behalf.
For the senior roles in banking and tech that he's pursuing, using AI to handle the entire application would be "disingenuous," Rogers, 34, said. "I want to put a lot more thought and care into it."
While employers use AI to screen applications, job seekers are using AI to whip up résumés and apply for jobs.
Yet as AI firms make it easier to identify a bot's helping hand — Anthropic recently said new Claude models would insert an "imperceptible watermark" into text that AI kicks out — the big question is how much AI is too much in the application process?
Business Insider spoke with headhunters and HR pros about best practices for using AI in your job hunt:
You don't need to hide AI
Job coaches said that candidates don't necessarily need to hide their use of AI. Employers are more focused on whether a candidate's claims hold up than on how polished their résumé looks.
"It's not really about whether AI helped write it," said Stephen Telford, a headhunter and career coach. "It's about whether the claim actually holds up once I start digging."
If a candidate claims they "improved sales by 30%" yet can't provide a detailed breakdown or point to evidence of how they achieved that result on their LinkedIn profile or elsewhere, Telford said he starts to lose trust.
"That tells me it's just AI-generated confidence," said Telford, who previously recruited for AWS.
He said candidates can use a simple test: Before letting AI phrase an accomplishment, ask whether the claim would hold up if a recruiter looked into it. Could you clearly explain the mechanics behind it, the starting point, what you did, and the outcome?
"If AI helped you say something you can't independently prove, that's where I'd draw the line," Telford said. "AI can help you tell your story better. It just can't be the source of the story."
Focus on your brand
In a sea of AI-generated cover letters using the same buzzwords and perfect grammar, maintaining a personal brand can help candidates stand out and seem authentic.
Liz Andora, chief people officer at DHI, parent company of tech career marketplace Dice, said that AI can be useful for structuring a résumé or sharpening the language, though candidates should make sure their apps still reflect them accurately.
"You want to make sure you're representing and putting forward who you are and what you offer to the potential employer," said Andora, who also does career coaching.
That extends beyond your résumé and cover letter. At a time when it can be difficult to tell whether you're interacting with a person or a bot, recruiters want to see evidence of the person behind the application. That doesn't mean leaving grammatical errors to prove you're human. However, candidates should keep their LinkedIn profile up-to-date and give hiring managers a clear sense of what they've accomplished.
Ron Porter, a senior client partner at the recruiting firm Korn Ferry, said he sometimes comes across materials with phrasing that is technically correct, but doesn't sound like the person who wrote it. Candidates should ensure the language reflects how they actually communicate and is something they could have written themselves.
Don't try to undermine the ATS
In a job market where getting past résumé-screening software can feel impossible, it may be tempting to try to game the system by doing something like hiding keywords in white text.
Andora said getting through ATS is a "legitimate issue." However, secretly stuffing applications with keywords that don't match your skills could backfire.
Telford said it can signal that a candidate is more focused on maximizing visibility than building credibility.
"If that keyword list doesn't match what's actually on their LinkedIn, their GitHub, or what they can speak to when I ask about it, it doesn't just hurt that one application. It makes me second-guess everything else they've told me, too," Telford said.
Job seekers' frustrations are understandable, said Xenia Wade, an AI adoption consultant. Employers "don't want the résumés to sound too much like AI, but they're filtering it out with AI," Wade said.
One way to sidestep the issue is to get a referral from someone inside the company. DHI Group's Andora said it's best to find an insider to make sure your application gets seen.
Applicant bots are risky
Applicants are sending out more applications on average, making the competition for each opening steeper. In the third quarter of 2025, hiring software company Greenhouse found that the average job opening received nearly triple the amount of applications from 2017, when the unemployment rate was comparable.
That doesn't mean using an AI bot to mass-send applications is the most effective way to land an interview.
One risk is that, if it's obvious, it can signal that the job wasn't worth the candidate's time or effort, Telford said. And in a competitive market, generic applications are unlikely to get you very far.
Throughout his job search, Rogers has leaned on AI. Nevertheless, he said, it took months of experimenting to get his résumé, cover letter, and application process where he wanted them.
"AI cannot do everything for you," Rogers said. He still checks its work and makes the final calls.
"It's the structure of the car, but it's not necessarily the engine," Rogers said. "You have to be able to drive it yourself."

Doctor Who, One Piece, Pokémon, Star Wars. Empty product boxes from these popular properties have been listed on eBay for $2,500 and up. It’s not too surprising to anyone familiar with modern nerd-dom that even the empty boxes for these perennial collectibles would command high prices.
But look what they’re joined by in that elite bracket: a Bottega Stardust Sparkling Rosé bottle and box (listed for $8,105), the box for a 1980s Rolex Explorer 1016 ($3,850), a “rare” Hermes Bolide box from Japan ($3,450), and a Suntory Hibiki bottle and box ($3,000).
One big reason for this is that buyers are paying big bucks to acquire the original packaging for an item they want to auction off; selling the collectable with an original box almost always boosts the resale price. For high-priced items—a secondhand Rolex Explorer 1016 sells for between $19,000 and $52,000—spending a couple grand on an original box is a worthwhile investment. It’s not just collectibles either; even for items like a Dyson Airwrap or Nintendo Switch, it can make sound financial sense for a seller to track down the original packaging.
There are currently over 160,000 “empty box” listings on eBay (many under $25), and over 140,000 on eBay UK. WIRED requested sales statistics on empty box sales from eBay, Vinted, and Poshmark; eBay declined to provide data, and Vinted and Poshmark did not respond.
There is also an illicit side to this business: Counterfeiters will acquire and use authentic boxes to ship fake products to buyers, hoping to bolster the illusion that the shipped item is real. Sometimes, sellers will ship an authentic box filled with nothing at all in what’s known as an empty box scam.
Buying Clout
A seller on Vinted with the username wildswhim, whose listings include jewelry packaging (Vivienne Westwood, Michael Kors) deliberately avoids including “actual empty tubes or containers” in sales to deter counterfeiters. The seller also frequently describes listings as being “for props, staging, or storage.”
Yes, props and staging: Often, these empty boxes are going to influencers and video producers who use them to decorate their film set. Independent creators and aspiring influencers will use empty boxes, bottles, and packaging to stage their Instagram posts and TikTok videos to give their clips a whiff of the luxury lifestyle.
There are currently over 1,500 listings on eBay specifically for the search term “empty box decor.” Listings include a “rare” empty Abercrombie & Fitch “PR box” listed for $50 and a “rare” empty Fenty Beauty “multi-tier influencer PR launch box” selling for $245. Both of these were originally sent out to select influencers by the companies’ respective public relations teams, indicating that the OG influencers are reselling the items to the next generation of creators coming up behind them.
The Vinted seller tonym528, who is based in London, sold an empty orange Louis Vuitton box for £23 (around $32) this month. He doesn’t ask his buyers questions but suspects that people are using “those kinds of boxes to show off fake wealth.” Seller MattyHornby, based in York, UK, has resold empty packaging from Supreme, Gucci, Balenciaga, Prada, retailer Selfridges, and skateboard and streetwear label Palace for similar prices per bag or box.
Seller Rafal tells WIRED that the “absolutely crazy” prices are why he started selling empty packaging (Nike, Apple, Puma, Dior) on Vinted. Seller mariaharris1967 also jumped on the trend. “I couldn’t believe it,” she tells WIRED. “I was able to get rid of loads. LV, Burberry, and Hermès sell super quickly.” She is one of the sellers who labels empty boxes and bags with descriptions such as “great for room staging,” “good for social media staging,” “decor, staging, or room props” and “#instagram” to target aspiring creators.
Signaling Success
Branded packaging arranged to appear in the shot—but in the background, not as the central focus —in social posts is often used to imply an association with an aspirational brand, says Tama Leaver, a social media researcher at Curtin University in Perth, Australia. Influencers are doing it, he says, “clearly with a view to making those intended relationships into real ones.”
Platforms like Giggster and Home Studio List, which rent out prestaged sets to influencers, are very good customers too. The Vinted seller wildswhim says “the studios catering to influencers are bulk buyers now” for empty packaging listings.
Creators posting piles of packaging—even basic cardboard boxes—are doing so to indicate not just that they can afford the luxury consumption lifestyle, but also that they’re successful at the game.
Instagram influencers will post behind-the-scenes images of “PR hauls,” “PR mountains,” or “a month’s worth of PR” showing the piles of products gifted to them by the public relations reps from aspirational companies. They’ll show the boxes littering their homes, or products clogging their luggage after returning from a trip.
Of course, not all of these PR hauls are authentic. Blessing Wuraola Akinsete, who runs the digital growth agency Wura Digital Concept in Lagos, Nigeria, has encountered emerging creators who buy empty high-end packaging just so they can post it for clout. “The pressure is to appear as though you are already receiving brand deals,” she says. “A new creator may see someone constantly posting PR packages and assume that person is far ahead of them, without knowing whether those products were gifted, purchased, or connected to a paid collaboration.”
In Nigeria, companies like Rent Now NG offer Lagosian influencers, celebs, and “fake life baddies” options such as its ultimate “fake life” package. For 6.5 million naira ($4,800), they get a mansion, a car, a chauffeur, a makeup artist, and a private chef for a day, plus plenty of luxury bags for photo shoots. Jason Koebler of 404 Media recently tried “LARPing” the faux-luxury life of a TikTok “hustlebro” by renting a fake set (inside a warehouse) that looks like the interior of a private jet, outsourcing high-energy video edits, and even faking Stripe dashboards, reports, and payment notifications to “prove” his earnings.
Established creators warn about the shortcuts of faking PR stacks. Tom Honeyands, the YouTube creator behind the series The Tech Chap, says these “fake it till you make it” tricks of staging shots with boxes is not sustainable. “Even if they achieve some growth with this kind of content,” he says, “most brands will be savvy enough to consider their whole profile and level of engagement before agreeing to work with them.”
Leaver suggests that staged luxury goods might still have a place in the creator world now that “the dial on authenticity has shifted” thanks to generative AI tools that can be used make any visual backdrop.
“At least with real physical objects like luxury-brand packaging, they can be actually shown, manipulated, and integrated into a video,” Leaver says. “Their realness in terms of being objects, even empty ones, is more valuable in an era of AI slop where everything can be faked.”
