Great camera. Strong battery life. Solid performance. Qi2 25W support. Slick contextual AI features.
TIRED
Not much is new. eSIM only in the US. Secure face unlock still doesn’t work in the dark.
The hot pink Hibiscus color is dazzling, but is Google’s 11th-generation Pixel just another iterative upgrade, or does it dial things up to 11? Diving beneath the surface, we find a slightly better chipset and camera, faster wireless charging, a fresh batch of AI features, and not much else. Don’t get me wrong: This is a slick smartphone, perhaps the best Android phone for folks who are comfortable with Google and Gemini AI, but it’s only a very slight improvement over last year’s Pixel 10.
Although it lands alongside the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, the Pixel 11 shares more in common with the new Pro Fold (review coming soon). The Pro models' more powerful camera system, with the gimmicky, glowing HiLight LED, is what sets them apart. The base model storage has finally jumped up to a more practical 256 GB, but that means the starting price of the Pixel 11 is $100 more than the 10 at $899 (not technically a price bump since the 256 GB model of the Pixel 10 was the same price).
Refinement has been the pattern in smartphones for the last few years, and the Pixel 11 does nothing to buck that trend. If you’ve got a 3-year-old handset and you’re in the market for a new phone, the Pixel 11 should be in the conversation, but if you’re looking for a justification to upgrade from last year’s Pixel 10, you won’t find it here.
Minor Makeover
Photograph: Simon Hill
The instantly recognizable design has been slightly refined; most notably, the pill-shaped camera bump is thinner and all-glass. Stick a case on the Pixel 11, and it will lie flat on a desk. It sports the same satin finish on the recycled aluminum frame and gloss finish on the glass back as last year’s phone, but with some fun new colors.
I was delighted to get Hibiscus (otherwise known as hot pink), but there’s also a more subtle Pistachio (warm green), and the usual Frost (white) and Obsidian (black). I’m sad they cut Indigo (surely everyone’s favorite from last year). Like Apple, Google seems to save the fun colors for the regular Pixel, and the Pros look more muted.
Despite a 6.3-inch screen, this is what passes for a small phone nowadays. Switching from last year's Pixel 10 Pro XL, I really appreciated how easy it was to handle the Pixel 11 one-handed. It’s a little thick, but it feels good in hand and has almost the same profile as the Pro, so you can use cases interchangeably. And I do recommend snagging a Pixel 11 case; I already scuffed the paintwork when I dropped it on the beach.
The screen is the same as last year’s: an excellent 6.3-inch OLED display with a 1080 x 2424-pixel resolution and refresh rates of 60 or 120 Hz. It’s a shame Google didn’t upgrade to a variable refresh rate (1 to 120 Hz) since it can save battery life. It also defaults to 60 Hz, and you have to dip into the Display settings to toggle on the smoother 120 Hz. The display is plenty bright with a 3,000-nit peak brightness; I never found myself squinting. Side by side with the Pro, it’s not quite as bright or sharp, and it has larger bezels, but you have to look closely to see the difference.
The fingerprint unlock is as good as any, but Google’s Face Unlock still doesn't work in the dark, which will annoy any iPhone defectors. US buyers will also have to do without a SIM slot, as the Pixel 11 is eSIM-only stateside. Physical SIM cards make switching between phones more straightforward, but phone makers and carriers have made that process smoother with eSIMs than in the past. Sure, it’s much easier to pop a card in than to go through your carrier when traveling abroad, but setting up an international eSIM isn't that complex. Both have benefits, but with US phones and carriers embracing eSIM over the past couple of years, it's become a nonissue.
Power Up
The new chip, Google’s Tensor G6, is supposed to deliver 20 percent gains in power efficiency, 25 percent faster browsing, and 15 percent faster app loading. The Pixel 11 has 12 GB of RAM and 256 or 512 GB of storage. For everyday use, it feels fast and responsive. I had no issues with loading apps or scrolling web pages, and the camera app feels a bit faster. Compared with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, I also noticed the Pixel 11 notified and loaded video from my Nest video doorbell a second or two faster.
I put it through its paces with the challenging mobile game Wuthering Waves. It was playable, but the action stuttered, and even on the Balanced (graphics and performance) setting, there were dropped frames aplenty during combat. After an hour, the Pixel 11 was warm, and the battery went from 40 to 26 percent. Less demanding games, like Mini Metro and Alto’s Odyssey, were fine, but dedicated gamers should still look elsewhere.
The 4,985-mAh battery is a disappointing 15-mAh jump over the Pixel 10, but Google claims battery life has improved 25 percent from 24 hours to 30 hours. I’m not sure it’s quite that much based on my first week of testing, but the Pixel 11 has seen me through very busy days without hitting empty, though I still think daily charging will be the norm for most folks.
The Pixel 11 charges at 30 watts wired (cable but no charger included), but support for Qi2 25W enables faster wireless charging. I recommend buying a Qi2 wireless charger. The magnetic Pixelsnap (Google's version of Apple's MagSafe on iPhones) feels a touch stronger than the one in the 10-series, and it’s such a handy feature that saves you from fumbling with cables. Google has also expanded the screensaver so you can have a multiple swipe function on the nightstand, including clock, weather, photos, charging status, and smart home controls.
Google has also switched to a MediaTek modem in the Pixel 11. I wouldn’t normally mention a modem, but the Samsung variant Google used in last year’s 10 series was prone to draining the battery and not holding a signal terribly well. Anecdotally, the Pixel 11 does better in a few spots where I’ve traditionally had trouble with my Pixel 10 Pro XL, which is great news for when you want to use your phone for calls. Your mileage may vary.
AI Everywhere
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google’s phones have always been about software over hardware, but the real-world value of AI features comes down to context. If I have to go digging or remember that a feature exists, I probably won’t get much value from it. This is why Google weaves its AI into everything, rather than applying it as a layer on top. The latest Gemini Intelligence features extend Google’s lead in this space.
Rambler improves the Pixel’s voice-to-text, cutting ums and ahs and letting you draft messages conversationally. I didn’t like it as much as my colleague, but I’m not really a speech-to-text guy, and I have a Scottish accent that it sometimes picks up wrong. I use the Pixel’s Recorder app a lot and love it for instantly transcribing my interviews, but Rambler doesn’t show the text as you talk like Recorder does; everything pops up after you’re done, which I don’t like as much.
AI overviews pop up right there in the Messages app when someone texts with a meet-up request, and you can add it to your calendar, or if they have a restaurant suggestion, you can tap to open it directly in Maps. Gemini can also dig details like flight numbers out of your Gmail to share via Messages if you let it. This is quite handy.
Fans of Circle to Search will be glad to know you don’t even have to snap a photo anymore; you can open the camera app, hold down the nav bar, and circle anything in the viewfinder to get info on it. You can also get location-based suggestions on the lock and home screen, such as a shortcut to your loyalty card in Google Wallet when you’re in a relevant store or recommendations for what to order at a restaurant from Maps.
There’s nothing groundbreaking here, but features like Call Screen for screening spam calls and Now Playing for surfacing the name of the song you can hear are still there, and those are the kinds of things that I miss when I switch away from a Pixel phone.
AI is firmly embedded in Google’s apps, and there’s no switch to turn it off completely, but you can choose to turn off Gemini, cut its access to apps like Photos and Messages, and turn off features like Circle to Search. Most of the camera app AI options are exactly that: options. But if this all sounds gimmicky and the idea of an AI-infused phone gives you the creeps, the Pixel line is not for you.
Camera Magician
The triple-lens rear camera is one of the top reasons to buy the Pixel 11. The camera feels faster, with less processing delay than the Pixel 10, and you can snap a shot and instantly load it into the gallery. Spec-wise, it’s almost identical, with a 48-megapixel main camera, 13-megapixel ultrawide, and 10.8-megapixel telephoto for 5x optical zoom. The main camera sensor is larger, enabling slightly better low-light performance, and the digital zoom capability is up from 20x to 30x. The 10.5-megapixel front-facing camera is the same.
Screenshot: Simon Hill
Everything works beautifully. Most people probably only ever use the main camera and the selfie camera, and reviewers can get too far into the weeds, but the bottom line is that you don’t need a particularly skilled hand or eye to snap great photos with the Pixel 11. I really appreciate the telephoto lens. I rarely have a use for the ultrawide, but the telephoto is great for zooming in from a distance, and though the 30x zoom is digitally enhanced by combining multiple images, there’s no generative AI at work, so you get a real image.
The camera app is feature-packed if you want to dive in. The most notable new features are the Camera Looks, which are like filters you select before you snap a shot. Phone cameras are typically tuned a certain way—Google’s phones tend to be punchy and high-contrast with realistic colors, while Samsung saturates colors and Apple prefers brighter images—but Camera Looks lets you tweak that to opt for warmer colors or dial up the shadows.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Google Pixel 11, main camera
Magic Capture is a clever new feature that lets you hold your phone up at a party or event and record video and select still shots simultaneously, without having to watch through the viewfinder. It’s a nice way to be more in the moment, and a safer way to hand your phone off to Mum and maybe get decent photos back.
No one really needs to upgrade their phone every year or two. It’s only by skipping a few releases that you’ll feel a real difference, and this is especially true for Google's phones because so much of what makes them special is on the software side, and many of those features will make it onto older phones too, though they might take a while.
For slick software features and a camera that’s easy to get great results from, the Pixel 11 is tough to beat in this bracket. If you want performance, both the Samsung Galaxy S26 and the Apple iPhone 17 are superior. Unless you’re a keen photographer, I don’t see a compelling case for paying more to get a Pro model. The Pixel 11 is the value sweet spot in Google’s new lineup, at least until the A-series next year.

Nearly 90,000 told to evacuate as wildfire approaches Reno, Nevada

Tens of thousands of people have been told to evacuate from an area close to Reno, Nevada, as a large wildfire reached the outskirts of the city.
Around 42,000 people have been ordered to leave their homes immediately, with a further 45,000 people urged to get ready to leave.
The fire, which was first reported on Saturday morning, had so far injured six people, officials said. Windy and unpredictable weather conditions have contributed to its spread.
Nevada's Governor Joe Lombardo has declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and ordered the National Guard to join firefighting and law enforcement efforts.
"This is an active and rapidly evolving situation and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said.
The fire was caused by humans and first reported at 11:15 local time (18:15 GMT) on Saturday, according to local officials.
They said that, as of Sunday evening, the fire had burned around 10,500 acres and was 0% contained.
Around 13,700 homes were inside the evacuation area, local emergency services said, with two shelters set up to take in displaced residents.
Of the six injured, three were emergency responders fighting the fire.
All Washoe County schools will be closed on Monday, except one, and mass road closures are in place.
Reno, in western Nevada, is located close to the state boundary with California and has a population of around 280,000 people.

Five features and one documentary have been nominated for the 2026 Nordic Council Film Prize. It’s awarded to a feature film or documentary produced in the Nordic countries that has been distributed in cinemas.
Some picks – announced at the Norwegian International Film Festival Haugesund – come as no surprise, as Joachim Trier’s Oscar-winning “Sentimental Value” and Hlynur Pálmason’s “The Love That Remains” have already enjoyed significant festival success.
However, the jury consisting of Jacob Ludvigsen, Jan Berg Jørgensen, Marjo Pipinen, Jóna Finnsdóttir, Anne Gjelsvik and Jonas Holmberg also recognized Jeanette Nordahl’s “Beginnings,” Búi Dam’s “Birita,” “A Light That Never Goes Out” by Lauri-Matti Parppei and “Kevlar Soul” directed by Maria Eriksson-Hecht.
Popular on Variety
“Kevlar Soul” focuses on two brothers who grow up terrorized by their alcoholic father.
“We are deeply honored by this nomination,” said Eriksson-Hecht.
“Being selected as Sweden’s entry for the Nordic Council Film Prize means a great deal to everyone involved, both in front of and behind the camera. We hope this recognition will help more people discover and see the film, bringing new attention to its themes.”
“Beginnings,” starring Trine Dyrholm and David Dencik, follows a couple that’s about to divorce – until Ane suffers a stroke.
“We wanted to explore the absolute loss of control, seen from all perspectives within a family. What happens when illness strikes, and how do we relate to each other when everything has changed?,” noted Nordahl, deciding to tell the story “without sentimentality or judgement, focusing on simple, everyday situations that might feel familiar.”
“So many families find themselves in this type of conflict, and our intention was to give them a film in which they could feel seen and validated. I think, and hope, this is why audiences have responded so strongly to it.”
In “Birita,” the only doc in the selection, Búi Dam decided to go personal.
“Making this film about my mother, an actress, and my relationship with her has been a journey of joy, love, and discovery. And, clichéd as it may sound, that has of course been the reward in itself,” he said. But the nomination is important for another reason as well.
“The Faroe Islands, a semi-autonomous part of the Danish realm, have long stood on the periphery of the Nordic community. Now, as we move towards independence – something that our Icelandic sister Björk encouraged us and Greenland to do in 2008 [in her song ‘Declare Independence’] – it feels important that we carve out a clear place for our own voice, our language, and our culture within the Nordic community.”
He added: “In that sense, this film is rebellious – just like my mother.”
Or like the protagonists of the music-heavy drama “A Light That Never Goes Out” by Lauri-Matti Parppei, who decide to start an experimental band, aka a “paramilitary noise art collective.” The film, which premiered at Cannes ACID, was a big winner at the Jussi Awards in its native Finland.
“My background is in the Finnish underground and DIY music scene. I never expected that a film based on those experiences would suddenly touch people around the world. And travel across borders and continents,” Parppei told Variety.
“As a Finn, I’ve always admired Nordic filmmakers and their long history of acclaimed cinema, even feeling a bit inferior. Even my favorite film of all time is from Sweden: ‘Fucking Åmål’ by Lukas Moodysson [also known as ‘Show Me Love’]. That’s why it means so much to me to be nominated alongside the works of my colleagues – and it feels like I might actually be a real Nordic filmmaker myself!”
Greenland did not submit a film for the 2026 Nordic Council Film Prize.
The prize comes with 300,000 Danish kroner, which will be shared equally among the screenwriters, directors and producers to emphasize “how film as an art form is brought about by the close collaboration of these three main contributors,” it was stated.
The winners will be announced on 20 October.
Here’s the full list of the nominees:
“Beginnings”
Nominated director: Jeanette Nordahl
Nominated writers: Rasmus Birch, Jeanette Nordahl
Nominated producers: Eva Jakobsen, Katrin Pors, Mikkel Jersin
“Birita”
Nominated director/writer: Búi Dam
Nominated producer: Jón Hammer, Durita Sumberg, Mark Steele
“Kevlar Soul”

Nominated writers: Pelle Rådström
Nominated producers: Ronny Fritsche, Lizette Jonjic
“A Light That Never Goes Out”

Nominated producer: Ilona Tolmunen
“The Love That Remains”

Its organisers announced in May that this year’s tournament was to be relocated to France because of the ongoing Middle East war.

Delhi HC notice to Abhijit Mitra, X, Google over Saurav Das’ privacy plea
The CJP leader has sought action against them for allegedly putting his residential details in public domain.
The Delhi High Court on Monday issued notices and summons to commentator Abhijit Iyer Mitra, and various law portals and media platforms on a privacy plea filed by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das. The CJP leader has sought action against them for allegedly putting his residential details in public domain.
X (formerly known as Twitter) told the Delhi high court on Monday that posts containing the residential address and other personal information of Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) spokesperson Saurav Das had been taken down and were no longer accessible.
The submission was made by X’s lawyer before a bench of Justice Sachin Datta in a suit filed by Das against political commentator Abhijit Iyer Mitra and several organisations, including media platform The Pamphlet, social media accounts associated with Jaipur Dialogues and Sunday Guardian, and legal news platform LawBeat.
In his suit, Das alleged that the defendants had violated his privacy by publishing the content in the public domain.
Justice Datta, however, issued summons in Das’s suit as well as in his application seeking to restrain the defendants from further publishing or disseminating such content.
In his suit, in which he has sought ₹2 crore in damages, Das, represented by senior advocate Akhil Sibal, alleged that he had been residing in a rented property in Greater Kailash since early 2025 and that representatives of The Pamphlet had trespassed onto the premises, recorded its interiors and subsequently published the footage on X on August 5. The video, the suit said, garnered more than 2.1 million views and was republished on August 10.
Das further alleged that Mitra disclosed details of his residence during a programme hosted by LawBeat, identifying his neighbour and incorrectly stating that the monthly rent was around ₹7 lakh. He claimed that Mitra subsequently published multiple posts containing the alleged personal information.
Besides damages, the suit also seeks an injunction restraining the defendants from further publishing or disseminating such content.
During the hearing, The Pamphlet’s lawyer, Abhinav Chandrachud, submitted that the X posts were no longer accessible, but sought time to file a response on the merits of the case.
Mitra’s lawyer opposed the suit, arguing that there was no cause of action against him.
The matter will now be heard on September 14.

Clark holds off McIlroy fightback to win BMW Championship

BMW Championship - final leaderboard
-16 W Clark (US); -14 P Cantlay (US); -13 R McIlroy (NI); -12 G Woodland (US), C Gotterup (US), C Morikawa (US); -10 R MacIntyre (Sco), M McNealy (US); -9 J Bridgeman (US); -8 S J Im (Kor), M Brennan (US).
Selected others: -7 S Scheffler (US), A Bhatia (US); -6 A Rai (Eng); -5 J Rose (Eng); -3 M Fitzpatrick (Eng); +2 T Fleetwood (Eng).
Wyndham Clark said he is "one of the best players in the world" after he survived a fightback from Rory McIlroy to win the BMW Championship in Missouri.
Clark held a five-shot lead going into the final day, but saw his advantage evaporate as McIlroy drew level with seven holes left to play.
But Northern Irishman McIlroy could not take several opportunities to move ahead, and successive Clark birdies enabled the American to post a fourth-round 71 and finish the week 17 under par.
After pushing Clark all the way, McIlroy ended the day one under par to finish 13 under, four shots behind the winner.
"It was weird - I wasn't nervous but I was kind of out of it, making double bogies, I can't believe I didn't make anything on the greens. But I kept trying to get myself going," Clark told CBS Sports.
"I really started to swing free down the end. I was proud I didn't let it get away and was mentally strong.
"I'm one of the best players in the world. Everyone gives me a hard time and roots for other people, but I've come into my own. It's my best season yet coming off my worst year."
After losing his first-day lead with a second-round 69, McIlroy said he needed a "heroic effort" to catch Clark on the final day.
The back-to-back Masters champion fought hard to gain two shots as Clark dropped three, but missed a put on the 14th with the scores tied - and from there Clark recovered.
"I can't be too disappointed, I'm not playing well enough to be too disappointed to no win," McIlroy told CBS Sports.
"I had my chances, but Wyndham stepped up. The way he played the last three holes, he showed a lot of character."

Normal deliveries are declining and C-section deliveries remain high at the Government Hospital for Women and Children at Kottaparamba in Kozhikode City, Keralam.
According to the Health department, there were a total of 5,201 deliveries (2,729 normal and 2,472 C-section) in 2020-21. This number came down to 2,238 (1,387 normal and 851 C-section) in 2025-26. A large number of people from the urban areas of Kozhikode are dependant on this hospital.
The data also reveal that between 2020-21 and 2022-23, a high number of deliveries were in the C-section category. In 2020-21, of the 5,201 deliveries, 2,472 were C-section; in 2021-22, of the 3,552 deliveries, 1,841 were C-section; and in 2022-23, of the 2,205 deliveries, 1,148 were C-section.
Though there were fewer C-section deliveries between 2023-24 and 2025-26, the percentage remained higher than the ideal population-level rate, between 10% and 15%, as suggested by the World Health Organisation. It is even higher than the national average of 21.5%, claims Satheesh Parannur, chairman of the Kozhikode-based rights organisation, Pouravakasha Samrakshana Samithi, who gathered the data through a Right to Information Act (RTI) query.
Mr. Parannur says that between 2020-21 and 2023-24, the number of total deliveries came down by 61% from 5,201 to 2,019. Though this number slightly went up to 2,238 in 2025-26, it was fewer than what was reported in 2020.
The RTI data show that in-patient admission dropped from 8,315 to 4,683 between 2020-21 and 2023-24. The next year, 5,089 people were admitted. The number again dropped to 4,838 in 2025-26. Meanwhile, a high number of people are seeking outpatient (OP) treatment. In 2020-21, a total of 81,329 people sought OP treatment and in 2024-25, this went up to 1,55,257 and slightly declined to 1,50,305 in 2025-26.
Inquiry sought
Mr. Parannur claims that though a large number of people could be approaching the hospital for medical check-up and medicines, at least some are not willing to get admitted there for deliveries.
He says the Health department should conduct a detailed inquiry into the decline in the number of deliveries and IP admission.

Consumer services company platform Urban Company has filed a defamation and disparagement suit against Kent RO Systems over advertisements questioning the safety and performance claims of the former’s Native water purifiers. In an exchange filing, Urban Company said it filed the suit before the Delhi High Court on August 11, alleging that Kent’s advertising campaign made false and misleading claims concerning the two-year filter life and two-year service life offered with Native water purifiers. The campaign included advertisements and social media content featuring several influencers, according to the filing. Kent allegedly described the two-year filter and service life claims as a “marketing gimmick” and suggested that using Native water purifiers was “unsafe” and “risky” for consumers. The advertisements referred to Urban Company’s Native M0, M1, M2, M1 Pro, and M2 Pro water purifiers. Urban Company alleged that the campaign disparaged both the company and its Native water purifiers and defamed them. During a hearing on August 12, Kent told the Delhi HC that it would remove the advertisements covered by the suit and would not run promotional content making the same or similar claims about water purifiers offering a two-year filter life or two-year no-servicing feature if such content disparaged Urban Company. Kent was asked to remove the advertisements and related social media content within 15 days of the hearing. The court passed its order on August 12, but it was uploaded to its website on August 22, the filing said. This is not the first legal dispute between Urban Company and Kent. Last year, Kent filed a patent infringement suit alleging that Urban Company’s Native water purifiers infringed its patent and sought a permanent injunction restraining their manufacturing and sale. Urban Company opposed the allegations and filed a counterclaim challenging the validity of Kent’s patent. The company has also filed a separate suit against Kent alleging tortious interference. Ask a sixteen-year-old about a social media ban, and you get an answer sharper than most adults arguing about bans. She says, “It doesn’t prepare us for the real world when we will have to deal with these distractions in our life”. The teenager’s response strikes at the core of the ban vs. no ban debate: the necessity to teach and develop self-regulation.
The argument for and against bans
Lawmakers banning social media are working from the angle that if we remove the option altogether, the posting, compulsive scrolling, and ensuing anxiety will go away with it. The opposing argument is that bans prevent self-regulation, built through practice with social media access readily available.
Behavioral science has a fairly precise answer for which of these arguments holds up.
The bans themselves are moving fast and in earnest around the world. Australia was the first country to impose a sweeping ban on social media outright for children under-16 in 2025. Multiple countries in the EU are attempting to follow suit. These decisions to ban social media rest on neuroscientific insights showing that the human brain’s reward circuitry matures years before the prefrontal cortex that reins it in, leaving adolescents genuinely more vulnerable to engineered design working actively to grab their attention. Lawmakers are right to take this seriously.
But are social media bans for teenagers the panacea that they are made out to be?
How social media functions
Social media platforms function like a Skinner box for the modern human: our engagement on them runs on the same reinforcement-based learning as B. F. Skinner’s animal experiments. People on social media post faster exactly when their recent rate of reward, meaning engagement, has been higher. A pattern known as the law of effect, more ‘likes’ leads to more posting. Engagement on every platform runs on an unpredictable schedule; we never know which posts are going to land. Rewards are also hyper-personalised: an unending carousel of perfectly-matched content delivered based on every prior click and scroll.
What makes matters worse is that social media’s unpredictable and personalised rewards are exactly the training that will make children persist on these platforms through the interruption that comes from a ban. When there are multiple ways to get on social media, our behavior distributes itself across those options in proportion to the corresponding rewards. Think of a building with many entrances: remove one entrance without touching the others and people will continue to be able to get in. Underlying behavior does not vanish; It simply reallocates to a different mode. If a regular account stops working, we create a bustling market for fake accounts and new platforms not covered by the bans, effectively pushing teenagers to unregulated corners of the internet.
Perhaps predictably so, Australia’s ban, sweeping on paper, is showing that an estimated 85% of children under-16 are still finding their way onto restricted platforms, through borrowed logins and fake accounts, in a recent study. Bans are leaky. Short of closing every door at once, children will simply find the ones still open. But setting up strict age verification measures can be seen as an infringement upon teenagers’ rights to a private life, one of the reasons France’s newly-enacted social media ban was recently struck down by their Constitution Council.
In any case, let’s assume we manage to pull off the most stringent enforcement of a ban. Children with support systems in place will now have time to learn skills, build hobbies, and form real relationships. What happens to the vulnerable teenagers without a supportive home environment? A ban restricts access, but it does not fix the environment around the child. For teenagers building their sense of autonomy, that restriction in itself can cause harm.
In April, a commentary drawing on a year-long international working group on digital safety noted that bans are “unlikely to be effective” because they overlook how social platforms can be redesigned to build resilience, and instead place all the onus on teenagers. A nuanced solution is one that addresses the problem from both sides.
What, then, can work?
Nobel Prize winner Richard Thaler coined the term ‘nudge’ to describe choices that reshape the environment. When workers avoided retirement plans, a nudge that automatically enrolled them in superannuation funds profoundly impacted their savings. On social media, forcing platforms to batch-deliver notifications into fixed windows instead of letting them arrive at all times, and adding friction to sharing sensitive content, and disabling autoplay and infinite-scroll by default are nudges. We mandate structural corrections on the platform side. A boost, on the other hand, gives young people the skills to manage their own actions instead of complete restriction. The option to use social media stays available. Decision rules around time on social media, and encouraging goal-setting for healthier digital habits are examples of boosts.
Which brings us back to that 16-year-old. She was right: a ban will not teach her self-regulation. But unfettered access to social media where she is left to fend for herself will not work either. What she actually needs is a nuanced alternative, one that is, unfortunately, not on offer in her school’s policy.
(Maithri Sivaraman is an assistant professor at Teachers College, Columbia University. maithri.sivaraman@tc.columbia.edu)

Bali jails Swiss tourist for insulting sacred Day of Silence
- Published
A Swiss tourist has been sentenced to one year in prison for insulting a sacred religious event on Indonesia's holiday island of Bali.
In a now-removed video, Luzian Andrin Zgraggen, 26, had filmed himself walking to an empty beach during the Hindu holiday of Nyepi, describing the scene as "crazy".
He was arrested in March after the video sparked widespread anger among Balinese on social media.
Nyepi, also known as the Day of Silence, is an annual holiday during which the usually bustling tourist island goes quiet, as people stay home and refrain from making loud noises. The restrictions apply to everyone on the island regardless of religion, including tourists.
On Nyepi, the island's airport shuts down and internet access is restricted.
Entertainment events are restricted and even the use of electricity is discouraged.
Residents typically stock up on groceries ahead of Nyepi so they can stay at home during the holiday.
On Nyepi, which fell on 19 March this year, Zgraggen filmed himself breaking the ban on going out, in an Instagram post captioned with expletives, local media reported.
"What the defendant did offended the Balinese people, hurt their faith and provoked public outrage," the presiding judge said, according to the Associated Press.
Zgraggen said during his trial that he did not understand the extent of Nyepi restrictions and did not mean to insult the Balinese.
"I deeply regret what I did, I apologise to the Balinese people," the Associated Press reported him as saying in court.
Tourists have previously been detained or deported for violating Nyepi restrictions.
Bali has seen tourist numbers recover past its pandemic lull. Last year it welcomed a record seven million international visitors.
But along with the surge in tourism comes misbehaviour that has vexed locals and Balinese authorities. Foreigners have been penalised for offensive acts at religious sites, forming exclusive tourist enclaves and flouting traffic laws.
Authorities have vowed to tighten scrutiny of the island's tourists and crackdown on unruly foreigners.

‘India will establish its own space station by 2035’: Isro chief V Narayanan
Narayanan highlighted India's growing capabilities in space technology and said the country is now using space-based applications across more than 50 areas.
India is working towards establishing its own space station by 2035, with the first module of the proposed Bharatiya Antariksha Station already approved, Isro Chairman Dr V Narayanan said on Sunday.
Speaking at the third National Space Day celebrations in Ahmedabad, Narayanan highlighted India's growing capabilities in space technology and said the country is now using space-based applications across more than 50 areas directly serving citizens.
"Today, we are celebrating the third National Space Day. The theme is very important: innovation, collaboration, and aspiring for global leadership in the space sector," Narayanan said.
He said India has been steadily expanding its capabilities since launching its space programme 64 years ago.
"India started its space programme 64 years ago, and today we are serving the common man in more than 50 areas, including Earth observation, remote sensing, telecommunications, television broadcasting, tele-education, disaster warning and mitigation, ensuring the safety and security of every citizen, navigation, real-time monitoring and tracking," the Isro chief said.
Narayanan also outlined some of the country's major upcoming space programmes, including the Gaganyaan human spaceflight mission and the development of India's own space station.
"Under the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, many programmes are in the pipeline. We are working on the Gaganyaan programme. We are also working towards establishing our own space station, the Bharatiya Antariksha Station," he said.
"The first module has already been approved, and we aim to establish the space station by 2035," Narayanan added.
The Isro chief's remarks came during celebrations marking India's achievements in space exploration and the third National Space Day.
Union Minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, who also addressed the event, recalled the significance of Chandrayaan-3's historic landing near the Moon's south polar region.
He said National Space Day was announced following the successful Chandrayaan mission and India's achievement of reaching the lunar south pole at the location named Shiv Shakti Point.
"Following the success of the Chandrayaan mission and the announcement by the Prime Minister, India will observe the day it set foot on the Moon's south pole-at the 'Shiv Shakti Point'-as National Space Day," Shekhawat said.
He said the third National Space Day was being celebrated in Ahmedabad under the aegis of the Space Applications Centre and highlighted the government's efforts to expand participation in the space sector.
"Under the Prime Minister's leadership, the privatisation of the space science sector has opened doors to immense possibilities for India," Shekhawat said.
He said the expansion of private participation had created new opportunities for India's space industry while also complementing the work being undertaken by Isro.
"Isro's workload has not decreased; rather, its operational capacity has expanded manifold," the Union Minister said.
Shekhawat further noted that the time taken for several space-related activities, including developing applications, manufacturing satellites, creating payloads and launching satellites, had been substantially reduced.
"These processes are now being executed with far greater proficiency," he said.

India's space programme has expanded significantly from its early focus on developing basic satellite and launch capabilities to missions involving lunar exploration, human spaceflight, advanced Earth observation and satellite-based applications.
The Chandrayaan-3 mission, which successfully landed on the Moon on August 23, 2023, became a landmark achievement for the country's space programme and is commemorated annually through National Space Day.
With Gaganyaan and the proposed Bharatiya Antariksha Station, India is now looking beyond lunar exploration towards sustained human activity in space and a larger role in the global space ecosystem.

Thai prime minister meets security chiefs after coordinated attacks in 3 southern provinces
Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has held an urgent meeting with security officials after coordinated violence erupted in three southern provinces
BANGKOK -- BANGKOK (AP) — Thailand ’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, already facing a flood crisis in the country’s north, held an urgent meeting on Sunday with high-level security officials in response to coordinated violence overnight in three southern provinces where a small-scale Muslim insurgency is active.
The meeting, held shortly before Anutin flew north to inspect the badly flooded province of Nan, followed 51 incidents on Saturday night in the southernmost provinces of Narathiwat, Pattani and Yala.
The attackers did not engage with military or police forces. Only three civilians were known to have been wounded, and they were reported to be recovering on Sunday.
The violence primarily involved small bombs, arson and other forms of property damage. The highest-profile target was a 7-Eleven convenience store in Pattani. A video circulating on social media appeared to show armed men stalking outside the store while customers and workers fled before it was set on fire.
A bomb that damaged rail tracks in Narathiwat forced the suspension of local and long-haul services. It was not clear when they would be restored due to the uncertain security situation.
As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions.
However, such attacks are generally believed to be carried out by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional Melayu Patani, or BRN. It is the major insurgent group in the south with the organizational means and support to stage such an action. It is also the group with which the Thai government has been holding on-again, off-again peace talks.
The three southernmost provinces are the only ones with Muslim majorities in predominantly Buddhist Thailand and the BRN has said that it is seeking self-rule for them.
Muslim residents have long complained of being treated like second-class citizens in Thailand, and separatist movements have been periodically active for decades.
Insurgent violence escalated sharply in 2004 and was met with heavy-handed crackdowns, further fueling discontent. According to Deep South Watch, a think tank based at the Prince of Songkla University’s campus in Pattani, 7,837 people have died in the violence in the past 22 years.
The last major flare-up came in July, when about 10 attackers opened fire and threw pipe bombs at soldiers at a security checkpoint in Narathiwat. Five paramilitary soldiers were killed and six civilians were wounded, including a 10-year-old boy.
Don Pathan, an independent security analyst, says the BRN carries out attacks largely for leverage as it negotiates with the Thai government.
“From the ground, BRN combatants are turned off by the boasting of military officials and wanted to use the spike in violence to demonstrate their capabilities," said Pathan. "Many of the targets in these latest incidents were civilians, but BRN combatants were not after body counts. They want to send a stern message to the Thais of what they are capable of doing.”

Within minutes of the BJP announcing its new social media team on Monday, August 17, a search on X revealed that the accounts of the four newly appointed social media co-convenors had either vanished or their posts had become inaccessible.
Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav were appointed as social media co-convenors by BJP national president Nitin Nabin. Gandhi’s profile initially remained accessible but her timeline showed no recent posts, suggesting that her tweets had been deleted. Soon after, her profile disappeared altogether, displaying X’s “account doesn’t exist” notice. The X profiles of the other three appointees are also currently inaccessible.
The X handles belonging to Shiwanand Dwivedi and Arun Yadav have been made private while Alok Bhatt’s X handle has been deactivated.
The appointments came as part of a rejig of the BJP’s national office bearers, with Amit Malviya, who had served as the party’s social media convenor since 2015, replaced by Deepak Mhaskey.
Deepak Mhaskey’s X account (@deepakmhaskey), which is not a verified handle as of August 18, offers a clear indication that posts were removed. At 5:19 pm on August 17, the account displayed 6,905 posts. The same account currently displays 5,563 posts — a reduction of 1,342 posts. (Screenshots below)
His timeline tells a more striking story: Only two original posts are currently visible, both posted on August 17, both concerning his appointment as the social media convenor of the party. The discrepancy is particularly noteworthy given Mhaskey’s new role.
At least three of the four newly appointed co-convenors have a documented history of amplifying communal rhetoric and spreading misinformation. Gandhi has been fact-checked by Alt News multiple times for disseminating communal misinformation. Her X activity shows repeated support for Nathuram Godse, including a tweet expressing her desire to have Godse as her last name instead of Gandhi.
In March 2014, Priti Gandhi was identified by WikiLeaks as the person responsible for amplifying a fabricated endorsement of Narendra Modi. Gandhi had promoted a fake quote falsely attributed to WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange, claiming he said Modi was “incorruptible,” complete with Assange’s forged signature. Modi’s online supporters then seized upon the false endorsement as a high-profile international validation of the BJP Prime Ministerial candidate’s credentials.
Alok Bhatt, meanwhile, has a pattern of publicly posting sexist and anti-Muslim slurs. He has even targeted journalists like Barkha Dutt using vitriolic language.
Arun Yadav, who was the BJP Haryana IT cell in-charge, was removed by the party on July 7, 2022, amid calls for his arrest over his Islamophobic tweets, dating between May 2022 and 2017. #ArrestArunYadav was trending at the time with over 184,000 tweets. The state BJP president said Yadav was removed with immediate effect but gave no reason.
Malviya congratulated the new office-bearers in an X post and said they have been appointed at a “crucial juncture”. Speaking specifically about the social media co-convenors, he said he had the “privilege of working closely with each of them” and that he was confident that under their leadership, the party’s digital communication would “achieve newer milestones and continue to shape India’s public discourse with conviction, creativity and clarity.”
Just as this report was getting published, the X account of Shiwanand Dwidevi (@shiwadwivedi) became accessible again. Notably, the total post count came down from 10,800 (as shows in the screenshot used in this story) to 10,200. This indicates that roughly around 600 posts were removed.

What Does a Trump Endorsement Actually Mean in 2026?
A few recent losses for Trump-endorsed politicians hardly mean a sea change in Trump’s power, but they do complicate his narrative.
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.
Cory Mills’s reelection campaign was in trouble before it even began. Washington, D.C., police investigated the Florida representative early last year after a woman alleged that he’d assaulted her; later in 2025, a different woman was granted a restraining order against him. Neither woman was his wife. Mills, who has denied any wrongdoing, was never charged with anything, and the woman who alleged that he’d assaulted her walked back her claim after it became public. Still, questions lingered. Then, in February, Donald Trump endorsed him anyway, calling him an “America First Patriot and Tremendous Champion” of his district.
Not everyone in Florida’s Republican establishment felt the same. Governor Ron DeSantis declined to back him, and Representatives Anna Paulina Luna and Mike Haridopolos threw their support behind his opponent. A House ethics probe is ongoing. On Tuesday, Mills lost his primary election—and despite never having rescinded his endorsement, Trump is now trying to back away from the congressman retroactively. “I told Congressman Cory Mills of Florida, a friend of mine, to get out of the Race, but he wouldn’t listen,” he posted on Truth Social yesterday morning. Mills’s opponent, Ryan Elijah—who already won the primary—now has Trump’s “Complete and Total Endorsement!”
What does a presidential endorsement mean for a Republican facing a primary election in 2026? If not enduring loyalty from the White House, then at least a reliable boost in the polls. The candidates that Trump supports still tend to win big; about 96 percent of the politicians he tapped this year (more than 300 of them) won their primary, according to Ballotpedia—an impressive ratio. Trump clearly enjoys the perception that his endorsement makes or breaks a candidate. “If they don’t get the endorsement, they don’t win,” he said in 2021.
For many voters, particularly in the MAGA camp, perceived loyalty to Trump remains a deciding factor. (Just ask Bill Cassidy.) But not every bet Trump makes pays off. An endorsement has never been an outright guarantee of victory, and the rare exceptions illuminate some truths about Trump and the GOP. Two of the president’s other picks lost their primary race on Tuesday: Megan Degenfelder, the head of Wyoming’s Department of Education, who was running for the state’s governorship, and the former Commerce Department adviser Catalina Lauf, who was up for an open House seat in southwest Florida. By CNN’s count, that makes 10 Trump-endorsed candidates who have so far lost their primary this year.
No single, unifying theory can explain these races. Sometimes, the timing makes a difference. When Trump endorsed Degenfelder as Wyoming’s best choice for the governorship, back in January, the state’s education chief hadn’t even entered the race. Once she did, the nod gave her campaign an early lead—an advantage she held on prediction markets for about seven months, despite being outraised and outspent by her main opponent in the GOP primary. In the end, she couldn’t sustain it. Lauf got her endorsement from Trump last week, almost a full year into her campaign, and well after mail-in voting had already begun. Her primary was always more of a toss-up than Degenfelder’s, but Trump’s endorsement may have arrived too late to make a difference.
 
 The president also cares more about some races than he does about others. In Indiana, he was able to use his endorsement power to punish those who had opposed his agenda. Trump vowed that Republican state senators who were up for reelection would lose their race if they rejected a gerrymandering plan he backed—and in May, after a concerted effort and successful fundraising from the MAGA base, most of those politicians did indeed lose their primary. Compare that with what he gave Lauf: not much more than a one-off Truth Social post.
Not every race is a blanket referendum on Trump’s endorsement power; the particulars always matter. The Republican strategist Doug Heye told me that “when the voters go in the voting booth, the word Trump doesn’t appear. It’s those candidates.” Mike Lindell, the Trump-endorsed MyPillow founder and MAGA stalwart, lost his bid for the Minnesota governorship earlier this month. He’d been leading in the polls, despite the fact that he was obviously unqualified—and that the state’s GOP leadership had declined to endorse him, suggesting that he’d be an “easy target” for Democrats. On Election Day, though, he lost to the experienced state House speaker Lisa Demuth. His adjacency to Trump couldn’t get him over the line.
As much as Trump likes the idea that he alone can propel a candidate to victory, he also seems to try to skew the odds in his favor. As NPR points out, the president has lately been backing more incumbents than he did during the 2018 midterms (75 percent of his choices this year have been sitting politicians), which suggests a greater aversion to risk. He also tends to make endorsements much earlier than he used to, getting involved from the outset and attempting to deter competition. Recent history is full of examples of races where Trump’s endorsement did make a big difference: The Ohio Senate seat that ultimately went to J. D. Vance in 2022 was fiercely contested until the president made his pick. Often, though, the president is simply playing the odds, betting on the candidate he thinks has the best chance.
That’s exactly what happened in Texas earlier this year. Ahead of the GOP primary for John Cornyn’s Senate seat, Trump was widely expected to endorse the incumbent. As my colleague Elaine Godfrey noted at the time, the senator tried to rename a highway after Trump in an effort to secure his support. But the president went with a competitor, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who’d been ahead in the polls despite being impeached a few years prior. Back in 2022, in the lead-up to Missouri’s Senate primary, Trump went with a more unusual strategy. He wrote on social media that he’d decided to endorse “ERIC”—but didn’t specify which of the three candidates named Eric he actually supported. Was it a gaffe, or a sly acknowledgment that he didn’t want to pick among them?
Trump has been more involved in primaries than his predecessors were, setting a new expectation for how active presidents should be in those races. Many of his endorsements have been a boon for his favored candidates. But not every election is about Donald Trump.

Despite making changes last fall to help block adults from messaging unknown children, Roblox is still failing to stop adults from creeping on kids in other ways, Australia’s eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, said on Thursday.
Suspecting that Roblox may not be doing enough to stop child exploitation, eSafety conducted testing earlier this year that flagged alarming gaps in Roblox safeguards. The agency found that adult strangers could still send connection requests to kids, whose “profiles and biographies, including account names, number and names of connections, avatar images, and non-sensitive biographical information such as their interests were visible to anyone on the Roblox platform, with no option to restrict the visibility of this information.”
Such requests did not trigger parental alerts, eSafety found, and bad actors could also search kids’ visible-to-anyone contact lists for more targets.
Perhaps even more concerning, adults could also search for kids and comment on their posts “without parental or carer consent” in “forums outside game environments,” eSafety said.
Australia’s Online Safety Act requires that platforms prevent unwanted contact between adults and minors. It also mandates setting children’s accounts to private by default. Although Roblox “believes it is meeting its obligations,” the online gaming platform—which 1.7 million Australian kids use—has entered a court-enforceable agreement to make changes in the next three months.
Upcoming measures will prevent adults from contacting kids without parental consent across the platform, Roblox has promised. Providing better protections for kids starts with “strengthening the account settings of children’s accounts so they are private by default,” eSafety said, and ends with Roblox making it easy to report unwanted contact and notifying users of outcomes after reports are made. Those are critical protections for Australia’s second most popular online game for kids, Inman Grant said.

Three Sundays ago, Payas Jain fell two points short of lifting the trophy at the Commonwealth Table Tennis Championship in his hometown New Delhi. On Sunday evening here, he didn’t let history repeat itself. For Payas, the three weeks since the CTTC have not been about chasing results but about sticking to a process.
That process bore fruit in emphatic fashion on Sunday, when Payas outplayed reigning National champion Manav Thakkar to win the season-opening National Ranking tournament at The Sportz Hub in Kanpur.
“Nothing has changed,” Payas told Sportstar after the victory. “Before the Commonwealth Championships, I was trying to follow the process. Even after the Commonwealth Championships, I was just trying to follow the process. Because the Asian Games is coming up, my main goal is to win a medal for India at the Asian Games. So, I am just looking at that.”
What changed on the table, however, was the manner in which Payas went about his business. Against one of the strongest defensive players in Indian men’s table tennis, Payas refused to be hurried. He stayed in the rallies, waited for the opportunity to turn and then passed Manav with the precision that had also been evident in his service receiving.
Everything, he insisted, was intentional. “Everything was intentional, whether it be my body language, my shot-making, my strategy or my tactics. The fact that everything was very intentional reflected on the table today,” he said.
“I know how Manav plays. He knows how I will play. So I was prepared for everything,” Payas said. “It was a great match. I played actually well and I was feeling very confident.”
That confidence grew as the final progressed. Payas sensed the rhythm after the opening game and, rather than attempting to force the issue, trusted his ability to remain in the exchanges until the opening appeared.
“I knew that he is not going to miss so soon and it is going to be a tough fight,” he said. “I was just ready to be on the table whether he is playing speed or power. I was just trying to put as much balls as possible. And whenever I was getting the chance, I was able to turn and pass.”
The title adds another significant marker to Payas’ rise. A member of India’s Asian Games squad, he has put together a strong domestic season and finished second in the national rankings, strengthening his claim for a place in the Indian team for major international competitions.
He is also closing in on a place in the world’s top 100. Payas is still awaiting inclusion in the Sports Authority of India’s Target Olympic Podium Scheme list of promising athletes. For now, though, he is less concerned about what may follow than about maintaining the process that has brought him this far. The Asian Games medal remains the larger target. Sunday’s title was simply another step towards it.

Student wellbeing in India declines sharply through the senior school years, the Student Well-Being Pulse Report by IC3 Institute has found. The report is a part of a wider study on student suicide aversion, which focuses on mental health and well-being. The proportion of students reporting high overall wellbeing fell from 62% in Grade 8 to 43% in Grade 12, the report has stated. The findings are based on the responses from 8,515 students across India, showing a consistent decline across wellbeing, happiness, confidence and motivation as students progress through school. The report was launched at the 10th Annual IC3 Conference and Expo in Mumbai on Thursday (August 20, 2026).
“The findings point to a widening gap between the pressures students experience and the support they seek. Happiness falls from 65% in Grade 8 to 48% in Grade 12, confidence from 64% to 47% and motivation from 64% to 49%. Negative emotions also intensify with age, with anxiety, low energy, frustration, loneliness and sadness all peaking among students in Grades 11 and 12. When students do seek help, they most commonly turn to friends and family, with 49% and 44% respectively. A smaller proportion also reach out to teachers (13%) and school counsellors (6%), while 2% report seeking support from therapists. Notably, 52% of students believe that therapy or counselling would be helpful, indicating openness to structured support when accessible,” a statement issued by IC3 stated.
Gender gap
As per the report, girls experience significantly higher levels of negative emotions than boys across every category. Across all five negative emotional states (anxiety, low energy, loneliness, frustration, and sadness), female students consistently report higher “Often/Always” levels than males. 33% girls experienced anxiety, while 23% boys reported experiencing it.
Also, negative emotions intensified steadily as students moved into higher grades. “Almost every emotion shows a clear upward trend from Grade 8 to Grade 12 in the “Often/Always” category. Seniors (Grade 11 and 12) show the worst overall emotional wellbeing profile. In every negative emotion category, Grades 11 and 12 have the highest, or among the highest, “Often/Always” responses. This reflects academic pressure, board exams, college planning, and burnout,” the report said.
High level of flourishing
Students generally reported high levels of flourishing, especially in social belonging and emotional connection. Across nearly all indicators, the majority of students fell in the ‘Strongly Agree/Agree’ category, often above 60–80%. Overall, 62% students felt happy at school while 78% have a close friend at school and 74% felt safe and included in school. Additionally, 64% said they took care of their physical and mental health, 78% said their friends and family support them and 70% said they feel hopeful of their future. Girls tend to flourish more socially and emotionally, while boys rate themselves higher on personal resilience measures.
Well-being declined steadily as students progressed to higher grades, with Grade 12 showing sharp drops. Across every indicator, Grade 8 students report the highest flourishing, and Grade 12 the lowest.
Sleep concern
According to the findings of the study, sleep declined steadily and sharply as students moved into higher grades. The grade-level trend showed a deterioration in sleep (recommended: 7-8 hours) as academic pressure increased.
“The senior grades (11 & 12) show the most worrying sleep patterns. Students in Grades 11 and 12 report that 19% slept for less than five hours, nearly half slept only 5–6 hours, while 22–23% got the recommended 7–8 hours of sleep. “These are the years where cognitive performance and emotional resilience are most needed and yet students appear to be the most sleep-deprived,” the report said.
The 2025 Student Well-being Pulse Report was conducted by the IC3 Institute in collaboration with the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations (CISCE). 8,515 students across India participated in the survey, with the majority of them being from Grades 8 through 12. The survey was developed using Google Forms and disseminated through email and WhatsApp.

Fast-moving wildfire threatens Reno, Nevada, forcing thousands to evacuate
Hawk Fire began Saturday and quickly grew to more than 60 square kilometres
A fast-moving wildfire that jumped over fire trucks and made it difficult for crews to reach hot spots destroyed homes in northwest Reno, Nevada, on Sunday. Shifting winds challenged firefighters trying to bring it under control, and authorities urged some 90,000 people to evacuate.
At least six people — three first responders and three civilians — were injured, officials said. Officials said the fire was "human-caused" but did not provide details on how they reached that conclusion, or whether it was intentionally set or accidental.
The Hawk Fire began Saturday and quickly grew to more than 60 square kilometres as it spread across the Peavine Peak area of the Humboldt–Toiyabe National Forest, where rugged foothills are ringed by homes and businesses near the California state line.
'Please get out'
Some 42,000 residents have been ordered evacuated as the "GO NOW" zone expanded, reaching the edge of the University of Nevada. An additional 45,000 people were in the adjacent evacuation warning zone. Authorities implored all of them to leave and be prepared to stay away for several days, because shifting and strengthening winds were expected to make the fire even more unpredictable.
"Please get out if you can right now," Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said.
Cari Kieffer said a video posted on social media showed her house entirely burned down, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing.
- Destructive wildfires prompt evacuations in Washington state
- Spokane wildfires displace thousands, but crews make progress containing flames
"I woke up this morning and just started crying — all my kids, they lost everything," Kieffer said Sunday. "We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone."
Kieffer had been watching her son's football game Saturday when she learned that their home on the outskirts of Reno was in the evacuation zone. An app the family used to track the fire's progress had been lagging significantly behind its actual location, she said, so they thought firefighters had kept the blaze from their neighbourhood.
Instead, Kieffer, her husband and their four children ages 3 to 16 raced to save their dogs and whatever possessions they could retrieve. Ash rained down, and the wind blew like an oven blast from a wall of flames advancing down the hillside toward their neighborhood, she said.
"I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked," Kieffer said. "I was like, we gotta go like now."
Eyes watering and throat burning, Kieffer grabbed a handful of clothes, a Bible, her wedding photos and her mother's ashes. In the frenzy, as firefighters yelled at her family to leave immediately, she said she forgot her family's birth certificates and was unable to salvage her childhood photos.
National Guard mobilized
The family drove to a friend's home but had to evacuate again. They learned later Saturday evening that their own home was gone.
Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the Nevada National Guard to support aerial firefighting with two helicopter crews as well as 60 troops to help police safeguard evacuated neighborhoods. Also responding were 800 fire personnel.

Nearly 10,000 customers were without power in Washoe County on Sunday, down from 60,000 on Saturday. Portions of U.S. Route 395, a major north-south highway, were closed due to the fire. Reno, with more than 280,000 residents, is the largest city in Nevada outside of metro Las Vegas.
Washoe County emergency officials opened the Reno-Sparks Convention Center to evacuees, but said they couldn't bring their pets — small animals and large animals were to be left at two other locations. Casinos in Reno offered discounts on hotel rooms to evacuees.
Fire quickly turned destructive
The fire was so small Saturday morning that it wasn't even a concern, said Tyler Duvall, who went camping over the weekend. By the next day, his house was in the evacuation zone.
"The wind really blew it up," Duvall said.
On Saturday alone, 15 new fires popped up across Nevada. Months of dry weather and a record lack of snow this past winter across the American West have created prime fire conditions. Earlier this month, wildfires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area, while three wildfires north of Reno forced more than 13,000 residents from their homes.
The University of Nevada, where many of the 20,000 undergraduates moved into their housing this weekend, was just outside the evacuation zone Sunday.
Two hospitals evacuated patients and the sheriff said his office was keeping a close watch on whether to evacuate the county jail.
The fire moved exceptionally fast Saturday night, jumping over fire trucks and making it difficult for responders to get to hot spots while residents were trying to get out, the sheriff said.
"It was extremely confusing," Balaam said, describing how changing winds sent the flames in different directions.

Dubai, Aug 24: The new head of Iran's top security body warned Sunday that Tehran will see any country's support for new US economic measures against the Islamic Republic as an “act of war,” while Iran's president defended an MoU with the US.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday is expected to announce the new measures after the US vowed to impose an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on a country that has lived for decades under sanctions. Also Monday, Pakistan's army chief is expected to visit Iran as mediators try to revive talks.
Meanwhile, attacks calmed on the Strait of Hormuz, but posturing did not, as a recently created Iranian authority listed dozens of vessels it said will face restrictions on future transits.
Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Sunday. Full coverage can be found here.
Iran's security chief sharpens warning to neighbours.
The hard-line leader of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, issued his latest warning on X, with the comments quickly shared by Iranian state media.
It came a day after Rezaei's most extensive public comments since being named to the post this month.
“If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” he had told the state broadcaster in an interview that aired late Saturday. He said Iran would target other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.
Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander and military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, was part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran's political and military stance.
Iranian president wants to move past neither war nor peace'
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian earlier Sunday said the memorandum of understanding signed in mid-June was the best way to move beyond a situation of “neither war nor peace," adding that Tehran can't attract investment nearly six months after the war began.
“There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation,” Pezeshkian said in a speech published by state-run IRNA. “The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path.”
The interim deal opened a 60-day period for talks aimed at ending the war and reaching an accord on Iran's nuclear program. That period ended last week with no signs of compromise or extension.
No attacks confirmed on the strait, but new restrictions
There were no confirmed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz over the past 48 hours, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said Sunday, with shipping traffic still at reduced levels. The US military said its blockade of Iranian ports had redirected 70 commercial ships and disabled three as of Sunday.
Iran's recently created Persian Gulf Strait Authority, sanctioned by the US, published a list of dozens of ships it said had violated arrangements for transiting the strait and would face future restrictions like fines or seizures. The strait had been considered an international waterway before the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.
Iran and Oman, on the strait's other side, are now discussing management of it, which likely will include ships paying fees.
Pakistan's army chief will visit Tehran
Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir will lead a delegation to Tehran on Monday, Iranian state television reported, citing Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei.
Two regional officials said the visit was part of Islamabad's efforts to de-escalate tensions between the United States and Iran and urge them to return to the negotiating table. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly.

The Iranian judiciary's Mizan news agency reported the latest execution connected to nationwide protests early this year, saying Majid Adineh was arrested January 9 in Mohammadshahr, west of Tehran.
The judiciary said forensic examinations indicated the handgun found on him had been fired on January 8-9.
Mizan said Adineh had joined the unrest following calls by groups opposed to Iran's government and alleged that he had received training from groups outside the country. He was convicted under Iran's law imposing harsher penalties for espionage and cooperation with hostile states.

Police arrested a 16-year-old boy from the Israeli settlement of Avigayil in the beating of a 61-year-old Palestinian, Saeed Muhammad Ibrahim Rabah, outside his home in the occupied West Bank, a year after he lost a leg after being shot by a settler.
