MPs call for UK to hold Israeli government to account for killing of journalists following Independent investigation
A joint investigation has uncovered evidence of possible war crimes committed by the Israeli military in an August 2025 attack that killed Independent Arabia’s Gaza correspondent Mariam Abu Dagga
MPs have urged Britain to “take the strongest measures” against the Israeli government in the wake of an investigation by The Independent into the killing of journalists, first responders and medics in a double-tap attack on one of the last functioning hospitals in Gaza.
They want Downing Street to increase sanctions and cease all trade with Israel rather than “accept weak justifications” for apparent war crimes and breaches of international humanitarian law.
It follows revelations by this publication along with Independent Arabia into the 25 August, 2025 incident that killed Gaza correspondent Mariam Abu Dagga and at least 19 others.
The investigation and reconstruction was based on 17 eyewitness accounts as well as the testimony of two Israeli whistleblowers, three weapons experts and international law experts.
Mariam was one of more than 20 people, including five journalists, killed by Israeli tank fire as she rushed to report on an earlier strike. The initial attack had taken place just eight minutes beforehand, killing Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri as he manned his live position at Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis.
The Independent and Independent Arabia’s investigation and reconstruction uncovered evidence that, according to international law experts, would point to the war crimes of intentionally attacking civilians and of launching a disproportionate attack, particularly with regard to the second attack.
The Israeli military said at the time it “regrets any harm to uninvolved individuals” and that it “does not target journalists as such”.
It later claimed the Golani Brigade, one of Israel’s elite infantry brigades, identified a camera “that was positioned by Hamas” to observe troops and identified six “terrorists” who were killed in the attack. The Israeli military has repeatedly denied committing any war crimes in Gaza.
But the investigation shows the camera in question was the Reuters live feed, placed on the fourth floor of an external stairwell that hundreds of journalists, including Mariam, regularly used to take videos, report live and access internet and mobile phone connections.
Mariam herself took a photo of the camera in the weeks before the attack, with Hussam al-Masri, and appeared in apparent Israeli military surveillance footage three days before.
The investigation found the military did not contact the hospital about the issue they had with the camera, despite having staffers’ phone numbers, or warn them of impending strikes, which they are obliged to do, according to international law experts spoken to by The Independent.
The investigation further found that in the first round of strikes there were likely two tank projectiles, one of which killed Hussam al-Masri, and destroyed his camera on the eastern stairwell.
Another hit an entirely different area within the hospital, near the operating theatre, called the “Titanic” where medics would rest.
Eight minutes later as journalists, medics, first responders and displaced civilians gathered on the stairwell to help and report – in full view of live-streamed cameras – two more tank projectiles were fired, killing more than 20 people.
Seven eyewitnesses we spoke to also reported seeing Israeli surveillance drones closely monitoring that stairwell and the activity of first responders between the attacks.
The Independent identified two of the six people labelled as “terrorists” killed in the attack as actually being a hospital worker and a member of the civil defence assisting in the rescue operation.
At the time, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu – who has an ICC arrest warrant out against him – called it a “tragic mishap”.
But whistleblowers said that an attack of this size on a hospital – a protected building under international law – would have required sign-off from at least battalion level and planning.
Kevin Jon Heller, a professor of international law at the University of Copenhagen's Centre for Military Studies, told The Independent after examining all the evidence, a prosecutor could "reasonably conclude” that the perpetrators had committed the war crimes “of intentionally attacking civilians and of launching a disproportionate attack, particularly with regard to the second attack".
The Independent shared all its findings with the Israeli military and asked for comments on each point. The military declined to respond, adding only “the review is still ongoing under the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism.”
In response to the investigation, International Development Committee chair and Labour MP Sarah Champion called on the government to ensure the Geneva Convention is upheld.
“Where is our outrage over journalists seemingly becoming a legitimate target? Is this the new reality; that killing civilians, medics, and humanitarian workers no longer has consequences?” she told The Independent.
“The Geneva Convention was written 77 years ago to provide some order and agreed responsibilities during the chaos of conflict. It is the international communities’ responsibility to make sure those conventions are upheld.
“Sadly, in the case of Gaza, it seems we are choosing to accept weak justifications rather than uphold international humanitarian law.”
Liberal Democrat MP Layla Moran said the investigation marked “yet another example of the reasons why we need the criminal case against Netanyahu and his ministers to go ahead at the International Criminal Court”.
“The targeting of the hospitals, but also the targeting of journalists has unfortunately become all too common. The lack of proportionality in the actions of the IDF is now well documented,” she said.
“This investigation is yet another example of the reasons why we need the criminal case against Netanyahu and his ministers to go ahead at the International Criminal Court, and for the International Court of Justice to move forward with its investigation into war crimes and genocide,” she continued. “It is right that it is ultimately decided in international courts.
“The moral case to end this war has never been clearer. And while there is a so-called ceasefire in place, we know attacks still continue to this day.”
She added she was concerned Britain could be “sitting on evidence that they haven’t put forward”, and called for reassurance from foreign secretary Ed Miliband and defence secretary Wes Streeting that there be “a no-questions-asked threshold if information is requested”.
“They should hand it over willingly and be proactive in making sure that that information gets to the right people so that it can be properly considered at the right level,” she said.
Baroness Helena Kennedy KC said there is “serious alarm” about the “failure to protect journalists” around the world and in the Middle East.
The Labour peer and chair of the High Level Legal Panel of the Media Freedom Coalition told The Independent there should be an international inquiry into the deaths of journalists in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank.
“What had happened in the Middle East is seriously alarming,” she said. “I firmly take the view that there should be an International Inquiry into the huge numbers of deaths of journalists in Gaza, Lebanon and the West Bank.
“The closure of Gaza to international news agencies was unconscionable. The world needs to be able to see and judge the conduct of a war. I support all steps to investigate what has taken place.”
Labour MP Rachael Maskell said the IDF must be held accountable through the international courts, and said the the UK government “must take the strongest measures” against the Israeli government.
“Having spoken to medics working in Gaza, they have reported to MPs that they have identified targeted war crimes, with precision targeting humanitarian workers including with sniper fire and drone use,” she said.
“The UK Government must take the strongest measures, including ceasing all trade and increasing sanctions against the Israeli government to hold it to account for the actions of the IDF.
“The evidence continues to mount of the war crimes that have been committed, and justice must be served through the international courts.”
A government spokesperson said: “Israel’s attack on Nasser hospital a year ago was horrific. It is vital that civilians are protected, and that journalists and humanitarian workers be able to carry out their essential work in safety.
“The Government of Israel must uphold its obligations under international law and ensure that it investigates any potential breaches when such incidents occur and ensures that those who are responsible are held to account.
“This government's record on Gaza is clear. We have recognised the state of Palestine, suspended the negotiations on a trade deal with Israel and the foreign secretary raised concerns over the humanitarian situation last week in a call with the Israeli foreign minister.”

Australian shark attack victim grateful for 'second chance at life'
- Published
An Australian woman bitten by a shark at a popular Sydney beach earlier this year says she has been given a "second chance at life" and will be making the most of it.
Leah Stewart, 35, was mauled by a shark during a morning swim at Coogee Beach in June, suffering multiple bites to her arms and legs, amid a spate of attacks in Australia.
The mother-of-one was placed in an induced coma and had several surgeries, including having one of her arms amputated.
In an online post on Monday, she thanked her supporters who have raised more than AU$550,000 (US$394,000; £289,000) for her, saying her recovery has been "incredibly difficult" but she is making "remarkable" progress.
"After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I'm so happy that I've progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this," Stewart wrote, in her first comments since the attack.
"I want you to know that I feel like I've been given a second chance at life, and I'm not going to waste it."
Stewart said she had been "overwhelmed" by the support from family, friends and "even strangers", adding that the "you've inspired me to get better, not bitter".
An online fundraiser for her would now be closed, she wrote, with the money raised giving her the chance to recover at home as well as "options for further medical treatment down the road".
"I still have a long way to go, but my recovery has been remarkable, and a huge part of that is because of the absolute army of love, support, prayers and encouragement surrounding my family and I from all over the world."
There have been a spate of shark attacks in Australia this year, with four attacks over a two-day period in January, including one on a 12-year-old boy who later died from his injuries.
In May, a man was killed by a shark in Queensland while spearfishing and in Western Australia, a father-of-two died after he was attacked by a 4m (13ft) shark.

“URGENT: Immediate Action Required” blasts into my eyeballs as I scroll through the impossibly giant email inbox looming directly in front of my face.
I’m reclined way back in a chair, wearing a pair of Xreal smart glasses. Tethered to my laptop via a USB-C cord, these glasses mirror the laptop screen and project it into a virtual display. The virtual screen is gigantic, equivalent to a 170-inch TV that feels about a foot away from my nose. I’m the only one who can see it, and so I’ve got this massive display all to myself.
With this technological marvel, I conjure the most riveting view imaginable: five workplace training modules about business principles and cybersecurity that my boss has repeatedly reminded me are very overdue. The text on the screen is blurry, but I complete them all within my virtual display. It takes several hours. By the time I’m done, the glasses have overheated, my forehead is sweaty, and I’m still not sure I can actually recognize a phishing email.
Virtual display glasses are a much more niche category of mixed-reality smart glasses than the camera-equipped, AI-powered frames that have dominated the product market—namely, Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses. Made by companies like Xreal, Viture, and Rokid, these glasses aim to bring a screen directly to your face. Like a portable monitor, plug the USB-C cable into the arm of the glasses, then stick the other end into the port of just about any laptop, phone, tablet, or handheld gaming console. Slap ’em on, and that screen mirrors in a holographic VR-style projection, right in your center of vision.
Wearing them, you can chill out in an airplane seat, lie prone, even dangle upside-down if you like, and the big screen stays right there with you. (No tech neck!) Yup, you're basically cosplaying the lazy humans in Wall-E. Hooray.
Virtual display glasses don’t get the heat of privacy issues that Meta’s “pervert glasses” do. No cameras, no recording—just sweet, sweet content consumption beamed out an inch from your eye holes. If you're feeling generous, the Xreal glasses could even be lauded for their privacy protections, at least for the user. Got sensitive documents or embarrassing videos you're trying to watch on a plane? A virtual display is one only the wearer can see. (The Xreal glasses also have speakers in the frames that do leak sound, so be careful with your audible content consumption.)
Display-only glasses make good on at least one promise made by other wearable mixed-reality devices. When Apple launched its flawed Vision Pro headset, one of its primary features was spatial computing that let you work and watch entertainment in a virtual workspace. But the device was too heavy and bulky to wear for long. Xreal’s specs are much simpler and less elegant but do accomplish most of that goal in a much lighter package. (We’ve also had a pretty great experience with Sightful’s Spacetop spatial computing interface, also powered by Xreal glasses.)
“The fundamental thing these glasses do well is that they just work,” says Anshel Sag, a principal analyst at the industry advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategies. Sag says he wears these kinds of glasses regularly on flights. “You plug them in, and you have faith that you're going to get a video signal on those glasses that mostly matches what's on the screen of the device they're plugged into.”
I’ve been swapping between two of the glasses. First, Xreal’s $849 ROG Xreal R1, available to preorder and expected to ship in September. It displays that 171-inch virtual screen in a 57-degree field of view, which you can anchor in place or have the screen stay dead center in your vision as you turn your head different directions.
I've also used the much cheaper, much lighter Xreal xbx A01+, which the company launched in May and started shipping in July. It costs $299 but has a smaller screen with a 50-degree field of view. It has less of a heat issue but also lower screen quality. Crucially, you can't anchor the screen, which can make watching stuff disorienting when the screen moves every time your head does.
Xreal’s primary selling point for these glasses is gaming or watching videos. The glasses don’t use batteries and instead sip power from your plugged-in device. I’ve connected both frames to my Steam Deck and blasted through seas of demons in Diablo IV on a giant virtual screen. I tried watching the extended editions of the Lord of the Rings films, but I had plugged the device into my phone, which died halfway through the first movie. I’ve also plugged the glasses into my laptop for regular browsing, lurking on social media, and being a nuisance in my workplace Slack.
The glasses don’t work with everything. I tried connecting them to my PlayStation 5, which required a much longer cord and more patience than I can muster in return for a not-so-great display across my vision.
The very stern faces of actors portraying harassment victims in my workplace training videos have an almost 3D-ified quality, their pouting chins jutting out past the blocks of text. The animations in this very good WIRED story hit way harder than they did on my lil’ laptop screen. Unfortunately, the smaller text in the article was almost too blurry to read.
Virtual displays still don’t have the resolution and fidelity that we’re used to on our laptops and smartphones. They tend to be fuzzy, and I almost feel like it’s a simulation of what it would be like to need a glasses prescription. After staring at that virtual screen for hours, I pop it off, and it feels like I’ve had my eyes crossed for too long and they’re ready to stay that way.
The glasses also aren’t exactly inconspicuous enough for me to feel comfortable walking around in them. You can pop off the projection lenses and wear them like regular glasses, but you probably won’t, because they look very chunky and won’t fool anyone. As I used them in the office, I asked a nearby coworker if I looked cool wearing them. She just laughed.
So the Xreal glasses aren’t perfect. They certainly aren’t something I want to wear all that long. But they are good enough at what they do to offer a glimpse of a smart glasses ecosystem coming into focus. They also seem to be growing in popularity. Tech analyst firm International Data Corporation wrote in a report that virtual monitor glasses, like Xreal and Viture, “represent the fastest-growing segment” of the smart glasses market. IDC projects them selling around 3 million units in 2026. That's a small part of the same projection that puts sales of all smart glasses at nearly 14 million units in 2026, but it ain’t nothing.
Xreal also has bigger ambitions that will take its products into another category of XR glasses—the ones with cameras and recording capabilities, though they’re still not designed to be something you wear walking about. Xreal’s Project Aura, a partnership with Google running on the Android XR platform, will launch later this year. All of Xreal’s efforts have been leading to this.
“These are a means to an end, and that end is Project Aura,” Sag says. He doesn’t think the existence of the Aura glasses—expected to cost under $1,500—spells the end of Xreal’s other offerings. “You have to be able to create access points for people at different prices,” Sag says. “And that's why I think these glasses will continue to exist, because you have to ramp people up to making a purchase over a thousand dollars.”

Guinea rubbish landfill collapse kills 30
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed after a mound of rubbish at a major waste site collapsed on to nearby homes in Guinea's capital Conakry, the government has said.
Another 22 people were injured, including six seriously, in the city's Dar-es-Salam area.
"Significant" resources and personnel - including the military - have been deployed to search for survivors after the collapse at about 02:00 local time following heavy rain overnight, the government added in a statement.
One woman told local media her five children had died in the disaster. There are fears that the death toll will rise further.
Rescuers were later seen using excavators to comb through a mountain of scattered rubbish at the site as local residents gathered nearby.
Guinea's Prime Minister Mamadou Oury Bah visited the scene to assess the situation and oversee the search efforts.
Neighbourhood leader Lancine Sylla had earlier told the AFP news agency he feared there would be a heavy death toll.
"We have pulled out 18 bodies that were taken to the morgue," he said.
Another landslide at the site killed 10 people in 2017.

Jadavpur University probe panel head resigns amid opposition from RSS-linked group
Professor Subha Shankar Sarkar resigned from the Jadavpur University panel probing the August 20 campus vandalism. His exit has intensified demands for a more credible and independent inquiry into the clash.
Professor Subha Shankar Sarkar has resigned as the head of a five-member committee set up by Jadavpur University to investigate the recent vandalism on its campus, with the university saying a new chairperson will be appointed soon. A university official said Sarkar stepped down, citing his inability to conduct the inquiry effectively.
The panel was formed after clashes broke out on the campus on August 20 between members of the ABVP and Left-leaning student groups, with both sides accusing each other of bringing outsiders into the university. Sarkar's resignation came hours before the RSS-linked teachers' body, Akhil Bhartiya Rashtriya Shaikshik Mahasangh, wrote to the vice-chancellor opposing his appointment.
Jadavpur University acting registrar Selim Box Mandal said, "Sarkar has communicated his inability to head the panel. A new chairperson would be appointed shortly." Sarkar informed Vice Chancellor Chiranjib Bhattacharjee through an email on Saturday that he would not be able to take up the assignment.
Explaining his decision, Sarkar told PTI on Monday, "I informed the Jadavpur University vice-chancellor immediately after receiving the communication about my appointment. I am currently in Delhi, and the inquiry would require regular interactions with the people who were present on the campus during the incident." Sarkar, a former vice-chancellor of Netaji Subhas Open University, said the university authorities had suggested that he could conduct the proceedings online, but he felt such an inquiry could not be carried out effectively through virtual interactions.
A clash had broken out early on August 20 between ABVP members and Left-leaning student groups at Jadavpur University, with both camps trading allegations over the presence of outsiders on the campus. The RSS-affiliated Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad alleged that members of Left student organisations, including the SFI and DSO-DSF, had started confrontations under the cover of a meeting of the Faculty of Engineering and Technology Students' Union. The Left-leaning groups, however, accused the ABVP of bringing outsiders into the campus and indulging in vandalism.
The university announced the formation of the committee on August 21 after a demonstration by students, teachers and citizens protesting against the alleged vandalism. In its letter to the vice-chancellor, the RSS-linked teachers' wing said Sarkar's appointment could raise doubts about the "credibility, independence and impartiality" of the proposed inquiry. It demanded that the panel be headed by a retired judge of the Calcutta High Court or the Supreme Court to ensure an independent and transparent investigation.
Bhaskar Sardar, president of the organisation's Jadavpur University unit, welcomed Sarkar's decision to resign. Referring to Sarkar's removal as chairman of the West Bengal School Service Commission in January 2022 following proceedings before the Calcutta High Court over alleged irregularities in recruitments, the organisation questioned his selection to lead the panel. Sardar claimed Sarkar had been appointed chairman of the commission in December 2020 while serving as vice-chancellor of Netaji Subhas Open University, and said the high court had expressed dissatisfaction over the functioning of the commission and questioned his continuation as its chairman. An ABVP spokesperson said, "Such a man cannot head an inquiry panel into attacks against us. A conspiracy was hatched against us for the damage of the university plaque."
With Sarkar stepping down, Jadavpur University is now set to appoint a new head for the inquiry panel as questions continue over the August 20 campus clash and the competing allegations made by the ABVP and Left-leaning student groups.

'It embarrasses me to be involved': Inside the National Guard D.C. deployment
As the sight of armed, uniformed National Guard troops became ubiquitous in Washington, D.C. over the past year, one voice has been notably absent from the public discourse around the deployment: the guard members themselves.
"I will say very frankly that the bad taste that this mission left in my mouth, it actually embarrasses me to be involved in any way," one guard member who was part of the deployment for several months recently told NPR.
Thousands of National Guard members have been patrolling the streets of Washington, D.C. for more than a year now, in what has become President Trump's largest and longest domestic military deployment. Their presence has become a common, and controversial, topic of conversation among D.C. residents and constitutional experts alike, raising concerns about the normalization of armed troops in a city for an extended period of time.
Members of the military are not allowed to speak to the press without authorization. Under this administration, those rules and the ramifications for breaking them have gotten even stricter.
But some members who are no longer a part of the mission have become more open to sharing their thoughts as the deployment enters its second year – and has been extended to the end of President Trump's term.
"I don't want to think about the National Guard. I don't want to necessarily discuss my affiliation with the National Guard. I don't want to fulfill my normal National Guard duties just because of the abuses of the National Guard in this D.C. mission," the guard member said, noting that isn't how he's felt after previous domestic deployments.
That guard member was one of three who spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity because they are still serving and are barred from speaking publicly. All of them were deployed as part of the D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission for many months and each has more than a decade of service.
In candid interviews, the guard members described their feelings throughout their time on the deployment, and their worries about the new norms it's establishing. They discussed the cost, which is expected to run into the billions. And they say they worry that Trump's unprecedented use of the troops is damaging the National Guard's reputation with the American public.
All were skeptical about the administration's original reason for the deployment – to help with law enforcement after declaring a "crime emergency", despite a 30-year low in violent crime in the city.
"Now, with it being a year, it's hard to feel like that justification holds any water," said one guard member. "It feels like the guard is being exploited in a sense."
Another said it feels more like a political stunt, pointing out the way the guard has been inserted into certain narratives by the administration, like being ordered to patrol the perimeter of the Reflecting Pool following its faulty renovation.
"I hope that there will be some accounting someday — probably after President Trump is gone — about why we were there, and was it worth it? But none of that is gonna happen right now," that member said.
NPR reached out to both the White House and the D.C. Joint Task Force regarding the concerns raised by the guard members.
The White House responded by reiterating how safe D.C. is now, without providing evidence that the guard is responsible for decreasing crime.
In a statement, Brig. Gen. Leland Blanchard II, the interim commanding general of the D.C. National Guard, called the deployment "unique," and pointed to "significant accomplishments" that guard members contributed in the past year including assisting law enforcement with apprehensions, rendering medical aid and reuniting lost children with their families.
"Whatever individual perspectives they carry away from their experience, their service and sacrifice deserve our respect," Blanchard wrote.
'My initial reaction was just shock'
Trump first deployed the D.C. National Guard in August of 2025 — something he can do since the president controls the District's guard. Hundreds of guard members in the district were pulled from their civilian jobs and immediately called up.
"My very initial reaction was just, I guess, shock and feeling like this context and this situation just felt like a very authoritarian move that kind of felt uncharacteristic of something you would see in our country," said one member of the D.C. guard, adding that the reasoning behind the deployment contributed to the confusion.
In the days and weeks that followed, Republican governors began sending members of their guard to help with the mission.
"Walking into it, we had no real specifics," one guard member who was deployed from West Virginia remembered thinking. "The president is calling out the guard to make D.C. safe. Well, what the what the f*** does that mean?"
All remembered a scramble in the early days to figure out what everyone should be doing, as more and more troops — who were all deputized as special law enforcement and armed with a handgun — arrived. They said despite the confusion there was a collective effort to figure out how to be useful and effective. Military members are trained to be apolitical and follow orders.
"All of these people showed up, and then it was more of an after-the-fact figure out what we're going to do," one said, saying everyone was really trying to be as helpful as possible to the community with whatever resources they were given, like providing Naloxone to counter the effects of an opioid overdose or helping a bicyclist who had been hit by a car. "We can argue about why they were there and whether they should be there, but soldiers and airmen were trying to do the best with what they had."
In the early days, troops were largely assigned to help with beautification projects around the city: clearing trash along the road, bagging leaves in public parks or trimming trees at the National Mall. The guard member from West Virginia said that many of the members he had arrived with – most of whom had raised their hand for the deployment – became quickly disillusioned.
"I know there were a lot of people that showed up from West Virginia specifically that were just like, I want to help, and then later they found out that they were taking out trash and setting up (logistical equipment). I think they later fell off mission as soon as they could get off," he said.
Patrolling the streets
As the deployment continued, troops were assigned less to beautification projects and more to presence patrols around the city — which the task force says are an effort to deter crime — and settled into a routine that one guard member described as "mundane" and another as "monotonous."
"At some point, I found myself going, well, at least this isn't that bad. At least I'm not doing anything illegal, and that's always counterbalanced with, like, this is wasting everyone's time," one said, adding that it became clear that the "point of the mission is presence."
One member who served in Afghanistan likened the patrols to tactics commonly used by the U.S. military during the War on Terror in communities to instill goodwill and monitor the opposition.
Another said the lack of clear goals made the deployment feel never-ending, even as Trump falsely claimed there was "almost zero crime" in D.C., and touted its success.
"If it's safe now, then why are we here?" one guard member asked. "You don't really know when good is good enough, or when we can go home. It's just a continuing thing."
Two recent studies have found that the National Guard presence has had no effect on violent crime in the city, while it has minimally decreased more opportunistic crime, like petty theft and vehicle break-ins. Both also found that local policing could produce better outcomes for less money.
The deployment comes with perks
A majority of the nearly 4,700 guard members deployed to D.C. are from other states or U.S. territories, most of which are led by Republicans, and have volunteered for the assignment. All three guard members said despite their concerns, they understood why people might raise their hand.
"It's a good paycheck, and I can't blame them for wanting to better their own financial situation when the economy is how it is right now," one said, noting that many of the troops are very young, come from more rural communities and might not have steady income back home.
There are a host of other incentives as well, from per diems to boosts to their retirement benefits.
The guard member from West Virginia said that normally, on domestic deployments, he was used to sleeping on the floor of an armory, maybe without electricity, and eating ready-to-eat military meals. But this D.C. deployment was much more comfortable.
"The food on the mission was very good. My hotel was very nice," he said, noting that was different even from other times he had come to D.C. on deployment for events like the inauguration.
The thousands of out-of-state guard members have been staying in hotels throughout the city for more than a year. Recently, the federal government awarded a nearly $300 million contract — the largest of its kind ever — to a local company for thousands of furnished, luxury apartments, saying the move would ultimately save money on extended lodging for the troops in D.C.
That guard member said when elected officials or other leaders would come visit the troops, they would always ask how they could make it better.
"There was never a discussion of whether you should be here. It was always, 'What do you need?'," he said. "Which is nice as a military member, but once we see what all this is going to cost in the very end, it's probably not going to feel so great."
An estimate from the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office found that the D.C. deployment at its current level costs about $3 million per day. The Pentagon estimates extending the deployment until 2029 will cost an additional $1.4 billion. A total cost estimate by the nonpartisan watchdog Project on Government Oversight for the deployment is around $3.4 billion.
A personal cost
The deployment has also had a human cost, after a gunman shot two guard members from West Virginia patrolling near the White House last November. One of those members, 20-year-old Specialist Sarah Beckstrom, was killed. It was a pivotal moment in the deployment.
"I remember feeling just really sad," one guard member said, starting to tear up a bit. "And I kept thinking – did they have to be here?"
Another said the killing similarly made him question the necessity of the deployment in real terms.
"The thing that really stuck out to me was how absolutely futile that death felt, and that was hard to live with," he said, noting he still thinks about Beckstrom almost daily and sometimes visits the spot where she was shot, even though he didn't know her personally. "After her death, this mission became untenable for me emotionally."
Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia called the shooting a "direct challenge to law and order in our capital," and the White House responded by adding hundreds more troops to the city.
The guard member from West Virginia said he's been specifically angry about the shooting, saying he's had to work in therapy about guilt he's felt for not being there when it happened.
"We were made a target, and I don't know that anybody did a very good job of planning for the worst case scenario," he said.
Blanchard refuted that, saying that "no mission is without risk" and the loss "remains deeply felt across the National Guard."
"Force protection and the safety of our Soldiers and Airmen remain paramount. We continually assess the operating environment and adapt to changing conditions to better protect the force while accomplishing the mission," he said in a statement.
A harm to the National Guard's reputation
The extended and growing deployment – and the administration's unprecedented use of the National Guard in other parts of the country – has led to a rising anti-guard sentiment, which all three members acknowledged.
Throughout D.C. in the areas most patrolled by the troops, signs are plastered on lampposts and chalked on sidewalks urging "National Guard Go Home" and "Troops out now." Residents regularly approach the patrols and speak their mind, sometimes with what one of the guard members called "misdirected anger."
The guard member from West Virginia said it was the first time he'd ever not had the community in a domestic deployment welcome the help, since the guard usually shows up after floods or natural disasters.
All were concerned that there was damage being done to the reputation of the National Guard.
"If we continue down this path, where this kind of 'presence patrol' mission becomes the new definitive image of the National Guard, it's going to completely rebrand everything that was noble about the National Guard into being mundane at best and threatening at worst," one guard member said.
"I would like to think there would be enough mechanisms to have checks and balances that would be able to say overtly that's not what we want to see in our country," another one said.
The member paused before adding: "I don't know if that's the case right now."

At an off-site leadership meeting held by Moderna in March 2023 — after mid-stage results of the biotech company’s cancer vaccine showed promise — CEO Stéphane Bancel had the floor. He asked if any of the 100 or so executives present had expected the experimental treatment to succeed. If they did, he said, please stand up.
Stephen Hoge, Moderna’s president, was standing on stage. He sat down. Then, Hoge recalled in an interview with STAT, Bancel sat down, too.
“None of us believed it,” Hoge said. It had taken time before he remembers feeling, “Oh my gosh. This is real.”
The rest of the world remained skeptical until last Wednesday, when Moderna and Merck revealed that a 1,137-volunteer study had shown the vaccine reduced the odds that melanoma that had been surgically removed would return or spread. Up to that point, investors were betting against Moderna’s stock. Even after the news, some observers argue researchers should wait for fuller data — while longtime skeptics of Moderna’s core mRNA technology do the same.
Top-line results from large pharmaceutical firms are rarely reversed when full data emerge, but doubt is nothing new for Moderna’s cancer treatment, called intismeran autogene. It has always been the breakthrough no one quite believed in.

John Leguizamo said his wife makes sure the glitz of his Hollywood career doesn't go to his head.
Speaking on the "Wild Card with Rachel Martin" podcast, Leguizamo reflected on more than two decades of marriage and the role his wife plays in supporting both his personal and creative life.
"My wife is my moral compass," Leguizamo said.
Leguizamo met his wife, Justine Maurer, while working on the crime drama "Carlito's Way," in which he played an up-and-coming gangster, and she worked in the costume department.
"We dated, and then we got married. We had kids, but she's always been sort of the north star, keeping our house together, keeping me together," he said.
"The Odyssey" actor said his wife understands that he needs certain freedoms and routines to create and write, and gives him the space to be the artist he wants to be.
However, her support also comes with plenty of honesty.
"She'll call me out, set me straight, put me in my place. She'll do all of that, which is great. Humbling," Leguizamo said.
He said that even after attending a premiere with Matt Damon or going to a major sporting event, Maurer makes sure he doesn't get too caught up in the glamour.
"Go take out the garbage. You're a big deal, yeah, yeah, yeah. Go clean the cat litter," Leguizamo said.
This isn't the first time Leguizamo has spoken about his relationship with his wife.
In a 2011 interview with AARP, he said his wife brought out the best in him.
"Being an actor, especially at first, tends to make you incredibly narcissistic. My wife… was my savior. I've achieved my best artistic levels, and it's all because of her," Leguizamo said.
In 2024, he told People that Maurer had given him a sense of stability amid the demands of his Hollywood career.
"I wanted peace. I wanted to have an oasis. And Justine gave me all of that," he said.
Other celebrities have also spoken about how their spouses have supported their careers.
In August 2025, Michelle Yeoh said her husband, Jean Todt, has always given her the freedom to pursue her career.
"I am so blessed because he's so supportive of what I do. I love my work. This is my passion. He never turns around and says, 'You spend a lot of time away from me,' which I have sometimes, but he's very understanding," she said.
In November, Ina Garten said her decadeslong marriage to her husband, Jeffrey, works because they make room for both of their priorities.
"And this is what Jeffrey taught me: Let's figure out how we can both do what we want to do. It's not about whether we get to do what you want to do or I want to do," Garten said.

Hayley Atwell was disappointed about the demise of Peggy Carter.
In an interview at the For the Love of Fantasy & Sci-Fi convention in London, Atwell told attendees that she was frustrated by Captain Carter’s storyline in 2022’s Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

DHS officials launch scathing attack on Trump’s pick to lead ICE as nomination stalls in the Senate: report
Critics inside DHS question the qualifications of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer
Department of Homeland Security officials are reportedly up in arms over President Donald Trump's controversial choice to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement — as his nomination remains in limbo over the fatal shootings of two American protesters in Minneapolis.
Critics inside DHS question the qualifications of former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer and want ICE's acting director, Dave Veturella, to keep running the agency, Politico reported Sunday, citing six unidentified officials and others familiar with the matter.
“We don’t want [Schroyer]. We don’t need him. Leave us alone. We are running better than ever,” one official said. “People need to stop telling us how to do what we do best.”
Some inside the department are also glad that Republican Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky has held up a confirmation hearing for Schroyer, who now works as a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Politico said.
Earlier this month, The Wall Street Journal reported that Paul told senior Homeland Security officials he would delay Schroyer’s hearing until he got more information about the January slayings of anti-ICE activists and American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
In a statement to The Independent, a White House official said, “Lance Schroyer remains President Trump’s nominee to lead ICE. Congressional scheduling should not be interpreted as any personnel announcements."
A DHS spokesperson also told The Independent that Mullin and the department “stand firmly behind President Trump’s nominee, Lance Schroyer, and look forward to him bringing nearly 30 years of law enforcement experience to lead the men and women of ICE.”
Schroyer, who served in the Marine Corps from 1992 to 1996, ran the security detail at Mullin's house when he represented Oklahoma in the U.S. Senate. The pair struck up a friendship after Mullin invited Schroyer inside for dinner, the WSJ reported in July.
But Schroyer, who retired as a state police major, has no federal government experience beyond having been deputized to make immigration arrests, according to the WSJ.
Under Trump, ICE has become the most well-funded federal law enforcement agency, with an $85 billion budget that was boosted by Trump-backed legislation known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Venturella, ICE's acting director, is an ally of White House border czar Tom Homan, and both he and deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, who oversees immigration matters, were “blindsided” by Schroyer’s nomination, according to a report by the Daily Beast and PunchUp. The White House said the reports were “fake news.”
The WSJ later reported that Homan only learned Schroyer had been nominated when Trump announced it on social media.
In the post, Trump called Schroyer a “PATRIOT with real operational experience” and touted him as a “proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst.”
Trump campaigned for re-election on a pledge to carry out the largest mass-deportation operation in U.S. history, and the White House has reportedly set a goal of 1 million deportations annually.
But ICE arrests haven't come anywhere near that figure, and CBS News reported in February that an internal DHS document showed less than 14 percent of nearly 400,000 people arrested during Trump's first year back in the White House had been convicted of or even charged with violent criminal offenses.
Mullin has reportedly drawn the ire of MAGA influencers and White House officials who are furious that he hasn’t boosted the arrest numbers, and Politico said Sunday that Schroyer’s stalled nomination has done little to bridge the divide.
ICE hasn’t had a Senate-approved director since Sarah Saldaña left the post at the end of President Barack Obama’s second term in January 2017.

Mexican governor indicted by the US seeks leave again after contentious return to office
Mexico’s Sinaloa governor has reversed his return to office after one day, bowing to party opposition over U.S. drug trafficking charges
MEXICO CITY -- The embattled governor of Mexico’s Sinaloa state has reversed his decision to return to his post, bowing to an extraordinary backlash from his own ruling party over accusations by U.S. prosecutors he conspired with a powerful cartel to smuggle drugs into the United States.
State lawmakers were expected Sunday to approve Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya’s request for an indefinite leave of absence, about a day and a half after he announced his return by claiming Mexican prosecutors had cleared him of the drug trafficking charges leveled against him by the U.S. Department of Justice in late April.
The rapid reversal demonstrated the authority Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum wields over her Morena party as she walks a fine line between placating U.S. President Donald Trump, who says cartels control Mexico and has repeatedly offered U.S. military help to fight them, and her progressive movement deeply wary of U.S. intervention.
After nearly four months on leave, Rocha Moya announced Friday that he was returning to office, claiming Mexico’s Attorney General’s Office had found “no evidence to support our participation in any criminal conduct.” He declared that he was back “as governor of Sinaloa with my head held high.”
That defiance lasted barely a day, as his return unleashed a torrent of criticism from governors, senators and other prominent figures in Morena, including Sheinbaum.
“No personal interest can ever come before the interests of the people and the nation,” she wrote Saturday in an apparent rebuke of Rocha Moya, without mentioning him by name. “Mexico deserves public servants who understand that positions are temporary, but responsibility to the nation is eternal.”
Morena said its national leadership had no prior knowledge of Rocha Moya’s return, calling it his “personal decision.” The party’s Senate bloc urged respect for the ongoing investigation, while Morena governors declared in a joint statement that “personal or group political projects have no place” when the country’s interests are at stake.
Ricardo Monreal, Morena’s leader in the lower house of Congress, publicly urged Rocha Moya, his longtime ally, to reconsider and remain on leave.
The coordinated response left Rocha Moya isolated. He announced later Saturday that he had asked the state legislature to allow him to step aside indefinitely. “Sinaloa, the nation and the transformation movement come first,” he wrote.
Rocha Moya had been on leave since early May, days after federal prosecutors in New York unsealed a bombshell indictment accusing him and nine other current and former Mexican officials of protecting Sinaloa cartel members in exchange for bribes as they trafficked fentanyl, heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine into the U.S.
The indictment marked the Trump administration’s most significant public action against what it calls official corruption enabling Mexico’s cartels, fueling new tension between the U.S. and Mexican governments. Sheinbaum has denied shielding Rocha Moya but rejected Washington’s request to arrest and extradite the defendants without credible evidence, insisting that any prosecution take place in Mexico.
Rocha Moya, 77, a staunch ally of Sheinbaum’s mentor, former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador, denied wrongdoing and described the charges as a politically motivated attack. He initially stepped aside so he could cooperate with the Mexican investigation without relying on the constitutional immunity attached to his office. Whether taking leave stripped him of that protection — and whether his latest request to step aside indefinitely would do so again — remains disputed among Mexican legal scholars.
After the indictment, the mayor of Culiacán, Sinaloa’s capital, and the state’s deputy attorney general also stepped down from their posts, while two former senior state officials surrendered to U.S. authorities.
Sinaloa has been engulfed for nearly two years in a bloody conflict between rival factions of the cartel that bears the state’s name.

Modular builder's sudden closure leaves customers wondering what's next
In short:
Perth-based manufacturer Bella Modular has told all its customers that it is ceasing work and handing its projects over to a new company.
It has left customers who paid substantial deposits wondering when their small modular buildings will be completed.
What's next?
Bella Modular has told customers they will receive more information in the next few weeks.
Perth-based manufacturer Bella Modular, which built transportable granny flats and home office buildings to order, wrote to all its customers to notify them it would be unable complete their projects and had already vacated its premises.
"Due to unforeseen and significant financial difficulties, Bella Modular is unable to complete your project directly," it wrote on Wednesday last week.
"To ensure your build is protected and delivered through to Practical Completion and final handover, Bella Modular has entered into an arrangement for an independent, fully resourced third-party modular builder to step in and take over the management and construction of your home."
The letter does not name the new third-party builder nor make mention of what has happened to customers' deposits, but said they would be given the new company's details within 14 days.
Customer Peter Elliot, who ordered a granny flat intended for his parents in May 2025, told Nadia Mitsopoulos on 102.5 ABC Perth he was shocked to receive the letter.
"About three weeks ago, I'd had a phone call with the production manager on site," he said.
"He told me that our steel was on site and just ready to be assembled."
There had already been substantial delays in the build.
Mr Elliot paid a $90,000 deposit — 50 per cent of the cost of building — to guarantee a three-month completion time and had been hoping to have his parents living in his backyard by Christmas 2025.
"My parents are devastated," he said.
"This was a disability-ready home for them to move into as they progress further in their lives."
Concern for deposits
Because the modular homes are built in a factory off-site and customers arrange transportation and cranes for the homes themselves, builders' indemnity insurance does not apply.
"The business model, which made sense to me at the time, was they construct a dwelling; we take ownership of the dwelling; we transport it and we are the owner-builder," Mr Elliot said.
He is uncertain how a new company is going to complete his modular building, or where his $90,000 deposit is now.
"I can't envisage another company taking on, effectively, the 50 per cent debt against the buildings that are either underway or promised to be underway," he said.
Another customer left wondering is Steve Evans, who has paid almost $160,000 towards a modular home from Bella Modular that is yet to be built.
He initially paid a deposit of $28,000, then was contacted by the company four weeks ago to ask for a further $130,000, which he paid.
"It had a due date, which I found very odd at the time, of four days after I received the invoice, which is highly unusual because you need time to arrange funds to be able to transfer into accounts," Mr Evans said.
"I feel like a bit of a patsy … and I've got a horrible pit in my stomach that I've lost the money."
A Credit Watch report shows the company has a debt to the Australian Taxation Office of $576,614.68. It is also facing three court actions for payments totalling just over $170,000.
Communication issues
On April 30 this year, Bella Modular wrote to clients apologising for the delays in their builds and the lack of communication with customers, promising improvements to its production schedule.
"Over the past 12 months, the level of customer service and communication you have received has been, quite frankly, atrocious," it wrote.
"We are currently playing catch-up, and while we are implementing solutions that should have been brought to you months ago, we do have a strategic plan in place."
Caroline Marsh, another of the company's former customers, said she received her building more than two years after first placing her order in March 2024.
"In May this year, we received the delivery of the two modules that we ordered, and it was a very stressful time," she said.
"We had basically no communication with barely any of the staff through that two and a half years. I had to constantly go down there to check if any progress was happening.
"A week before we actually got delivery of ours, we were told it was definitely finished so I went down there and I looked at it and it wasn't finished.
"I still had a checklist of things that they hadn't done."
Bella Modular's owners have been contacted for comment.

Women and child healthcare were among the key priorities in the announcements made by Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj in the Legislative Assembly on Monday (August 17, 2026). In a first, the State government will formulate a ‘Peri-Menopausal Care Policy’ to enable early identification of the physical and mental health needs of women in the peri-menopausal age group, along with screening, counselling and treatment services.
Bluetooth-enabled blood pressure (BP) monitors will be introduced to track BP in pregnant women, with real-time transmission of data to facilitate timely intervention, while children under 18 with type 1 diabetes will receive free year-round insulin supply in government hospitals at a cost of ₹9.94 crore.
In the first phase, the BP apparatus will be provided to nearly 10,000 pregnant women in 14 districts, including Kallakurichi, Nilgiris, Tirupattur, Dharmapuri, Dindigul and Namakkal.
According to the announcement, under the peri-menopausal policy, camps would be conducted on a specific day every week at all primary health centres (PHC) and urban PHCs for symptomatic assessment, basic tests, counselling and referrals for treatment at district headquarters hospitals and government medical college hospitals.
“Irumbu Kanmani” - School Anaemia Prevention will be rolled out at a cost of ₹6.37 crore. Haemoglobin estimation will be done for nearly 16.5 lakh adolescents studying in classes VI, IX and XI in government and government-aided schools and appropriate treatment and monitoring will be done.
The department will launch rare genetic disease screening for newborns. Nearly 4.5 lakh babies delivered in all government hospitals in the State will be screened for seven rare genetic diseases in a hub-and-spoke model. This will include congenital hypothyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, galactosemia and biotinidase deficiency.
Neo Genesis Unit for extreme low birth weight babies will be set up at a cost of ₹16.81 crore. The intrauterine/womb-like environments will be set up at the Institute of Obstetrics and Gynaecology in Chennai and government medical college hospitals in Madurai, Coimbatore, Tirunelveli, Chengalpattu and Tiruchi.
An Autism Early Detection Programme will be launched to screen children for autism spectrum disorder. For this, 12,456 village health nurses and 5,000 doctors will be trained. A Childhood Obesity Prevention Programme will be launched in schools, while a School Orthodontic Treatment programme will be rolled out in five districts — Cuddalore, Nagapattinam, Kancheepuram, Kallakurichi and Virudhunagar — covering 1,500 children at a cost of ₹1.80 crore.
Newborn hearing screening facilities such as Otoacoustic Emission and Sound Proof Room will be established. The monthly financial assistance for children affected by or living with HIV/AIDS will be increased and additional funds to the tune of ₹1.21 crore will be allotted.
Transport ventilators for newborns, modern equipment for human milk banks, mother and newborn care units, administration of ferric carboxy maltose injections for pregnant women with moderate anaemia and adolescent girls with severe anaemia and strengthening maternal and child care infrastructure were among other announcements.

Ajit Doval to visit China for boundary talks ahead of Xi’s India trip
Doval’s visit assumes greater significance as it comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected trip to India next month
National security adviser Ajit Doval is expected to visit China on Monday for a meeting of the Special Representatives on the boundary issue, which is part of efforts by the two sides to normalise ties, people familiar with the matter said on Sunday.
Doval is expected to meet his counterpart for the Special Representatives mechanism, Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi, on Tuesday, the people said on condition of anonymity. This will be the 25th round of talks under the mechanism, established in 2003 to work out a framework for resolving the dispute over the 3,488-km border.
Doval’s visit assumes greater significance as it comes ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s expected trip to India next month to participate in the BRICS Summit in New Delhi. Though both sides have not made an official announcement in this regard, Xi is expected to join the summit to be held during September 12-13, the people said.
This will be Xi’s first visit to India in seven years. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Xi last met in August 2025 on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Summit in China.
The talks between the Special Representatives is being held against the backdrop of a recent standoff between Indian and Chinese troops in the Arunachal Pradesh sector of the Line of Actual Control (LAC). External affairs minister S Jaishankar reiterated at a media conclave on Saturday that the state of the border will determine the course of the overall India-China relationship.
“I think we went through a particularly bad patch between the summer of 2020 and the autumn of 2024, and that was primarily an outcome of the situation in the border areas,” Jaishankar said, referring to a military face-off in the Ladakh sector of the LAC that lasted more than four years and took bilateral ties to a six-decade low.
After the two sides reached an understanding on ending the face-off in Ladakh in October 2024, Xi and Modi met in Russia and agreed on measures to normalise ties and address the border dispute. Though the two sides have taken steps such as reviving the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, resuming direct flights and easing visa restrictions for Chinese nationals, there has been no forward movement on de-escalation on the LAC.
At the last round of Special Representatives’ talks in New Delhi a year ago, the two sides reiterated the “importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity” on the border to promote the overall development of ties.
According to an Indian readout issued at the time, the Special Representatives agreed on the need for a “political perspective” while working on a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable framework for settling the boundary question in line with the Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for Settlement of the India-China Boundary Question of 2005.
They also agreed to set up an expert group under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination (WMCC) on India-China Border Affairs to “explore early harvest in boundary delimitation”, and a working group under the WMCC to advance effective border management.
They further agreed to create general-level mechanisms in the eastern and middle sectors of the border, in addition to the existing general-level mechanism in the western sector.
There has been no word from both sides on what, if any, progress has been made on these matters.
The latest meeting of the WMCC, held in New Delhi on August 6, saw the two sides having detailed exchanges on “boundary delimitation, border management, mechanism‑building and trans‑border cooperation” as a follow-up to the last round of talks between the Special Representatives, according to an Indian readout.

London is famous for its great trees. More than 70% are at risk due to climate change, research finds
Successive heat waves and drought are putting stress on London's trees
In the middle of a heat wave and severe drought this summer, Divya Hariramani was pruning a plum tree in south London when she noticed something wrong with one of the tree's branches.
The branch was beginning to split completely from the tree. The workers at Mitcham Community Orchard told her it was because the fruit tree was stressed.
"Because of the heat essentially. Like, when the trees can't provide enough water to its parts and like some parts will just drop," said Hariramani, who documents fruit trees and the people who tend to them across the city on a social media account called Fruity Walks.
While London’s stone architecture may be more famous to some tourists, the 2,000-year-old city is also renowned for its mature urban forest, which has been called the largest in the world.
This year has proven difficult for the normally lush canopy, though, as five successive heat waves and a serious lack of rain have strained plants and wildlife.
And it’s projected to get much worse for the city’s eight million trees.
By the end of the century, according to a recent report from Royal Botanic Gardens Kew forecasting the vulnerability of London’s urban forest, some 73 per cent of the city’s trees could be at risk of dying due to climate change.
Driest July on record
The Kew Gardens tree collections and arboriculture team worked with the Greater London Authority to assess a sample of over a million public trees and found that 62 per cent of them already have "low suitability" to the climate conditions that can be expected by 2090 without action to reduce emissions. On top of that, nearly 11 per cent are “vulnerable."
It’s not just a future problem. In 2022, 400 of Kew's 11,000 trees died amid extreme heat and drought conditions. The gardens have left the skeleton of one red oak standing, and painted it red as a symbol of what climate change is already doing to London's trees.
Kew highlighted the findings and unveiled the red tree ahead of Climate Action Week in June, when Britain and Europe were already in the throes of a second heat wave. By August, there had been two more and a major drought was declared in much of England and Wales. Virtually no rain fell in July, resulting in the driest July on record in Britain.
Farmers lost crops, warned of food shortages and had to dip into winter feed reserves for cattle. Wildfires in parts of the country prompted an emergency cellphone alert in August. In the city, park grass turned yellow and brittle; tree branches and leaves looked droopier than usual. In some places, trees lost their leaves altogether, giving an autumnal look to the ground in the middle of summer.
The week in June when Kew publicized its report, Hariramani, in an ironic twist of fate, had to cancel a group walk she had organized in light of Climate Action Week due to the heat.
"Literally one of the most important walks in a way, for such an important situation and we couldn't even do it," said Hariramani, whose day job is in sustainable design.
More like Barcelona?
With a London that’s getting warmer than its current trees can handle, botanists are exploring whether they should start planting different trees.
"From most projections, we're expecting the climate in London in 2050 to look more like Barcelona's is now," Joe Richomme, a botanical horticulturist at Kew Gardens, told CBC on a recent visit to Kew’s Carbon Garden, where 35 trees and 6,500 plants have been selected to show how different species respond to changing conditions.
Richomme explained that Kew has been exploring what types of tree species could fare better in hotter, drier weather, while also being able to withstand England’s notorious wetter winters.
For example, English oak, which are native to Britain, have struggled in the heat, but have also adapted to grow in warmer places, such as the southern United States.
'They’re irreplaceable’
Paul Wood has written four books and two maps about London's trees, which he attributes to growing up playing in the forests of southern England — and also, his name.
"It's called nominative determinism," Wood said over the phone in mid-August with a chuckle, referring to the idea that people gravitate toward work that suits their name.
He too has made a career of writing about the British capital's storied tree canopy, and the cooling and relaxing benefits it brings to residents and visitors.
But these days he worries about what could happen to London's leafy streets and pockets of ancient woodland in the future as he sees the city struggling in record extreme heat and drought.
"Places like Highgate Woods and Sydenham Hill Woods, Oxleas Woods, Hampstead Heath, where there is native woodland which is really struggling in the current climate," Wood said.
Trees as old as 1,000 years live in some of those places, meaning they’ve stood through the Norman conquest, the Magna Carta and Shakespeare. They saw Victorian railways being built and felt the first rumblings of the London Underground.
"That would be really devastating to lose," Wood said, noting it's not just the trees' history that's valuable but the biodiversity they support as well.
"They're irreplaceable."

Zelensky has 'questions to answer' about corruption in his government, sacked minister tells BBC
- Published
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has "questions to answer" about corruption in his government, his sacked defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov has told the BBC.
Fedorov, a popular minister who modernised the armed forces and pioneered drone warfare, was fired last month after reportedly falling out with the head of Ukraine's armed forces.
He told the BBC a money laundering investigation announced last week raised questions about Zelensky's awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.
Fedorov also reiterated that "democracy should not be the hostage of Putin" - but stopped short of declaring his own political ambitions days after he posted a video calling for elections in Ukraine.
- Sacked Ukrainian defence minister calls for presidential election 
  - Published3 days ago
Supporters have protested on Kyiv's streets weekly since he was sacked, calling on the president to reinstate him.
Asked whether he missed his old job, the 35-year-old replied "No", citing the relentless stress of managing Ukraine's war with Russia while transforming its defence ministry.
The protests ended on Wednesday, after Fedorov's replacement was confirmed, hours after he posted a video on YouTube calling for political reform.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, meaning elections are suspended.
But Fedorov said it was his "moral right" to start the conversation about elections.
"We should not be afraid of discussing it. That's what democracy is all about. If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?"
If elections were never held, he said, "then we are no longer a democracy".
In his earlier video statement Fedorov had argued that "people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made".
He shied away from criticising the president directly and declined to answer whether he backs Zelensky to win any election.
On Sunday, Zelensky said he believed wartime elections would currently be too dangerous for Ukraine.
"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk," he said. "Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine."

Ukraine's anti-corruption bureau said it had uncovered a scheme to misappropriate more than $3m (£2.2m) in Ukrainian currency to pay bail for a former energy minister accused of money laundering.
A senior official in Zelensky's office, alleged to be involved, was sacked.
Fedorov said the case raised questions about the president's awareness of potential corruption in his inner circle.
"Let him answer this question... I believe that he's ready for such questions. It's his responsibility to tell us all whether he was aware of all that or not... I don't want to make any assumptions."
A spokesperson for the president had earlier told BBC News: "Since the former minister was part of every government since 2019, it's strange that he phrases it as though these were somehow different governments without him. As everyone remembers, we didn't hear any strong statements from him back then."
Fedorov claimed he had rooted out elements of corruption from defence procurement but warned it was still affecting Ukraine's frontline capacity.
The former minister said he'd had no contact with the president for "a couple of weeks", and had no evidence the president was personally corrupt.
"In all the time that I worked with him, not a single time have I received from him any task or assignment that would go against law or my sense of integrity. So that's my personal experience with him."
As defence minister and previously digital transformation minister, Fedorov is credited with innovating to replace soldiers with an "army of drones", saving lives on the battlefield and enabling long-range Ukrainian strikes on Russian military targets, oil refineries and distribution warehouses - thousands of kilometres over the border.
He said he would continue to promote new ways to fight the war and confirmed a visit to the United States in the coming weeks, where he hopes to meet Elon Musk.
The billionaire businessman's Starlink satellite communications system has been key in Ukraine's success. Fedorov aims to convince Musk to extend the technology into Russian airspace to assist Ukrainian strikes, without the Kremlin benefiting from access.
"The best tech companies in the world are supporting us and they will be investing in our victory, in ending this war. And we need to stay in touch with them regardless of my position. I have a previous successful track record of working with them and I need to stay in touch with them for my country," he said.
Fedorov criticised bureaucracy in the UK and other countries supporting Ukraine for delays in supplying weapons.
The UK is a longstanding supporter of Ukraine, spending £16bn supplying weapons since the war began. It was confirmed last week that British-made drones have been used to attack Russian targets.
Fedorov said he was grateful for British support but blamed "bureaucracy and red tape" for delays in receiving promised equipment.
"Governments are lagging behind the realities on the ground. It's not only the issue for UK, but for other countries as well that announce some assistance and we are not getting it until the end of the year."
Fedorov urged direct funding of the latest Ukrainian drone production, in place of outdated skills and equipment from other nations: "We don't need repairs of tanks when we no longer use tanks."
He said timely deliveries would help save not just Ukrainian lives.
"Unfortunately, our losses, our blood, our military experience is beneficial to all of you guys. You can get this experience for all the assistance that you give us."
Fedorov denied having immediate political ambitions but didn't rule out a future run for president.
"It will all depend on how soon we'll be able to relaunch this democratic election process, [...] how much energy I would have, whether I will preserve my team, whether I will be able to respond to the question myself, whether I can handle this position of the president or not.

A drug called Tavneos used to treat rare autoimmune diseases will be pulled from the shelves in France, the country's medicine watchdog said Wednesday, after it was linked to 20 deaths in Japan.
"The recall of all batches available in France will begin on August 19," France's medicine safety agency ANSM said in a statement.
The agency noted that the European Commission revoked the drug's marketing authorisation earlier this month because "the benefits are no longer proven to outweigh its risks".
Tavneos is made by the U.S. biotech firm Amgen and is sold by different partner pharmaceutical companies around the world.
It is used to treat adults with severe and rare autoimmune diseases which cause inflammation of the blood vessels.
Kissei Pharmaceutical, which sells the drug in Japan, said in May that 20 deaths had been reported among people using the it since 2022.
The company warned doctors of "the risk of severe liver dysfunction" and asked them to stop prescribing it.
Both Kissei and Amgen said the deaths included cases for which no causal link to the medicine could be determined.
But the warning raised doubts about the rigour of the study that was submitted to various regulatory authorities to determine whether it should be authorised for sale.
The European Medicines Agency reassessed the data and recommended in July that the drug be stripped of its market authorisation.
The European Commission endorsed that recommendation earlier this month.
In France, the drug is prescribed to 600 patients, according to the ANSM.
"Abruptly stopping Tavneos without switching to an alternative should be avoided to prevent the condition worsening," the agency warned, advising patients to consult a doctor about alternatives.
In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration offered Amgen the option of voluntarily withdrawing Tavneos from shelves.
But the company refused, so a procedure is underway to determine whether they will be forced to pull the drug.

Swimming pools are fun. Cleaning swimming pools is not fun.
I learned this simple logic as a kid growing up in and around pools—it’s the only way to survive summer in Houston. Four years ago, I became a pool owner myself, and I found that the rule still holds. Jumping into the pool on a hot day remains a rare treat, but if the pool is filled with leaves and dirt, that treat becomes a lot less delightful. And when the thermometer is reading over 100 degrees Fahrenheit, the thought of laboring on the pool deck, scooping out debris with a net, is downright cruel.
Robotic pool cleaners were a thing when I was growing up in the ’80s, but there was really only one technology available: pressure-side cleaners that attach to a pump on the surface and use water pressure, not electricity, to move around the pool. These types of cleaners are still around; you’ll recognize them by the length of tubing that floats in the water and connects to a jet set into the wall of the pool.
Today, the market is gravitating to electronic cleaners that don’t require a pump or that big, ugly hose in the water. And while corded cleaners are still an option—essentially running off of a long extension cord connected to wall power—battery-powered robotic cleaners are the future of the industry.
Battery-powered cleaners have many benefits, including the lack of hoses or cords and the ability to be removed from the water on demand, leaving your pool unencumbered by obstacles when you want to swim in it. Of the ones I've tested, the Beatbot AquaSense 2 Ultra is the best all-around, but I've also found options for other budgets and preferences.
