Relief for Iraola but Liverpool have work to do
- Published
When Liverpool came to Newcastle last August, there was utter jubilation as Rio Ngumoha scored a remarkable 100th-minute winner.
They scored late again this time around, through Dominik Szoboszlai's 99th-minute penalty, but it felt more like a sense of relief than joy as they rescued a point.
Andoni Iraola said afterwards that his side did not deserve to lose and, to their credit, they never gave up as they earned a 2-2 draw.
A defeat would have been Liverpool's first on the opening weekend since 2012-13. A draw will do wonders for their spirit but it will certainly not mask their concerns.
"It's probably not the result you want when you come in before the game but we definitely deserve this point and even more," Iraola told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"The team has never given up and we've recovered one point and probably the taste is better because we score in the last minute."
Iraola will be content with the outcome, given his side trailed twice at a raucous St James' Park.
But on the flight back to Merseyside on Sunday evening, he would have had time to consider the performance, which highlighted why his squad needs more depth.
"You're expecting Liverpool to get top four this season at least but they didn't look like a top four team today," former Scotland winger Pat Nevin told 5 Live.
"There are more players to come in, so you can't make a real decision on how their season is going to go.
"There's a definite lack of creativity and somehow they must get the best out of Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak because you certainly didn't get the best out of them today."
All eyes were on Wirtz and Isak - the Sweden striker, signed from Newcastle in a drawn-out saga last September, was booed relentlessly whenever he touched the ball. Wirtz did start positively, but was replaced just after the hour mark after Newcastle went 2-1 up.
Isak had 28 touches and looked fired up but wasted a brilliant opportunity in the second half - the kind of which he would take regularly when he was at Newcastle.
Both of them, signed for nine-figure fees last summer, will know that their overall output and connection must improve over the coming weeks and months.
'I've liked a lot of things I've seen'
This remains a Liverpool side offering more questions than answers.
One significant question is the Cody Gakpo conundrum, which will roll into the final week of the transfer window.
If Liverpool do bring in two more attacking players then Gakpo may leave.
The club have been linked with Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye and have had two bids rejected for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh.
Yet Dutchman Gakpo was Liverpool's best player at Newcastle and took his goal brilliantly - while there was another positive in the performance of Spanish forward Victor Munoz on his Liverpool debut from the bench.
Munoz won the late penalty after replacing Ngumoha but Iraola's decision to take off the English teenager off after just over an hour summed up how much he struggled down the right.
Ngumoha will turn 18 next week and has preferred to play down the left throughout his youth career but failed to have an impact on the other side.
With Iraola determined to have his wingers able to play on both sides, it remains to be seen if that experiment persists once Liverpool get more attackers in.
What is for certain is that Iraola needs more options. Once Munoz and Alexis Mac Allister came on in the 63rd minute, Iraola's remaining bench options were: Giorgi Mamardashvili, Ronald Araujo, Wataru Endo, Kostas Tsimikas, Trey Nyoni, James McConnell and Lewis Koumas.
Defensively, both Milos Kerkez and Jeremie Frimpong had poor games at full-back and Liverpool were undone on the counter attack for both of the goals they conceded.
The lack of a defensive midfielder showed and it was revealing to see Iraola use Mac Allister just ahead of the back four after Joe Willock put Newcastle 2-1 up.
Liverpool have now conceded more goals via fast breaks in all competitions than any other Premier League team since the start of last season - nine.
All that and more will be food for thought for the new Liverpool boss but this was a relatively positive start to life under Iraola - who prefers to wait until the day after the match for a debrief.
"I've liked a lot of the things I've seen from the team," he said. "There's definitely things to improve like the goals but I've seen a lot of things I've liked from the team. I've liked the energy, especially the players coming from the bench. I think we finished the game quite strong physically."
"We will never give up. I can guarantee you that," Szoboszlai told Sky Sports. "We have to fight every time - all day long during the 90 minutes. Everybody who came off the bench also made an impact as well. We need the whole squad and we need to be ready."
That desire was never a cause for concern on Tyneside. But this Liverpool squad must improve, both in terms of quality and quantity.

U.S. drugmakers Merck and Moderna said Wednesday a personalized cancer treatment had shown success in reducing the recurrence of melanoma tumors in a late-stage trial hailed by experts as a "breakthrough."
The news sent shares in Moderna soaring 145% to $154 while Merck's stock was up more than 12% to $152.
The drug, called "intismeran autogene," is based on the same messenger RNA (mRNA) technology behind Covid-19 vaccines.
Researchers have for years been trying to apply mRNA treatments against cancer, but this was the first time such a drug showed positive results in a large, late-stage clinical trial.
"Today marks an extraordinary milestone for Moderna, for mRNA science and, most importantly, for patients with cancer," Moderna CEO Stephane Bancel said in a statement.
The trial lasted approximately a year and involved 1,137 patients who, following surgical removal of their cancers, were randomized into groups, with two-thirds receiving the new treatment plus pembrolizumab -- the current standard-of-care drug -- while the rest received pembrolizumab alone.
The companies said they would present their data at an upcoming international conference and begin filings with regulators for approval.
Proof of principle
Lennard Lee, an oncologist and assistant professor at the University of Oxford who was not involved in the trial, called the results "very encouraging," adding: "We should now look forward to seeing the complete data."
Oncologist Marco Gerlinger, a professor at London's Barts Cancer Institute, added that beyond being good news for patients with melanoma, it was "proof of principle that personalised cancer vaccines work."
"I think it is fair to call it a breakthrough in the development of new cancer immunotherapies," he added, while also noting the press release was short on details.
The treatment works by taking a sample of the patient's tumor and identifying its unique mutational signature, or "fingerprint," then using mRNA technology to fight it.
Messenger RNA technology uses synthetic molecular instructions encased in tiny fat bubbles that temporarily enter cells, causing them to produce targets that train the body's immune system.
The technology was first conceived decades ago but came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Moderna and Pfizer developed vaccines that were highly effective against serious forms of the illness.
Melanoma is one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer, with more than 330,000 new cases diagnosed worldwide in 2022.
"Together with Merck, we are now studying intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab and other anti-cancer therapies, and as a monotherapy, across multiple tumor types and stages of disease, including melanoma, lung, bladder and kidney cancers," said Bancel.

Alex Lanier walked into history books and An Se-young reiterated her supremacy after being crowned world champions in style at the 2026 World Badminton Championships.
Lanier, at 21-years-old, became the first French men’s singles champion with a clinical, one-sided 21-11, 21-11 dismantling of Japan’s Kodai Naraoka in the final to make it a double delight for the French.
The mixed doubles pair of Thom Gicquel and Delphine Delrue became the first-ever French champions in the morning, defeating the top-ranked pair of Feng Yan Zhe & Huang Dong Ping 22-20, 19-21, 21-15.
The Chinese pair was one of three in the running for a title here but only the men’s pair of Liang Wei Keng and Wang Chang managed to come out on top, defeating Malaysia’s Aaron Chia and Soh Wooi Yik 21-17, 21-16 to ensure China returned with at least one title in every edition of the marquee event starting 1983.
Top-ranked Se-young, meanwhile, extended her win streak against World No. 2 and defending champion Akane Yamaguchi to six matches in their 35th encounter with a 21-17, 21-14 win to regain the title.
The 10th ranked Lanier was all over Naraoka for a large part of the final, never letting the Japanese settle or find his rhythm. The two were circumspect early on, probing, lifting and dropping tentatively rather than going all out on the attack. Leading 11-9 in the opening game, Lanier shifted gears, increasing the pace and becoming more aggressive, forcing Naraoka into errors and pushing him hard, dictating the play to win 21-11.
The second game was more of the same as Naraoka tried everything but was unable to find any gaps in Lanier’s defence and unable to find a way to repel his smashes. At 11-14, he seemed to have all but given up as Lanier raced through the next seven points to seal the deal.
The women’s final was on expected lines with high intensity, high speed action to the delight of the more than 8000 strong crowd that packed the stands. The opening game was close with both Se-young and Yamaguchi exchanging the lead, the gap never more than three points between the two. Se-young led 15-12 before Yamaguchi took four straight points to go ahead 16-15 but the Korean came out on top to win 21-17.
Things continued in the same vein in the second game, Yamaguchi leading but Se-young landed a couple of winners to go up 11-7. A combination of unforced errors and missed chances from Yamaguchi saw Se-young lead 17-13 before wrapping up the win. For someone coming into the tournament with fitness concerns and a dodgy knee, this was her ninth win on the trot without dropping a game.
In the women’s doubles, the Korean pair of Baek Ha Na and Lee So Hee beat top-seed Sheng Shu Liu and Ning Tan of China 21-15, 21-15 to break a five match losing streak and their first win in straight games since the World Tour Finals in 2024. In the process, they also became only the second Korean women’s doubles champions after 31 years, the last being Gil Young-ah and Jang Hye-ock in 1995.

Can you tell when someone nearby is wearing Meta AI glasses?
As millions of people buy into the smart glasses fad each year, the odds are increasing that you could be secretly recorded while simply going about your day.
Meta is not the only smart glasses maker, but its AI glasses are by far the most popular. And as the devices become more common, some public places, including schools, courts, restaurants, and entertainment venues, have begun to ban them. Even tech lovers have rejected Meta glasses in certain settings. The hackers behind DEF CON 2026 reportedly banned smart glasses with no exceptions, reminding attendees with prescription pairs to “be sure to pack non-violating eyewear if you need them.”
But a ban is only as effective as the people enforcing it. Spotting a pair of smart glasses can require tech-savvy security staff, and enforcement may depend on users voluntarily disclosing their devices—or on watchful observers speaking up.
Those bans are an important way to push back against the potential for abuse. But privacy advocates know that increasing the social friction around nonconsensual recording can’t stop the practice by itself.
Until comprehensive consumer privacy laws are passed, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has warned that Meta seems prepared to make the tech even more invasive in its bid to sell more glasses and stay ahead of rivals in the burgeoning industry.
And as AI advances, EFF staff technologist Cooper Quintin told Ars, potential new features such as facial recognition could raise the stakes further, potentially allowing the devices to be used to create convincing deepfakes or nonconsensual intimate imagery of people who may not be aware that cameras are rolling.
“I think that there are a lot of other concerns there beyond just being recorded without your knowledge,” Quintin told Ars.
EFF has warned that smart glasses makers will likely be tempted to add facial-recognition features unless lawmakers intervene and give people a private right to sue companies whose products violate their biometric privacy rights. In the meantime, the group has released a guide for smart-glasses users that lays out ways to resist facial recognition, develop responsible recording habits, and better understand the privacy risks of continuous recording. It also urges users to consider blurring strangers’ faces before posting videos online.
For people unknowingly targeted in secret recordings, the only safety feature Meta provides is nearly “useless,” Quintin told Ars.
A tiny recording light that can be easily covered with a sticker is unlikely to deter bad actors intent on abusing the glasses, whether stalkers or creepy partners secretly recording women in public bathrooms or private bedrooms. The tech has also controversially been used in immigration raids, 404 Media reported, and to harass sex workers and retail workers. And on social media, videos show a range of other unwanted recordings, from relatively inoffensive pranks to more harmful videos featuring bullying or harassment.
The volume of these videos online suggests the LED feature “is better than nothing, but not by much,” Quintin said.
Hobbyists build apps to detect glasses
Experts have noted that Meta may already have plans to diminish that limited safety feature. The company is supposedly “testing a prototype of ‘super sensing’ AI glasses that would use cameras and audio recordings to capture a wearer’s every moment,” the Financial Times reported last month. According to sources familiar with Meta’s thinking, executives “are planning not to activate the LED when the super-sensing features are being used,” even though “that would make it harder for bystanders to know when they were being recorded.”
Meta execs’ plans may change if the public’s privacy concerns remain a sticking point, though, sources have suggested. And backlash will likely be sustained as more people wear the glasses, since digital rights experts have accused Meta of failing to consider civil rights or privacy ramifications when designing new features. Perhaps most troublingly, Meta recently backpedaled and deleted an unreleased facial recognition system from its smart-glasses app that Wired and EFF revealed had been quietly installed on 50 million phones in June.
It’s unclear if or when Meta might try to bring the facial recognition system back. Meta did not respond to Ars’ request to comment on this story.
As Meta glasses have become more commonplace, hobbyist programmers have been building apps to detect when smart glasses are nearby so people can steer clear of them.
These civil defense apps, Quintin said, aren’t a perfect solution to the social problem of smart-glasses recording without consent. But when used in combination with bans, the apps can offer wary members of the public a way to check if a ban is being enforced or whether a nearby device may begin recording at a sensitive time. Society needs both solutions, Quintin said, especially because the most popular and recognizable smart glasses available today will likely one day come in a wider assortment of trendy models, making them harder to spot in the wild.
“You need to have the social construct around these being unwelcome, and you also need to be able to find when people are using these,” Quintin said. “Right now, they’re pretty easy to just detect with your eyes. They’re pretty obvious, but that might not always be the case. So technologies like this are also important to supplement that.”
“I can do something about it”
Since February, engineers have been releasing and updating apps that help people detect glasses like Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, or Snap Spectacles.
“It is completely unsurprising that people are building apps to fight back against Meta glasses and other surreptitious public recording,” Quintin told Ars. Many people “have a deep revulsion to being recorded without their consent, which is understandable,” and that remains “the biggest problem with these glasses,” Quintin said.
Smart-glasses detector apps aren’t perfect. At best, they can alert users when nearby glasses are turned on by detecting the Bluetooth signal used to pair the glasses with a phone. Most importantly, the apps cannot determine whether the glasses are actively recording, and users are cautioned to never assume that someone wearing smart glasses is recording them. App makers also advise against confrontation and accept no liability for false positives or misunderstandings. Additionally, detection may be unreliable if a wall or other obstacle, like a human body, interferes with a signal.
Users don’t seem to consider these flaws deal-breakers. They simply want some way to scan a room, and some are eager to provide feedback to improve the apps, even expressing an emotional investment in seeing the technology develop.
One of the first apps, Nearby Glasses, is available for $2.99 on both iOS and Android. It has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store and remains the most popular such app, despite the developer, Yves Jeanrenaud, warning on GitHub that he’s “no pro developer” and that “detecting Bluetooth LE devices might sometimes just not work as expected,” and “false positives are likely.”
Released in response to online content showing that smart glasses are “an intolerable intrusion, consent neglecting, horrible piece of tech,” Jeanrenaud said, he kept his goals humble. On GitHub, he wrote that “I hope this app is useful for someone,” but “I do not want to promote techsolutionism, nor do I want people to feel falsely secure. It’s still an imperfect approach,” and it probably “always will be.”
By July, another detector, Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner, was nearing the top of iPhone charts, also charging $3 for the service. One high school teacher reviewing the app called it the “best $3 I’ve spent,” writing that she was concerned that her students could use AI glasses to take unwanted recordings in class.
Ars tested the most recently released app, Zuckoff, which launched for free on iPhone in early August and is currently seeking 12 testers to launch on Android devices later this year.
Already, thousands of users have downloaded the iPhone app, with some eagerly submitting feedback that has helped improve key functionality, including the ability to detect AI glasses and receive alerts when the app is closed. Perpetual scanning is an optional feature that costs about $10 a year. The subscription helps cover the costs of “continuous support” for the app, Zuckoff’s creator, Pawel Szydlowski, told Ars.
Like Jeanrenaud’s app, Zuckoff collects no data and was created partly in response to toxic Meta glasses content flooding social media. Szydlowski told Ars that he built the app in one week after finishing another project that scans for nearby Bluetooth devices and deciding, “Let’s see how far we can go with detecting those glasses.”
Without researching whether other apps had already sought to solve the problem, Szydlowski decided to put his 10 years of iPhone developer experience to work. “I was like, ‘I can do something about it, so let’s go,’” Szydlowski told Ars.
Building a Meta glasses detector
Szydlowski’s biggest challenge was collecting the unique identifiers that manufacturers use to label different products for regulatory purposes. Zuckoff uses these identifiers to help users detect specific smart-glasses models while ignoring Bluetooth signals from less creepy devices. To compile as comprehensive a list as possible, Szydlowski crawled Instagram and Reddit for photos of people wearing different types of smart glasses.
“I see you have those glasses,” Szydlowski would say in messages to early Meta glasses adopters, who agreed to help despite presumably approving of the technology. “Can you help me with this little name? I want to know the unique identifier that’s broadcasting.”
To catch glasses with identifiers that Zuckoff hasn’t yet logged, Szydlowski created a workaround that first flags devices by their advertised names. It’s less precise, he said, but it gives users some indication that a pair of smart glasses may be nearby, even without a known identifier. He’s currently working on another solution that should widen discovery even further, he told Ars.
Szydlowski’s app first alerted him to nearby smart glasses when he ran into two colleagues wearing them at a recent Apple event in Poland. That helped him confirm the tech was working as he hoped.
When you load Zuckoff, the app “estimates distance from signal strength and puts a confidence level on every hit rather than a hard yes or no,” Szydlowski explained. Esitmates tell users if glasses are very close (within arm’s length), close (in the same room), near (nearby) and far. This feature also makes it possible to see when you may be approaching an area with a larger concentration of smart glasses, like in a tourist trap such as the Las Vegas strip.
Ars replicated the test, thanks to this writer’s brother-in-law, who agreed to use the app to detect his own Ray-Bans. He likes to use his smart glasses to record nature sightings when he goes boating or to take action shots of his bulldog playing fetch along the lake, and he had the glasses on him when I called to see if he could run the test.
After putting the glasses on, my brother-in-law loaded the app, which detected the glasses in minutes and warned that “one possible pair” was “within arm’s length.” (In this case, the message was very literal, since he was wearing the glasses while looking at the phone in his hand.)
The app then references the identifier to help the user detect exactly which model is nearby, and my brother-in-law confirmed that Zuckoff correctly labeled his smart glasses.
For Szydlowski, the toughest challenge was figuring out how Apple might allow the app to run in the background, since the company is “very strict when it comes to apps working in the background all the time.” He worried some users wouldn’t find the app as beneficial without that functionality. Eventually, he settled on a solution that scans continuously, but rather than flagging all known devices the moment they’re turned on, Apple allows only a fixed list of known Bluetooth service identifiers to be detected in that mode. Extra-cautious users should therefore also open the app to see the full list of potential devices in the area.
“This background feature, it’s so crucial,” Szydlowski said.
Android may allow him to offer faster detection through background functionality, Szydlowski suggested, because unlike Apple devices, Android allows background activities to be “possible to exempt from battery optimization,” Szydlowski said. That means Zuckoff “can continue using the battery in the background” without Android protocols that “wipe out the apps that are consuming your battery,” he said.
Although people have mostly grown accustomed to the idea of being recorded without consent in public, smart glasses have the potential to expand mass surveillance in ways that deeply concern privacy advocates.
Meta could introduce technical solutions, like automatically blurring faces, as Google does in Street View images, but Szydlowski doubts Meta would voluntarily make such a privacy-conscious change without regulatory or public pressure. The creator of Zuckoff, a name that takes a cheeky dig at Meta’s founder, also said that “I’m pretty sure they’re not going to be happy with this app existing.”
He likens malicious smart-glasses recording to the earliest harms of Apple’s AirTags. When that technology was released in 2021, the easy-to-hide tracking devices were soon implicated in stalking cases. But there still is no federal law targeting AirTag abuses, and it took the first states to act on the emerging privacy threat roughly three to five years to pass legislation prohibiting the invasive tracking.
Szydlowski worries lawmakers will be similarly slow to react to threats from Meta glasses. He told Ars he thinks the best solution might be rules mandating companies like Meta to advertise a specific Bluetooth service identifier while recording. That would improve civil defense apps like his.
In the meantime, he hopes people will find the detector app that they like best and use it to spread awareness of the risk that smart glasses may be present in a room where they’re unexpected or explicitly forbidden.
“The goal of this app was just making people aware because a lot of people won’t be aware until it becomes a major problem, which was the case with AirTags, basically,” Szydlowski said.
Meta expects demand to explode
Last December, analysts forecasted that 2026 would be a breakthrough year for smart glasses. And it’s clear by now that Meta wants this to be the year that AI glasses are suddenly everywhere you look.
The tech giant invested heavily in promoting them, collaborating with celebrity influencer Kylie Jenner on a pair of Ray-Bans featuring an AI assistant that speaks in her voice. The campaign featured billboard ads and a video spot showing Kylie simply enjoying wearing the glasses, without necessarily highlighting their practical features. The partnership was rumored to have paid Jenner millions of dollars and was intended to position the technology as a fashionable, practical accessory—and perhaps buff out the public perception of them as “pervert glasses.” But critics have argued that the ads seem narrowly designed to encourage more people to use their glasses for continuous recording.
Though the Jenner campaign was supposedly viewed as a success internally at Meta, it also prompted global backlash. On social media, the protest collective “Everyone Hates Elon” razed Jenner, The Huffington Post reported, saying that “recording everything we see and do constantly? It’s giving fascism, not fashion,” “hun.” And pop singer Lorde stopped a festival performance to tell her fans, “Fuck the glasses. Don’t get the glasses. Not sexy.”
Salon’s Andi Zeisler slammed the Kylie Edition glasses for trying to lull women into a false sense of security, even as Meta knows the technology has been used to record women without their knowledge, both in public and private. In London, activists took that criticism a step further, replacing bus stop ads of Jenner smiling in the glasses with a spoof in which her face transforms into a skeletal grin above the warning that at Meta, “We’re always watching.”
But despite protests, the glasses aren’t going away any time soon, as Meta plans to move millions more into production. In 2025, the company sold more than 7 million AI glasses—up from 2 million sold in the prior two years combined—then quickly made plans to double its Ray-Ban outputs, Bloomberg reported. By the end of 2026, Meta expects to start producing at least 20 million glasses annually to meet demand, or perhaps as many as 30 million if the market continues trending strongly.
Beyond the backlash, regulating the glasses is a touchy subject, Quintin told Ars. No civil rights group would advocate banning recording in public, a practice that can be crucial for holding police and government officials accountable. What may prove just as useful as thoughtful privacy regulations, Quintin suggested, is a broader effort to ban the technology at the community level.
Szydlowski told Ars that he’s personally not bothered by Meta’s AI glasses, only by the gross content made with them. But other critics, like Quintin, think the tech is “disgusting” and “unacceptable,” and he has little hope that technical solutions can solve the problem and abundant concern that the privacy risks will compound as enthusiasm for the technology grows.
Right now, there’s less social friction around using glasses to record than there was when people first started using phones to record public interactions, Quintin suggested. As a father of young children, he recently saw another dad using glasses to film kids at a birthday party, a moment that illustrates how smart glasses have shifted the power dynamic.
Previously, “if you wanted to record somebody, you had to take out your phone, shove it in their face,” Quintin said. “And they know they’re being recorded. That is a useful social friction. And the glasses remove that and put the friction on the other end. The friction is now on me, calling you a pervert for wearing glasses and telling you to stop recording my kids.”
Szydlowski somewhat agreed. He told Ars there’s value in being able to record hands-free from eye level, but he created Zuckoff because he draws the line at posting harmful smart-glasses recordings online.
“People are using it in a bad way,” Szydlowski said. “That was the first part that annoyed me. I was like, ‘I don’t like it. I just don’t enjoy the content, and I don’t think it’s valid’ because myself, I wouldn’t have a way to react to being recorded because I’m used to people holding the phone and actually pointing at me. Then I can say, ‘Hold on a second. This is not scrolling. Someone is actually recording.’”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

The Durand Cup, Asia’s oldest football tournament, has undergone a remarkable transformation in recent years. From its long association with Delhi and Kolkata, the competition has evolved into a multi-state tournament with growing support from fans, state governments and sponsors.
The latest edition has also demonstrated football’s ability to bring communities together, particularly in Manipur, where matches drew enthusiastic crowds despite the state’s challenges.
In an interview with Sportstar, Major General Dinesh Kumar Singh, General Officer Commanding, Bengal Sub Area and Vice Chairman, Durand Cup Organising Committee, discusses the tournament’s revival, the importance of balancing Indian Super League (ISL) clubs with local teams, plans to expand into new regions, and the role of infrastructure and grassroots development in Indian football.
He also explains how the Durand Cup can become a catalyst for nurturing talent and strengthening the sport across the country.
Q: How has the revamped Durand Cup done so far?
A: The Durand Cup has a long legacy, dating back to 1888. Over the years, however, it went through several changes as football’s popularity evolved across the country.
From 1940, it was held in Delhi, but in 2014 it moved to Goa because Delhi was not providing the required spectatorship and traction. After two years in Goa, it returned to Delhi.
In 2019, the Eastern Command of the Army took over its organisation. Since then, the tournament has grown considerably.
I would attribute this growth to three factors: tremendous support from spectators and fans, particularly in the Northeast; strong support from state governments; and increasing sponsorship.
The tournament has expanded from being largely Kolkata-centric to being hosted across five states—Manipur, Meghalaya, Assam, Jharkhand and West Bengal. The Army, Navy and Air Force have also provided tremendous support, along with the President of India.
Q: Given the success, are you looking to expand the tournament further?
A: Yes, certainly. But when we talk about expansion, we are not necessarily looking at increasing the number of participating teams. We would continue with six groups, but in the next edition, we are looking at moving one of the groups outside the Northeast.
We are in discussions with a number of state governments to see where it would be feasible to hold the competition. The format, by and large, will remain the same.
Having said that, there is always scope for making a competition better. Our immediate objective is to improve the quality of the competition, get greater support and bring more spectators to the stadiums. That is what we want to achieve in the foreseeable future.
Q: Sport is often described as a leveller and something that brings people together. How did the Manipur leg work out, particularly given the distress and difficulties in the state?
A: As you rightly said, sport brings people together. It creates camaraderie and teamwork, and it does not matter which region, religion or background you come from.
I wish you had been there in Imphal. I went for the opening game, and I have also been following the matches through live coverage. The stadium was sold out. The cheering, accompanied by Mexican waves, continued throughout the game. There was genuine support for football.
There were around 5,000 to 6,000 people waiting outside to get in. Despite the problems in the region, sport - and football in particular - has been a binding factor.
We also organised a friendly match between two women’s teams in Imphal as a precursor to the tournament, and that too was played in an almost packed stadium.
So, in whatever small way sport can bring happiness and bring society together, it certainly helps. We intend to continue with this in future editions as well.
Q: A number of ISL teams did not participate this time. Is that linked to the crisis Indian football is going through, particularly with uncertainty over when the ISL season will begin?
A: Traditionally, we have had around eight or nine ISL teams, plus or minus one or two, participating in the Durand Cup. It is the season opener in the AIFF calendar. But we must understand the objective of the Durand Cup. Its aim is to nurture talent, provide opportunities and do whatever we can to improve the standard of football.
If all the ISL teams participate, then what is the difference between the ISL and the Durand Cup? We therefore want a healthy mix of ISL teams, other football league teams and local clubs.
For example, FC Raengdai reached the quarterfinals. From nowhere, they have suddenly come to that level. Imagine the exposure the young players of that club are getting.
This time there were several new entrants, including clubs from Assam, Meghalaya and Manipur. There were around seven or eight new clubs. They got an opportunity to play against some of the best teams, many of which have foreign players.
When a youngster plays alongside and against seasoned Indian players and foreign players, the exposure he gets is extremely valuable. That is why I believe this healthy mix of teams is important.
Q: What about Mizoram? It is another state that contributes a lot of talent; were clubs from there invited?
A: Invitations go to several clubs, but participation also depends on their preparation and circumstances. Unfortunately, Mizoram currently does not have infrastructure approved by the AIFF.
We would certainly like clubs from Mizoram to participate, but the infrastructure has to meet the required FIFA and AIFF standards.
Q: We have seen the Indian Army support sport through initiatives such as the Army Sports Institute in Pune, where top athletes are trained. Is there any possibility of a similar dedicated academy or setup for football?
A: The Army already has a system of sports nodes, where different establishments are assigned responsibility for particular sports. Our Army football team, for instance, is based in Bengaluru, which serves as a football node.
The Army also contributes at the grassroots level through initiatives such as the Sadbhavna schemes. At the school and district levels, tournaments are organised, and wherever equipment is required, it is provided.
We also have the Boys Sports Company system, through which we identify talented youngsters at an early age. If the parents agree, the Army takes responsibility for the child’s education as well as sporting training. This gives the youngster an opportunity to develop his talent in a structured environment while continuing his studies.
The system has already demonstrated its impact in other sports, including at events such as the Commonwealth Games. So, while we do not currently have a separate, dedicated football academy on the lines of the Army Sports Institute, the existing sports-node and Boys Sports Company systems provide a pathway through which promising footballers can be identified, trained and eventually channelled into the Army football system.
Q: Could this be taken further for football - identifying young players and developing them in a structured environment?
A: As a dedicated football academy, we do not have such a system at present. However, the Boys Sports Company is already functioning and provides a structured pathway for identifying and developing young talent.
Once a talented youngster is identified, he can be brought into the system with the consent of his parents, while the Army takes care of both his education and sporting training. From there, the player can be channelled into the Army football system and get the opportunity to train and compete at a higher level.
The important aspect is that it is not only about developing a footballer. If the youngster is interested in joining the Army, we can also provide him with a career pathway within the armed forces. At the same time, those who demonstrate the potential and desire to pursue football professionally can continue along that route.
So, while a dedicated football academy could certainly take this effort further, the existing system already provides a foundation for identifying young talent, giving them proper training and education, and helping them build a future either in football or in the Army.
Q: Is there anything else you would like to add about the Durand Cup and your plans for the future?
A: There is always scope for improvement. Once the tournament concludes, we will assess what could have been done better.
Our aim is to achieve a practical 10 - 15 per cent improvement each year - in participation, crowd support, infrastructure, administration or the teams’ stay.
We also try to minimise team travel because it increases costs. The tournament operates on a no-profit, no-loss basis and we do not charge participation fees, which helps local clubs take part.

I hope several young players from this edition will be noticed by bigger clubs and eventually represent India. But the larger challenge is grassroots development. We need to start with schools and districts, where many children do not even have proper playgrounds. We have discussed this with sports ministers and chief ministers, and there is interest in taking the tournament to smaller towns. However, the necessary infrastructure must first be created.
This year, we moved from Jamshedpur to Ranchi and from Kokrajhar to Guwahati. Taking the tournament to new locations encourages states to invest in infrastructure and creates more opportunities for young players.
Across the Northeast, we rely largely on state infrastructure. It is a synergistic effort involving the armed forces, state governments, sponsors, clubs and, most importantly, supporters.
Q: How do you view the participation of so many states as hosts?
A: We have received tremendous support from all the states and are grateful for it.
West Bengal has traditionally been a football powerhouse, while states such as Nagaland and Mizoram have good football but face infrastructure constraints. Assam has also expressed interest in taking the tournament to more districts, although suitable facilities remain a challenge.
Initially, we were sceptical about Guwahati and Ranchi, but the stadiums have been full. That shows that people are interested in football when the quality of competition and organisation are good.
The Durand Cup is increasingly becoming a platform that brings together states, the armed forces, sponsors, clubs and supporters. That collective effort is driving the tournament’s growth.

Water is supposed to be the simplest thing we consume. The premium bottled water industry has transformed it into something that requires a backstory.
Supermarket shelves now distinguish between glacial, iceberg, volcanic, spring, mineral, and alkaline water. Restaurants are introducing water menus, while trained water sommeliers assess bottles by their mineral composition, mouthfeel and provenance. At the extreme end of the category, Svalbarði Polar Iceberg Water sells Arctic water for as much as €100 (around $116) a bottle.
The category’s growth rests on a mixture of verifiable differences and carefully constructed associations. Water can contain different minerals. Those minerals can change how it tastes. But claims about purity, alkaline pH, and remote natural sources can also create the impression that expensive water must be healthier.
According to Michael Mascha, who founded the platform FineWaters in 2002 to train water sommeliers and drag premium bottled products out of the commodity aisle, prices often reflect remote sourcing and difficult transport rather than superior health benefits. Luxury water, he argues, is better understood as a dining experience than as a more effective source of hydration.
Does Expensive Water Hydrate You Better?
There is no established evidence that luxury water hydrates an otherwise healthy person better simply because it is more expensive or comes from a celebrated source.
“Fundamentally, true hydration is about consuming enough water throughout the day to replace daily losses rather than brand status or origin,” says Lucy Semerjian, associate professor of environmental science and technology at the University of Sharjah in the United Arab Emirates.
What matters most is drinking enough safe water to replace the fluid the body loses. Its chemical and microbial composition must also remain within safe limits.
Are the Minerals in Bottled Water Better for You?
Minerals are responsible for some of the genuine differences between waters. As water travels through soil and rock, it can absorb calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, sodium, and other dissolved substances. Their type and concentration depend partly on the geology surrounding the source.
These minerals are already dissolved into ionized forms, meaning the gastrointestinal tract can absorb them. Mineral water can therefore contribute to a person’s calcium or magnesium intake, although its nutritional significance depends on the concentration, the quantity consumed, and the rest of that person’s diet.
The word “mineral,” however, does not tell consumers how much of any particular nutrient is present.
“People see terms like rich in minerals, high TDS numbers, or alkaline pH on a premium label and assume those are automatically markers of superior quality,” says Maria Abi Hanna, cofounder and CEO of nutrition intelligence software Food Label Maker, “when in reality none of those numbers tell you anything on their own.”
Total dissolved solids, or TDS, measures the combined concentration of dissolved substances in water. A higher number does not function as a score for safety, purity, or health. It mainly describes the water’s mineral load.
The same problem applies to alkaline water. Its higher pH is frequently positioned as a wellness advantage, but pH alone does not establish that a bottle is healthier. The stomach is already highly acidic, and the body tightly regulates the pH of the blood.
Consumers should instead look at which minerals appear on the label and in what concentrations. People limiting their sodium intake, for example, may have different priorities from someone specifically looking for a water containing calcium or magnesium.
Does Mineral Content Change How Water Tastes?
Minerals may not transform hydration, but they can transform taste.
“Some waters taste very light because they have very low mineral content,” Mascha says.
Rainwater that has had little contact with the ground may contain very few dissolved minerals. Iceberg and some glacial waters can also fall towards the low end of the TDS scale, producing a relatively light or neutral taste.
At the other end, water containing upwards of 2,000mg of mineral content can have a noticeably heavier mouthfeel and a stronger flavor. Individual minerals can introduce salty, bitter, chalky, or slightly sweet characteristics.
The differences are real. The leap from “tastes different” to “is healthier,” however, is usually where the marketing begins to outrun the evidence. Luxury water makes the most sense when treated as a taste category: something selected for a particular mineral profile, dining experience, or personal preference. The price is not a reliable shorthand for its nutritional value.
Is Glass-Bottled Water Safer Than Plastic?
The most consequential thing about a bottle of water, though, may not be the water itself.
Premium brands often use glass packaging, reinforcing the perception that the water is both luxurious and protected from the concerns surrounding plastic.
“Plastic bottles are sensitive to thermal stress, UV radiation, or extended storage times,” says Nidia Rodriguez-Sanchez, senior lecturer in physiology and nutrition at Scotland’s University of Stirling.
This is particularly relevant in hot climates. Leaving bottled water inside a vehicle or storing it for prolonged periods at high temperatures can increase the migration of substances from PET into the water. Studies have found that heat can increase the release of antimony, a substance used during PET manufacturing, although the concentrations vary by bottle, temperature, and storage time.
Glass is not an entirely plastic-free solution. A 2025 study led by France’s Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety, or ANSES, found microplastics in beverages packaged in glass.
The glass itself was not identified as the main source. Researchers traced many of the particles to the painted coating on metal bottle caps, which could become scratched as the caps rubbed together during storage.
The results also varied by beverage. Soft drinks and beer in glass bottles contained considerably more particles than the same drinks in other packaging. Water contained far fewer particles overall, although glass-bottled water averaged slightly more than water packaged in plastic or cartons.
The study does not prove that glass packaging is more dangerous than plastic. It demonstrates that changing the bottle material does not eliminate every other potential source of plastic exposure.
Mascha’s response to all this is that the anxiety is selectively applied. “Everyone talks about microplastics in water. There’s also microplastics in wine, in beer, and in Coke,” he says.

Vietnamese found-footage horror film “Lầu Chú Hoả: The Deadliest Mansion” is opening in North American theaters on Sept. 4, with Mockingbird Pictures placing the title across AMC, Regal and Cinemark circuits.
Directed by Hùng Trần, the film became Vietnam‘s first theatrical found-footage horror release and turned into a breakout hit after its June debut. It topped the local box office, drew more than one million admissions and crossed VND78 billion ($3 million) in cumulative grosses.
The story pulls from a well-known Vietnamese urban legend: a band of young streamers force their way into the notoriously haunted Hứa family estate, hoping the stunt will bring them fame and money. Instead their broadcast captures a dormant, malevolent force stirring back to life, pulling them into the century-old tale of the “Ghost of the Hứa Family.” The entire film was shot in found-footage style.
Popular on Variety
“Lầu Chú Hoả: The Deadliest Mansion” was produced by Runup Vietnam alongside South Korea’s Hive Media Corp, marking the Korean company’s first production investment outside its home market. Hive has backed several of Korea’s biggest recent releases, including “12.12: The Day,” “Inside Men,” “The Man Standing Next” and “Harbin,” along with the found-footage horror title “Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum,” which drew more than 2.6 million admissions in South Korea.
“Found footage has the power to make audiences feel as though they are experiencing the horror themselves,” said producer Lee Jin Sung. “Working with Hive Media Corp allowed us to bring that experience to a uniquely Vietnamese legend while preserving the identity and atmosphere that make the story distinctive.”
Mockingbird Pictures is overseeing the North American theatrical rollout as part of its broader effort to bring Vietnamese commercial films to international audiences.
“‘Lầu Chú Hoả: The Deadliest Mansion’ delivers one of the most intense Vietnamese horror experiences in recent years,” said Phong Duong, business director of Mockingbird Pictures and one of the executive producers at sister company Bluebells Studios. “We believe this is a film that can travel, and we want audiences around the world to experience that fear for themselves.”
Mockingbird Pictures’ distribution footprint spans more than 60 new theatrical releases a year in Vietnam and upwards of 100 titles across post-theatrical platforms, reflecting the company’s growing focus on bringing Southeast Asian films to international audiences.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Every summer evening, Gulshan follows the same routine. She washes the floor of her one-room home several times so it cools a little for her four children to sleep on. Last summer, the family saved enough to buy a desert cooler, which uses evaporation as a cheaper alternative to air conditioning.
The family uses the appliance cautiously to save on energy costs. But even when it is on, Gulshan, who does not use a surname, has to dampeneveryone’s clothes before sleeping. The 39-year-old and her children now have rashes and one has a skin infection from the wet cloth against their skin.
This summer, Gulshan started jotting down these coping strategies in a garmi khata, or heat registry. “I feel relieved that at least somebody might read my family’s experiences,” she says.
They are one of 40 households in Sunder Nagri, a slum in north-east Delhi, documenting their experiences of surviving the city’s increasingly longer and more frequent heatwaves.
Over the last few years, cities across India have begun drawing up heat action plans – agreements formulated by a municipality or district administration on how to prepare for and respond to extreme heat.
While some incorporate data such as satellite-derived land surface temperatures to identify heat hotspots, there are still significant gaps in information on people, making it difficult to understand how heat is experienced differently across communities.
Aravind Unni, an urban planner and researcher in Delhi, says: “Experiences of heat are vastly different depending on geography, income, occupation, gender, caste, class.
“While we have some meteorological data on heat, what’s absolutely missing is people, community – what they feel, what they experience.”
Most data collated in heat planning is usually just meteorological, such as air temperatures and heatwave thresholds.. The idea for the heat diaries was to “move beyond just the numbers”, says Nibedita Saha, a Greenpeace India researcher who worked on the project.
Aakiz Farooq, a senior campaigner at the group, says the team contemplated how best to encapsulate experiences and thought: “What if they become their own storytellers, they write their own evidence, they write their own testimonies?”
Arshi, 19, who lives in one room with five other family members, is a distance-learning student at Delhi University. She also works at home making decorative tassels for trucks.
She makes about 150 rupees (£1.17) working with her mother and sister for a day. “Sometimes I go to the college library just to sit in the air-conditioned space for a while. But I have to come back home so I can help my sister and mother,” she says. These experiences are part of Arshi’s diary.
The diaries, which ask about daily routines, work, home, mood and families, are intended to serve as comprehensive journals of residents’ daily lives.
Arshi’s small brick house is extremely humid, and while the temperatures are lower after rain, the combination of heat and humidity means everyone is sweating profusely.
The ambient air temperature insideis 29.3C (85F), but with relative humidity at 84.6%, the “feels-like” temperature is 36.3C (97F).
Raja, a 21-year-old street vendor, experiences temperatures as high as 45C during peak summer months as he sells vegetables from his pushcart. The fresh produce spoils quickly, leading to losses, and he has noticed a drastic drop in numbers of people on the street, which also reduces his income.
Every night, he returns to a home with limited ventilation and no cooling source beyond a ceiling fan. As the gap between day and night temperatures narrows year after year in Delhi, people in homes such as Raja’s get no respite, even after the sun sets. “I started sleeping out on the roof in May so I could feel some air,” he says.
Workers such as Raja, Unni says, could be better protected by public policy if the state knew of their experiences at a micro-level and establish systems to provide compensation.
When Sunder Nagri’s residents set out to map heat indices within their neighbourhood, they found that some streets, including where Raja sells vegetables, reflected temperatures on the ground of more than 54C (129F). The residents are attempting to find pragmatic solutions, such as shade, water sources or increased greenery.
This summer, satellite analysis found striking differences across Delhi. For instance, an analysis by the news magazine India Today found an average land-surface temperature of nearly 44C in the south-west district of Mahipalpur, by the airport, compared with about 37C just 2 miles (3km) away in the leafy, upmarket suburb of Vasant Kunj.
Unni feels the diaries and community heat mapping can help form urban resilience policy, but says a big stumbling block is that “Indian cities do not have the administrative capacity or infrastructure to have decentralised action”.
The diaries have now been submitted to India’s National Human Rights Commission, urging it to recognise extreme heat as a human rights issue and recommend measures to protect people.
Farooq says the team also plans to share the testimonies with ministries, policymakers and MPs to push for more targeted measures to protect people from extreme heat.
He says they are also working to develop the testimonies into evidence of impacts and injuries that could be used for lawsuits to increase accountability, given the supreme court’s 2024 ruling that protection from the most adverse impacts of the climate crisis forms part of the right to life.
On 4 August, India’s government added heatwaves to the list of nationally notified disasters, allowing states to access emergency relief funds.
Unni and Farooq say it “would be ideal” if the decision meant funds could support local action guided by community participation.
Arshi also feels more hopeful after the new guidelines. “Even if the government sees something as small as our rising medical and electricity costs and tries to help with that, it would feel like a win for me. At least they would have seen what we are going through,” she says.

India's first 100% indigenised AK-203 ‘Sher’ rifle made, test-fired at factory in UP's Amethi
“We have successfully produced and fired the first AK-203 (Sher) rifle made with 100% Indian components and input materials,” IRRPL CEO Major Gen Sharma said.
India has manufactured and tested a prototype of the 100 per cent indigenised AK-203 ‘Sher’ rifle, with army trials for the weapon to begin in September this year, Major General SK Sharma said on Sunday, while sharing a video of the test firing.
The rifles are manufactured by the Indo-Russian Rifles Private Limited, a joint-venture of the Indian Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs), along with Concern Kalashnikov and Rosoboron export from Russia. Maj Gen S K Sharma, who is the CEO and managing director of IRRPL, said the testing of the prototype was “a moment of immense pride” for the company.
Also Read | Indian Army to get loitering munitions worth ₹1,577 crore
“We have successfully produced and fired the first AK-203 (Sher) rifle made with 100% Indian components and input materials,” Major Gen Sharma said in a post on LinkedIn.
‘Every single component, input material sourced from India’
Ever single component and input material which has gone into manufacturing the rifle is sourced from the Indian industry, Major Gen Sharma said in the post. He said this was not just “localisation of selected components”, but was a “true, end-to-end ‘100% genuine indigenisation’ of the rifle.”
He said the prototype of the first 100 per cent indigenised vehicle had “successfully undergone firing, including burst firing”, adding that the initial results were “extremely encouraging.”
“A proud moment for IRRPL, our partners (AWEIL & OSL) and MSMEs, and the entire Indian Defence Industry. This is Atmanirbhar Bharat in action!!” Major Gen Sharma said.
Also Read | India imposes phased ban on import of 405 defence items to boost domestic production
‘IRRPL moving towards production rate of one AK-203 every 100 seconds’
Major Gen Sharma said that with the successful testing of the first prototype, IRRPL would now focus on producing the requisite number of 100 per cent indigenised AK-203 ‘Sher’ rifles for trials to the Indian Armed Forces in September, 2026.
The IRRPL CEO said the company will be “moving towards a production rate of one AK-203 (Sher) every 100 seconds,” adding that there is “much more ahead.” Major Gen Sharma further said that IRRPL was also looking to prepone the delivery timeline of the approximately 6 lakh rifles that it has to supply to the Indian Army “by almost one year”. He credited the company's efforts towards “capacity enhancement, indigenisation and production optimisation” for the efficiency.
IRRPL is mandated under a ₹5,200 crore contract to supply 6,01,427 rifles to the armed forces by October 2032. However, Major Gen Sharma had earlier too said that the company plans to finish deliveries by December 2030.

Good morning. Nick Visser here to get the news going. Here’s what’s on deck:
Leah Stewart, the woman who was bitten by a shark at Sydney’s Coogee beach, issued a thankyou to those who supported her after the attack.
She wrote on GoFundMe: “After what has been an incredibly difficult few months, I’m so happy that I’ve progressed enough to build some independence, and I can finally see some light after all of this.”

Meanwhile authorities have begun vaccinating as many of Phillip Island’s little penguins as they can against the H5 strain of bird flu. The island, south-west of Melbourne, has a 5,000-strong colony, which sees a nightly ritual of the penguins returning to the same burrow, along the same path, making them ideal candidates for vaccination. It comes a day after authorities revealed the death of a seal from the flu, the first confirmed mainland mammal fatality.
Watt says fur seal death from H5 bird flu ‘very serious’, but government prepared
Murray Watt, the environment minister, said the confirmed death of a fur seal, was a “very serious development”.
Watt spoke to ABC News Breakfast, saying the government had warned the H5 strain of bird flu was likely to spread and more mass mortality events were likely, but officials have also been preparing for that eventuality. He said:
What we’ve been doing over the last couple of years is trying to build up larger populations of these mammals, so if we do have bird flu come, and it does kill some of them, we still have resilient populations for the future. …
I know it’s a distressing thing for Australians to hear but we need to be realistic. This is the sort of thing we have seen overseas. We’re very fortunate we’re the last continent to have the bird flu happen. But we’ve been preparing for this, for some time.
Watt said the government would continue to do “everything we can to ensure these beautiful creatures will be here for us for a long time to come”.
Phillip Island’s penguin parade gets vaccinated for bird flu
The nightly parade of penguins on Phillip Island is a tourist favourite, but has recently taken on a more serious tone, AAP reports.
As the little penguins toddled up the Victorian beach on Sunday night, many were corralled into pens to receive the first of two vaccinations against bird flu. The H5 strain of bird flu first reached Australia’s shores in June and is already confirmed to have claimed the life of one of the penguins in the colony.
With case numbers on the rise, authorities have stepped in to do what they can to defend the 5,000-strong colony of little penguins living on Phillip Island, south-west of Melbourne.
The penguin’s nightly ritual of returning the same burrow, along the same path, made them ideal candidates for vaccination, said Phillip Island nature parks reserve manager Ben Thomas:
We started on some of the quieter penguin pathways to fine-tune the whole process and and get it working as quickly as we can, so we can process as many penguins as we can each night.
We’ve now moved to the western end of the penguin parade, where the larger numbers are, and it’s working really well.
A second long-nosed fur seal is suspected to have died in South Australia from H5 bird flu, just a day after officials confirmed the first death of a mammal on the Australian mainland.
The South Australian government said the second fur seal death occurred offshore at the Pages conservation park. More than 1,000 dead crested terns were found across Troubridge Island and the Pages islands in recent weeks, with the latter a known breeding site for a colony of endangered Australian sea lions, with long-nosed fur seals known to visit the area.
Samples will be taken for confirmatory testing, with results expected in the coming days. The South Australian government maintained that there are no H5 bird flu detections in poultry or livestock and the risk to humans remains low.
“South Australians are encouraged to continue being vigilant in reporting sick and dead birds and other wildlife,” the government said in a statement.

Sarah Basford Canales

The Greens should not be eclipsed by the Burnham bounce - this is their moment
In recent years, the Green Party has firmly established itself as the primary electoral outlet for left-leaning voters in England and Wales disillusioned by Labour’s domestic, economic and foreign policy. Its more combative approach under Zack Polanski, its firm stance in support of Palestinian liberation and left-populist economic policies have all enabled it to make significant inroads into Labour’s fragmenting progressive base.
By eating into the Labour Party’s support among young voters and those from minority backgrounds, particularly British Muslims angered and alienated by Keir Starmer’s active complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza, the Greens also played their part in hastening Starmer’s political demise, contributing to the sense that Labour was facing an existential wipeout unless it rapidly found some way of changing course - or at least giving the appearance of having done so.
But Andy Burnham’s rise to the Labour leadership, and the premiership, poses the Greens with a thornier challenge. Certainly, Burnham is a far more capable and charismatic politician than Starmer, and has the benefit of having spent a considerable amount of time outside the Westminster bubble (even if Burnham’s much-vaunted “Manchesterism” is little more than a buzzword). There are good reasons to doubt whether Burnham’s ambitious rhetoric has any underlying substance, but it has been enough to stall the Greens’ momentum.
Last month's mayoral election in Greater Manchester is a case in point. The Greens ran a peculiar, confused campaign, trying to position themselves as the only party that could stop Reform UK’s Sian Astley from winning, even though it was clear that Labour was the party to beat. In the event, the Green Party’s Geraldine Coggins won nearly 200,000 fewer first-preference votes than the winning Labour candidate, Manchester City Council leader Bev Craig, albeit on the lowest turnout since the city-region mayoralty was introduced.
Granted, expectations for the Greens are much higher than they were just a couple of years ago, but this can only be regarded as a disappointing showing. Even so, it is wise not to over-analyse a single result.

Burnham won his three Greater Manchester mayoral contests with more than 60 percent of the vote on each occasion, and even in his absence, Labour was always going to be difficult to beat on his former turf so soon after his departure for Downing Street.
So overwhelming was Starmer’s unpopularity by the end of his tenure, his removal was inevitably going to give Labour a lift in the opinion polls. Some of the Greens’ softer support has drifted back to Labour in the hope that Burnham can deliver some noticeable kind of change; as a result, Labour is now neck-and-neck in the polls with Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, which has seen its own momentum weaken in recent months. But the thing about honeymoons is that they’re typically shortlived.
Media hostility
The Greens are also being subjected to a level of media hostility they have not seriously encountered before now, a tacit recognition that they have emerged as a significant national political force. Inevitably, and by design, this amplification of social media controversies and internal discord - as with Labour under Jeremy Corbyn - deflects attention away from policy in favour of trivia. The media cycle revolves around culture-war flashpoints and outrages, making it extremely difficult to keep the focus on matters of actual substance.
Nevertheless, the Greens do appear divided over how they should respond to Burnham. One tendency is prepared to offer tacit support for Burnham in the hope that he can nudge Labour back towards a more centre-left position. The party’s left wing, on the other hand, argues that the Greens should stick to their guns and hold to an oppositional, left-populist orientation, continuing to attack and expose Labour’s limitations.
Influential Green Party figures, including Caroline Lucas, Adrian Ramsay and Ellie Chowns, seem to favour a softly-softly approach towards Burnham’s Labour; Lucas publicly urged the Greens to effectively stand aside for Burnham in the Makerfield by-election back in June. Such a strategy, however, risks leading the party into a cul-de-sac. The Labour Party has historically sought to discipline and neuter parties to its left while offering as few concessions as it can get away with in return. The Greens should be mindful of this.
Proportional representation is the most obvious example. This is the Greens’ single biggest constitutional objective. While Burnham has previously expressed support for reform, the ingrained resistance to PR within the Labour hierarchy runs much deeper than any individual leader, and Burnham has a history of folding when faced with serious institutional pressure. The Greens could therefore be jeopardising their political independence, and their distinctive appeal, for promises that fail to materialise.
There is no reason for panic. The Greens have made impressive progress in a relatively short period of time, establishing themselves as a serious national electoral force capable of challenging and beating Labour in many of its urban heartlands. It was always probable that when Starmer was eventually deposed, a lull in their polling would follow. Setbacks like this should be kept in perspective.
Anti-establishment appeal
Falling into line behind Labour would be a serious mistake for the Green Party, depriving it of much of its anti-establishment appeal. Much of the Greens’ recent success has been predicated on positioning the party as a left-wing alternative to the Tweedledum and Tweedledee show at Westminster, not as a prospective junior partner to a marginally less unpalatable Labour Party. Lining up alongside Burnham’s Labour now would risk undoing the work that has enabled their growth to this point.
Climate change is now a tangible feature of everyday
life, exacerbating the cost-of-living crisis that Burnham has sworn to tackle
In any case, Burnham’s room for manoeuvre is likely to prove much narrower than his more naive supporters are hoping. His new Chancellor, John Healey, has already warned ministers that they must brace themselves for further spending cuts to fund commitments elsewhere, specifically on arms expenditure. After 16 years of austerity and underinvestment, there is precious little left to trim without inflicting yet more damage on living standards and the social fabric as a whole.
The impact of the climate crisis, too, grows ever more egregious while Burnham prepares to drill for more North Sea oil - at the behest of the White House. Britain’s exceptionally hot, dry summer has already resulted in England’s earliest harvest ever, with warnings that rising prices and some food shortages could soon follow. Climate change is now a tangible feature of everyday life, exacerbating the cost-of-living crisis that Burnham has sworn to tackle.
Burnham has undeniably won back some wavering Labour voters, but their loyalty to Labour is already conditional. Before too long, they will want to see Burnham’s warm words backed up by meaningful action. The Greens should therefore resist the temptation to retreat. Rather, they should insist on the need for fundamental social and economic transformation, instead of cosying up to a Labour Party that remains incapable of delivering either.

Trump says Canada wants 'benefits' of being US state after trade talks collapse
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said Canada wants "the benefits of being a State, without being one" after trade talks between the two countries collapsed late on Friday.
In his first comments since negotiations broke down, triggering new 50% US tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, Trump also said American farmers had been charged "massive amounts of Tariffs" for years.
It comes after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the fresh tariffs a "miscalculation" designed to "hurt and divide us".
Carney confirmed he would match Trump's tariffs "dollar-for-dollar" from 8 September, including levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The US and Canada are now in a trade "war", he said.
"They asked too much and they offered too little," Carney said on Saturday. "You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he added.
Trump's latest comments echo his repeated references to making Canada the "51st state" of America since returning to office, sparking frustration among its leaders and residents.
The collapse of the trade talks upended a deeply integrated trading relationship, with no clear path to resolution.
"We cannot accept what they've offered, and we will not give what they've asked," Carney said.
Both countries were optimistic of a deal earlier in the week, but talks fell apart after both sides accused the other of making last-minute changes.
The new 50% US tariffs will apply to a range of Canadian goods, in addition to existing US tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium, automobiles and lumber.
They are limited in scope, covering about $20bn (£15bn; C$28bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% in total, including wine, dairy, cement, clothing and hockey equipment.
The prime minister said Canada was retaliating "reluctantly" to protect its interests. Details of the counter-measures will be released in the coming days, he said.
- Carney faces crucial test after walking away from Trump's deal 
  - Published15 hours ago
Leaders of other federal parties in Canada, including the Conservative opposition, voiced support for the prime minister, as have the leaders of some Canadian provinces.
Tariffs - a tax placed on imports from other countries - have been a key component of Trump's trade policy, with the US president arguing they will boost American manufacturing and create jobs at home.
Critics, however, say tariffs have raised prices for American consumers and have disrupted and damaged the global economy.
Carney's speech on Saturday was his first address to Canadians after he announced late on Friday night that a deal would not be reached, accusing the Americans of making "last-minute changes" that were "unfair" and "uneconomic".
US negotiators, meanwhile, accused Canada of making "new demands and walk backs" on terms which had been previously agreed.
On Saturday, US trade representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News there were no plans to resume talks.
He added that the US had been prepared to cut some of its tariffs on Canada as part of the ill-fated deal.
Carney, however, said the US presented "unacceptable" terms that were too restrictive, including curbing Canada's ability to strike new trade deals with other countries.
He also rejected the assertion that Canada had made last-minute requests: "We clarified what was on offer and were continually disappointed by the answers."
Doug Ford, the leader of Canada's most populous province Ontario, backed Carney and said Trump "can't be trusted".
British Columbia Premier David Eby said the US demand for restrictions on Canada's ability to have other trade deals "would reduce us to the economic equivalent of the 51st state".
"It was never acceptable to Canadians," Eby said.
The Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also appeared to support Carney, calling the latest US levies "unjustified".
Quebec's premier, Christine Fréchette, warned jobs would likely be lost as a result of the new US tariffs.
"Behind these numbers are real people," she said, vowing to introduce measures to support impacted sectors.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, whose oil-rich province has worked to make inroads with the Trump administration, urged both sides to resume talks.
The collapse comes after more than a year of on-again, off-again trade talks, which intensified in recent weeks after a US-imposed deadline to strike a deal or face further tariffs.
The two countries were also engaged in a mandatory review of an existing North American free trade agreement, known as USMCA, with Mexico.
The pact was signed by Trump during his first term to replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. It underpins $1.6tn (£1.2tn) in annual trilateral trade across Canada, the US and Mexico.
Earlier this summer, Canada and Mexico had formally requested for USMCA to be renewed for another 16 years. The US, however, declined to renew it in its current form.
Asked how Friday's trade talk collapse would impact the North American free trade pact, Carney said it was "certainly not good news".
